questions.statement: A network engineer is designing a system where two hosts must communicate without any established connection, prioritizing speed over reliability. Which transport protocol should be used?
questions.option_a: TCP
questions.option_b: FTP
questions.option_c: UDP
questions.option_d: SCTP
questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery, ordering, or error correction. This makes it faster than TCP and suitable for real-time applications (video streaming, gaming, DNS) where speed is preferred over reliability.

questions.statement: What does the acronym IP stand for in networking?
questions.option_a: Internet Protocol
questions.option_b: Internal Protocol
questions.option_c: Interface Protocol
questions.option_d: Integrated Protocol
questions.explanation: IP stands for Internet Protocol. The distractors all use the same initial letters (I and P) as required: Internal Protocol, Interface Protocol, and Integrated Protocol are plausible-sounding but incorrect expansions.

questions.statement: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for end-to-end error detection and flow control between two communicating hosts?
questions.option_a: Network Layer (Layer 3)
questions.option_b: Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
questions.option_c: Transport Layer (Layer 4)
questions.option_d: Session Layer (Layer 5)
questions.explanation: The Transport Layer (Layer 4) provides end-to-end communication services including error detection, flow control, and segmentation/reassembly (TCP). The Data Link Layer provides node-to-node error detection only within a single link.

questions.statement: A packet travels from Host A to Host B through 3 routers. At each router, the packet's destination IP address is used to determine the next hop. This is the function of which OSI layer?
questions.option_a: Data Link Layer
questions.option_b: Physical Layer
questions.option_c: Network Layer
questions.option_d: Transport Layer
questions.explanation: Routing (forwarding packets based on IP addresses) is the primary function of the Network Layer (Layer 3). The Data Link Layer handles MAC addresses within a single network segment. The Transport Layer handles end-to-end delivery.

questions.statement: Which cloud computing service model provides virtualized computing infrastructure (servers, storage, networking) over the internet?
questions.option_a: SaaS (Software as a Service)
questions.option_b: PaaS (Platform as a Service)
questions.option_c: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
questions.option_d: FaaS (Function as a Service)
questions.explanation: IaaS provides virtualized computing infrastructure. PaaS provides platforms for application development. SaaS provides complete software applications. FaaS provides serverless function execution. IaaS gives the most control over underlying resources.

questions.statement: In CSMA/CD, after a collision is detected, a station waits a random backoff time before retransmitting. The algorithm used to calculate this backoff time is:
questions.option_a: Round-robin scheduling
questions.option_b: Token passing
questions.option_c: Binary exponential backoff
questions.option_d: Fixed-interval scheduling
questions.explanation: Binary exponential backoff doubles the maximum random waiting interval after each successive collision. After the kth collision, the station waits a random number of slot times in [0, 2^min(k,10) - 1]. This reduces collision probability progressively.

questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)?
questions.option_a: Translating domain names to IP addresses
questions.option_b: Mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network
questions.option_c: Routing packets between different networks
questions.option_d: Encrypting data before transmission
questions.explanation: ARP resolves (maps) a known IP address to its corresponding MAC address on a local network segment. DNS maps domain names to IP addresses. Routing is performed by routers. Encryption is handled by protocols like TLS/SSL.

questions.statement: A company uses NAT (Network Address Translation). The primary benefit of NAT is:
questions.option_a: Increasing network speed by reducing packet size
questions.option_b: Allowing multiple devices with private IP addresses to share a single public IP address
questions.option_c: Encrypting all traffic leaving the network
questions.option_d: Providing QoS (Quality of Service) prioritization
questions.explanation: NAT allows multiple internal devices with private IP addresses (RFC 1918) to share one or a few public IP addresses. This conserves public IPv4 addresses and provides a basic form of security by hiding internal network topology.

questions.statement: Which DNS record type maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?
questions.option_a: MX record
questions.option_b: CNAME record
questions.option_c: A record
questions.option_d: AAAA record
questions.explanation: An A (Address) record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address. AAAA maps to IPv6. MX specifies mail servers. CNAME creates an alias pointing to another domain name.

questions.statement: In TCP, the 'three-way handshake' establishes a connection using which message sequence?
questions.option_a: SYN → ACK → SYN-ACK
questions.option_b: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
questions.option_c: ACK → SYN → SYN-ACK
questions.option_d: FIN → ACK → FIN-ACK
questions.explanation: TCP's three-way handshake: Client sends SYN, Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client responds with ACK. This establishes initial sequence numbers and confirms both parties can send and receive. FIN/ACK is used to terminate connections.

questions.statement: A network administrator subnetworks 192.168.1.0/24 into subnets with the mask /26. How many subnets are created?
questions.option_a: 2 subnets
questions.option_b: 4 subnets
questions.option_c: 8 subnets
questions.option_d: 16 subnets
questions.explanation: /24 to /26 borrows 2 bits from the host portion (26-24=2). Number of subnets = 2² = 4. Each subnet has 2^(32-26) - 2 = 62 usable host addresses. The four subnets span .0-.63, .64-.127, .128-.191, .192-.255.

questions.statement: Which routing protocol uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm and is classified as a distance-vector protocol?
questions.option_a: OSPF
questions.option_b: BGP
questions.option_c: RIP
questions.option_d: IS-IS
questions.explanation: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) is a distance-vector protocol using Bellman-Ford. OSPF uses Dijkstra's algorithm and is a link-state protocol. BGP is a path-vector protocol. IS-IS is a link-state protocol.

questions.statement: What does the acronym OSPF stand for?
questions.option_a: Open Shortest Path First
questions.option_b: Optimal Shortest Path First
questions.option_c: Open Secure Path First
questions.option_d: Open System Path First
questions.explanation: OSPF stands for Open Shortest Path First. The distractors use the same O, S, P, F initials: Optimal Shortest Path First, Open Secure Path First, and Open System Path First are plausible-sounding but incorrect expansions.

questions.statement: In cloud computing, 'elasticity' refers to:
questions.option_a: The ability to keep data highly encrypted
questions.option_b: The ability to automatically scale resources up or down based on demand
questions.option_c: The ability to recover from hardware failures automatically
questions.option_d: The ability to deploy to multiple geographic regions
questions.explanation: Elasticity in cloud computing means the ability to automatically and rapidly scale computing resources up when demand increases and down when demand decreases, matching supply to demand without manual intervention.

questions.statement: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for data compression, encryption, and format conversion?
questions.option_a: Application Layer (Layer 7)
questions.option_b: Session Layer (Layer 5)
questions.option_c: Presentation Layer (Layer 6)
questions.option_d: Transport Layer (Layer 4)
questions.explanation: The Presentation Layer (Layer 6) handles data formatting, compression, and encryption/decryption. It ensures data is in a readable format for the application layer. Examples: SSL/TLS, JPEG, MPEG are associated with this layer.

questions.statement: A network device that operates at Layer 2 (Data Link) and forwards frames based on MAC address tables is called a:
questions.option_a: Router
questions.option_b: Hub
questions.option_c: Switch
questions.option_d: Firewall
questions.explanation: A switch operates at Layer 2 and forwards frames based on MAC addresses, learning which MAC addresses are on which ports. A router operates at Layer 3. A hub broadcasts to all ports (Layer 1). A firewall filters traffic at Layer 3/4.

questions.statement: What is the maximum data rate of Fast Ethernet?
questions.option_a: 10 Mbps
questions.option_b: 100 Mbps
questions.option_c: 1 Gbps
questions.option_d: 10 Gbps
questions.explanation: Fast Ethernet (IEEE 802.3u) operates at 100 Mbps. Standard Ethernet is 10 Mbps. Gigabit Ethernet is 1 Gbps. 10 Gbps Ethernet is 10GbE. 'Fast Ethernet' specifically refers to the 100 Mbps standard.

questions.statement: A TCP connection is sending data. If the receiver's window size is 0, what should the sender do?
questions.option_a: Terminate the connection immediately
questions.option_b: Continue sending data at a reduced rate
questions.option_c: Stop sending data and wait for a non-zero window advertisement
questions.option_d: Retransmit all unacknowledged segments
questions.explanation: A zero window size means the receiver's buffer is full—the sender must stop sending data. TCP's flow control uses the receiver window to prevent the sender from overwhelming the receiver. The sender waits for a window update advertisement before resuming.

questions.statement: In the context of cloud computing, which deployment model provides cloud services exclusively to a single organization and is not shared with other organizations?
questions.option_a: Public cloud
questions.option_b: Hybrid cloud
questions.option_c: Community cloud
questions.option_d: Private cloud
questions.explanation: A private cloud provides cloud infrastructure dedicated to a single organization, not shared with others. Public clouds serve multiple tenants. Hybrid clouds combine public and private. Community clouds are shared among organizations with common concerns.

questions.statement: Which protocol operates at the Application Layer and is used to transfer files between a client and a server?
questions.option_a: TCP
questions.option_b: UDP
questions.option_c: FTP
questions.option_d: ICMP
questions.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) operates at the Application Layer (Layer 7) and transfers files between hosts. TCP and UDP are Transport Layer protocols. ICMP is a Network Layer protocol for diagnostics (ping, traceroute).

questions.statement: A router receives a packet destined for 10.0.0.25. Its routing table has entries for 10.0.0.0/8, 10.0.0.0/24, and 0.0.0.0/0. Which route is selected?
questions.option_a: 0.0.0.0/0 (default route)
questions.option_d: The packet is dropped
questions.explanation: Routers apply the 'longest prefix match' rule: select the route with the most specific (longest) matching prefix. 10.0.0.0/24 (24-bit mask) is more specific than 10.0.0.0/8 (8-bit mask) for 10.0.0.25. The default route (0.0.0.0/0) is least specific.

questions.statement: In WiFi (IEEE 802.11), the CSMA/CA protocol is used instead of CSMA/CD because:
questions.option_a: Wireless channels are faster than wired channels
questions.option_b: Collision detection is impractical on wireless media due to the hidden node problem and the inability to transmit and listen simultaneously
questions.option_c: Wireless networks do not experience collisions
questions.option_d: CSMA/CA provides higher throughput than CSMA/CD
questions.explanation: Wireless stations cannot reliably detect collisions while transmitting (they cannot listen to the channel while transmitting) and the hidden node problem makes collision detection impractical. CSMA/CA avoids collisions by waiting and using random backoff before transmitting.

questions.statement: What is the primary function of DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)?
questions.option_a: Resolving domain names to IP addresses
questions.option_b: Automatically assigning IP addresses and network configuration to hosts
questions.option_c: Encrypting data between hosts
questions.option_d: Routing packets across different networks
questions.explanation: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS server addresses to hosts when they join a network. DNS resolves domain names. Routing is performed by routers. Encryption is handled by TLS/SSL.

questions.statement: In which cloud service model does the provider manage the operating system, middleware, and runtime, while the customer manages only the application and data?
questions.option_a: IaaS
questions.option_b: SaaS
questions.option_c: PaaS
questions.option_d: DaaS
questions.explanation: PaaS (Platform as a Service) manages OS, middleware, and runtime, allowing developers to focus on building applications without managing infrastructure. IaaS gives OS-level control. SaaS provides the complete application; the user manages nothing. DaaS provides virtual desktops.

questions.statement: TCP uses 'sliding window' flow control. If the window size is 4 and the sender has sent segments 1-4, but only received ACK for 1, which segments can the sender transmit next?
questions.option_a: Segments 5-8
questions.option_b: Only segment 5
questions.option_c: No new segments (must wait)
questions.option_d: Segments 2-5
questions.explanation: With a window size of 4 and ACK for segment 1 received, the window slides forward by 1: the sender can now send segment 5. Segments 2, 3, 4 are still unacknowledged and within the window. The sender cannot send segments 6-8 until further ACKs arrive.

questions.statement: What type of address does IPv6 use?
questions.option_a: 32-bit address
questions.option_b: 64-bit address
questions.option_c: 128-bit address
questions.option_d: 256-bit address
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, typically written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits (e.g., 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334). IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses. IPv6 provides 2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.4×10³⁸ unique addresses.

questions.statement: A company wants to prevent external users from accessing its internal web server's admin port (8080) while allowing normal HTTP (80) traffic. The best tool for this is:
questions.option_a: A network switch
questions.option_b: A hub
questions.option_c: A firewall with port filtering rules
questions.option_d: A DNS server
questions.explanation: A firewall can be configured with packet filtering rules to allow traffic on port 80 while blocking port 8080 for external sources. Switches and hubs do not perform traffic filtering based on port numbers.

questions.statement: In BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), the protocol used between different Autonomous Systems (AS) to exchange routing information is called:
questions.option_a: IBGP (Internal BGP)
questions.option_b: EBGP (External BGP)
questions.option_c: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
questions.option_d: RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
questions.explanation: EBGP (External BGP) exchanges routing information between different Autonomous Systems. IBGP is used within the same AS. OSPF and RIP are intra-AS (IGP) routing protocols not used for inter-AS routing.

questions.statement: The maximum number of usable host addresses in a /27 subnet is:
questions.option_a: 30 hosts
questions.option_b: 32 hosts
questions.option_c: 14 hosts
questions.option_d: 62 hosts
questions.explanation: A /27 subnet has 32 addresses (2^5 = 32). Subtracting the network address and broadcast address: 32 - 2 = 30 usable host addresses. /28 gives 14, /26 gives 62. The formula is 2^(32-prefix) - 2.

questions.statement: Which cloud computing characteristic ensures that resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers, with physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned?
questions.option_a: On-demand self-service
questions.option_b: Resource pooling (multi-tenancy)
questions.option_c: Rapid elasticity
questions.option_d: Measured service
questions.explanation: Resource pooling (multi-tenancy) allows the cloud provider to serve multiple consumers using shared physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned. On-demand self-service allows provisioning without provider interaction. Elasticity means automatic scaling.

questions.statement: In the context of network security, what does a 'man-in-the-middle' (MITM) attack involve?
questions.option_a: Flooding a server with requests to cause denial of service
questions.option_b: An attacker secretly intercepting and potentially altering communication between two parties
questions.option_c: Scanning a network to map active hosts and open ports
questions.option_d: Embedding malicious code in a legitimate website
questions.explanation: A MITM attack positions the attacker between two communicating parties, intercepting and potentially modifying messages without either party's knowledge. DDoS flooding is option A. Port scanning is option C. XSS is option D.

questions.statement: Which protocol provides reliable, in-order, byte-stream delivery with congestion control?
questions.option_a: UDP
questions.option_b: ICMP
questions.option_c: TCP
questions.option_d: ARP
questions.explanation: TCP provides reliable (guaranteed delivery), in-order byte-stream delivery, flow control, and congestion control. UDP is unreliable and connectionless. ICMP is for diagnostics. ARP is for address resolution.

questions.statement: A cloud provider offers a service where customers pay only for the exact compute time their functions consume, with no server management. This is:
questions.option_a: Virtual Machine hosting
questions.option_b: Container orchestration (Kubernetes)
questions.option_c: Serverless computing (FaaS)
questions.option_d: Managed database service
questions.explanation: Serverless computing (FaaS - Function as a Service) executes code in response to events, charging only for compute time consumed. The provider manages all infrastructure. AWS Lambda and Azure Functions are examples. No server provisioning or management is required.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the TTL (Time To Live) field in an IP packet header?
questions.option_a: To specify the packet's priority level
questions.option_b: To limit the lifespan of a packet by decrementing at each hop, preventing infinite routing loops
questions.option_c: To indicate the packet's encryption status
questions.option_d: To specify the packet's total size in bytes
questions.explanation: TTL prevents routing loops by starting at a value (e.g., 64 or 128) and decrementing by 1 at each router. When TTL reaches 0, the packet is discarded and an ICMP 'Time Exceeded' message is sent to the source. This prevents packets from circulating indefinitely.

questions.statement: Which wireless network standard operates in the 5 GHz band, providing less interference but shorter range than 2.4 GHz standards?
questions.option_a: IEEE 802.11b
questions.option_b: IEEE 802.11g
questions.option_c: IEEE 802.11a
questions.option_d: IEEE 802.11n
questions.explanation: IEEE 802.11a operates exclusively at 5 GHz, avoiding the congested 2.4 GHz band used by 802.11b and 802.11g. The 5 GHz band has less interference but shorter range due to higher frequency. 802.11n operates on both bands.

questions.statement: In HTTP, which status code indicates that the requested resource has been permanently moved to a new URL?
questions.option_a: 200 OK
questions.option_b: 404 Not Found
questions.option_c: 301 Moved Permanently
questions.option_d: 500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: HTTP 301 indicates a permanent redirect—clients should update their URLs and use the new location for all future requests. 200 is success. 404 is resource not found. 302 is a temporary redirect. 500 is a server error.

questions.statement: What is the difference between half-duplex and full-duplex communication?
questions.option_a: Half-duplex is faster; full-duplex supports longer distances
questions.option_b: Half-duplex allows transmission in both directions but not simultaneously; full-duplex allows simultaneous bidirectional communication
questions.option_c: Half-duplex requires a wired medium; full-duplex works wirelessly
questions.option_d: Half-duplex uses UDP; full-duplex uses TCP
questions.explanation: Half-duplex allows both-direction communication but only one direction at a time (walkie-talkies). Full-duplex allows simultaneous bidirectional communication (telephone). Most Ethernet switches support full-duplex, eliminating collisions.

questions.statement: A network engineer observes high latency on a WAN link. Which quality of service (QoS) mechanism prioritizes latency-sensitive traffic (e.g., VoIP) over bulk data transfers?
questions.option_a: CSMA/CD
questions.option_b: Traffic shaping and queuing prioritization
questions.option_c: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
questions.option_d: Link-state advertisement flooding
questions.explanation: QoS traffic shaping and queuing mechanisms (e.g., DiffServ, priority queuing) classify packets and ensure latency-sensitive traffic (VoIP, video) is transmitted before bulk data. CSMA/CD is a collision detection mechanism for shared media.

questions.statement: Which protocol is used to send email from a mail client to a mail server?
questions.option_a: POP3
questions.option_b: IMAP
questions.option_c: SMTP
questions.option_d: FTP
questions.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is used to send email from a client to a server and between mail servers. POP3 and IMAP are used to retrieve email from a server. FTP is for file transfer.

questions.statement: In cloud architecture, what is a 'CDN' (Content Delivery Network)?
questions.option_a: A private network connecting cloud data centers
questions.option_b: A geographically distributed system of servers that delivers content to users from the nearest location
questions.option_c: A network protocol for container communication
questions.option_d: A type of virtual private cloud network
questions.explanation: A CDN distributes copies of content across geographically distributed servers (edge nodes), serving users from the closest node to minimize latency and improve performance. It is widely used for static assets, video streaming, and large file distribution.

questions.statement: Which layer of the OSI model handles physical addressing (MAC addresses) and access to the transmission medium?
questions.option_a: Physical Layer (Layer 1)
questions.option_b: Network Layer (Layer 3)
questions.option_c: Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
questions.option_d: Transport Layer (Layer 4)
questions.explanation: The Data Link Layer (Layer 2) handles MAC addresses, framing, error detection (CRC), and media access control (CSMA/CD). The Physical Layer handles bit transmission over the medium. The Network Layer handles IP addresses.

questions.statement: In TCP congestion control, when a packet loss is detected via timeout (not triple duplicate ACK), the sender sets its congestion window (cwnd) to:
questions.option_a: Half of its current value
questions.option_b: The maximum window size
questions.option_c: 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size)
questions.option_d: 0, then slowly increases
questions.explanation: TCP's Tahoe/Reno congestion control: on timeout (severe congestion), cwnd is reset to 1 MSS and slow start threshold (ssthresh) is halved. On triple duplicate ACK (Fast Retransmit), Reno halves cwnd (less severe congestion).

questions.statement: What is the role of a 'load balancer' in cloud infrastructure?
questions.option_a: Encrypting traffic between clients and servers
questions.option_b: Distributing incoming network traffic across multiple servers to prevent overload
questions.option_c: Compressing data to reduce bandwidth usage
questions.option_d: Managing virtual machine snapshots
questions.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers, ensuring no single server is overwhelmed, improving availability and scalability. Round-robin, least connections, and IP hash are common load balancing algorithms.

questions.statement: In VLAN (Virtual LAN) technology, what primary problem does it solve?
questions.option_a: Increasing the physical range of a network
questions.option_b: Logically segmenting a single physical network into multiple isolated broadcast domains
questions.option_c: Encrypting traffic between switches
questions.option_d: Automatically assigning IP addresses to network devices
questions.explanation: VLANs partition a single physical switched network into multiple logical broadcast domains. Traffic from one VLAN cannot reach another without a router or Layer 3 switch. This improves security, reduces broadcast traffic, and enables flexible network design.

questions.statement: What does TLS (Transport Layer Security) primarily protect against in network communications?
questions.option_a: IP address spoofing attacks
questions.option_b: Eavesdropping and tampering during data transmission
questions.option_c: MAC address flooding attacks
questions.option_d: DHCP starvation attacks
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts data in transit and authenticates the server (and optionally the client), protecting against eavesdropping (confidentiality) and tampering (integrity). SSL is TLS's predecessor. MAC flooding and DHCP starvation are Layer 2 attacks.

questions.statement: Which AWS service is equivalent to a 'virtual machine' in cloud computing?
questions.option_a: AWS S3
questions.option_b: AWS EC2
questions.option_c: AWS RDS
questions.option_d: AWS Lambda
questions.explanation: AWS EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides virtual machines (instances) in the cloud. S3 is object storage. RDS is managed relational database service. Lambda is serverless function execution (FaaS).

questions.statement: In the context of network protocols, what is 'encapsulation'?
questions.option_a: Encrypting data at each layer
questions.option_b: Adding protocol-specific headers (and trailers) as data moves down the OSI layers before transmission
questions.option_c: Removing headers as data moves up the OSI layers
questions.option_d: Compressing data to reduce transmission size
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is the process of adding protocol-specific headers (and sometimes trailers) at each layer as data moves from the application layer down to the physical layer. De-encapsulation is the reverse process at the receiver.

questions.statement: A 'ping' command uses which protocol to test network connectivity?
questions.option_a: TCP
questions.option_b: UDP
questions.option_c: ICMP
questions.option_d: ARP
questions.explanation: Ping uses ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Echo Request and Echo Reply messages to test connectivity and measure round-trip time. ICMP operates at the Network Layer. TCP and UDP are Transport Layer protocols.

questions.statement: In cloud computing, 'SLA' (Service Level Agreement) defines:
questions.option_a: The technical architecture of the cloud service
questions.option_b: The guaranteed minimum performance, availability, and support standards the provider commits to
questions.option_c: The pricing model for cloud resource consumption
questions.option_d: The physical location of cloud data centers
questions.explanation: An SLA defines the guaranteed performance and availability standards (e.g., 99.9% uptime) that a cloud provider commits to, along with remedies (credits) if standards are not met. It is a contractual agreement, not a technical specification.

questions.statement: A packet arrives at a router with destination IP 172.16.5.14. The router's table has: 172.16.0.0/16 via R1, 172.16.5.0/24 via R2, default via R3. Which next hop is chosen?
questions.option_a: R1
questions.option_b: R2
questions.option_c: R3
questions.option_d: The packet is dropped
questions.explanation: The longest prefix match rule selects 172.16.5.0/24 (24-bit prefix) over 172.16.0.0/16 (16-bit prefix) because /24 is more specific. The default route is only used if no other route matches. The packet is forwarded to R2.

questions.statement: What is the primary difference between TCP and UDP at the Transport Layer?
questions.option_a: TCP is faster; UDP provides error correction
questions.option_b: TCP provides reliable, connection-oriented delivery; UDP provides unreliable, connectionless delivery
questions.option_c: TCP uses 8-byte headers; UDP uses 20-byte headers
questions.option_d: TCP is for file transfer only; UDP is for streaming only
questions.explanation: TCP establishes connections, guarantees delivery, order, and error correction, and implements flow/congestion control. UDP is connectionless with minimal overhead, used where speed matters more than reliability. TCP has 20-byte headers (minimum); UDP has 8-byte headers.

questions.statement: In DNS resolution, what is the role of a 'recursive resolver'?
questions.option_a: Answering queries by searching its own zone files
questions.option_b: Performing the full query resolution on behalf of the client by querying root, TLD, and authoritative servers
questions.option_c: Storing cached DNS records for performance
questions.option_d: Delegating queries to authoritative name servers only
questions.explanation: A recursive resolver (usually operated by an ISP or public service like 8.8.8.8) accepts a query from a client and performs the full iterative resolution—querying root servers, then TLD servers, then authoritative servers—returning the final answer to the client.

questions.statement: Which cloud storage type is most appropriate for storing large amounts of unstructured data such as images, videos, and backups?
questions.option_a: Block storage
questions.option_b: File storage (NFS)
questions.option_c: Object storage
questions.option_d: Database storage
questions.explanation: Object storage (e.g., AWS S3, Azure Blob) is designed for large-scale unstructured data like images, videos, and backups. It stores data as objects with metadata and provides HTTP-based access. Block storage provides raw disk access; file storage provides hierarchical directories.

questions.statement: In network terminology, the difference between 'bandwidth' and 'throughput' is:
questions.option_a: Bandwidth is measured in seconds; throughput is measured in bits
questions.option_b: Bandwidth is the maximum theoretical data rate; throughput is the actual data rate achieved under real conditions
questions.option_c: Bandwidth applies to wireless; throughput applies to wired networks
questions.option_d: Bandwidth and throughput are identical concepts
questions.explanation: Bandwidth is the maximum capacity of a link (theoretical maximum). Throughput is the actual data rate achieved, which is always ≤ bandwidth due to protocol overhead, congestion, errors, and other real-world factors.

questions.statement: What does 'stateless' mean in the context of HTTP protocol design?
questions.option_a: The server maintains no memory of previous client requests by default
questions.option_b: The server stores all client session data permanently
questions.option_c: HTTP connections are always encrypted
questions.option_d: HTTP cannot be used without a session cookie
questions.explanation: HTTP is stateless by design: each request from a client to server is independent, with no memory of previous requests. State must be explicitly maintained using cookies, sessions, or tokens. This simplifies server design but requires external state management for applications.

questions.statement: In the context of next-generation networks, SDN (Software-Defined Networking) separates which two planes?
questions.option_a: Application and transport planes
questions.option_b: Data plane and control plane
questions.option_c: Physical and virtual planes
questions.option_d: WAN and LAN planes
questions.explanation: SDN separates the data plane (forwarding: what to do with packets) from the control plane (deciding how to forward: routing logic). The control plane is centralized in an SDN controller, enabling programmable, software-driven network management.

questions.statement: A user connects to a company VPN. The primary security benefit provided is:
questions.option_a: Faster internet access
questions.option_b: Encrypted, tunneled communication between the user's device and the company network
questions.option_c: Blocking all incoming connections
questions.option_d: Automatic two-factor authentication
questions.explanation: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel between the user's device and the company network, protecting data from eavesdropping on untrusted networks. It authenticates users but does not inherently block connections or provide 2FA.

questions.statement: Which of the following correctly describes the 'cloud shared responsibility model'?
questions.option_a: The provider is responsible for all security aspects, including customer data
questions.option_b: Security responsibilities are divided: the provider secures the infrastructure; the customer secures their data, applications, and identity
questions.option_c: The customer is responsible for all security, including physical data center security
questions.option_d: Security responsibility is entirely determined by the SLA
questions.explanation: The shared responsibility model divides security: the cloud provider secures the physical infrastructure, hypervisor, and core services; the customer secures their data, applications, access controls, and OS (for IaaS). The division varies by service model.

questions.statement: In Ethernet framing, the CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) field is used to:
questions.option_a: Encrypt the frame contents for security
questions.option_b: Detect transmission errors in the received frame
questions.option_c: Identify the source and destination MAC addresses
questions.option_d: Control the frame's transmission speed
questions.explanation: The CRC field in an Ethernet frame allows the receiver to detect errors introduced during transmission. The receiver recomputes the CRC over the received data and compares it to the received CRC. A mismatch indicates a transmission error, and the frame is discarded.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the 'subnet mask' in IP networking?
questions.option_a: Encrypting traffic within a subnet
questions.option_b: Determining which portion of an IP address identifies the network and which identifies the host
questions.option_c: Assigning IP addresses automatically to hosts
questions.option_d: Routing packets between different subnets
questions.explanation: A subnet mask (e.g., 255.255.255.0 or /24) is a 32-bit number that identifies the network portion (1 bits) and host portion (0 bits) of an IP address. ANDing an IP address with its subnet mask yields the network address.

questions.statement: Which network layer protocol is responsible for reporting errors and sending operational information about IP packet processing?
questions.option_a: TCP
questions.option_b: UDP
questions.option_c: ICMP
questions.option_d: RIP
questions.explanation: ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) reports errors (destination unreachable, TTL expired) and operational messages (ping echo request/reply). It is a Network Layer protocol used by routers and hosts, not for user data.

questions.statement: In the context of cloud auto-scaling, a 'scale-in' event refers to:
questions.option_a: Adding more compute instances to handle increased load
questions.option_b: Reducing the number of compute instances when load decreases
questions.option_c: Moving workloads to a larger instance type
questions.option_d: Upgrading the instance's CPU and RAM
questions.explanation: Scale-in (scale down) removes instances when load decreases to reduce costs. Scale-out (scale up horizontally) adds instances when load increases. Vertical scaling (scale up) upgrades instance size. Cloud auto-scaling performs both scale-out and scale-in automatically.

questions.statement: In OSPF, each router maintains a complete map of the network topology called:
questions.option_a: A routing table
questions.option_b: A link-state database (LSDB)
questions.option_c: A distance vector table
questions.option_d: A forwarding information base
questions.explanation: OSPF routers maintain a Link-State Database (LSDB) containing LSAs (Link-State Advertisements) from all routers, providing a complete topology map. Each router independently runs Dijkstra's SPF algorithm on the LSDB to compute shortest paths.

questions.statement: What is the difference between 'unicast', 'multicast', and 'broadcast' transmission?
questions.option_a: Unicast is to all; multicast is to one; broadcast is to a group
questions.option_b: Unicast is to one; multicast is to a specific group; broadcast is to all on the network
questions.option_c: Unicast is to a group; broadcast is to one; multicast is to all
questions.option_d: All three transmit to the same number of recipients
questions.explanation: Unicast sends to a single specific destination. Multicast sends to a specific group of interested subscribers. Broadcast sends to all hosts on a network segment. Each has different addressing and forwarding behavior.

questions.statement: A developer is building a microservices application. Which cloud-native feature ensures that if one service instance fails, traffic is automatically redirected to healthy instances?
questions.option_a: Auto-scaling groups
questions.option_b: Health checks combined with load balancing
questions.option_c: Serverless functions
questions.option_d: Multi-region replication
questions.explanation: Load balancers perform health checks on backend instances and stop routing traffic to unhealthy ones, ensuring fault tolerance. This automatic redirection to healthy instances is a fundamental cloud-native reliability pattern.

questions.statement: In the OSI model, the 'Session Layer' (Layer 5) is responsible for:
questions.option_a: Packet routing between networks
questions.option_b: Establishing, managing, and terminating sessions between applications
questions.option_c: Physical bit transmission over the medium
questions.option_d: Data compression and format conversion
questions.explanation: The Session Layer establishes, manages, and terminates dialog sessions between applications. It handles checkpointing and recovery for long data transfers. Examples: NetBIOS, RPC. Routing is Network Layer; compression is Presentation Layer.

questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of HTTPS compared to HTTP?
questions.option_a: HTTPS transmits data faster than HTTP
questions.option_b: HTTPS encrypts the HTTP communication using TLS, providing confidentiality and integrity
questions.option_c: HTTPS uses a different port (80) than HTTP (443)
questions.option_d: HTTPS only works on wired networks
questions.explanation: HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS encryption, protecting data from eavesdropping and tampering. HTTP is unencrypted. HTTPS uses port 443; HTTP uses port 80 (not the other way around). HTTPS works on any network medium.

questions.statement: Which protocol is used for secure remote login and command execution on a Linux server?
questions.option_a: Telnet
questions.option_b: FTP
questions.option_c: SSH
questions.option_d: RDP
questions.explanation: SSH (Secure Shell) provides encrypted remote login, command execution, and tunneling. Telnet is insecure (unencrypted). FTP is for file transfer. RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) is primarily for Windows GUI remote access.

questions.statement: In cloud computing, 'multi-tenancy' means:
questions.option_a: Each customer has a dedicated physical server
questions.option_b: Multiple customers share the same underlying physical infrastructure while remaining logically isolated
questions.option_c: The cloud service is deployed across multiple geographic regions
questions.option_d: Multiple applications run on separate virtual machines
questions.explanation: Multi-tenancy means multiple customers (tenants) share the same physical infrastructure (servers, storage, network), with the cloud provider using virtualization and logical isolation to ensure each tenant's data and workloads remain separate.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the 'gateway' in a TCP/IP network configuration?
questions.option_a: Assigning IP addresses to local hosts
questions.option_b: Translating domain names to IP addresses
questions.option_c: Forwarding packets to destinations outside the local network
questions.option_d: Encrypting local network traffic
questions.explanation: The default gateway is the router that forwards packets to destinations outside the local subnet. Hosts send all traffic destined for other networks to the gateway. DHCP assigns addresses; DNS resolves names.

questions.statement: A company wants to store relational data in the cloud with managed backups, patching, and high availability. Which cloud service is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: AWS EC2
questions.option_b: AWS S3
questions.option_c: AWS RDS
questions.option_d: AWS CloudFront
questions.explanation: AWS RDS (Relational Database Service) is a managed database service providing automated backups, patching, and high availability (Multi-AZ) for relational databases. EC2 is for VMs; S3 is object storage; CloudFront is a CDN.

questions.statement: In wireless networking, what is the 'hidden node problem'?
questions.option_a: A node whose IP address is not visible in the routing table
questions.option_b: Two nodes that can communicate with an access point but cannot directly sense each other, leading to collisions at the AP
questions.option_c: A node that is physically hidden in a building causing signal degradation
questions.option_d: A node that cannot receive broadcast messages from the AP
questions.explanation: The hidden node problem: Node A and Node C are both in range of AP but not each other. Both may transmit simultaneously to the AP, causing a collision the AP cannot detect. CSMA/CA with RTS/CTS mechanism mitigates this.

questions.statement: Which protocol provides time synchronization between network devices?
questions.option_a: SNMP
questions.option_b: NTP
questions.option_c: DHCP
questions.option_d: DNS
questions.explanation: NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronizes clocks across networked devices to a reference time source. Accurate time is essential for log correlation, security certificates, and distributed transactions. SNMP manages network devices; DHCP assigns addresses.

questions.statement: In a TCP connection, what does the 'FIN' flag signify?
questions.option_a: A request to restart the connection
questions.option_b: An acknowledgment of received data
questions.option_c: A request to terminate the connection
questions.option_d: A notification of packet loss
questions.explanation: The FIN flag signals the sender has finished sending data and wishes to close its half of the TCP connection. TCP uses a four-way handshake for termination: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK. Each side independently closes its direction.

questions.statement: What is 'network latency'?
questions.option_a: The maximum bandwidth available on a link
questions.option_b: The time delay for a packet to travel from source to destination
questions.option_c: The rate of packet loss on a network link
questions.option_d: The number of hops between two hosts
questions.explanation: Latency is the time delay (usually in milliseconds) for a packet to travel from source to destination. It is influenced by propagation delay, transmission delay, queuing delay, and processing delay. Bandwidth is the capacity; packet loss is a reliability metric.

questions.statement: In the context of cloud security, 'IAM' (Identity and Access Management) primarily controls:
questions.option_a: Physical access to data centers
questions.option_b: Network traffic flow between services
questions.option_c: Who can access which cloud resources and what actions they can perform
questions.option_d: Encryption keys for data at rest
questions.explanation: IAM manages identities (users, roles, groups) and defines policies specifying what actions each identity can perform on which resources. It implements the principle of least privilege. IAM controls logical access, not physical or network access.

questions.statement: Which Ethernet standard uses twisted-pair cables and supports data rates up to 1 Gbps?
questions.option_a: 10BASE-T
questions.option_b: 100BASE-TX
questions.option_c: 1000BASE-T
questions.option_d: 10GBASE-T
questions.explanation: 1000BASE-T (IEEE 802.3ab) supports Gigabit Ethernet (1 Gbps) over Category 5e or better twisted-pair cables up to 100m. 10BASE-T is 10 Mbps; 100BASE-TX is 100 Mbps; 10GBASE-T is 10 Gbps.

questions.statement: A company is migrating to microservices. Which cloud networking concept allows services to discover each other without hardcoded IP addresses?
questions.option_a: Static routing
questions.option_b: Service discovery (via DNS or service registry)
questions.option_c: NAT traversal
questions.option_d: Port forwarding
questions.explanation: Service discovery allows microservices to find each other dynamically without hardcoded IPs. Services register themselves and query a registry (e.g., Consul, Kubernetes DNS) to locate others. This supports auto-scaling and fault tolerance where IPs change dynamically.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) in data center networking?
questions.option_a: Providing encryption for all VM traffic
questions.option_b: Extending Layer 2 networks over Layer 3 IP networks to connect VMs across different physical locations
questions.option_c: Replacing IP addresses with MAC addresses for routing
questions.option_d: Increasing the number of available VLANs beyond 4094
questions.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates Layer 2 frames within Layer 3 UDP packets, allowing Layer 2 network segments to span across routed Layer 3 networks. This connects VMs in different physical locations as if they're on the same LAN. It also increases the VLAN limit from 4094 to ~16 million.

questions.statement: In TCP's slow start algorithm, how does the congestion window (cwnd) grow initially?
questions.option_a: It remains constant at 1 MSS
questions.option_b: It grows linearly by 1 MSS per RTT
questions.option_c: It doubles with each RTT (exponential growth) until reaching ssthresh
questions.option_d: It immediately jumps to the receiver's advertised window size
questions.explanation: TCP slow start begins with cwnd = 1 MSS and doubles it every RTT (one ACK per segment increments cwnd by 1 MSS, so receiving a full window of ACKs doubles cwnd). This exponential growth continues until cwnd reaches ssthresh, after which congestion avoidance (linear growth) begins.

questions.statement: In cloud architecture, what is 'high availability' (HA)?
questions.option_a: A system that processes requests faster than competing systems
questions.option_b: A system designed to operate continuously with minimal downtime, typically using redundancy
questions.option_c: A system with the lowest latency in the geographic region
questions.option_d: A system that is accessible by the maximum number of users simultaneously
questions.explanation: High availability means designing systems to minimize downtime by eliminating single points of failure through redundancy (multiple servers, AZs, regions). HA is measured in 'nines' of uptime (e.g., 99.99% = 52.6 minutes downtime per year).

questions.statement: Which protocol automatically discovers the MAC address of a device given its IPv4 address on a local network?
questions.option_a: RARP
questions.option_b: ICMP
questions.option_c: ARP
questions.option_d: DNS
questions.explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) broadcasts a request asking 'who has this IP?' and the device with that IP responds with its MAC address. RARP is the reverse (MAC to IP, obsolete). DNS maps domain names to IPs. ICMP is for diagnostics.

questions.statement: What is the primary advantage of 'Infrastructure as Code' (IaC) in cloud environments?
questions.option_a: Manually controlling each server for fine-grained configuration
questions.option_b: Automating infrastructure provisioning through code, enabling version control, reproducibility, and consistency
questions.option_c: Replacing virtual machines with physical servers for better performance
questions.option_d: Providing real-time monitoring of all infrastructure components
questions.explanation: IaC (tools like Terraform, CloudFormation) defines infrastructure in code, enabling automated, reproducible provisioning. Benefits include version control, peer review, consistency across environments, and rapid recovery. Manual configuration is error-prone and slow.

questions.statement: In the OSI model, what unit of data does the Data Link Layer work with?
questions.option_a: Bits
questions.option_b: Packets
questions.option_c: Frames
questions.option_d: Segments
questions.explanation: Each OSI layer has a specific protocol data unit (PDU): Physical=Bits, Data Link=Frames, Network=Packets, Transport=Segments, Session/Presentation/Application=Data. Frames contain MAC addresses, data payload, and CRC.

questions.statement: A developer notices that their application receives DNS responses even for incorrect domain names, always resolving to a specific IP. This is likely caused by:
questions.option_a: A firewall blocking legitimate DNS traffic
questions.option_b: DNS hijacking or DNS spoofing
questions.option_c: An incorrectly configured DHCP server
questions.option_d: A BGP routing anomaly
questions.explanation: DNS hijacking or spoofing redirects DNS queries to malicious IPs. Attackers either compromise DNS servers or inject forged DNS responses. Symptoms include resolving all domains (including incorrect ones) to a specific attacker-controlled IP.

questions.statement: In cloud computing, 'fault tolerance' means:
questions.option_a: A system that never experiences hardware failures
questions.option_b: A system that continues operating correctly even when some components fail
questions.option_c: A system that automatically scales to handle load
questions.option_d: A system with geographic distribution across continents
questions.explanation: Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to continue operating correctly despite component failures. It requires redundancy (active-active or active-passive failover). A fault-tolerant system has no single point of failure.

questions.statement: Which HTTPS certificate type validates only domain ownership (no identity verification) and is fastest to obtain?
questions.option_a: Extended Validation (EV) certificate
questions.option_b: Organization Validation (OV) certificate
questions.option_c: Domain Validation (DV) certificate
questions.option_d: Wildcard certificate
questions.explanation: A DV (Domain Validation) certificate only verifies that the applicant controls the domain—no identity check. It is issued quickly (minutes) and automatically. OV verifies the organization. EV requires extensive identity verification. Wildcard covers all subdomains.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of port numbers in TCP/UDP communication?
questions.option_a: Identifying the source and destination computers
questions.option_b: Identifying the specific application or service on a host that should receive the data
questions.option_c: Encrypting the data payload of packets
questions.option_d: Routing packets between different network segments
questions.explanation: Port numbers (0-65535) identify specific applications or services on a host. Combined with an IP address, they form a socket. Well-known ports: HTTP=80, HTTPS=443, SSH=22, DNS=53. The IP address identifies the host; the port identifies the process.

questions.statement: A company's cloud application experiences high traffic on Monday mornings and low traffic on weekends. Which cloud feature directly addresses cost optimization for this pattern?
questions.option_a: Reserved instances (always-on, discounted pricing)
questions.option_b: Auto-scaling with on-demand pricing
questions.option_c: Dedicated hosts for performance
questions.option_d: Multi-region deployment for redundancy
questions.explanation: Auto-scaling with on-demand pricing scales resources up on Monday mornings and down on weekends, paying only for what is used. Reserved instances commit to always-on capacity, wasting money during low-traffic periods. This pattern suits auto-scaling.

questions.statement: In the context of network protocols, what does 'full-mesh topology' in a WAN mean?
questions.option_a: Every site connects to a central hub site
questions.option_b: Every site has a direct connection to every other site
questions.option_c: Sites connect in a ring pattern
questions.option_d: Sites connect hierarchically
questions.explanation: In a full-mesh WAN, every site has a direct link to every other site, providing maximum redundancy and performance but at high cost. For n sites, n(n-1)/2 links are required. Hub-and-spoke (star) is more cost-effective but less resilient.

questions.statement: What does 'jitter' measure in network performance?
questions.option_a: The maximum bandwidth of a network link
questions.option_b: The variation in packet arrival times (inconsistency in latency)
questions.option_c: The percentage of packets lost during transmission
questions.option_d: The total round-trip time for a packet
questions.explanation: Jitter is the variation in delay between packet arrivals. Consistent latency is ideal for real-time applications (VoIP, video). High jitter causes choppy audio/video. Jitter buffers compensate for jitter by buffering packets and playing them at a constant rate.

questions.statement: Which cloud service model is most appropriate for a company that needs to deploy a web application without managing underlying servers or operating systems?
questions.option_a: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
questions.option_b: SaaS (Software as a Service)
questions.option_c: PaaS (Platform as a Service)
questions.option_d: DaaS (Desktop as a Service)
questions.explanation: PaaS provides a platform for deploying applications (web servers, databases, runtimes) without managing the underlying OS, hardware, or infrastructure. The provider handles patching, scaling, and availability. IaaS requires OS management. SaaS is for end-user applications.

questions.statement: In Ethernet, what is the purpose of the preamble field at the beginning of a frame?
questions.option_a: Identifying the source and destination MAC addresses
questions.option_b: Allowing the receiver to synchronize its clock with the incoming bit stream before the actual data arrives
questions.option_c: Detecting errors in the frame payload
questions.option_d: Indicating the length of the data payload
questions.explanation: The 7-byte preamble (alternating 1s and 0s) allows the receiver's hardware to synchronize its clock with the incoming bit stream. The 8th byte (Start Frame Delimiter, SFD) signals the start of the actual frame. MAC addresses come after the preamble.

questions.statement: Which mechanism does TCP use to ensure the sender does not overwhelm a slow receiver?
questions.option_a: Congestion control (adjusting to network capacity)
questions.option_b: Error correction (retransmitting lost packets)
questions.option_c: Flow control (receiver-advertised window size)
questions.option_d: Checksum verification (error detection)
questions.explanation: TCP flow control uses the receiver's advertised window (rwnd) to tell the sender how much buffer space is available. The sender limits outstanding data to min(cwnd, rwnd). Congestion control prevents overwhelming the network, not the receiver.

questions.statement: Which of the five components of data communication defines the rules governing how data is formatted, transmitted, and received?
questions.option_a: Message
questions.option_b: Sender
questions.option_c: Medium
questions.option_d: Protocol
questions.explanation: Protocol defines the rules — format, timing, sequence, error control. Without agreed protocols, even if the signal arrives perfectly, sender and receiver cannot understand each other. TCP/IP, HTTP, and SMTP are all protocols.

questions.statement: A doctor uses a stethoscope connected via Bluetooth to her tablet which automatically records patient heart sounds. This is an example of which transmission mode?
questions.option_a: Simplex
questions.option_b: Half-duplex
questions.option_c: Full-duplex
questions.option_d: Broadcast
questions.explanation: The stethoscope ONLY sends data to the tablet. The tablet doesn't send data back to the stethoscope. One-way only = Simplex.

questions.statement: Why is fiber optic cable preferred over copper for submarine (undersea) cables?
questions.option_a: Fiber is cheaper than copper
questions.option_b: Fiber is immune to electromagnetic interference, has much higher bandwidth, and can span thousands of kilometers with few repeaters
questions.option_c: Fiber is easier to repair underwater
questions.option_d: Fiber uses less power than copper
questions.explanation: Fiber optic advantages for long-distance: completely EMI-immune (electrical fields exist underwater from ships), terabit-per-second capacity, minimal signal loss over thousands of km (attenuation ~0.2 dB/km vs copper's ~3 dB/km). Pakistan's internet arrives on undersea fiber (SEA-ME-WE cables).

questions.statement: A 100 Mbps link has a propagation delay of 50ms. A single 1000-bit packet is sent. What is the TOTAL delay to transmit this packet from end to end?
questions.option_a: 50ms
questions.option_d: 100ms
questions.explanation: Transmission delay = 1000 bits / 100,000,000 bps = 0.00001 seconds = 0.01ms. Propagation delay = 50ms. Total = 50ms + 0.01ms = 50.01ms. Transmission delay is negligible compared to propagation on high-speed long-distance links.

questions.statement: CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) is used at which layer for error detection in Ethernet?
questions.option_a: Physical Layer (Layer 1)
questions.option_b: Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
questions.option_c: Network Layer (Layer 3)
questions.option_d: Transport Layer (Layer 4)
questions.explanation: CRC is computed by the sender and appended to the Ethernet frame at Layer 2. The receiver recomputes CRC and compares. This is a Data Link Layer function. TCP also has a checksum (Layer 4), but Ethernet CRC is a Layer 2 mechanism.

questions.statement: What is the main limitation of Stop-and-Wait protocol compared to Sliding Window?
questions.option_a: Stop-and-Wait cannot detect errors
questions.option_b: Stop-and-Wait is extremely inefficient — the sender sits idle waiting for ACK during the full round-trip time
questions.option_c: Stop-and-Wait requires more memory
questions.option_d: Stop-and-Wait doesn't work with wireless networks
questions.explanation: In Stop-and-Wait, the sender transmits one frame, then waits for an ACK before sending the next. During the RTT (often milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds), the sender is completely idle. On high-speed, high-latency links, efficiency approaches 0%. Sliding Window allows multiple frames in flight simultaneously.

questions.statement: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for ROUTING packets between different networks?
questions.option_a: Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
questions.option_b: Transport Layer (Layer 4)
questions.option_c: Network Layer (Layer 3)
questions.option_d: Session Layer (Layer 5)
questions.explanation: Routing is a Layer 3 function. Routers operate at Layer 3, using IP addresses to determine the path packets should take across interconnected networks. Layer 2 (Data Link) handles delivery between adjacent nodes on the SAME network.

questions.statement: The MAC address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF represents:
questions.option_a: An invalid MAC address
questions.option_b: A multicast MAC address
questions.option_c: The Layer 2 broadcast address — sent to all devices on the local network
questions.option_d: The default gateway's MAC address
questions.explanation: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is the Ethernet broadcast address. A frame sent to this MAC is delivered to ALL devices on the local network segment. Used by ARP requests, DHCP Discover, and other broadcasts.

questions.statement: CSMA/CA is used instead of CSMA/CD in WiFi networks because:
questions.option_a: WiFi devices cannot transmit and receive simultaneously, making collision detection impossible
questions.option_b: CSMA/CA is faster than CSMA/CD
questions.option_c: Wireless networks don't have collisions
questions.option_d: CSMA/CD requires too much power for mobile devices
questions.explanation: In wireless, a device's own transmitted signal (much stronger) would overwhelm any other signal being received simultaneously — making it impossible to detect that a collision occurred. So WiFi avoids collisions proactively (CSMA/CA) rather than detecting them after the fact (CSMA/CD).

questions.statement: A university network has 200 computers in one building. The network uses switches, not hubs. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.option_a: All 200 computers share the same bandwidth (e.g., 100 Mbps shared)
questions.option_b: Each computer gets its own dedicated bandwidth to the switch (e.g., 1 Gbps full-duplex each)
questions.option_c: Collisions occur between all 200 computers
questions.option_d: Maximum 24 computers can be connected to a single switch
questions.explanation: Unlike hubs (which create one collision domain and share bandwidth), switches give each port its own dedicated bandwidth. Each of the 200 computers has its own 1 Gbps full-duplex link to the switch. No collisions, no sharing. This is a fundamental advantage of switches over hubs.

questions.statement: The TTL (Time to Live) field in an IPv4 packet is decremented by routers. What happens when TTL reaches 0?
questions.option_a: The packet is immediately delivered to the destination
questions.option_b: The packet is duplicated and sent on multiple paths
questions.option_c: The router discards the packet and sends an ICMP "Time Exceeded" message to the source
questions.option_d: The packet is stored until the TTL is refreshed
questions.explanation: TTL prevents infinite routing loops. When a router decrements TTL to 0, it discards the packet and sends ICMP Type 11 (Time Exceeded) back to the original sender. Traceroute exploits this by sending packets with TTL=1, 2, 3... to map the route.

questions.statement: Which IP addresses are considered PRIVATE (RFC 1918) and cannot be routed on the public internet?
questions.option_b: All addresses beginning with 192
questions.option_d: Any address with subnet mask /24 or higher
questions.explanation: RFC 1918 defines three private ranges: 10.0.0.0/8 (Class A), 172.16.0.0/12 (Class B range), 192.168.0.0/16 (Class C range). These are used in homes and organizations, translated to public IPs by NAT at the router.

questions.statement: What does BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) route traffic between?
questions.option_a: Routers within a single company's network
questions.option_b: Different Autonomous Systems (AS) — the routing protocol of the internet
questions.option_c: Switches within a VLAN
questions.option_d: Client devices and their default gateway
questions.explanation: BGP is an Exterior Gateway Protocol that routes between Autonomous Systems. Each ISP, large enterprise, or university is an AS. BGP is literally the protocol that holds the internet together, determining how traffic travels between different organizations' networks.

questions.statement: In the DHCP DORA process, why does the client broadcast the REQUEST message rather than unicasting directly to the server that made the OFFER?
questions.option_a: DHCP clients don't know the server's MAC address
questions.option_b: Multiple DHCP servers may have made offers; the broadcast informs ALL servers which offer was accepted, so others can withdraw their offers
questions.option_c: Unicast is not supported at this stage of DHCP
questions.option_d: Broadcasting is faster than unicasting
questions.explanation: Multiple DHCP servers on the network may have all responded with OFFERs. The client selects one but must inform ALL servers. By broadcasting the REQUEST, all servers see which one was chosen — the selected server confirms, and others know to release their reserved addresses.

questions.statement: Which DNS record type would you look up to find the mail server for the domain "example.pk"?
questions.option_a: A record
questions.option_b: CNAME record
questions.option_c: MX record
questions.option_d: PTR record
questions.explanation: MX (Mail Exchange) records specify the mail servers responsible for accepting email for a domain. When Gmail sends email to someone@example.pk, it looks up example.pk's MX records to find the destination mail server.

questions.statement: The "three-way handshake" in TCP (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) is necessary because:
questions.option_a: TCP requires three packets to establish a connection for reliability
questions.option_b: Both client and server must establish their initial sequence numbers and confirm each other's sequence numbers — requiring a minimum of three messages
questions.option_c: The third packet carries the first data payload
questions.option_d: It prevents SYN flood attacks
questions.explanation: The handshake is about synchronizing sequence numbers bidirectionally. Client tells server its ISN (SYN). Server acknowledges and tells client its ISN (SYN-ACK). Client acknowledges server's ISN (ACK). Each direction requires one message to send the ISN and one to acknowledge it — three messages total (the SYN-ACK combines two).

questions.statement: TCP's "fast retransmit" is triggered by:
questions.option_a: A retransmission timeout (RTO) expiry
questions.option_b: Three duplicate ACKs for the same sequence number
questions.option_c: The receiver sending a NACK (Negative Acknowledgment)
questions.option_d: The congestion window reaching zero
questions.explanation: Three duplicate ACKs (same ACK number received 4 times total) strongly suggest that one specific segment was lost while subsequent segments arrived. Instead of waiting for the RTO timer (which could be hundreds of milliseconds), TCP retransmits the lost segment immediately.

questions.statement: What distinguishes UDP from TCP regarding reliability?
questions.option_a: UDP uses checksums while TCP doesn't
questions.option_b: UDP is reliable for small packets only
questions.option_c: UDP provides no delivery guarantees — no ACKs, no retransmission, no ordering, no flow control
questions.option_d: UDP is reliable only within a single LAN
questions.explanation: UDP is a best-effort protocol. It sends datagrams and doesn't track whether they arrived. No handshake, no ACKs, no retransmission, no sequence numbers for ordering, no flow/congestion control. This makes it fast and low-overhead — appropriate when the application handles reliability itself or doesn't need it.

questions.statement: Which of the following is the BEST example of an application that should use UDP rather than TCP?
questions.option_a: Email (SMTP)
questions.option_b: File download (FTP)
questions.option_c: Online banking transaction
questions.option_d: Real-time video conference (Zoom/Google Meet)
questions.explanation: Real-time video conferencing requires low latency above all. A slightly delayed or missing packet causing a momentary glitch is acceptable. TCP's retransmission would cause a delayed packet to arrive when it's already outdated — making video jerk and audio stutter. UDP drops late packets; applications use jitter buffers to smooth playback.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of NAT (Network Address Translation) in home/office routers?
questions.option_a: Increase network speed by caching DNS responses
questions.option_b: Allow multiple devices with private IP addresses to share a single public IP address for internet access
questions.option_c: Translate between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
questions.option_d: Provide wireless access point functionality
questions.explanation: NAT allows an entire home or office network (with private IPs like 192.168.x.x) to share one public IP address assigned by the ISP. The router maintains a translation table mapping private IP:port → public IP:port for each connection. Enables the internet to scale despite IPv4 address exhaustion.

questions.statement: How does a switch determine which port to forward a frame to?
questions.option_a: It broadcasts every frame to all ports (like a hub)
questions.option_b: It uses IP addresses from a routing table
questions.option_c: It uses its MAC address table, which maps destination MAC addresses to specific ports
questions.option_d: It uses spanning tree protocol to find the shortest path
questions.explanation: A switch builds a MAC address table by learning source MAC addresses as frames arrive on each port. When a frame arrives, the switch looks up the destination MAC in this table and forwards ONLY to the correct port. If the destination MAC is unknown, it floods to all ports except the incoming one.

questions.statement: VLANs provide which primary benefit in enterprise networking?
questions.option_a: They double the available bandwidth
questions.option_b: They allow wireless devices to connect to wired networks
questions.option_c: They logically segment a physical network — providing security isolation, broadcast domain reduction, and flexible user grouping
questions.option_d: They replace the need for subnetting
questions.explanation: VLANs create virtual separate networks on shared physical infrastructure. Devices on different VLANs cannot communicate without a Layer 3 device (router/firewall) — providing security isolation. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain (smaller, better performance). Users can be grouped logically regardless of physical location.

questions.statement: What is the difference between a router and a Layer 3 switch?
questions.option_a: Routers operate at Layer 2; Layer 3 switches operate at Layer 3
questions.option_b: Both route between networks, but Layer 3 switches route using ASICs (hardware) at wire speed; traditional routers use software routing (typically slower)
questions.option_c: Layer 3 switches can only route within a VLAN; routers route between different sites
questions.option_d: They are identical — Layer 3 switch is just another name for a router
questions.explanation: Both make Layer 3 forwarding decisions. The key difference is speed and use case. Layer 3 switches use specialized hardware (ASICs) for line-rate inter-VLAN routing within a LAN. Traditional routers use software (CPU-based) for routing, often connecting different WAN types with more features (NAT, VPN, QoS policies).

questions.statement: What is the purpose of ARP in networking?
questions.option_a: Assign IP addresses automatically to devices
questions.option_b: Map IP addresses to MAC addresses so frames can be properly addressed on the local network
questions.option_c: Translate domain names to IP addresses
questions.option_d: Establish encrypted connections between hosts
questions.explanation: ARP resolves IP → MAC. When a device wants to send to 192.168.1.50 on the same subnet, it needs the MAC address to build the Ethernet frame. ARP broadcasts "Who has 192.168.1.50? Tell 192.168.1.10." The device with that IP responds with its MAC address.

questions.statement: Which routing protocol is specifically designed for routing BETWEEN different ISPs and Autonomous Systems on the internet?
questions.option_a: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
questions.option_b: RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
questions.option_c: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
questions.option_d: EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol)
questions.explanation: BGP is the Exterior Gateway Protocol that routes between Autonomous Systems. OSPF and EIGRP are Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) used WITHIN an organization's network. BGP is the only routing protocol designed for the scale and policy requirements of inter-AS (inter-ISP) routing on the global internet.

questions.statement: An OSPF router sends Link State Advertisements (LSAs) to all other OSPF routers. What does each router do with this information?
questions.option_a: Forward LSAs to the default gateway only
questions.option_b: Build a complete topology map of the network and run Dijkstra's SPF algorithm to calculate best routes
questions.option_c: Simply add the advertised routes directly to its routing table
questions.option_d: Use LSAs only for backup routing when the primary path fails
questions.explanation: OSPF link state: Each router floods its LSAs (its direct connections and their costs) to ALL routers. Every router builds an identical topology database (map of the entire network). Then each router independently runs Dijkstra's Shortest Path First algorithm to compute the best path to every destination.

questions.statement: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) in switched networks is designed to:
questions.option_a: Increase network bandwidth by using all available links simultaneously
questions.option_b: Prevent Layer 2 switching loops by blocking redundant paths, then activating them if the primary path fails
questions.option_c: Enable routers to exchange routing information
questions.option_d: Authenticate users before allowing network access
questions.explanation: In a network with redundant switch links (for fault tolerance), Layer 2 loops cause broadcast storms — a broadcast frame loops forever, consuming all bandwidth. STP logically blocks redundant ports, creating a loop-free tree topology. If the primary path fails, STP unblocks the previously blocked path.

questions.statement: WiFi uses CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD. The "Avoidance" approach uses which mechanism to reduce collisions?
questions.option_a: Transmitting as fast as possible before others can start
questions.option_b: Carrier sensing + random backoff after channel becomes idle + ACK confirmation
questions.option_c: Using dedicated time slots for each device (TDMA)
questions.option_d: Encrypting transmissions so only the intended receiver responds
questions.explanation: CSMA/CA: (1) Sense carrier — wait if busy. (2) When idle, wait IFS period. (3) Wait random backoff period. (4) Transmit. (5) Receiver sends ACK. If no ACK received, collision assumed — retry with increased backoff. The random backoff reduces probability of multiple devices transmitting simultaneously.

questions.statement: What is the "hidden terminal problem" in WiFi, and what is its standard solution?
questions.option_a: WiFi passwords can be hidden from users; solved by WPA3
questions.option_b: Two devices can both hear the AP but not each other — both transmit simultaneously causing collision at the AP; solved by RTS/CTS
questions.option_c: The AP's SSID can be hidden; solved by broadcasting the SSID
questions.option_d: Devices at the edge of WiFi range can't see the AP; solved by range extenders
questions.explanation: Device A and Device C are both in range of AP B but out of range of each other. Both sense the channel as idle (they can't hear each other) and transmit simultaneously → collision at AP B. RTS/CTS: A sends RTS to AP. AP broadcasts CTS — C hears it and defers. Only A transmits.

questions.statement: What is the key advantage of WiFi 6 (802.11ax) over WiFi 5 (802.11ac) in dense environments like stadiums?
questions.option_a: Higher maximum single-device speed
questions.option_b: OFDMA — allows the AP to serve multiple clients simultaneously on different portions of the channel
questions.option_c: Support for 60 GHz frequencies for extremely high speeds
questions.option_d: Reduced battery drain compared to 802.11ac
questions.explanation: OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) divides a channel into smaller resource units, allowing simultaneous service to multiple clients. WiFi 5's MU-MIMO helps but has limitations in dense environments. OFDMA dramatically improves efficiency when hundreds of devices are connected — crucial for stadiums, airports, and offices.

questions.statement: WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) improves over WPA2's PSK because:
questions.option_a: SAE uses a longer password by default
questions.option_b: SAE is immune to offline dictionary attacks — an attacker cannot capture WiFi frames and brute-force the password offline
questions.option_c: SAE eliminates the need for a WiFi password entirely
questions.option_d: SAE only works on 5 GHz networks
questions.explanation: WPA2 PSK: An attacker can capture the 4-way handshake and try millions of passwords offline using a GPU. WPA3 SAE: Uses Dragonfly key exchange — an attacker must interact with the network for EACH password guess (online attack only). Makes brute-force attacks impractical. Also provides forward secrecy.

questions.statement: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, providing approximately how many possible addresses?
questions.option_a: 4.3 billion (2³²)
questions.option_b: 4.3 trillion (2⁴²)
questions.option_c: 340 undecillion (3.4 × 10³⁸) (2¹²⁸)
questions.option_d: 4.3 quintillion (2⁶²)
questions.explanation: IPv6 = 128 bits = 2¹²⁸ = approximately 3.4 × 10³⁸ addresses — 340 undecillion. Enough to assign billions of IPs to every grain of sand on Earth. Designed to eliminate address exhaustion permanently.

questions.statement: The IPv6 address ::1 is equivalent to which IPv4 address?
questions.option_c: 127.0.0.1 (localhost/loopback)
questions.explanation: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback address (short for 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001). Like 127.0.0.1 in IPv4, it refers to the device itself. ping ::1 tests the local TCP/IP stack without sending traffic onto the network.

questions.statement: Which 5G service category enables remote surgery and industrial robot control requiring 1ms latency?
questions.option_a: eMBB (Enhanced Mobile Broadband)
questions.option_b: mMTC (Massive Machine Type Communications)
questions.option_c: URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications)
questions.option_d: NSA (Non-Standalone Architecture)
questions.explanation: URLLC targets 1ms end-to-end latency with 99.9999% reliability (six nines). Essential for applications where delay or failure is catastrophic: autonomous vehicles (brake decisions), remote surgery (haptic feedback), industrial automation (real-time robot control). eMBB is for high-speed data. mMTC is for massive IoT sensor deployments.

questions.statement: What does the "hop count" metric in RIP represent, and what is its maximum value?
questions.option_a: Number of bytes transmitted; maximum 65,535
questions.option_b: Number of routers a packet passes through; maximum 15 (16 = infinity/unreachable)
questions.option_c: Number of available paths; maximum 8
questions.option_d: Bandwidth consumed per route; maximum determined dynamically
questions.explanation: RIP uses hop count as its sole metric — the number of routers a packet must traverse. Maximum useful metric is 15 hops. A route with 16 hops is considered unreachable (infinity). This limits RIP to small networks — a network larger than 15 hops in diameter cannot use RIP.

questions.statement: What is the primary function of a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) in network security?
questions.option_a: A wireless network zone with no security restrictions
questions.option_b: A network segment hosting public-facing services (web, email) isolated from the internal network — compromise of DMZ servers doesn't expose internal systems
