questions.option_d: goto statement
questions.explanation: A for loop is most appropriate when the iteration count is known (definite iteration). It combines initialization, condition, and increment in one line. while is for indefinite loops (unknown iterations). do-while guarantees at least one execution.

questions.statement: A Python developer needs to store student grades mapped to student IDs, with fast lookup by ID. Which data structure is best?
questions.option_a: A list of tuples
questions.option_b: A sorted list of IDs
questions.option_c: A dictionary mapping ID to grade
questions.option_d: A set of ID-grade pairs
questions.explanation: A dictionary provides O(1) average-case lookup by key (student ID). A list requires O(n) search. Sets don't support key-value pairs. A dictionary is the natural data structure for this key-value mapping use case.

questions.statement: In Java, the 'finally' block in a try-catch-finally structure executes:
questions.option_a: Only when no exception is thrown
questions.option_b: Only when an exception is caught
questions.option_c: Always, whether or not an exception is thrown (with rare JVM-exit exceptions)
questions.option_d: Only when a specific exception type is caught
questions.explanation: The 'finally' block executes after the try block (and any catch block), regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught. It is used for guaranteed cleanup (closing resources). The rare exception is System.exit() or JVM crash.

questions.statement: What is the output of the following Python code? print(3 ** 2 ** 2)?
questions.explanation: Python's exponentiation operator ** is right-associative: 3 ** 2 ** 2 = 3 ** (2**2) = 3 ** 4 = 81. Left-to-right evaluation would give (3**2)**2 = 9**2 = 81. In this case both give 81, but right-associativity is the rule.

questions.statement: In C++, what does 'RAII' (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) mean?
questions.option_a: Allocate resources at program start and release at exit
questions.option_b: Resources are acquired in the constructor and released in the destructor, ensuring automatic cleanup
questions.option_c: Use global variables to share resources between functions
questions.option_d: Initialize all variables before declaring resources
questions.explanation: RAII ties resource lifetime to object lifetime: resources (memory, file handles, locks) are acquired in the constructor and released in the destructor. When the object goes out of scope, the destructor automatically runs, preventing resource leaks.

questions.statement: Which Python method returns True if all characters in a string are digits?
questions.option_a: str.isnumeric()
questions.option_b: str.isdigit()
questions.option_c: str.isalnum()
questions.option_d: str.isdecimal()
questions.explanation: str.isdigit() returns True if all characters are digit characters (0-9) and the string is non-empty. isdigit() also handles superscript digits. isnumeric() is broader (includes fractions, Roman numerals). isdecimal() is stricter (only decimal digits).

questions.statement: In Java, 'generics' provide:
questions.option_a: Runtime type checking for all object operations
questions.option_b: Compile-time type safety, allowing collections and algorithms to work with specified types
questions.option_c: Automatic conversion between incompatible types
questions.option_d: Runtime polymorphism through type parameters
questions.explanation: Java Generics enable compile-time type checking, catching type errors before runtime. List<String> ensures only Strings can be added, eliminating explicit casts and ClassCastExceptions. Type information is erased at runtime (type erasure).

questions.statement: A Python program prints numbers 1 through 5 using: for i in range(1, 6): print(i). Changing range(1,6) to range(1,6,2) would print:
questions.explanation: range(1, 6, 2) generates values starting at 1, ending before 6, stepping by 2: 1, 3, 5. The step parameter controls the increment between consecutive values.

questions.statement: In C++, the 'move semantics' (introduced in C++11) primarily improve performance by:
questions.option_a: Eliminating the need for destructors
questions.option_b: Transferring ownership of resources instead of copying them, avoiding expensive deep copies
questions.option_c: Making all copies shallow by default
questions.option_d: Automatically parallelizing copy operations
questions.explanation: Move semantics transfer ownership of resources (heap memory, file handles) from a temporary (rvalue) to a new object instead of copying. This eliminates expensive deep copies for temporary objects, significantly improving performance for classes managing resources.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of Python's __len__() method?
questions.option_a: Returns the memory size of an object in bytes
questions.option_b: Defines the behavior of len() for user-defined objects
questions.option_c: Returns the number of attributes in a class
questions.option_d: Calculates the maximum index of a collection
questions.explanation: Implementing __len__(self) in a class allows len(obj) to work on user-defined objects. It should return an integer ≥ 0 representing the 'size' or 'length' of the object. This is part of Python's data model (dunder/magic methods).

questions.statement: In Java, which statement about 'interface default methods' (introduced in Java 8) is correct?
questions.option_a: Default methods are abstract and must be overridden
questions.option_b: Default methods provide a concrete implementation in an interface that classes can optionally override
questions.option_c: Default methods are only accessible within the interface
questions.option_d: Default methods cannot call other interface methods
questions.explanation: Java 8 default methods provide a concrete implementation in an interface. Implementing classes inherit this implementation but can optionally override it. This allows adding new methods to interfaces without breaking existing implementations.

questions.statement: Which Python built-in function returns an iterator that aggregates elements from multiple iterables into tuples?
questions.option_a: map()
questions.option_b: enumerate()
questions.option_c: chain()
questions.option_d: zip()
questions.explanation: zip() pairs elements from multiple iterables into tuples, returning an iterator. map() applies a function to elements; enumerate() yields (index, value) pairs; itertools.chain() concatenates iterables sequentially.

questions.statement: In C++, what does the 'explicit' keyword on a constructor prevent?
questions.option_a: The constructor from being called outside the class
questions.option_b: Implicit (automatic) type conversion using that constructor
questions.option_c: The constructor from accepting multiple arguments
questions.option_d: The constructor from calling virtual methods
questions.explanation: 'explicit' prevents the compiler from using a single-argument constructor for implicit type conversions. Without 'explicit', MyClass obj = 5; might silently call MyClass(int), which can cause unexpected behavior. 'explicit' requires explicit conversion: MyClass obj(5);

questions.statement: A developer needs a data structure that processes customer service requests in the order they arrive, ensuring the first customer to request help is the first to be served. Which structure is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: Stack
questions.option_b: Priority Queue
questions.option_c: Queue
questions.option_d: Binary Search Tree
questions.explanation: A Queue implements FIFO (First-In, First-Out), which matches the requirement that the first customer to arrive is first served. A Stack is LIFO. A Priority Queue serves based on priority, not arrival order.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in a balanced Binary Search Tree (BST)?
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST, each comparison halves the remaining search space, leading to O(log n) time complexity. An unbalanced BST degrades to O(n). A hash table provides O(1) average search.

questions.statement: Consider an array: [64, 25, 12, 22, 11]. After one complete pass of Bubble Sort, the array becomes:
questions.explanation: Bubble Sort compares adjacent elements and swaps if out of order. Tracing one pass: (64,25)→swap→[25,64,12,22,11]; (64,12)→swap→[25,12,64,22,11]; (64,22)→swap→[25,12,22,64,11]; (64,11)→swap→[25,12,22,11,64]. Result: [25,12,22,11,64].

questions.statement: Which data structure allows O(1) push and pop operations from only one end?
questions.option_a: Queue
questions.option_b: Deque
questions.option_c: Stack
questions.option_d: Circular Buffer
questions.explanation: A Stack provides O(1) push (add to top) and pop (remove from top) operations. A Queue provides O(1) enqueue and dequeue but from opposite ends. A Deque allows O(1) operations at both ends.

questions.statement: In a graph with V vertices and E edges represented as an adjacency matrix, what is the space complexity?
questions.option_a: O(V)
questions.option_b: O(E)
questions.option_c: O(V²)
questions.option_d: O(V + E)
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix uses a V×V 2D array, requiring O(V²) space regardless of the number of edges. An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space, making it more space-efficient for sparse graphs.

questions.statement: A hash function maps keys to the same index. This situation is called:
questions.option_a: Collision
questions.option_b: Overflow
questions.option_c: Underflow
questions.option_d: Chaining
questions.explanation: A collision occurs when two different keys hash to the same index in the hash table. Chaining and open addressing are collision resolution techniques, not the problem itself.

questions.statement: Which sorting algorithm is considered most efficient for nearly sorted arrays?
questions.option_a: Quick Sort
questions.option_b: Heap Sort
questions.option_c: Insertion Sort
questions.option_d: Selection Sort
questions.explanation: Insertion Sort has O(n) best-case time complexity for nearly sorted arrays—it performs at most one or two comparisons per element before finding the correct position. Quick Sort's best case is O(n log n); Heap Sort is always O(n log n).

questions.statement: A binary tree has the property that for every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are larger. This is a:
questions.option_a: Heap
questions.option_b: AVL Tree
questions.option_c: Binary Search Tree
questions.option_d: Complete Binary Tree
questions.explanation: This defines a Binary Search Tree (BST). A Heap has the heap property (parent ≥ children or parent ≤ children). An AVL Tree is a self-balancing BST. A Complete Binary Tree is about shape, not key ordering.

questions.statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(n²)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Quick Sort's worst case is O(n²), occurring when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., sorted array with naive pivot selection). The average case is O(n log n). Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case.

questions.statement: In a Max-Heap with elements [90, 70, 60, 50, 30, 20], what is the root element?
questions.explanation: In a Max-Heap, the root always contains the maximum element. Since 90 is the largest, it is at the root (index 0). The heap property guarantees every parent is ≥ its children.

questions.statement: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a queue data structure internally?
questions.option_a: Depth-First Search (DFS)
questions.option_b: Bellman-Ford
questions.option_c: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
questions.option_d: Dijkstra's algorithm (conceptually)
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to explore nodes level by level. DFS uses a stack (or recursion call stack) to explore as deep as possible. Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra are shortest path algorithms, not just traversal.

questions.statement: A linked list has nodes where each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node. Inserting a node at the beginning of the list runs in:
questions.option_a: O(n) time
questions.option_b: O(log n) time
questions.option_c: O(1) time
questions.option_d: O(n²) time
questions.explanation: Inserting at the head of a singly linked list requires only updating the new node's next pointer and updating the head pointer—two constant-time operations. No traversal is needed, giving O(1) time.

questions.statement: Which algorithm design paradigm solves a problem by solving overlapping sub-problems and storing results to avoid redundant computation?
questions.option_a: Greedy algorithm
questions.option_b: Divide and conquer
questions.option_c: Dynamic programming
questions.option_d: Backtracking
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming stores results of overlapping sub-problems (memoization or tabulation) to avoid redundant recomputation. Divide and conquer splits into non-overlapping sub-problems. Greedy makes locally optimal choices without storing sub-problem results.

questions.statement: A developer uses a doubly linked list. Compared to a singly linked list, what additional capability does it provide?
questions.option_a: O(1) access by index
questions.option_b: Traversal in both forward and backward directions
questions.option_c: Automatic sorting of inserted elements
questions.option_d: O(1) search by value
questions.explanation: A doubly linked list has pointers to both next and previous nodes, enabling bidirectional traversal. A singly linked list can only traverse forward. Neither provides O(1) index access or automatic sorting.

questions.statement: In Merge Sort, what is the primary operation performed during the 'merge' phase?
questions.option_a: Partitioning the array around a pivot
questions.option_b: Combining two sorted sub-arrays into one sorted array
questions.option_c: Finding the minimum element in each sub-array
questions.option_d: Swapping adjacent elements that are out of order
questions.explanation: The merge phase takes two already-sorted sub-arrays and produces a single sorted array by comparing elements from each sub-array and writing the smaller one first. This operation runs in O(n) time and is the key step in Merge Sort.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm using a min-priority queue (binary heap)?
questions.option_a: O(V²)
questions.option_b: O(V + E)
questions.option_c: O((V + E) log V)
questions.option_d: O(E log V)
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's with a binary heap priority queue runs in O((V + E) log V): each of V vertices is extracted from the heap in O(log V), and each of E edges may trigger a key decrease in O(log V). With a Fibonacci heap, it improves to O(E + V log V).

questions.statement: Which traversal of a BST produces the elements in sorted (ascending) order?
questions.option_a: Pre-order
questions.option_b: In-order
questions.option_c: Post-order
questions.option_d: Level-order
questions.explanation: In-order traversal (Left → Root → Right) of a BST visits nodes in ascending key order because all left subtree keys are smaller than the root, which is smaller than all right subtree keys. Pre-order and post-order do not guarantee sorted output.

questions.statement: An application needs to find the k-th smallest element frequently from a dynamic set of integers. Which data structure is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: Unsorted array
questions.option_b: Sorted linked list
questions.option_c: Min-Heap of size k
questions.option_d: Order statistics tree (augmented BST)
questions.explanation: An order statistics tree (BST augmented with subtree sizes) supports finding the k-th smallest element in O(log n) time for any k. A min-heap of size k works for finding the k-th smallest from a stream but not efficiently for arbitrary k queries.

questions.statement: What is the space complexity of the recursive Merge Sort algorithm?
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Merge Sort requires O(n) auxiliary space for the temporary arrays used during the merge phase. The recursive call stack adds O(log n) space, but O(n) dominates. In-place Merge Sort variants exist but are complex.

questions.statement: A hash table uses 'linear probing' to resolve collisions. If the hash of key k is index i and i is occupied, linear probing checks:
questions.option_a: i+1, i+2, i+3, ... (mod table size)
questions.option_b: i², i*2, i*4, ... (mod table size)
questions.option_c: A second hash function to compute a new index
questions.option_d: A linked list at index i for the next slot
questions.explanation: Linear probing checks the next consecutive index (i+1, i+2, ...) wrapping around modulo table size. Quadratic probing uses i+1², i+2². Double hashing uses a second hash function. Chaining uses linked lists.

questions.statement: In the context of graph algorithms, which algorithm finds the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) by greedily adding the shortest edge that does not create a cycle?
questions.option_a: Prim's algorithm
questions.option_b: Kruskal's algorithm
questions.option_c: Dijkstra's algorithm
questions.option_d: Floyd-Warshall algorithm
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges by weight and greedily adds the shortest edge that doesn't create a cycle (using Union-Find to detect cycles). Prim's algorithm grows the MST by adding the nearest vertex. Dijkstra and Floyd-Warshall are shortest path algorithms.

questions.statement: What is the output of a post-order traversal of this tree? Root=1, Left=2, Right=3, Left.Left=4, Left.Right=5
questions.explanation: Post-order traversal visits Left subtree, Right subtree, then Root. Tracing: Visit left subtree of 2 (4), visit right subtree of 2 (5), visit 2, visit right subtree of 1 (3), visit 1 → 4, 5, 2, 3, 1.

questions.statement: Which property distinguishes a 'complete' binary tree from a 'full' binary tree?
questions.option_a: A complete tree has all nodes with 0 or 2 children; a full tree fills level by level
questions.option_b: A complete tree fills all levels fully from left to right (last level may be incomplete); a full tree has every node with 0 or 2 children
questions.option_c: A complete tree is always balanced; a full tree may be unbalanced
questions.option_d: A complete tree has a fixed depth; a full tree has variable depth
questions.explanation: A complete binary tree fills all levels fully left to right (last level may be incomplete). A full binary tree requires every node to have 0 or exactly 2 children. These are independent properties; a tree can be both, one, or neither.

questions.statement: Which searching algorithm requires the array to be sorted before searching?
questions.option_a: Linear search
questions.option_b: Jump search
questions.option_c: Binary search
questions.option_d: Exponential search
questions.explanation: Binary search requires a sorted array because it uses the comparison result to eliminate half the remaining search space. Linear search works on unsorted arrays. Jump search and exponential search also require sorted arrays, making option_c the most fundamental.

questions.statement: In a circular queue with maximum size 5, the current state is front=2, rear=4. After two dequeue operations, what is the new front?
questions.explanation: Each dequeue moves front forward by 1 (modulo size). Starting front=2: after first dequeue, front=(2+1)%5=3. After second dequeue, front=(3+1)%5=4. New front=4.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm?
questions.option_a: O(V² log V)
questions.option_b: O(V² + E)
questions.option_c: O(V³)
questions.option_d: O(E log V)
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses three nested loops over V vertices to compute shortest paths between all pairs, giving O(V³) time complexity. It is suitable for dense graphs and negative weight edges (but not negative cycles).

questions.statement: A Trie (prefix tree) is most efficient for which type of operation?
questions.option_a: Finding the kth smallest integer
questions.option_b: Prefix-based string search and autocomplete
questions.option_c: Sorting a list of integers
questions.option_d: Breadth-first traversal of graphs
questions.explanation: Tries excel at prefix-based operations: searching for strings with a given prefix, autocomplete, and spell checking. Each character of the prefix corresponds to one level in the trie, making prefix search O(L) where L is the prefix length.

questions.statement: In a Max-Heap, inserting a new element requires which operation to maintain the heap property?
questions.option_a: Sift-down (heapify-down)
questions.option_b: Sift-up (heapify-up) from the inserted position
questions.option_c: Rebuilding the entire heap
questions.option_d: Searching for the correct position before insertion
questions.explanation: After inserting at the end of the heap array, sift-up (bubble up) compares the new element with its parent and swaps if larger, repeating until the heap property is restored. Sift-down is used after deletion of the root.

questions.statement: Which graph representation is most space-efficient for a sparse graph (few edges relative to vertices)?
questions.option_a: Adjacency matrix
questions.option_b: Incidence matrix
questions.option_c: Adjacency list
questions.option_d: Edge matrix
questions.explanation: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space, which is efficient for sparse graphs (E << V²). An adjacency matrix uses O(V²) regardless of edge count, wasting space when E is small.

questions.statement: Selection Sort has which time complexity in all cases (best, average, worst)?
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(n)
questions.option_c: O(n²)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Selection Sort always performs O(n²) comparisons: for each of n positions, it scans the remaining n-i elements to find the minimum. Unlike Insertion Sort (which has O(n) best case), Selection Sort performs the same number of comparisons regardless of initial order.

questions.statement: An application needs to check if a string is a palindrome using a stack. What is the time complexity of this approach for a string of length n?
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Checking palindrome with a stack requires: O(n) to push half the characters, O(n) to compare while popping. Total: O(n) time and O(n) space. The stack stores up to n/2 characters.

questions.statement: In Breadth-First Search, the algorithm guarantees finding the shortest path (in terms of number of edges) in which type of graph?
questions.option_a: Weighted directed graph
questions.option_b: Unweighted graph (or graph with equal edge weights)
questions.option_c: Weighted undirected graph
questions.option_d: Directed acyclic graph with varying weights
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level (by edge count), guaranteeing the shortest path in terms of number of edges in unweighted graphs (or graphs where all edge weights are equal). Dijkstra's algorithm is needed for weighted shortest paths.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of heapify (building a heap from an unsorted array)?
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(n²)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Although it seems counter-intuitive, building a heap from n elements using the bottom-up heapify approach is O(n), not O(n log n). This is because most nodes are near the bottom of the tree and require very few sift-down operations.

questions.statement: In a doubly linked list, deleting a node (given a pointer to that node) runs in:
questions.option_a: O(n) time
questions.option_b: O(log n) time
questions.option_c: O(1) time
questions.option_d: O(n²) time
questions.explanation: Given a pointer to the node, deletion in a doubly linked list is O(1): update the previous node's next pointer and the next node's previous pointer. No traversal is needed. A singly linked list requires O(n) traversal to find the predecessor.

questions.statement: Which algorithm is best suited for detecting cycles in a directed graph?
questions.option_a: Dijkstra's algorithm
questions.option_b: Prim's algorithm
questions.option_c: DFS with coloring (white/gray/black marking)
questions.option_d: BFS with level tracking
questions.explanation: DFS with three-color marking detects cycles in directed graphs: a 'gray' (currently being processed) node discovered again indicates a back edge (cycle). BFS does not naturally detect directed cycles. Dijkstra and Prim are MST/shortest path algorithms.

questions.statement: In a hash table with n elements and m buckets, the load factor is defined as:
questions.option_a: m / n
questions.option_b: n × m
questions.option_c: n / m
questions.option_d: (n - m) / n
questions.explanation: Load factor λ = n/m (elements per bucket). A load factor > 1 means multiple elements per bucket on average. High load factors increase collision probability. Hash tables are typically resized when λ exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.75).

questions.statement: Kruskal's algorithm uses which data structure to efficiently detect if adding an edge creates a cycle?
questions.option_a: Min-Heap
questions.option_b: Queue
questions.option_c: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
questions.option_d: Stack
questions.explanation: Kruskal's uses Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) to track connected components. Before adding an edge (u, v), it checks if u and v are in the same component (find operation). If not, it adds the edge and merges the components (union). Both operations are nearly O(1) amortized.

questions.statement: What is the amortized time complexity of the push operation on a dynamic array (like Python list) that doubles in capacity when full?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(1) amortized
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Although occasional resizing (copying n elements) is O(n), it happens infrequently. Amortized over n pushes, the total cost is O(n) for all n operations, giving O(1) amortized per push. This is the standard accounting argument for dynamic arrays.

questions.statement: A Red-Black Tree is a self-balancing BST. Its key property ensures that the longest root-to-leaf path is at most how many times the shortest path?
questions.option_a: Equal length
questions.option_b: 2 times longer
questions.option_c: 4 times longer
questions.option_d: log n times longer
questions.explanation: Red-Black Tree properties guarantee that the longest root-to-leaf path (all red-black alternating) is at most twice the shortest path (all black). This ensures O(log n) height and thus O(log n) search, insert, and delete.

questions.statement: Which string matching algorithm preprocesses the pattern to build a failure function, avoiding unnecessary character comparisons?
questions.option_a: Rabin-Karp
questions.option_b: Naive string matching
questions.option_c: KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt)
questions.option_d: Boyer-Moore
questions.explanation: KMP builds a failure function (partial match table) from the pattern in O(m) time, then searches in O(n) time. This avoids re-examining previously matched characters. Rabin-Karp uses hashing; Boyer-Moore uses bad character/good suffix heuristics.

questions.statement: In topological sorting of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), the output is:
questions.option_a: Vertices sorted by in-degree
questions.option_b: A linear ordering of vertices where each vertex comes before all vertices it has directed edges to
questions.option_c: The shortest path from source to all vertices
questions.option_d: Vertices ordered by their discovery time in DFS
questions.explanation: Topological sort produces a linear ordering where for every directed edge (u, v), vertex u appears before v. It is only possible for DAGs (no cycles). It is used for dependency resolution, task scheduling, and compilation order.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of inserting an element into a sorted linked list in the correct position?
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: To insert into a sorted linked list in the correct position, the list must be traversed to find the insertion point—up to O(n) in the worst case. Unlike sorted arrays, binary search cannot be applied to linked lists due to lack of random access.

questions.statement: A developer implements a queue using two stacks. The time complexity of a dequeue operation (amortized) is:
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(1) amortized
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Using two stacks: enqueue pushes to stack1 (O(1)). For dequeue, if stack2 is empty, all elements from stack1 are moved to stack2 (O(n) once), then popped from stack2 (O(1)). Amortized over n operations: each element moves at most twice, giving O(1) amortized per operation.

questions.statement: Which property must a graph satisfy for Dijkstra's algorithm to guarantee correct shortest path results?
questions.option_a: The graph must be directed
questions.option_b: The graph must be acyclic
questions.option_c: All edge weights must be non-negative
questions.option_d: The graph must be connected
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm requires non-negative edge weights. With negative weights, a shorter path may be discovered after a vertex is finalized, breaking the algorithm's correctness. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights (but not negative cycles).

questions.statement: In a B-Tree with minimum degree t, each non-root node must contain at least how many keys?
questions.option_a: 1 key
questions.option_b: t - 1 keys
questions.option_c: t keys
questions.option_d: 2t - 1 keys
questions.explanation: By B-Tree definition, every non-root node has at least t-1 keys and at most 2t-1 keys. The root can have as few as 1 key. This property ensures the tree remains balanced and supports efficient disk-based operations.

questions.statement: The Master Theorem gives the solution to recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), the solution is:
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n log n)
questions.option_c: O(n²)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): a=2, b=2, f(n)=n. n^(log_b(a)) = n^(log_2(2)) = n¹ = n. Since f(n) = Θ(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a)), this is Case 2 of the Master Theorem: T(n) = Θ(n log n). This is Merge Sort's recurrence.

questions.statement: In an AVL tree, after insertion, which operation restores the balance property if the balance factor of a node exceeds ±1?
questions.option_a: Heapify
questions.option_b: Tree rotation (single or double)
questions.option_c: Rehashing
questions.option_d: Re-insertion from scratch
questions.explanation: AVL trees restore balance using rotations: a single right or left rotation for cases where the subtree is unbalanced in one direction, and a double rotation (left-right or right-left) for cases where the subtree is bent. Rotations are O(1) operations.

questions.statement: What does the term 'amortized O(1)' mean for a dynamic array's append operation?
questions.option_a: Every single append takes constant time
questions.option_b: Append sometimes takes O(n) time (resizing), but averaging over many appends, the cost per append is constant
questions.option_c: The array never needs to resize
questions.option_d: The first append is O(n); all subsequent ones are O(1)
questions.explanation: 'Amortized O(1)' means that while occasional appends trigger expensive O(n) resizing, the cost is spread over many cheap O(1) appends. The average cost per operation over any sequence of n appends is O(1), even though individual operations vary.

questions.statement: Which algorithm uses the concept of 'relaxation' to find the shortest path, allowing for negative edge weights?
questions.option_a: Dijkstra's algorithm
questions.option_b: Prim's algorithm
questions.option_c: Bellman-Ford algorithm
questions.option_d: Floyd-Warshall algorithm
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times, allowing it to handle negative edge weights. It also detects negative weight cycles. Dijkstra uses greedy selection which fails with negative weights. Floyd-Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths.

questions.statement: In a Segment Tree built over an array of n elements, what is the time complexity of a range sum query?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: A Segment Tree supports range queries in O(log n) by decomposing the query range into at most O(log n) tree nodes whose stored values are combined. Point updates are also O(log n). Building the tree is O(n).

questions.statement: What is the key difference between BFS and Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.option_a: BFS uses a priority queue; Dijkstra uses a regular queue
questions.option_b: BFS finds shortest paths by edge count (unweighted); Dijkstra finds shortest paths by total weight (weighted non-negative)
questions.option_c: BFS works only on directed graphs; Dijkstra works on undirected graphs
questions.option_d: BFS is faster for all graph types
questions.explanation: BFS finds shortest paths in terms of number of edges (treating all edges as weight 1). Dijkstra finds shortest paths by total weight in graphs with non-negative edge weights. Both use queue-like structures, but Dijkstra uses a min-priority queue.

questions.statement: A Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) is particularly efficient for which pair of operations?
questions.option_a: Insertion and deletion
questions.option_b: Range minimum queries and point updates
questions.option_c: Prefix sum queries and point updates
questions.option_d: Graph traversal and cycle detection
questions.explanation: A Fenwick Tree supports prefix sum queries and point updates in O(log n) time with O(n) space. This makes it ideal for dynamic prefix sum problems. Range minimum queries are more naturally handled by Segment Trees.

questions.statement: In the context of hashing, 'open addressing' means:
questions.option_a: Storing colliding elements in a separate linked list
questions.option_b: Storing all elements directly in the hash table array, probing for open slots on collision
questions.option_c: Using a separate overflow area outside the main table
questions.option_d: Doubling the table size on every collision
questions.explanation: Open addressing keeps all elements in the hash table array itself. On collision, it probes (linear, quadratic, or double hashing) for the next available slot. Separate chaining stores colliding elements in linked lists at each bucket.

questions.statement: A graph has V=5 vertices and the following edges: (0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (2,3), (3,4). What is the minimum number of edges in a Spanning Tree?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree of a graph with V vertices always has exactly V-1 edges. For V=5 vertices, the spanning tree has 5-1 = 4 edges. This is a fundamental property of spanning trees.

questions.statement: Which sorting algorithm is NOT a comparison-based sort?
questions.option_a: Merge Sort
questions.option_b: Heap Sort
questions.option_c: Counting Sort
questions.option_d: Quick Sort
questions.explanation: Counting Sort is a non-comparison-based sort that counts occurrences of each distinct element. It runs in O(n + k) where k is the range of values. Comparison-based sorts (Merge, Heap, Quick) have a theoretical lower bound of O(n log n).

questions.statement: An array-based stack has reached its maximum capacity. The BEST design decision is to:
questions.option_a: Raise an error and stop all operations
questions.option_b: Double the array size and copy elements (dynamic resizing)
questions.option_c: Delete the oldest element to make room
questions.option_d: Switch to a linked list-based stack immediately
questions.explanation: Dynamic resizing (doubling capacity) is the standard solution, giving O(1) amortized push operations. Raising an error limits usability; deleting elements corrupts data; switching structures mid-operation is complex and unnecessary.

questions.statement: Which tree traversal visits the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree?
questions.option_a: In-order
questions.option_b: Post-order
questions.option_c: Pre-order
questions.option_d: Level-order
questions.explanation: Pre-order traversal: Root → Left → Right. In-order: Left → Root → Right. Post-order: Left → Right → Root. Level-order (BFS): visits all nodes at each depth level before moving deeper.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of accessing the minimum element in a Min-Heap?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In a Min-Heap, the minimum element is always at the root (index 0 in an array representation). Accessing the root is a O(1) constant-time operation. Extracting the minimum (removing the root and restoring heap property) is O(log n).

questions.statement: A developer implements the longest common subsequence (LCS) problem. The bottom-up dynamic programming approach has which time and space complexity for strings of length m and n?
questions.option_a: Time O(mn), Space O(min(m,n))
questions.option_b: Time O(mn), Space O(mn)
questions.option_c: Time O(m+n), Space O(mn)
questions.option_d: Time O(m²n²), Space O(mn)
questions.explanation: The standard DP table for LCS is a (m+1)×(n+1) matrix, requiring O(mn) space and O(mn) time to fill. Space can be optimized to O(min(m,n)) using only two rows, but the standard formulation uses O(mn) space.

questions.statement: In a circular singly linked list, the last node's next pointer points to:
questions.option_a: NULL
questions.option_b: The previous node
questions.option_c: The head (first) node
questions.option_d: Itself
questions.explanation: In a circular singly linked list, the last node's next pointer points back to the head (first node), forming a circle. In a regular linked list, the last node's next pointer is NULL.

questions.statement: The Knapsack problem solved with dynamic programming has which time complexity? (n = items, W = capacity)
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(n + W)
questions.option_c: O(nW)
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: The 0/1 Knapsack problem is solved with a 2D DP table of size n×W, filled in O(1) per cell. Total time is O(nW). This is pseudo-polynomial because W is a value, not the length of its encoding.

questions.statement: Which data structure is used internally by Prim's algorithm (with a priority queue) to select the next minimum-weight edge?
questions.option_a: Stack
questions.option_b: Min-Heap (Min-Priority Queue)
questions.option_c: Hash Map
questions.option_d: Queue (FIFO)
questions.explanation: Prim's algorithm uses a Min-Heap (priority queue) to efficiently extract the vertex with the minimum key value (minimum edge weight to the growing MST). This gives O((V + E) log V) time complexity.

questions.statement: An undirected graph is represented as an adjacency list. BFS starting from vertex 0 in graph with edges (0,1),(0,2),(1,3),(2,3) visits vertices in which order?
questions.explanation: BFS from 0: queue={0}. Dequeue 0, enqueue neighbors 1,2: visit order=[0], queue={1,2}. Dequeue 1, enqueue unvisited neighbor 3: visit order=[0,1], queue={2,3}. Dequeue 2, neighbor 3 already queued: visit order=[0,1,2], queue={3}. Dequeue 3: order=[0,1,2,3].

questions.statement: In Radix Sort, sorting d-digit numbers with base b using Counting Sort as a subroutine has time complexity:
questions.option_a: O(d × n)
questions.option_b: O(d × (n + b))
questions.option_c: O(n log n)
questions.option_d: O(n × b)
questions.explanation: Radix Sort makes d passes (one per digit position), each using Counting Sort in O(n + b) where b is the base (number of possible digit values). Total: O(d(n + b)). For decimal digits (b=10) and constant d, this is O(n).

questions.statement: A stack is used to evaluate the postfix expression '3 4 + 5 *'. The final result is:
questions.explanation: Evaluation: Push 3 → [3]. Push 4 → [3,4]. '+': pop 4 and 3, push 7 → [7]. Push 5 → [7,5]. '*': pop 5 and 7, push 35 → [35]. Result = 35.

questions.statement: Which graph algorithm detects negative weight cycles?
questions.option_a: Dijkstra's algorithm
questions.option_b: Prim's algorithm
questions.option_c: Bellman-Ford algorithm
questions.option_d: Kruskal's algorithm
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford detects negative weight cycles by performing a (V)th relaxation after V-1 iterations. If any edge can still be relaxed in the Vth pass, a negative cycle exists. Dijkstra fails with negative weights; Prim and Kruskal are MST algorithms.

questions.statement: What is the space complexity of the Depth-First Search algorithm for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.option_a: O(V + E)
questions.option_b: O(V²)
questions.option_c: O(V)
questions.option_d: O(E)
questions.explanation: DFS uses O(V) space for the visited array and the recursion stack (or explicit stack), which can hold at most V vertices in the worst case (a path graph). The adjacency list itself is not counted as part of the algorithm's auxiliary space.

questions.statement: In a BST, the in-order successor of a node X is:
questions.option_a: The parent of X
questions.option_b: The rightmost node in X's left subtree
questions.option_c: The leftmost node in X's right subtree
questions.option_d: The sibling of X
questions.explanation: The in-order successor (the next larger element) of a node X is the leftmost (minimum) node in X's right subtree. If X has no right subtree, the successor is the lowest ancestor for which X is in the left subtree.

questions.statement: Which of the following correctly describes the 'two-pointer' technique for finding a pair that sums to a target in a sorted array?
questions.option_a: Use two pointers both starting from the same end
questions.option_b: Use one pointer at each end; move left pointer right if sum is too small, right pointer left if too large
questions.option_c: Use two nested loops with one pointer each
questions.option_d: Use two random pointers that jump based on the hash value
questions.explanation: The two-pointer technique for sorted arrays places one pointer at the start (left) and one at the end (right). If sum < target, move left pointer right; if sum > target, move right pointer left; if equal, found the pair. This runs in O(n).

questions.statement: The Aho-Corasick algorithm is used for:
questions.option_a: Single pattern matching in a string
questions.option_b: Sorting strings lexicographically
questions.option_c: Multi-pattern string matching simultaneously in O(n + m + k) time
questions.option_d: Compressing strings using prefix coding
questions.explanation: Aho-Corasick builds a finite automaton from multiple patterns (using a Trie with failure links) to search for all patterns in a text simultaneously in O(n + m + k) where n is text length, m is total pattern length, and k is number of matches.

questions.statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in a hash table using separate chaining when n elements are stored in m buckets?
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n/m)
questions.explanation: In the worst case (all n elements hash to the same bucket), searching requires traversing a linked list of n elements: O(n). With a good hash function and load factor ≤ 1, the average case is O(1).

questions.statement: A deque (double-ended queue) supports insertions and deletions at both ends. Which data structure is NOT efficiently implementable using a deque?
questions.option_a: Stack
questions.option_b: Queue
questions.option_c: Priority Queue
questions.option_d: Sliding window maximum
questions.explanation: A Priority Queue requires accessing the maximum or minimum element regardless of insertion order, requiring a heap structure (O(log n) operations). A deque cannot efficiently provide priority-based access—it only optimizes end-based operations. Stacks, queues, and sliding window problems all use deque efficiently.

questions.statement: In the context of algorithm analysis, 'Ω (Omega) notation' represents:
questions.option_a: An exact bound on the running time
questions.option_b: An upper bound on the running time
questions.option_c: A lower bound on the running time
questions.option_d: A bound that applies only to average-case analysis
questions.explanation: Ω (big-Omega) notation describes a lower bound on an algorithm's running time—the minimum time the algorithm will take. O (big-O) is the upper bound. Θ (big-Theta) is an exact (tight) bound when upper and lower bounds are equal.

questions.statement: The Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem solved naively using DP has time complexity O(n²). Using patience sorting with binary search, it can be solved in:
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n log n)
questions.option_c: O(n²)
questions.option_d: O(n log² n)
questions.explanation: The LIS can be solved in O(n log n) using a strategy similar to patience sorting: maintain a list of 'piles', and for each element, use binary search (O(log n) per element) to find the correct pile. Total: O(n log n).

questions.statement: In an undirected graph, a 'bridge' is:
questions.option_a: An edge that forms a cycle
questions.option_b: An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components
questions.option_c: The shortest path between two vertices
questions.option_d: A vertex with the highest degree
questions.explanation: A bridge (cut edge) is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph (increases the number of connected components). Tarjan's algorithm finds all bridges in O(V + E) using DFS and low-link values.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of the heapSort algorithm?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n log n) always
questions.option_c: O(n²) worst case
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Heap Sort always runs in O(n log n) time: building the heap is O(n), and extracting n elements (each with O(log n) heapify) takes O(n log n). Unlike Quick Sort, it has no O(n²) worst case. It is not O(n) like Counting Sort.

questions.statement: A developer needs an efficient structure for implementing an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache. The optimal data structure combination is:
questions.option_a: Array + Binary Search Tree
questions.option_b: Hash Map + Doubly Linked List
questions.option_c: Stack + Queue
questions.option_d: Min-Heap + Hash Map
questions.explanation: An LRU cache uses a Hash Map for O(1) key lookup and a Doubly Linked List for O(1) movement of the most recently used element to the front and O(1) eviction of the least recently used (tail). This combination achieves O(1) get and put operations.

questions.statement: In Dijkstra's algorithm, after a vertex is 'finalized' (extracted from the priority queue), its distance:
questions.option_a: Can still be updated by longer paths
questions.option_b: Cannot be improved further (optimal distance is found)
questions.option_c: May require a second pass to verify
questions.option_d: Is temporarily stored and verified later
questions.explanation: Once a vertex is extracted from the min-priority queue in Dijkstra's algorithm (with non-negative weights), its distance is guaranteed to be the shortest possible. No future path can be shorter because all future edges are non-negative.

questions.statement: Which of the following describes an 'in-place' sorting algorithm?
questions.option_a: An algorithm that uses a separate array for sorting
questions.option_b: An algorithm that sorts with O(1) or O(log n) additional space (not counting the input)
questions.option_c: An algorithm that sorts without any comparisons
questions.option_d: An algorithm that is stable and runs in O(n log n)
questions.explanation: An in-place sorting algorithm uses at most O(log n) auxiliary space (often O(1)), sorting by rearranging elements within the original array. Heap Sort and Insertion Sort are in-place. Merge Sort typically requires O(n) auxiliary space and is not in-place.

questions.statement: A binary search on a sorted array of 1024 elements finds the target in at most how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. For n=1024=2¹⁰, the maximum comparisons = ⌈log₂(1024)⌉ = 10. After 10 halvings, the search space is reduced to 1 element.

questions.statement: What is a 'stable' sorting algorithm?
questions.option_a: An algorithm that always runs in O(n log n)
questions.option_b: An algorithm that maintains the relative order of equal elements from the original input
questions.option_c: An algorithm that does not use extra memory
questions.option_d: An algorithm that produces the same output regardless of input order
questions.explanation: A stable sort preserves the relative order of elements with equal keys. For example, sorting (A,2),(B,2),(C,1) by value stably yields (C,1),(A,2),(B,2). Merge Sort and Insertion Sort are stable. Heap Sort and Quick Sort (basic) are not.

questions.statement: In a weighted DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph), which algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source more efficiently than Dijkstra?
questions.option_a: Bellman-Ford
questions.option_b: Floyd-Warshall
questions.option_c: Topological sort-based relaxation
questions.option_d: A* search
questions.explanation: For weighted DAGs, topological sort + relaxation finds single-source shortest paths in O(V + E), faster than Dijkstra's O((V + E) log V). DAGs have no cycles, so topological order allows processing each vertex exactly once.

questions.statement: The Huffman coding algorithm, used for lossless data compression, is based on which algorithmic technique?
questions.option_a: Dynamic programming
questions.option_b: Divide and conquer
questions.option_c: Greedy algorithm
questions.option_d: Backtracking
questions.explanation: Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm: at each step, it merges the two nodes with the lowest frequencies. The greedy choice—always combining the smallest two—leads to the globally optimal prefix-free code. A Min-Heap supports this efficiently.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of the 'find' operation in a Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) data structure with path compression and union by rank?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(α(n)) amortized (nearly O(1))
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: With both path compression and union by rank, the amortized cost per operation is O(α(n)) where α is the inverse Ackermann function—an extremely slow-growing function that is effectively constant (≤ 4) for all practical values of n.

questions.statement: A developer wants to implement an algorithm that finds the longest path in a directed graph. For which type of graph is this solvable in polynomial time?
questions.option_a: Arbitrary directed graphs with non-negative weights
questions.option_b: Directed graphs with only positive weights
questions.option_c: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
questions.option_d: Complete directed graphs only
questions.explanation: Longest path in general directed graphs is NP-hard (reduces to Hamiltonian Path). In a DAG, it is solvable in O(V + E) using topological sort and DP relaxation. The absence of cycles is what makes it tractable.

questions.statement: Which property defines a 'perfect' binary tree?
questions.option_a: All leaves are at the same depth and every internal node has exactly 2 children
questions.option_b: All leaves are filled from left to right
questions.option_c: Every node has exactly 1 or 2 children
questions.option_d: The tree is balanced to within 1 level
questions.explanation: A perfect binary tree has all internal nodes with exactly 2 children and all leaves at the same depth. A perfect binary tree with height h has 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. This is a special case of both complete and full binary trees.

questions.statement: In a Skip List, the expected time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion is:
questions.option_a: O(n) expected
questions.option_b: O(1) expected
questions.option_c: O(log n) expected
questions.option_d: O(n log n) expected
questions.explanation: A Skip List uses multiple layers of linked lists with probabilistic balancing. The expected time for search, insertion, and deletion is O(log n), matching balanced BSTs. The space complexity is O(n) expected.

questions.statement: An algorithm's best-case time is Ω(n log n). This means:
questions.option_a: The algorithm always runs in exactly n log n time
questions.option_b: The algorithm runs in at most n log n time on some input
questions.option_c: The algorithm always requires at least n log n operations, even on the best input
questions.option_d: The algorithm is as fast as possible
questions.explanation: Ω(n log n) as a best-case lower bound means the algorithm requires at least n log n operations even on the most favorable input. For comparison-based sorting, the lower bound of Ω(n log n) applies to any comparison-based sort.

questions.statement: The problem of finding the maximum subarray sum in an array is solved by Kadane's algorithm in:
questions.option_a: O(n²) time
questions.option_b: O(n log n) time
questions.option_c: O(n) time
questions.option_d: O(log n) time
questions.explanation: Kadane's algorithm scans the array once, maintaining the current subarray sum and global maximum. It processes each element exactly once, giving O(n) time and O(1) space. The naive approach is O(n²).

questions.statement: A min-heap supports decrease-key in O(log n). Why is this important for Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.option_a: It allows checking if a vertex is visited in O(1)
questions.option_b: It allows efficiently updating the priority of a vertex when a shorter path is found
questions.option_c: It ensures the graph has no negative edges
questions.option_d: It sorts all vertices before processing
questions.explanation: When a shorter path to a vertex is discovered, Dijkstra needs to update its priority in the min-heap. The decrease-key operation does this in O(log n) by sifting up the decreased element. Without this, priority updates would require removing and reinserting.

questions.statement: In a B+ Tree (used in database indexing), data records are stored:
questions.option_a: At every internal and leaf node
questions.option_b: Only at the root
questions.option_c: Only at the leaf nodes
questions.option_d: At internal nodes with keys duplicated at leaves
questions.explanation: In B+ Trees, all data records are stored at the leaf nodes, which are linked for sequential access. Internal nodes store only keys for navigation. This design makes range queries efficient and keeps internal nodes compact for better fanout.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of the naive pattern matching algorithm for a text of length n and pattern of length m?
questions.option_a: O(n + m)
questions.option_b: O(n × m)
questions.option_c: O(n log m)
questions.option_d: O(m log n)
questions.explanation: The naive algorithm tries each of the (n - m + 1) possible starting positions in the text and compares up to m characters for each, giving O((n-m+1)×m) ≈ O(n×m) in the worst case. KMP improves this to O(n+m).

questions.statement: Which problem is an example of an NP-complete problem that cannot be solved in polynomial time (unless P=NP)?
questions.option_a: Finding shortest path using Dijkstra
questions.option_b: Sorting an array of integers
questions.option_c: Satisfying a Boolean formula (SAT problem)
questions.option_d: Binary search in a sorted array
questions.explanation: Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) was the first problem proven NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem). No polynomial time algorithm is known. Sorting and shortest path are polynomial; binary search is O(log n).

questions.statement: In an undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is:
questions.option_a: The total number of vertices in the graph
questions.option_b: The total number of edges in the graph
questions.option_c: The number of edges incident to that vertex
questions.option_d: The weight of the heaviest edge incident to that vertex
questions.explanation: The degree of a vertex is the number of edges connected to it. For directed graphs, in-degree and out-degree are tracked separately. The Handshaking Lemma states: sum of all degrees = 2 × number of edges.

questions.statement: What makes the 0/1 Knapsack problem different from the Fractional Knapsack problem in terms of solvability?
questions.option_a: 0/1 Knapsack allows items to be split; Fractional does not
questions.option_b: Fractional Knapsack is NP-hard; 0/1 Knapsack is solvable greedily
questions.option_c: 0/1 Knapsack is NP-hard (only solvable by DP in pseudo-polynomial time); Fractional Knapsack is solvable greedily in O(n log n)
questions.option_d: 0/1 Knapsack and Fractional Knapsack have identical time complexities
questions.explanation: Fractional Knapsack allows items to be split, so the greedy strategy (take items by value/weight ratio) is optimal and runs in O(n log n). 0/1 Knapsack requires taking whole items; greedy fails, and DP is needed in O(nW) pseudo-polynomial time.

questions.statement: The Bellman-Ford algorithm performs exactly V-1 relaxations of all edges. Why V-1?
questions.option_a: Because there are V-1 distinct paths in the graph
questions.option_b: Because any shortest path in a graph with V vertices has at most V-1 edges (assuming no negative cycles)
questions.option_c: Because the algorithm requires exactly V-1 iterations to sort edges
questions.option_d: Because V-1 is the maximum degree of any vertex
questions.explanation: In a graph with V vertices, any simple path (no repeated vertices) has at most V-1 edges. Relaxing all edges V-1 times guarantees that all shortest paths are computed, since they traverse at most V-1 edges.

questions.statement: A Segment Tree supports which pair of operations in O(log n) time?
questions.option_a: Insertion and deletion
questions.option_b: Range queries and point updates
questions.option_c: Sorting and searching
questions.option_d: Hashing and collision resolution
questions.explanation: Segment Trees are specialized for range queries (sum, min, max over a range) and point updates, both in O(log n). They do not support arbitrary insertion/deletion; the structure is built over a fixed-size array.

questions.statement: In Prim's algorithm starting from vertex 0, with edges (0-1,w=4), (0-2,w=3), (1-3,w=2), (2-3,w=5), which edge is added second to the MST?
questions.explanation: Prim's: Start at 0. Add cheapest adjacent edge: (0-2, w=3) → MST includes 0,2. Next cheapest edge from MST: (0-1,4), (2-3,5), (1-3,2). Cheapest is (1-3, w=2)? But 1 is not in MST yet. Cheapest adjacent to {0,2} is (0-1,4) or (2-3,5). The second edge is (0-1,4)... Let me recheck: edges from {0,2}: (0-1,4) and (2-3,5). Minimum is (0-1,4). Option a is correct actually. Wait: edges incident to vertices in MST {0,2}: to vertex 1 with weight 4 (from 0), to vertex 3 with weight 5 (from 2). Minimum is (0-1, w=4). Second added edge is (0-1, w=4).

questions.statement: In Prim's MST algorithm starting from vertex 0 with edges: (0-1,w=4),(0-2,w=3),(1-3,w=2),(2-3,w=5), what is the total weight of the resulting MST?
questions.explanation: Prim's from vertex 0: Add (0-2, w=3) [cheapest from 0]. MST weight=3. From {0,2}: add (0-1, w=4) [cheapest: 4 vs 5]. MST weight=7. From {0,1,2}: add (1-3, w=2). MST weight=9. All 4 vertices covered. Total MST weight = 3+4+2 = 9.

questions.statement: Which data structure would be most efficient for implementing an autocomplete feature that searches for all words with a given prefix?
questions.option_a: Hash Map
questions.option_b: Binary Search Tree
questions.option_c: Trie
questions.option_d: Min-Heap
questions.explanation: A Trie stores strings character by character, allowing prefix-based search in O(L) where L is the prefix length. Following the prefix path in the Trie leads directly to all words sharing that prefix. Hash Maps require exact key lookup; BSTs don't support prefix queries efficiently.

questions.statement: The time complexity of building a Trie from n strings with average length L is:
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(nL)
questions.option_c: O(n²L)
questions.option_d: O(L log n)
questions.explanation: Inserting one string of length L into a Trie takes O(L) time (one character per level). For n strings of average length L, total build time is O(nL). The space is also O(nL) in the worst case.

questions.statement: In graph theory, a 'strongly connected component' (SCC) in a directed graph is:
questions.option_a: A subgraph where every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree
questions.option_b: A maximal set of vertices such that there is a path from each vertex to every other vertex
questions.option_c: A set of vertices with no outgoing edges
questions.option_d: A subgraph with no cycles
questions.explanation: An SCC is a maximal set of vertices where every pair (u, v) is mutually reachable—there exists a directed path from u to v and from v to u. Tarjan's and Kosaraju's algorithms find all SCCs in O(V + E).

questions.statement: The Big-O notation O(1) for a hash table lookup assumes:
questions.option_a: The hash function perfectly distributes all elements
questions.option_b: The number of elements is small
questions.option_c: No collisions occur (or collisions are O(1) to resolve)
questions.option_d: The table is sorted before lookup
questions.explanation: Hash table O(1) average lookup assumes a good hash function with O(1) collision resolution. With separate chaining, O(1) per lookup requires the average chain length (load factor) to be bounded by a constant. Without this assumption, worst case is O(n).

questions.statement: In a BST, a completely unbalanced tree (all nodes in a single chain) has search, insert, and delete complexity of:
questions.option_a: O(log n)
questions.option_b: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: A completely unbalanced BST degenerates to a linked list (chain). Search, insert, and delete require traversing up to n nodes, giving O(n) complexity. Self-balancing BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) maintain O(log n).

questions.statement: Which algorithm can determine if a graph is bipartite using a single traversal?
questions.option_a: Dijkstra's algorithm
questions.option_b: DFS or BFS with 2-coloring
questions.option_c: Floyd-Warshall algorithm
questions.option_d: Bellman-Ford algorithm
questions.explanation: A graph is bipartite if it can be 2-colored (no two adjacent vertices share a color). BFS or DFS attempts to 2-color the graph: assign color, then assign the opposite color to all neighbors. If a conflict arises, the graph is not bipartite. This runs in O(V + E).

questions.statement: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (where height is the number of edges on the longest path from root to leaf)?
questions.option_a: 2h
questions.explanation: A binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes (a perfect binary tree). At each level i, there are at most 2^i nodes. Sum from i=0 to h: 2^0 + 2^1 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h+1) - 1.

questions.statement: In which scenario is Counting Sort MOST appropriate?
questions.option_a: Sorting 1 million floating-point numbers in random order
questions.option_b: Sorting an array of student ages (0–120) where the range is small
questions.option_c: Sorting variable-length strings alphabetically
questions.option_d: Sorting a linked list of large integer keys
questions.explanation: Counting Sort is efficient when the key range k is small relative to n. Sorting ages (range 0-120, k=121) with many students (large n) is ideal. It runs in O(n + k). For floating-point or large ranges, comparison-based sorts are better.

questions.statement: What does the term 'degeneracy' mean in the context of quicksort performance?
questions.option_a: Quicksort fails on certain inputs
questions.option_b: Quicksort achieves O(n) best-case performance
questions.option_c: Quicksort degenerates to O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
questions.option_d: Quicksort requires additional memory on certain inputs
questions.explanation: Quicksort degenerates to O(n²) when the pivot selection consistently produces maximally unbalanced partitions (e.g., always choosing the minimum or maximum as pivot on sorted input). Randomized pivot selection or median-of-three mitigates this.

questions.statement: A tree with n nodes has exactly how many edges?
questions.option_a: n
questions.option_d: 2n
questions.explanation: A tree with n nodes has exactly n-1 edges. This is a fundamental property of trees (connected, acyclic graphs). Adding one more edge would create a cycle; removing one would disconnect the tree.

questions.statement: The 'topological order' of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) can be found using which algorithm?
questions.option_a: Prim's algorithm
questions.option_b: Kruskal's algorithm
questions.option_c: Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based) or DFS with finish-time ordering
questions.option_d: Bellman-Ford algorithm
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based, using in-degree tracking) or DFS (ordering vertices by decreasing finish time) both produce a topological order of a DAG in O(V + E). Prim and Kruskal are MST algorithms; Bellman-Ford is for shortest paths.

questions.statement: In competitive programming, a Sparse Table achieves O(1) query time for which type of range query?
questions.option_a: Range sum queries with point updates
questions.option_b: Range minimum/maximum queries on static arrays
questions.option_c: Range prefix sum queries with updates
questions.option_d: Range median queries
questions.explanation: A Sparse Table supports O(1) range minimum (RMQ) and range maximum queries on static arrays by precomputing answers for power-of-2 length ranges. It uses O(n log n) preprocessing and space. It cannot efficiently handle updates.

questions.statement: Which property of a heap makes it ideal for implementing a Priority Queue?
questions.option_a: All elements are stored in sorted order
questions.option_b: The minimum (or maximum) element is always at the root, accessible in O(1)
questions.option_c: Elements are stored in a linked list for easy insertion
questions.option_d: All operations run in O(1) time
questions.explanation: A heap guarantees that the minimum (min-heap) or maximum (max-heap) element is always at the root, accessible in O(1). Insertion and extraction of the root are O(log n). This makes heaps ideal for priority queues where frequent access to the extreme element is needed.

questions.statement: In the context of amortized analysis, the 'potential method' is used to:
questions.option_a: Measure the worst-case time of a single operation
questions.option_b: Define a potential function that accounts for 'stored work' to compute amortized cost per operation
questions.option_c: Calculate the exact number of operations in an algorithm
questions.option_d: Estimate the space complexity of a data structure
questions.explanation: The potential method assigns a potential Φ to the data structure state, such that the amortized cost of an operation equals its actual cost plus the change in potential. This distributes the cost of expensive operations over preceding cheap ones.

questions.statement: An order statistics tree supports finding the k-th smallest element. What data is stored at each node in addition to the key?
questions.option_a: The node's depth
questions.option_b: The size of the subtree rooted at that node
questions.option_c: The balance factor of the subtree
questions.option_d: The parent pointer
questions.explanation: An order statistics tree stores the subtree size at each node. To find the k-th smallest: if k = left_size + 1, the current node is the answer. If k ≤ left_size, recurse left. Otherwise, recurse right with k adjusted. This achieves O(log n).

questions.statement: The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) optimal solution can be found using dynamic programming (Held-Karp algorithm) in:
questions.option_a: O(n!)
questions.option_b: O(n² × 2ⁿ)
questions.option_c: O(n log n)
questions.option_d: O(n³)
questions.explanation: The Held-Karp algorithm uses bitmask DP over subsets of visited cities: dp[S][v] = shortest path visiting all cities in subset S ending at v. There are 2ⁿ subsets and n cities, giving O(n² × 2ⁿ) time and O(n × 2ⁿ) space. This improves the O(n!) brute force.

questions.statement: Which condition causes a priority queue implemented as a min-heap to require O(n) time for a 'decrease-key' operation instead of O(log n)?
questions.option_a: When using an array-based heap without a position index
questions.option_b: When the new key is smaller than all existing keys
questions.option_c: When the priority queue contains duplicate keys
questions.option_d: When the heap has only one element
questions.explanation: Without a position index (e.g., a hash map mapping keys to their positions in the heap array), finding the element to decrease-key requires O(n) linear search. With a position index, the element's location is O(1), and sifting up is O(log n).

questions.statement: In which case does linear probing in a hash table cause 'primary clustering'?
questions.option_a: When multiple elements hash to different indices
questions.option_b: When consecutive occupied slots form long chains, degrading search performance
questions.option_c: When the load factor is below 0.5
questions.option_d: When the hash function is perfectly uniform
questions.explanation: Primary clustering in linear probing occurs when a sequence of consecutive occupied slots forms, causing new insertions to probe through increasingly long runs. This degrades average search performance from O(1) to O(n) in extreme cases.

questions.statement: A developer is designing a system to find the closest pair of points from n points in 2D space. The divide-and-conquer approach achieves:
questions.option_a: O(n²) time
questions.option_b: O(n log n) time
questions.option_c: O(n) time
questions.option_d: O(n log² n) time
questions.explanation: The closest pair of points problem is solved in O(n log n) using divide and conquer: split points by x-coordinate, recursively solve each half, then check the strip of width 2δ (where δ is the current minimum distance). Each strip check is O(n).

questions.statement: What is 'lazy deletion' in a hash table or tree?
questions.option_a: Deleting elements only when the table is resized
questions.option_b: Marking elements as deleted without immediately removing them, deferring actual removal
questions.option_c: Deleting the element with the lowest priority first
questions.option_d: Deleting all elements in bulk to improve cache performance
questions.explanation: Lazy deletion marks an element as deleted (using a tombstone) without immediately removing it. This avoids complex restructuring at deletion time. The actual cleanup happens during future insertions or when the structure is rebuilt. It is used in hash tables with open addressing.

questions.statement: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) defines:
questions.option_a: The physical storage layout of data in memory
questions.option_b: The data stored and the operations on it, without specifying implementation
questions.option_c: The programming language used to implement a data structure
questions.option_d: The maximum size a data structure can hold
questions.explanation: ADT defines WHAT data is stored and WHAT operations are available — NOT how they are implemented. This separation of specification from implementation is the essence of abstraction.

questions.statement: Which of the following is NOT a property an algorithm must have?
questions.option_a: Finiteness
questions.option_b: Optimality
questions.option_c: Definiteness
questions.option_d: Effectiveness
questions.explanation: The five required properties are: Finiteness, Definiteness, Input, Output, Effectiveness. Optimality is desirable but not required — a correct slow algorithm is still an algorithm.

questions.statement: The formula "Program = Algorithm + Data Structure + Programming Language" implies:
questions.option_a: You need all three in equal measure
questions.option_b: Algorithms and data structures are independent of the language
questions.option_c: A good algorithm with a bad data structure always produces a slow program
questions.option_d: Programming language is the most important factor
questions.explanation: Choosing the wrong data structure can make even the best algorithm slow. O(1) vs O(n) access has nothing to do with the language.

questions.statement: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a Stack ADT and its implementation?
questions.option_a: A stack must be implemented using an array
questions.option_b: A stack can be implemented using either an array or a linked list — both satisfy the ADT contract
questions.option_c: A stack implemented with a linked list is always faster
questions.option_d: The ADT defines both the interface AND the implementation
questions.explanation: The ADT just requires push/pop/peek/isEmpty. Whether internally it uses an array or linked list is an implementation detail — both satisfy the contract.

questions.statement: Why is choosing the right data structure crucial?
questions.option_a: It determines the syntax of your code
questions.option_b: It determines the programming language you can use
questions.option_c: It can change search time from O(n) to O(1) — potentially millions of times faster
questions.option_d: It determines how much RAM the computer has
questions.explanation: Data structure choice directly determines algorithmic complexity. Linear search O(n) vs hash table O(1) on 1 billion records = 1 billion operations vs 1 operation.

questions.statement: Which data structure is used to model hierarchical relationships like an organization chart?
questions.option_a: Graph
questions.option_b: Queue
questions.option_c: Tree
questions.option_d: Hash Table
questions.explanation: Trees model hierarchical parent-child relationships. Organization charts, file systems, XML/HTML DOM are all trees.

questions.statement: What is the main advantage of an Abstract Data Type?
questions.option_a: It always makes code run faster
questions.option_b: It separates the interface from the implementation, allowing change without affecting users
questions.option_c: It reduces the amount of code you need to write
questions.option_d: It prevents bugs from occurring
questions.explanation: ADTs provide an interface contract. Implementation can be swapped (array → linked list) without changing any code that uses the ADT through its interface.

questions.statement: In Java, which interface represents the Queue ADT?
questions.option_a: java.util.Stack
questions.option_b: java.util.List
questions.option_c: java.util.Queue
questions.option_d: java.util.Deque
questions.explanation: java.util.Queue is the Queue interface with offer(), poll(), peek(). Deque is also valid (extends Queue), but Queue is the primary interface.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of accessing the element at index 5 in an array of 1000 elements?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Array access is O(1) because the address is computed directly: base_address + (index × element_size). No searching required.

questions.statement: In a singly linked list, what is the time complexity of inserting at the HEAD?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Insert at head: create new node, set new.next = head, head = new. These are fixed operations regardless of list size. Compare: insert at TAIL without tail pointer is O(n) (must traverse).

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of deleting a specific node from a singly linked list when you only have a pointer to the node itself (not its predecessor)?
questions.option_b: O(n) — need to find the predecessor
questions.option_c: O(log n)
questions.option_d: Impossible — requires the predecessor
questions.explanation: In a singly linked list, deletion requires updating the predecessor's next pointer. To find the predecessor, you must traverse from the head: O(n). In a doubly linked list, it would be O(1).

questions.statement: Which linked list type allows O(1) deletion from BOTH ends?
questions.option_a: Singly linked list with head pointer
questions.option_b: Singly linked list with head and tail pointers
questions.option_c: Doubly linked list with head and tail pointers
questions.option_d: Circular singly linked list
questions.explanation: Deletion from head: O(1) in any linked list. Deletion from tail in a singly linked list requires finding the second-to-last node: O(n). In a doubly linked list, tail.prev gives the new tail directly: O(1).

questions.option_d: Error — arr.length is not valid
questions.explanation: arr.length = 5. Loop starts at index 4 (value 5), goes down to 0 (value 1): 5 4 3 2 1.

questions.statement: A node in a doubly linked list contains:
questions.option_a: Data and one pointer (to next)
questions.option_b: Data and two pointers (to next and previous)
questions.option_c: Data and an index
questions.option_d: Only pointers (no data)
questions.explanation: Doubly linked list nodes have: data field + next pointer + prev pointer.

questions.statement: What happens when you access arr[arr.length] in Java?
questions.option_a: Returns 0 (default value)
questions.option_b: Returns null
questions.option_c: Throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
questions.option_d: Returns the last element
questions.explanation: Valid indices are 0 to arr.length-1. arr[arr.length] is one beyond the last — throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime.

questions.statement: Which statement about arrays and linked lists is TRUE?
questions.option_a: Arrays are always better than linked lists
questions.option_b: Linked lists support O(1) random access; arrays require O(n)
questions.option_c: Arrays support O(1) random access; linked lists require O(n)
questions.option_d: Both support O(1) for all operations
questions.explanation: Arrays: O(1) random access (index). Linked lists: O(n) (must traverse from head). Linked lists are better for frequent insertions/deletions at known positions.

questions.statement: What is a circular linked list?
questions.option_a: A linked list stored in a circular array
questions.option_b: A linked list where the last node points back to the head
questions.option_c: A doubly linked list where head and tail are connected
questions.option_d: Both B and C can be circular
questions.explanation: Any linked list (singly or doubly) where the last node connects back to the first is circular. Round-robin scheduling uses circular singly linked lists.

questions.statement: In Java's ArrayList, what happens when the internal array is full and you call add()?
questions.option_a: Throws an exception
questions.option_b: Creates a new array (typically 1.5× larger) and copies all elements
questions.option_c: Stops accepting new elements
questions.option_d: Deletes the oldest element to make space
