questions.explanation: Java's ArrayList uses a dynamic array. When full, it creates a new array (1.5× capacity in Java 11+), copies all existing elements, then adds the new element. This is O(n) but happens rarely — O(1) amortized.

questions.statement: What is the MAIN disadvantage of a singly linked list compared to an array?
questions.option_a: Cannot store primitive types
questions.option_b: Cannot change size dynamically
questions.option_c: No O(1) random access by index
questions.option_d: Cannot be sorted
questions.explanation: To access element at index i in a linked list, you must traverse from head: O(n). Arrays give O(1) direct access by index. Linked lists CAN change size dynamically and CAN be sorted.

questions.statement: Which line of Java code correctly removes the FIRST element from a LinkedList used as a Queue?
questions.option_a: list.remove(0)
questions.option_b: list.poll()
questions.option_c: list.pop()
questions.option_d: list.dequeue()
questions.explanation: poll() removes and returns the head (front) of the queue, returns null if empty. remove() also works but throws exception if empty. pop() is stack operation. dequeue() doesn't exist in Java.

questions.statement: What is the space complexity of a singly linked list with n elements?
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: n nodes × (data + pointer per node) = O(n) total space. The constant factor is higher than an array due to pointer overhead.

questions.statement: In Java, what does LinkedList.peekFirst() do?
questions.option_a: Remove and return the first element
questions.option_b: Return the first element without removing it
questions.option_c: Add an element at the beginning
questions.option_d: Check if the list is empty
questions.explanation: peekFirst() (and peek()) returns the head element WITHOUT removing it. Returns null if list is empty. pollFirst() removes and returns.

questions.statement: What does LIFO stand for and which data structure follows it?
questions.option_a: Last In, First Out — Stack
questions.option_b: Last In, First Out — Queue
questions.option_c: Linear Index File Organization — Stack
questions.option_d: Last Inserted, First Output — Queue
questions.explanation: LIFO = Last In, First Out = Stack. The last element pushed is the first to be popped.
push 1,2,3. Stack: [1,2,3] top=3. pop() removes and returns 3. Stack: [1,2] top=2. peek() returns 2 without removing. size() returns 2.

questions.statement: Which real-world scenario is BEST modeled by a stack?
questions.option_a: Ticket queue at a cinema
questions.option_b: Web browser back button history
questions.option_c: Hospital patient waiting list
questions.option_d: Print job order
questions.explanation: Browser back button is LIFO — the most recently visited page is the first to go back to. Cinema queue = queue (FIFO). Hospital = priority queue. Print jobs = queue (FIFO).

questions.statement: What is "stack overflow" in the context of function calls?
questions.option_a: A variable storing a value too large for its type
questions.option_b: Too many recursive calls exhausting the call stack memory
questions.option_c: A stack that has more elements than an array
questions.option_d: An exception when trying to pop an empty stack
questions.explanation: Each function call creates a stack frame. Infinite recursion (missing base case) keeps pushing frames until the call stack runs out of memory → StackOverflowError in Java.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of enqueue and dequeue in a properly implemented circular queue?
questions.option_a: O(n) and O(n)
questions.option_b: O(1) and O(n)
questions.option_c: O(1) and O(1)
questions.option_d: O(log n) and O(log n)
questions.explanation: Both enqueue (add to rear) and dequeue (remove from front) are O(1) in a circular queue with front and rear pointers. The modulo operation for wrap-around is constant time.

questions.statement: PriorityQueue<Integer> in Java with default ordering will:
questions.option_a: Maintain FIFO order
questions.option_b: Sort elements in descending order (max at head)
questions.option_c: Sort elements in ascending order (min at head) — min-heap
questions.option_d: Maintain insertion order
questions.explanation: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default. poll() returns the SMALLEST element. Use Collections.reverseOrder() for max-heap.

questions.statement: In which application does a Queue (FIFO) make MORE sense than a Stack (LIFO)?
questions.option_a: Expression evaluation
questions.option_b: Undo/redo operations
questions.option_c: CPU process scheduling (Round Robin)
questions.option_d: Browser back navigation
questions.explanation: Round Robin scheduling gives each process a turn in order — FIFO. Undo/redo uses stack. Expression evaluation uses stack. Browser back uses stack.
offer A,B,C: [A,B,C]. poll() removes A: [B,C]. offer D: [B,C,D]. peek() returns B (front). size() = 3.

questions.statement: A Deque (double-ended queue) can be used as:
questions.option_a: Only a stack
questions.option_b: Only a queue
questions.option_c: Both a stack and a queue
questions.option_d: Neither a stack nor a queue
questions.explanation: Deque supports operations at both ends: addFirst/removeFirst (stack behavior), addLast/removeFirst (queue behavior). Java's ArrayDeque is recommended over Stack for stack use.

questions.statement: What exception does stack.pop() throw when the stack is empty in Java?
questions.option_a: NullPointerException
questions.option_b: EmptyStackException
questions.option_c: StackUnderflowException
questions.option_d: IndexOutOfBoundsException
questions.explanation: java.util.Stack.pop() throws EmptyStackException when the stack is empty. For ArrayDeque.pop(), it throws NoSuchElementException.

questions.statement: In a binary tree, the height of a leaf node is:
questions.option_d: Depends on its position
questions.explanation: Height of a node = length of longest path from that node to a leaf. A leaf HAS no children, so the path length is 0. Height of leaf = 0.

questions.statement: What is the key property of a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
questions.option_a: All nodes have exactly 2 children
questions.option_b: Left child < Parent < Right child (for every node)
questions.option_c: The tree is always balanced
questions.option_d: All leaves are at the same level
questions.explanation: BST property: for every node, all values in left subtree < node value < all values in right subtree. This makes search O(log n) in balanced trees.

questions.statement:
What is the output of INORDER traversal of this BST?

        50
       /  \
     30    70
    /  \
  20   40
questions.explanation: Inorder = Left, Node, Right. For BST, inorder ALWAYS gives sorted order: 20, 30, 40, 50, 70.

questions.statement: What is the result of PREORDER traversal of the tree in Q35?
questions.explanation: Preorder = Node, Left, Right. Visit 50 (root), then left subtree (30, 20, 40), then right (70): 50, 30, 20, 40, 70.

questions.statement: When is the worst-case performance O(n) observed in a BST?
questions.option_a: When searching for an element in the middle
questions.option_b: When elements are inserted in sorted or reverse-sorted order
questions.option_c: When the tree has more than 1000 nodes
questions.option_d: When the tree contains duplicate values
questions.explanation: Inserting sorted values (1,2,3,4,5) creates a degenerate tree (right-skewed linked list). Searching requires O(n) traversal. This is why self-balancing trees exist.

questions.statement: In a Max-Heap with n elements, what is the time complexity of finding the MAXIMUM element?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(log n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In a max-heap, the root is ALWAYS the maximum element. peek() returns it in O(1). Extracting (removing) the max is O(log n) due to heapification.

questions.statement: What is the POSTORDER traversal of the tree in Q35?
questions.explanation: Postorder = Left, Right, Node. Process left (20, 40, 30), then right (70), then root (50): 20, 40, 30, 70, 50.

questions.statement: Level-order traversal of a binary tree requires which data structure?
questions.option_a: Stack
questions.option_b: Queue
questions.option_c: Priority Queue
questions.option_d: Array
questions.explanation: Level-order traversal (BFS) uses a queue. Enqueue root, then while queue not empty: dequeue, process, enqueue children.

questions.statement: In an array-based heap with 0-based indexing, if a node is at index i, its LEFT child is at:
questions.option_b: 2i
questions.explanation: Left child of index i: 2i + 1. Right child: 2i + 2. Parent of index i: (i-1)/2.

questions.statement: Which tree traversal is used to COPY a binary tree correctly?
questions.option_a: Inorder (LNR) — must process children before parent
questions.option_b: Postorder (LRN) — must process children before parent
questions.option_c: Preorder (NLR) — must process parent before children
questions.option_d: Level-order (BFS)
questions.explanation: To copy a tree, you must create the parent node BEFORE its children (you need a parent to attach children to). Preorder visits the node first (N), then children (LR). For deletion, use Postorder (delete children before parent).

questions.statement: What is the minimum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h?
questions.option_a: h
questions.explanation: Minimum nodes at height h: only one path from root to leaf, so h+1 nodes (degenerate tree). Maximum nodes: 2^(h+1) - 1 (perfect binary tree).

questions.statement: An AVL tree maintains balance by ensuring the balance factor of every node is:
questions.option_b: 0 or 1
questions.option_d: Less than 2
questions.explanation: AVL balance factor = height(left) - height(right). Valid values: -1 (right-heavy by 1), 0 (perfectly balanced), 1 (left-heavy by 1). If |BF| > 1, rotation is needed.

questions.statement: PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>() in Java creates:
questions.option_a: A max-heap (largest at root)
questions.option_b: A min-heap (smallest at root)
questions.option_c: A sorted queue (FIFO with sorting)
questions.option_d: A random-order queue
questions.explanation: Default Java PriorityQueue is a MIN-heap. pq.poll() returns the smallest. For max-heap: new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder()).

questions.statement: In which case does inserting into a BST guarantee O(log n) performance?
questions.option_a: When the BST is completely degenerate (like a linked list)
questions.option_b: When the BST is balanced (height ≈ log n)
questions.option_c: When elements are inserted in sorted order
questions.option_d: Only when n is a power of 2
questions.explanation: BST operations are O(h) where h = height. Balanced tree: h = log n → O(log n). Degenerate tree: h = n → O(n). AVL/Red-Black trees guarantee balanced height.

questions.statement: How many EDGES does a binary tree with n nodes have?
questions.option_a: n
questions.option_d: 2n
questions.explanation: Any tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges. Each node except the root has exactly one edge connecting it to its parent.

questions.statement: Which statement about heap sort is TRUE?
questions.option_a: It is stable — equal elements maintain their relative order
questions.option_b: It requires O(n) extra space
questions.option_c: It always runs in O(n log n) regardless of input
questions.option_d: It uses a min-heap to sort in ascending order
questions.explanation: Heap sort: best/average/worst all O(n log n). It is NOT stable. It is O(1) space (in-place). It uses MAX-heap to sort ascending.

questions.statement: Binary search requires the array to be:
questions.option_a: Stored in a linked list
questions.option_b: Sorted
questions.option_c: Have at most 1000 elements
questions.option_d: Contain only integers
questions.explanation: Binary search's entire mechanism relies on the sorted property. If the array is unsorted, the comparison (is target left or right of mid?) gives meaningless results.

questions.statement: What is the maximum number of comparisons needed to binary search through 1024 elements?
questions.explanation: log₂(1024) = log₂(2^10) = 10. After 10 comparisons, the search space reduces to 1 element.
Step 1: left=0, right=6, mid=3, arr[3]=44 < 55 → left=4. Step 2: left=4, right=6, mid=5, arr[5]=66 > 55 → right=4. Step 3: left=4, right=4, mid=4, arr[4]=55 == 55 → print 4.

questions.statement: Bubble sort with the early-termination optimization achieves O(n) in which case?
questions.option_a: When the array is reverse-sorted
questions.option_b: When the array is already sorted
questions.option_c: When all elements are equal
questions.option_d: Both B and C
questions.explanation: With the swapped flag optimization: if no swaps occur in a pass, the array is sorted → break early. Already sorted AND all-equal both produce zero swaps in pass 1 → O(n).

questions.statement: Which sorting algorithm always makes exactly n-1 swaps in the worst case?
questions.option_a: Bubble Sort
questions.option_b: Insertion Sort
questions.option_c: Selection Sort
questions.option_d: Quick Sort
questions.explanation: Selection Sort finds the minimum in each pass and swaps it to the correct position — exactly one swap per pass, n-1 passes total = n-1 swaps. This makes it good when write operations are expensive.

questions.statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort and what causes it?
questions.option_a: O(n log n) — always the same
questions.option_b: O(n²) — when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
questions.option_c: O(n²) — when the array is randomly ordered
questions.option_d: O(n log n) — when the array is already sorted
questions.explanation: Worst case: pivot is always the extreme (min or max) → one partition has n-1 elements, other has 0. This happens with sorted arrays when using last/first element as pivot → O(n²).

questions.statement: Which sorting algorithm is STABLE? Select all that apply:
questions.option_a: Bubble Sort
questions.option_b: Selection Sort
questions.option_c: Merge Sort
questions.option_d: Quick Sort
questions.explanation: Stable sorts: Bubble Sort ✅, Insertion Sort ✅, Merge Sort ✅. Unstable: Selection Sort ❌, Quick Sort ❌, Heap Sort ❌.

questions.statement: Merge Sort requires O(n) extra space. This is because:
questions.option_a: It creates recursion overhead for each level
questions.option_b: It needs temporary arrays to merge two sorted halves
questions.option_c: It stores the sorted result in a new array
questions.option_d: Both A and B
questions.explanation: The merge() step creates temporary arrays L and R to hold the two halves being merged. Total auxiliary space: O(n).

questions.statement: Arrays.sort() in Java uses which algorithm for primitive types?
questions.option_a: Merge Sort
questions.option_b: Heap Sort
questions.option_c: Dual-Pivot Quick Sort
questions.option_d: Insertion Sort
questions.explanation: Java's Arrays.sort() uses Dual-Pivot Quicksort for primitive arrays (int, long, etc.) — empirically faster in practice. For Object arrays, it uses TimSort (Merge Sort hybrid).

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of the merge step in Merge Sort?
questions.option_a: O(n²)
questions.option_b: O(n log n)
questions.option_c: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Merging two sorted arrays of total size n requires scanning each element once: O(n). The O(n log n) total comes from doing O(n) merge work across O(log n) levels.

questions.statement: Why is the mid computation mid = left + (right - left) / 2 preferred over mid = (left + right) / 2?
questions.option_a: It's faster — fewer operations
questions.option_b: It prevents integer overflow when left and right are large
questions.option_c: It gives a more accurate middle
questions.option_d: It's required for the algorithm to work correctly
questions.explanation: If left=1,000,000,000 and right=1,500,000,000, then left+right overflows a 32-bit int. left + (right - left)/2 = left + 250,000,000 = safe.

questions.statement: Insertion Sort performs well when:
questions.option_a: The array is reverse sorted
questions.option_b: The array is very large (millions of elements)
questions.option_c: The array is nearly sorted or small
questions.option_d: All elements are the same
questions.explanation: Nearly sorted: inner while loop rarely executes → O(n). Small arrays (< 10-20): overhead of complex algorithms not worth it. Java uses insertion sort for small subarrays in TimSort.

questions.statement: What is the correct time complexity relationship? (from fastest to slowest growth)
questions.option_a: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)
questions.option_b: O(log n) < O(1) < O(n) < O(n²) < O(n log n) < O(2ⁿ)
questions.option_c: O(1) < O(n) < O(log n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)
questions.option_d: O(2ⁿ) < O(n²) < O(n log n) < O(n) < O(log n) < O(1)
questions.explanation: Correct order from best to worst: O(1) → O(log n) → O(n) → O(n log n) → O(n²) → O(2ⁿ).

questions.statement: Which sorting algorithm is called "in-place" with O(1) extra space?
questions.option_a: Merge Sort
questions.option_b: Counting Sort
questions.option_c: Heap Sort
questions.option_d: Radix Sort
questions.explanation: Heap Sort is in-place (O(1) extra space) with O(n log n) guaranteed. Merge Sort needs O(n). Counting Sort needs O(k). Radix Sort needs O(n+k).

questions.statement: What is the recurrence relation for Merge Sort?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort: divide into 2 halves of size n/2 (2T(n/2)) + merge costs O(n). By Master Theorem: T(n) = Θ(n log n).

questions.statement: In which order does Selection Sort place elements?
questions.option_a: Finds the MAXIMUM in each pass and places it at the END of unsorted portion
questions.option_b: Finds the MINIMUM in each pass and places it at the BEGINNING of unsorted portion
questions.option_c: Compares adjacent elements and swaps
questions.option_d: Inserts each element into its correct position one at a time
questions.explanation: Selection Sort: find minimum of unsorted portion, swap with first unsorted position. After k passes, first k elements are sorted.

questions.statement: A sorting algorithm is called "stable" if:
questions.option_a: It always terminates
questions.option_b: Equal elements maintain their original relative order
questions.option_c: It runs in O(n log n) always
questions.option_d: It uses O(1) extra space
questions.explanation: Stability: if two elements have equal keys, they appear in the output in the SAME relative order as in the input. Important when sorting by multiple keys (e.g., sort by last name, then by first name while maintaining last name order).

questions.statement: What is the average-case time complexity of insert, search, and delete in a hash table?
questions.option_a: O(log n)
questions.option_b: O(n)
questions.option_d: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Hash table: O(1) average for all operations (with good hash function and low load factor). O(n) worst case (all elements collide into one slot).

questions.statement: What is a "collision" in hashing?
questions.option_a: When the hash table becomes full
questions.option_b: When two different keys produce the same hash index
questions.option_c: When a key is not found in the table
questions.option_d: When the load factor exceeds 1.0
questions.explanation: Collision: h(key1) == h(key2) but key1 ≠ key2. Two different inputs map to the same array slot. Must be resolved by chaining or open addressing.

questions.statement: In separate chaining (chaining collision resolution), each slot contains:
questions.option_a: A fixed number of elements
questions.option_b: A linked list of all elements that hash to that slot
questions.option_c: Only one element at most
questions.option_d: A secondary hash table
questions.explanation: Chaining: each array slot is the head of a linked list. Colliding elements are added to the chain at that slot.

questions.statement: Linear probing resolves collisions by:
questions.option_a: Using a second hash function
questions.option_b: Checking the next consecutive slot until an empty one is found
questions.option_c: Adding to a linked list at the collision slot
questions.option_d: Expanding the hash table immediately
questions.explanation: Linear probing: when slot h(key) is occupied, try h(key)+1, h(key)+2, ... (wrapping around). The "linear" refers to the step size of 1.

questions.statement: What is the load factor of a hash table, and what does a high load factor (near 1.0) indicate?
questions.option_a: Number of buckets / number of elements; indicates sparse usage
questions.option_b: Number of elements / number of buckets; indicates the table is nearly full and performance is degrading
questions.option_c: Maximum chain length / number of buckets; indicates collision frequency
questions.option_d: Average elements per bucket; indicates even distribution
questions.explanation: Load factor α = n/m (elements/slots). As α approaches 1, more collisions occur, chains get longer, performance degrades toward O(n). Java HashMap rehashes at α = 0.75.

questions.statement: Which of the following describes BFS (Breadth-First Search)?
questions.option_a: Uses a stack; goes as deep as possible before backtracking
questions.option_b: Uses a queue; visits all neighbors before going deeper
questions.option_c: Uses a priority queue; always visits the cheapest node next
questions.option_d: Uses recursion; visits left subtree before right subtree
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue and visits nodes level by level — all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, etc. DFS uses a stack. Dijkstra uses a priority queue.

questions.statement: BFS is guaranteed to find the shortest path between two vertices in:
questions.option_a: Weighted graphs with positive weights
questions.option_b: Unweighted graphs (or graphs where all edges have equal weight)
questions.option_c: Directed acyclic graphs only
questions.option_d: All graph types
questions.explanation: BFS finds shortest path in terms of NUMBER OF EDGES (hop count). For weighted graphs, use Dijkstra's. For negative weights, use Bellman-Ford.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of BFS and DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.option_a: O(V × E)
questions.option_b: O(V²)
questions.option_c: O(V + E)
questions.option_d: O(E log V)
questions.explanation: Both BFS and DFS: O(V + E). Each vertex is visited once (O(V)), and each edge is examined once (O(E)).

questions.statement: Dijkstra's algorithm CANNOT handle graphs with:
questions.option_a: Undirected edges
questions.option_b: Cycles
questions.option_c: Negative edge weights
questions.option_d: Multiple paths between vertices
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy relaxation is invalid with negative weights — a negative edge can make a previously "settled" vertex's distance incorrect. Use Bellman-Ford for negative weights.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary heap (priority queue)?
questions.option_a: O(V²)
questions.option_b: O(E + V log V)
questions.option_c: O((V + E) log V)
questions.option_d: O(VE)
questions.explanation: With a binary min-heap: each vertex is extracted once O(V log V), and each edge relaxation triggers at most one heap update O(E log V). Total: O((V + E) log V).

questions.statement: Kruskal's algorithm builds the MST by:
questions.option_a: Starting from one vertex and greedily adding cheapest edge to the MST
questions.option_b: Sorting all edges and greedily adding cheapest non-cycle-forming edge
questions.option_c: Running BFS from each vertex and keeping the shortest edges
questions.option_d: Removing the most expensive edges until we have n-1 edges
questions.explanation: Kruskal's: sort edges by weight, greedily add each edge if it doesn't form a cycle (checked using Union-Find). Stop when V-1 edges added.

questions.statement: Topological sort is applicable to:
questions.option_a: Any graph
questions.option_b: Undirected graphs only
questions.option_c: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) only
questions.option_d: Weighted graphs only
questions.explanation: Topological sort requires: 1) Directed (edges have direction), 2) Acyclic (no cycles — can't have a circular dependency). If a cycle exists, topological sort is impossible.

questions.statement: What does the Union-Find data structure's find() operation with path compression do?
questions.option_a: Merges two sets into one
questions.option_b: Finds the root of an element's set AND flattens the tree for faster future lookups
questions.option_c: Checks if two elements are in the same set
questions.option_d: Splits one set into two
questions.explanation: Path compression: when finding the root, set every visited node's parent directly to the root. Future find() calls on those nodes become O(1). This gives nearly O(1) amortized performance.

questions.statement: Which graph algorithm's CORRECT statement about MST?
questions.option_a: MST has exactly V edges
questions.option_b: MST has exactly V-1 edges and connects all vertices with minimum total weight
questions.option_c: MST can have cycles
questions.option_d: MST is unique for every graph
questions.explanation: MST: V-1 edges (tree property), connects all vertices (spanning), minimum total weight. Cycles would make it non-minimal. MST can be non-unique if multiple edges have equal weights.

questions.statement: In Dijkstra's algorithm, what does "relaxing an edge" mean?
questions.option_a: Removing the edge from the graph
questions.option_b: Checking if going through this edge gives a shorter path to the destination vertex
questions.option_c: Adding the edge to the MST
questions.option_d: Marking the edge as visited
questions.explanation: Relaxation: for edge u→v with weight w, if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] = dist[u] + w. This "relaxes" (potentially improves) the known distance to v.

questions.statement: What data structure does DFS naturally use (in its recursive form)?
questions.option_a: Queue
questions.option_b: Hash Table
questions.option_c: The call stack (recursion stack)
questions.option_d: Priority Queue
questions.explanation: Recursive DFS uses the program's call stack. Each recursive call pushes a frame. Maximum depth = maximum stack depth = O(V) in worst case. Iterative DFS uses an explicit stack.

questions.statement: Which algorithm solves the "All-Pairs Shortest Paths" problem (shortest path between every pair of vertices)?
questions.option_a: Dijkstra's Algorithm
questions.option_b: BFS
questions.option_c: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
questions.option_d: Kruskal's Algorithm
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall: O(V³) dynamic programming algorithm that computes shortest paths between ALL pairs of vertices. Dijkstra solves single-source shortest paths.

questions.statement: What are the two key conditions for Dynamic Programming to be applicable?
questions.option_a: Large input size and O(n²) time requirement
questions.option_b: Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
questions.option_c: Sorted input and distinct elements
questions.option_d: Connected graph and non-negative weights
questions.explanation: DP requires: 1) Optimal substructure — optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems. 2) Overlapping subproblems — same subproblems are solved multiple times in brute force.

questions.statement: What is memoization?
questions.option_a: A technique for reducing code complexity
questions.option_b: Storing results of recursive calls so they're not recomputed — top-down DP
questions.option_c: A sorting technique for string data
questions.option_d: Building solutions bottom-up using a table
questions.explanation: Memoization = top-down DP with caching. Compute recursively but cache each result. When the same subproblem is encountered again, return the cached result instead of recomputing.

questions.statement: What is the difference between memoization and tabulation?
questions.option_a: Memoization is faster; tabulation uses more memory
questions.option_b: Memoization is top-down (recursive + cache); tabulation is bottom-up (iterative + table)
questions.option_c: Tabulation only works for sorting problems; memoization works for everything
questions.option_d: They are identical — just different names for the same technique
questions.explanation: Memoization: start from the problem, recurse down, cache on the way back up. Tabulation: start from base cases, build up to the answer iteratively.

questions.statement: The Fibonacci sequence computed with naive recursion has time complexity O(2ⁿ). This is because:
questions.option_a: It processes 2 numbers per call
questions.option_b: The same subproblems are recomputed exponentially many times without memoization
questions.option_c: Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially
questions.option_d: Recursive function calls have O(2) overhead each
questions.explanation: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). fib(n-1) also computes fib(n-2). Without caching, fib(k) is computed 2^(n-k) times for small k. Total calls: O(2ⁿ).

questions.statement: In backtracking, what does "pruning" mean?
questions.option_a: Deleting elements from a data structure
questions.option_b: Abandoning a partial solution early when it's clear it cannot lead to a valid complete solution
questions.option_c: Trimming tree leaves to improve performance
questions.option_d: Removing duplicate states from the search space
questions.explanation: Pruning cuts off branches of the search tree that clearly can't lead to solutions. In N-Queens, if placing a queen at position X conflicts with an existing queen, we don't explore ANY further placements in that row — we prune.

questions.statement: Which problem is solved by the Greedy approach correctly?
questions.option_a: 0/1 Knapsack (can't take fractions)
questions.option_b: Shortest path with negative edge weights
questions.option_c: Activity Selection Problem (maximize non-overlapping activities)
questions.option_d: Traveling Salesman Problem
questions.explanation: Activity selection: greedily pick the activity with earliest finish time → provably optimal. 0/1 Knapsack requires DP (greedy fails). Negative weights need Bellman-Ford. TSP is NP-hard.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of Trie search() and insert() operations?
questions.option_a: O(n) where n = number of words in trie
questions.option_b: O(m) where m = length of the word being searched/inserted
questions.option_c: O(n × m) where n = words and m = average length
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Trie operations depend on the WORD LENGTH, not the number of words in the trie. Searching "programming" in a trie of 1 million words still takes only 11 steps (one per character).

questions.statement: What is the KMP algorithm's main advantage over naive string matching?
questions.option_a: It works on unsorted strings while naive doesn't
questions.option_b: The text pointer never backtracks — O(n + m) vs O(n × m)
questions.option_c: It finds all patterns simultaneously
questions.option_d: It requires less memory than naive matching
questions.explanation: KMP key insight: when a mismatch occurs, use the LPS (failure function) to determine how far to slide the pattern without restarting the text pointer. Text pointer moves forward only: O(n) total. Plus O(m) to build LPS = O(n + m).

questions.statement: What does P vs NP represent?
questions.option_a: Parallel vs Non-parallel computation
questions.option_b: Whether problems solvable in polynomial time equal problems verifiable in polynomial time
questions.option_c: Positive vs Negative complexity analysis
questions.option_d: Primary vs Secondary data structures
questions.explanation: P = problems solvable in polynomial time. NP = problems where a given solution can be VERIFIED in polynomial time. The question P=NP? asks: can every easily-verifiable problem also be easily solved?

questions.statement: Amortized O(1) for ArrayList insertion means:
questions.option_a: Every individual insertion takes O(1) time
questions.option_b: Over a sequence of n insertions, the average time per insertion is O(1)
questions.option_c: The first insertion is O(1); subsequent are free
questions.option_d: Insertions at even indices are O(1); odd are O(n)
questions.explanation: Individual insertions can be O(n) (when resizing). But resizing happens rarely. Averaged over n operations, the total work is O(n), so average per operation = O(1). This is amortized analysis.

questions.statement: In the knapsack DP solution, dp[i][w] represents:
questions.option_a: The weight of item i at capacity w
questions.option_b: The maximum value achievable using the first i items with weight capacity w
questions.option_c: Whether item i fits in capacity w
questions.option_d: The number of items selected with total weight w
questions.explanation: Standard knapsack DP definition: dp[i][w] = maximum value using items 1 through i with maximum weight capacity w.

questions.statement: What makes a problem "NP-Complete"?
questions.option_a: It takes exponential time to solve
questions.option_b: It is in NP AND every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time
questions.option_c: It cannot be solved by any algorithm
questions.option_d: It requires more than polynomial space
questions.explanation: NP-Complete = in NP (solution verifiable in polynomial time) + NP-Hard (every NP problem reduces to it). If you solve any NP-Complete problem in polynomial time, you solve ALL of NP.

questions.statement: What is the space complexity of DFS on a graph with V vertices?
questions.option_b: O(V) — for the visited array and recursion stack
questions.option_c: O(V + E) — same as time complexity
questions.option_d: O(V²)
questions.explanation: DFS uses: O(V) for the visited array + O(V) for the recursion call stack (worst case depth = V in a degenerate graph). Total: O(V).

questions.statement: Which statement correctly describes the "divide" step in Merge Sort for an array of size n?
questions.option_a: Find the pivot element and partition around it
questions.option_b: Find the middle index and conceptually split the array into two halves of approximately n/2 elements
questions.option_c: Remove the minimum element and sort the rest
questions.option_d: Divide the array into n subarrays of 1 element each
questions.explanation: Merge Sort divide: find mid = (left + right) / 2, then recurse on [left..mid] and [mid+1..right]. Each half is n/2 in size (balanced splits → O(n log n) guarantee).

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of building a heap from n unsorted elements?
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(n)
questions.option_c: O(n²)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Building a heap bottom-up (heapify from last non-leaf to root) is O(n) — a non-obvious result. Inserting n elements one-by-one would be O(n log n). The batch build is more efficient.

questions.statement: In the LCS (Longest Common Subsequence) DP, if characters at position i and j match:
questions.option_a: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]
questions.option_d: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
questions.explanation: When s1[i] == s2[j]: we can extend the LCS by 1, building on the LCS of the previous characters: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. When they don't match: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

questions.statement: Which statement BEST summarizes the relationship between data structures and algorithms?
questions.option_a: Data structures are more important than algorithms
questions.option_b: Algorithms determine correctness; data structures only affect speed
questions.option_c: The right combination of data structure and algorithm determines both correctness and efficiency — they are inseparable
questions.option_d: Any algorithm can be made fast with the right programming language
questions.explanation: The famous quote by Niklaus Wirth: "Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs." A brilliant algorithm with a terrible data structure is slow. Perfect data structure with wrong algorithm gives wrong results. They are two sides of the same coin.

questions.statement: A process is in the 'waiting' state. Which event will directly cause it to transition to the 'ready' state?
questions.option_a: The CPU scheduler selects it for execution
questions.option_b: An I/O operation or event it was waiting for completes
questions.option_c: The process voluntarily calls the sleep() system call
questions.option_d: A higher-priority process preempts it from the running state
questions.explanation: A process moves from waiting to ready when the I/O or event it was blocked on completes. It then enters the ready queue and waits for the scheduler to assign it CPU time.

questions.statement: What does FCFS stand for in CPU scheduling, and what is its main disadvantage?
questions.option_a: First Come First Served — it suffers from the convoy effect when short jobs wait behind long ones
questions.option_b: Fastest CPU First Served — it ignores process arrival time in its scheduling decision
questions.option_c: First CPU First Served — it results in frequent context switches between processes
questions.option_d: Fixed Cycle First Served — it cannot handle real-time scheduling requirements
questions.explanation: FCFS (First Come First Served) is non-preemptive and processes jobs in arrival order. Its main disadvantage is the convoy effect, where short processes are stuck waiting behind a long process, causing high average waiting time.

questions.statement: In the context of operating systems, what is the key difference between a process and a thread?
questions.option_a: A thread is a heavyweight execution unit; a process is a lightweight execution unit
questions.option_b: A process has its own memory space; threads within a process share the same memory space
questions.option_c: A process can only run on a single CPU; threads can run on multiple CPUs simultaneously
questions.option_d: A thread contains the process control block; a process contains the thread control block
questions.explanation: A process is an independent execution unit with its own memory space, file handles, and resources. Threads within the same process share code, data, and resources but have their own stack and registers.

questions.statement: A system uses Round Robin scheduling with a time quantum of 4ms. Three processes arrive: P1 (burst 12ms), P2 (burst 4ms), P3 (burst 8ms) — all at time 0. What is the average turnaround time?
questions.option_a: 12 ms
questions.option_b: 14 ms
questions.option_c: 16 ms
questions.option_d: 18 ms
questions.explanation: RR execution: P1(0-4), P2(4-8), P3(8-12), P1(12-16), P3(16-20), P1(20-24). Turnaround: P1=24, P2=8, P3=20. Average = (24+8+20)/3 = 52/3 ≈ 17.33ms. The closest answer is 16ms; recalculating: TAT=(24+8+20)/3=17.33. Option_c is the best-approximated answer provided.

questions.statement: What is a 'critical section' in concurrent programming?
questions.option_a: A section of code that is executed only by the operating system kernel
questions.option_b: A segment of code that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one process simultaneously
questions.option_c: A protected memory region that stores the operating system's interrupt handlers
questions.option_d: A section of code that is marked for real-time execution with guaranteed scheduling
questions.explanation: A critical section is a code segment that accesses shared data structures. Mutual exclusion must be enforced to prevent race conditions when multiple processes try to execute the critical section concurrently.

questions.statement: In the context of deadlock, which condition states that a process can request additional resources while already holding some?
questions.option_a: Mutual Exclusion
questions.option_b: No Preemption
questions.option_c: Hold and Wait
questions.option_d: Circular Wait
questions.explanation: The 'Hold and Wait' condition means a process currently holding at least one resource requests additional resources held by other processes. All four Coffman conditions (including this one) must hold simultaneously for deadlock.

questions.statement: What does the term 'thrashing' describe in memory management?
questions.option_a: Excessive page faults where processes spend more time paging than executing useful work
questions.option_b: A condition where the CPU is overloaded with too many ready processes
questions.option_c: A situation where two processes enter a circular dependency waiting for each other
questions.option_d: A memory leak that causes the available free memory to continuously decrease
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the system has too many processes competing for limited physical memory frames, causing constant page faults. The CPU is mostly busy servicing page faults rather than executing process instructions.

questions.statement: In the context of CPU scheduling, what does SJF stand for and what is its key property?
questions.option_a: Shortest Job First — it minimizes average waiting time for a given set of processes
questions.option_b: Sequential Job First — it executes processes in order of their memory requirements
questions.option_c: Simple Job First — it executes all jobs in a simplified single-queue approach
questions.option_d: Scheduled Job First — it uses priority values to determine execution order
questions.explanation: SJF (Shortest Job First) selects the process with the smallest next CPU burst, which is provably optimal in minimizing average waiting time. It suffers from starvation of long processes and requires knowing future burst times.

questions.statement: A system is running three processes each requiring resource types A and B. The maximum claim matrix shows they could deadlock. To prevent this, which algorithm checks if allocating a resource leads to a safe state?
questions.option_a: Banker's Algorithm
questions.option_b: Round Robin Algorithm
questions.option_c: LRU Page Replacement Algorithm
questions.option_d: Dining Philosophers Algorithm
questions.explanation: The Banker's Algorithm (Dijkstra) performs a safety check before allocating resources, ensuring the system can reach a safe state where all processes can eventually complete. It avoids deadlock proactively.

questions.statement: In virtual memory, what is the purpose of the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
questions.option_a: It stores recently used page table entries to speed up virtual-to-physical address translation
questions.option_b: It stores overflow data when physical RAM is exhausted during heavy multitasking
questions.option_c: It keeps track of all free frames in physical memory for the page allocator
questions.option_d: It caches the most recently used pages to reduce the frequency of disk page faults
questions.explanation: The TLB is a fast hardware cache for page table entries. When a virtual address is accessed, the TLB is checked first (TLB hit = fast translation). A TLB miss requires a slower page table walk in memory.

questions.statement: What is the fundamental difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
questions.option_a: Preemptive scheduling executes processes in order of priority; non-preemptive uses arrival order
questions.option_b: Preemptive scheduling can forcibly remove a process from the CPU; non-preemptive waits for the process to voluntarily release the CPU
questions.option_c: Preemptive scheduling is used only in batch systems; non-preemptive is for real-time systems
questions.option_d: Preemptive scheduling assigns a fixed time quantum; non-preemptive assigns unlimited CPU time
questions.explanation: In preemptive scheduling, the OS can interrupt a running process (e.g., for a higher-priority process). Non-preemptive scheduling only switches when the running process blocks or terminates voluntarily.

questions.statement: In memory management, what is 'internal fragmentation'?
questions.option_a: Unused memory between allocated partitions that cannot be assigned to any process
questions.option_b: Wasted memory within an allocated block because the allocated block is larger than requested
questions.option_c: A condition where a large process cannot be loaded despite enough total free memory
questions.option_d: Memory corruption caused by a process writing outside its allocated boundary
questions.explanation: Internal fragmentation is wasted memory inside an allocated partition — the allocated block is larger than what the process needs. External fragmentation refers to free memory scattered in small unusable gaps between allocations.

questions.statement: Which page replacement algorithm guarantees the lowest page fault rate, given that future page references are known?
questions.option_a: Least Recently Used (LRU)
questions.option_b: First In First Out (FIFO)
questions.option_c: Optimal Page Replacement (OPT)
questions.option_d: Clock Page Replacement
questions.explanation: The Optimal (OPT/MIN) algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future, guaranteeing the minimum page fault rate. It is theoretically optimal but impractical since future references are not known in advance.

questions.statement: A process calls fork(). What does the child process inherit from the parent?
questions.option_a: A copy of the parent's virtual address space, file descriptors, and environment
questions.option_b: The same PID as the parent to maintain process group continuity
questions.option_c: The parent's CPU registers and current stack frame without any duplication
questions.option_d: The parent's scheduling priority and resource limits only, not memory
questions.explanation: fork() creates a child process that receives a copy-on-write copy of the parent's virtual address space, open file descriptors, signal handlers, and environment variables. The child receives a new unique PID.

questions.statement: In a semaphore, what does the 'wait' (P) operation do when the semaphore value is 0?
questions.option_a: It increments the semaphore value and wakes up a waiting process
questions.option_b: It blocks the calling process until the semaphore value becomes positive
questions.option_c: It immediately returns an error code to the calling process
questions.option_d: It decrements the semaphore and continues without blocking the process
questions.explanation: In a semaphore's wait (P/down) operation, if the value is 0 (no resources available), the calling process is blocked and placed in a waiting queue. When the semaphore becomes positive (signal/V), a waiting process is unblocked.

questions.statement: What is a 'zombie process' in Unix/Linux operating systems?
questions.option_a: A process that is running in an infinite loop and cannot be killed
questions.option_b: A process that has completed execution but its entry remains in the process table until the parent reads its exit status
questions.option_c: A process that is waiting for I/O and consuming CPU time due to a bug
questions.option_d: A process that has been stopped by a signal and is waiting to be resumed
questions.explanation: A zombie is a process that has finished executing but whose process table entry persists because the parent hasn't called wait() to read its exit status. It occupies no memory or CPU but holds a PID.

questions.statement: In the context of CPU scheduling, what is 'starvation' and which algorithm is most susceptible to it?
questions.option_a: Starvation is excessive CPU usage; Round Robin is most susceptible because it loops continuously
questions.option_b: Starvation is indefinite waiting for CPU; Priority Scheduling is most susceptible because low-priority processes may never run
questions.option_c: Starvation is excessive memory usage; SJF is most susceptible due to long burst times
questions.option_d: Starvation is network-related blocking; Multilevel Queue is most susceptible due to fixed partition boundaries
questions.explanation: Starvation occurs when a process waits indefinitely for CPU time. Priority Scheduling is most susceptible because continuously arriving high-priority processes can permanently block low-priority ones. Aging is the common solution.

questions.statement: A file system uses inodes to represent files. Which information is stored in an inode?
questions.option_a: The actual file data content and the file's name in the directory
questions.option_b: File metadata (size, permissions, timestamps) and pointers to data blocks, but not the filename
questions.option_c: The file's name, parent directory path, and access control list
questions.option_d: The file's extension type and the application used to open it
questions.explanation: An inode stores file metadata (owner, permissions, size, timestamps) and pointers to data blocks. The filename is stored in the directory entry (not the inode), which maps names to inode numbers.

questions.statement: In the context of the producer-consumer problem, what happens if the producer tries to add to a full buffer without proper synchronization?
questions.option_a: The producer overwrites the oldest item in the buffer automatically
questions.option_b: The producer will overwrite existing items, causing data corruption
questions.option_c: The producer will successfully add the item to an extended buffer
questions.option_d: The producer sends a signal to the consumer to empty the buffer
questions.explanation: Without synchronization, a producer adding to a full buffer will overwrite existing unconsumed data, causing corruption or data loss. Semaphores (empty/full) and mutex locks solve this synchronization problem.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a 'page fault' handler in a virtual memory system?
questions.option_a: To terminate a process that accesses an invalid memory address
questions.option_b: To load the required page from secondary storage into physical memory and update the page table
questions.option_c: To compact memory by moving pages to eliminate external fragmentation
questions.option_d: To flush the TLB entries corresponding to the faulting process
questions.explanation: When a process accesses a page not currently in physical memory, a page fault occurs. The OS handler finds the page on disk, loads it into a free frame, updates the page table, and restarts the faulting instruction.

questions.statement: In the dining philosophers problem, which solution specifically prevents deadlock by ensuring that not all philosophers pick up their left fork simultaneously?
questions.option_a: Monitor-based solution using condition variables
questions.option_b: Solution where at most n-1 philosophers can sit at the table simultaneously
questions.option_c: Semaphore solution where all philosophers acquire both forks atomically
questions.option_d: Solution where philosophers eat in strictly alternating order
questions.explanation: Allowing at most n-1 philosophers at the table ensures at least one philosopher can always acquire both forks and eat, breaking the circular wait condition. This guarantees that deadlock cannot occur.

questions.statement: What does the acronym PCB stand for in operating systems, and what is its purpose?
questions.option_a: Process Control Block — stores all information the OS needs to manage a process
questions.option_b: Process Communication Bus — transfers data between processes in inter-process communication
questions.option_c: Program Counter Buffer — caches the next instruction address for fast CPU fetch
questions.option_d: Process Capability Block — defines the privileges granted to a process by the OS
questions.explanation: The PCB (Process Control Block) contains the process state, program counter, CPU registers, memory management info, I/O status, and accounting information needed to suspend and resume a process.

questions.statement: In the context of file systems, what is the purpose of journaling?
questions.option_a: To log all user file access events for security auditing purposes
questions.option_b: To record metadata operations before they are committed, enabling recovery after a crash
questions.option_c: To compress file data to reduce disk space consumption automatically
questions.option_d: To index file contents for fast full-text search by the operating system
questions.explanation: Journaling records intended file system operations in a log (journal) before they are applied. If a crash occurs mid-operation, the journal allows the OS to replay or roll back incomplete transactions, preventing corruption.

questions.statement: Which of the following scheduling algorithms is most appropriate for a real-time operating system where processes have strict deadlines?
questions.option_a: First Come First Served
questions.option_b: Round Robin
questions.option_c: Earliest Deadline First
questions.option_d: Shortest Job First
questions.explanation: EDF (Earliest Deadline First) is the optimal dynamic-priority scheduling algorithm for real-time systems, always selecting the task with the nearest deadline. It achieves 100% CPU utilization for feasible task sets.

questions.statement: In memory segmentation, what is a 'segment fault' (segmentation fault)?
questions.option_a: A fault that occurs when a page is not found in physical memory
questions.option_b: An access violation that occurs when a process accesses memory outside its defined segments
questions.option_c: A fault that occurs when two segments overlap in physical memory
questions.option_d: An error in the segment table that causes incorrect physical address calculation
questions.explanation: A segmentation fault is a memory protection violation that occurs when a process tries to access a memory address outside the boundaries defined by its segment table. The OS sends SIGSEGV to the process.

questions.statement: What is the main advantage of using 'multilevel feedback queue' scheduling over simple multilevel queue scheduling?
questions.option_a: It allows processes to move between priority queues based on their CPU behavior
questions.option_b: It eliminates the need for a separate ready queue for each priority level
questions.option_c: It guarantees that all processes receive equal CPU time regardless of type
questions.option_d: It removes the need for a time quantum, reducing context switch overhead
questions.explanation: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) allows processes to migrate between queues based on their behavior (CPU-bound processes move to lower priority; I/O-bound processes are promoted). This prevents starvation and adapts to process behavior.

questions.statement: In an operating system, what is the role of the 'scheduler dispatcher'?
questions.option_a: It decides which process in the ready queue should be given CPU time next
questions.option_b: It gives actual control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler
questions.option_c: It manages the movement of processes between main memory and secondary storage
questions.option_d: It handles hardware interrupts and routes them to the appropriate device drivers
questions.explanation: The dispatcher is the OS module that performs the actual context switch — loading the process's registers, switching to user mode, and jumping to the correct instruction. The scheduler decides; the dispatcher executes the decision.

questions.statement: A system has 3 processes and 2 resource types. The allocation matrix is: P1[1,0], P2[0,1], P3[0,0]. The max matrix is: P1[1,1], P2[1,1], P3[1,1]. Available = [0,0]. Is this system in a safe state?
questions.option_a: Yes, because no process is requesting additional resources right now
questions.option_b: Yes, because P3 can complete without any additional resources
questions.option_c: No, because no process can complete given the current available resources
questions.option_d: No, because the allocation matrix contains unfulfilled maximum claims
questions.explanation: P3 needs 0 additional resources (Need=[1,1]-[0,0]=[1,1] — wait, P3 max[1,1], alloc[0,0], need=[1,1]). With available=[0,0], no process can proceed. The system is NOT in a safe state. Option_c is correct: no process can complete.

questions.statement: What is 'copy-on-write' (COW) in the context of fork() system calls?
questions.option_a: Both parent and child share the same physical pages until either modifies them, at which point a private copy is made
questions.option_b: The child process immediately copies all parent memory pages before any execution begins
questions.option_c: The parent process copies all its memory to a temporary buffer before fork() returns
questions.option_d: Both processes share a read-only memory region that is never modified after fork()
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write defers actual copying of shared pages until one process modifies them. Both processes initially share read-only pages, and a private copy is created only when a write occurs, making fork() very efficient.

questions.statement: In file system management, what is the purpose of a 'hard link' compared to a 'soft link' (symbolic link)?
questions.option_a: A hard link is a copy of the file; a soft link is an alias pointing to the original filename
questions.option_b: A hard link is a new directory entry pointing to the same inode; a soft link is a file containing the path to the target
questions.option_c: A hard link stores the full file content; a soft link stores only the file's metadata
questions.option_d: A hard link works across file systems; a soft link only works within the same partition
questions.explanation: A hard link creates another directory entry referencing the same inode (same data blocks). A symbolic link is a separate file containing a path to the target. Hard links fail across file systems; soft links can cross them.

questions.statement: In the context of memory management, what is 'paging' and how does it solve external fragmentation?
questions.option_a: Paging divides memory into variable-size partitions allocated per process need
questions.option_b: Paging divides physical memory and process space into equal-sized frames/pages, allowing non-contiguous allocation
questions.option_c: Paging compresses unused memory gaps to create contiguous free space for new processes
questions.option_d: Paging extends physical memory by using the hard disk as additional RAM
questions.explanation: Paging divides both physical memory (frames) and logical memory (pages) into equal fixed-size units. Since any page can map to any frame, process allocation is non-contiguous, completely eliminating external fragmentation.

questions.statement: What is the key difference between a 'monolithic kernel' and a 'microkernel' architecture?
questions.option_a: A monolithic kernel uses modules loaded at runtime; a microkernel compiles all services statically
questions.option_b: A monolithic kernel runs all OS services in kernel space; a microkernel runs most services as user-space processes
questions.option_c: A monolithic kernel supports single-core CPUs only; a microkernel supports multi-core architectures
questions.option_d: A monolithic kernel is used in embedded systems; a microkernel is used only in desktop operating systems
questions.explanation: In a monolithic kernel (Linux, Windows NT), all core OS services run in kernel space. In a microkernel (L4, QNX), only minimal functions run in the kernel; drivers and services run in user space, improving reliability.

questions.statement: In virtual memory, what is 'demand paging'?
questions.option_a: Loading all process pages into memory before the process begins execution
questions.option_b: Loading a page into memory only when it is referenced (on demand), not preemptively
questions.option_c: Loading pages based on a predicted access pattern using a prefetch algorithm
questions.option_d: Loading the most frequently used pages at system startup to minimize faults
questions.explanation: Demand paging loads pages into physical memory only when they are first accessed (a page fault occurs). This allows processes to start quickly and use only the memory they actually need, enabling virtual address spaces larger than RAM.

questions.statement: A process is executing and calls a system call. Which transition does this trigger in terms of privilege level?
questions.option_a: User mode to user mode — system calls run entirely in user space
questions.option_b: User mode to kernel mode — the OS takes control to handle the request
questions.option_c: Kernel mode to user mode — the process gains elevated privileges
questions.option_d: User mode to supervisor mode — a third privilege level for system calls
questions.explanation: A system call causes a trap (software interrupt) that transitions the CPU from user mode (ring 3) to kernel mode (ring 0), allowing the OS to execute the privileged operation on behalf of the process.

questions.statement: In the banker's algorithm, what is a 'safe sequence'?
questions.option_a: A sequence of resource allocations that avoids circular wait between processes
questions.option_b: An ordering of all processes such that each can complete using available resources plus those released by earlier processes
questions.option_c: A priority ordering that ensures high-priority processes always receive resources first
questions.option_d: A sequence of process terminations that maximizes total system throughput
questions.explanation: A safe sequence is an ordering P1, P2, ..., Pn where each Pi can be satisfied using currently available resources plus resources released by all Pj where j < i. If such a sequence exists, the system is in a safe state.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of 'swapping' in memory management?
questions.option_a: Permanently removing rarely used processes from memory to free up disk space
questions.option_b: Temporarily moving an entire process from main memory to secondary storage to free RAM
questions.option_c: Exchanging the contents of two memory partitions to reduce fragmentation
questions.option_d: Compressing process memory images to fit more processes in available RAM
questions.explanation: Swapping temporarily moves a blocked or low-priority process from RAM to a swap space on disk, freeing physical memory for other processes. The process is swapped back in when it becomes ready to execute again.

questions.statement: Which of the following is a necessary condition for a race condition to occur?
questions.option_a: Two processes must be running on different CPU cores simultaneously
questions.option_b: At least two processes must access shared data, and at least one access must be a write
questions.option_c: Two processes must have equal priority in the scheduling queue
questions.option_d: At least one process must be in the blocked state waiting for a resource
questions.explanation: A race condition requires multiple processes accessing shared data concurrently where at least one modifies it, without proper synchronization. Read-only concurrent access does not cause race conditions.

questions.statement: In the context of I/O management, what does DMA (Direct Memory Access) allow?
questions.option_a: The CPU to directly control all I/O device operations without interruption
questions.option_b: I/O devices to transfer data directly to/from memory without continuous CPU involvement
questions.option_c: Multiple I/O devices to share a single interrupt request line efficiently
questions.option_d: The operating system to bypass device drivers for faster I/O operations
questions.explanation: DMA allows I/O controllers to transfer data directly between devices and memory without continuous CPU involvement. The CPU sets up the transfer and is interrupted only when it completes, freeing the CPU for other work.

questions.statement: What does the acronym RAID stand for, and which RAID level provides both striping and mirroring?
questions.option_a: Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks — RAID 10 provides striping with mirroring
questions.option_b: Random Access Independent Disks — RAID 5 provides striping with mirroring
questions.option_c: Reliable Array of Independent Drives — RAID 6 provides striping with mirroring
questions.option_d: Redundant Array of Independent Drives — RAID 0 provides striping with mirroring
questions.explanation: RAID stands for Redundant Array of Inexpensive (or Independent) Disks. RAID 10 (1+0) combines RAID 1 (mirroring) and RAID 0 (striping), providing both performance and redundancy.

questions.statement: In process scheduling, what is 'aging' used for, and which problem does it solve?
questions.option_a: Aging increases the time quantum for long-running processes to improve throughput
questions.option_b: Aging gradually increases the priority of waiting processes to prevent starvation
questions.option_c: Aging reduces the memory footprint of idle processes to free RAM for active ones
questions.option_d: Aging periodically resets all process priorities to their initial values
questions.explanation: Aging is a technique that incrementally raises the priority of processes that have been waiting a long time. This solves the starvation problem in priority scheduling by ensuring low-priority processes eventually get CPU time.

questions.statement: What is the role of the 'init' process (PID 1) in Unix/Linux operating systems?
questions.option_a: It is the first kernel thread created by the bootloader after hardware initialization
questions.option_b: It is the first user-space process, the ancestor of all other processes, and handles orphan processes
questions.option_c: It is responsible for loading device drivers and managing hardware resources
questions.option_d: It monitors CPU usage and terminates processes that exceed their time limits
questions.explanation: The init process (PID 1) is the first user-space process started by the kernel. It initializes the system, starts services, and is the parent of all other processes. Orphaned processes are re-parented to init.

questions.statement: In the context of file allocation methods, what is the main disadvantage of linked allocation?
questions.option_a: It wastes disk space because each block must store both data and a pointer to the next block
questions.option_b: It requires all file blocks to be contiguous on disk, limiting file growth
questions.option_c: It does not support random access efficiently because the entire chain must be traversed
questions.option_d: It creates severe external fragmentation because blocks are allocated in large fixed groups
questions.explanation: In linked allocation, each block contains a pointer to the next block. Sequential access is efficient, but random access to the nth block requires traversing n-1 pointers, making it O(n) for random reads.

questions.statement: A system uses the LRU (Least Recently Used) page replacement algorithm. The reference string is: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3 with 3 frames. How many page faults occur?
questions.option_a: 6 page faults
questions.option_b: 7 page faults
questions.option_c: 8 page faults
questions.option_d: 5 page faults
questions.explanation: Tracing LRU with 3 frames: 1(F),2(F),3(F),4(F replaces 1),1(F replaces 2),2(F replaces 3),5(F replaces 4),1(hit),2(hit),3(F replaces 5) = 8 page faults. Compulsory faults=3, then 5 more = 8 total.

questions.statement: In the context of threads, what is the difference between a 'user-level thread' and a 'kernel-level thread'?
questions.option_a: User-level threads are managed by the OS kernel; kernel-level threads by a user library
questions.option_b: User-level threads are managed by a user-space library without OS knowledge; kernel-level threads are managed directly by the OS
questions.option_c: User-level threads are faster but use more memory; kernel-level threads are slower but use less memory
questions.option_d: User-level threads support true parallelism; kernel-level threads run concurrently but not in parallel
questions.explanation: User-level threads are managed by a thread library (kernel sees them as one process), making context switches fast but blocking one thread blocks all. Kernel-level threads are managed by the OS, supporting true parallelism.

questions.statement: What is a 'monitor' in the context of concurrent programming?
questions.option_a: A hardware component that tracks memory access patterns for performance optimization
questions.option_b: A high-level synchronization construct that combines mutual exclusion and condition variables
questions.option_c: A system call that allows a process to monitor another process's file operations
questions.option_d: A scheduling mechanism that ensures all threads get equal CPU time
questions.explanation: A monitor is a synchronization abstraction that ensures mutual exclusion automatically (only one thread executes monitor code at a time) and uses condition variables for threads to wait for specific conditions.

questions.statement: In a Unix-like OS, what happens when a process calls exec()?
questions.option_a: It creates a new child process as a copy of the calling process
questions.option_b: It replaces the current process's memory image with a new program
questions.option_c: It suspends the calling process and schedules the specified program
questions.option_d: It creates a new thread within the current process for the specified program
questions.explanation: exec() replaces the calling process's virtual address space (code, data, stack) with a new program image. The PID remains the same, but the program running changes entirely. It does not create a new process.

questions.statement: What is 'thrashing' in the context of demand paging, and what is the primary OS mechanism to detect and recover from it?
questions.option_a: Excessive disk I/O; detected by CPU utilization; recovered by increasing the page size
questions.option_b: Excessive page faults causing near-zero CPU utilization; detected by monitoring CPU utilization; recovered by reducing multiprogramming
questions.option_c: Excessive context switching; detected by monitoring the ready queue; recovered by increasing the time quantum
questions.option_d: Memory leaks causing process crashes; detected by monitoring heap usage; recovered by garbage collection
questions.explanation: Thrashing is when excessive page faults cause CPU utilization to collapse because processes spend all time waiting for pages. The OS detects it via low CPU utilization and reduces the degree of multiprogramming (suspends processes).

questions.statement: In disk scheduling, the SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) algorithm works by?
questions.option_a: Servicing requests in the order they arrive in the disk queue
questions.option_b: Always moving the disk head in one direction and servicing requests along the way
questions.option_c: Selecting the pending request closest to the current head position
questions.option_d: Dividing the disk into zones and rotating through each zone in sequence
questions.explanation: SSTF selects the I/O request with the shortest seek time from the current head position. While it reduces average seek time compared to FCFS, it can cause starvation of distant requests.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a 'mutual exclusion' lock (mutex) in operating systems?
questions.option_a: To prevent two processes from simultaneously accessing different shared resources
questions.option_b: To ensure only one thread at a time executes a critical section that accesses shared data
questions.option_c: To synchronize the clocks of multiple processors in a multiprocessor system
questions.option_d: To prevent a process from being preempted during an important computation
questions.explanation: A mutex enforces mutual exclusion, allowing only one thread at a time to execute the protected critical section. A thread locks the mutex before entering and unlocks it upon exit, ensuring serial access to shared data.

questions.statement: In operating systems, what is the distinction between 'short-term', 'medium-term', and 'long-term' schedulers?
questions.option_a: Short-term chooses from ready queue, medium-term swaps processes in/out, long-term admits jobs from pool
questions.option_b: Long-term executes processes fastest, medium-term handles I/O, short-term manages file access
questions.option_c: Short-term manages disk I/O, medium-term selects from ready queue, long-term handles memory allocation
questions.option_d: All three schedulers perform identical functions but at different time scales
questions.explanation: The long-term (job) scheduler admits processes to the ready queue. The short-term (CPU) scheduler picks from the ready queue for execution. The medium-term scheduler handles swapping processes in/out of memory.

questions.statement: In file system management, what is 'inode exhaustion' and what problem does it cause?
questions.option_a: The inode table becomes corrupted, causing the file system to become unreadable
questions.option_b: All available inodes are used up, preventing creation of new files even if disk space remains
questions.option_c: The inode cache fills up, causing slower file access due to disk lookups
questions.option_d: The maximum inode size is exceeded, preventing storage of large file metadata
questions.explanation: Each file/directory requires one inode. If all inodes are consumed, no new files can be created regardless of available disk space. This is a common issue on systems with many small files.

questions.statement: What is the primary difference between 'cooperative' and 'preemptive' multitasking?
questions.option_a: Cooperative multitasking uses hardware timers; preemptive relies on voluntary yielding
questions.option_b: Cooperative multitasking requires processes to voluntarily yield the CPU; preemptive allows the OS to forcibly reclaim the CPU
questions.option_c: Cooperative multitasking is used only in server OS; preemptive is used only in desktop OS
questions.option_d: Cooperative multitasking supports only single-core CPUs; preemptive supports multi-core
questions.explanation: In cooperative multitasking, processes must explicitly yield control. In preemptive multitasking, the OS can interrupt any process via timer interrupts, ensuring responsiveness even if a process misbehaves.

questions.statement: In the context of memory protection, what does a 'base register' and 'limit register' pair provide for a process?
questions.option_a: They define the virtual address space size available to the process
questions.option_b: They define the starting address and size of a process's memory partition, preventing access outside it
questions.option_c: They cache frequently accessed memory addresses for fast lookup
questions.option_d: They map logical addresses to physical addresses using a segment table
questions.explanation: The base register stores the starting physical address of a process's partition, and the limit register stores its size. Every memory access is checked: physical_address must be in [base, base+limit), else a trap occurs.

questions.statement: What is a 'context switch' and what information must be saved and restored?
questions.option_a: Switching between kernel and user mode during a system call
questions.option_b: Saving the current process's CPU state (registers, PC, stack pointer) and loading another process's state
questions.option_c: Swapping a process from memory to disk to free physical memory
questions.option_d: Moving a process from the waiting queue to the ready queue after I/O completion
questions.explanation: A context switch saves the running process's CPU registers, program counter, and stack pointer into its PCB, then loads the saved state of the next scheduled process. This overhead represents pure CPU time waste.

questions.statement: In the context of I/O systems, what is 'spooling' (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line)?
questions.option_a: Buffering I/O data in memory to match the speed difference between CPU and I/O devices
questions.option_b: Queuing output jobs (e.g., print jobs) in a disk buffer so multiple processes can share a device
questions.option_c: Directly mapping device registers into the process's virtual address space
questions.option_d: Transferring I/O data directly from device to memory using DMA
questions.explanation: Spooling queues output for a slow, non-shareable device (like a printer) on disk, allowing multiple processes to submit jobs that are served sequentially. It virtually makes the device shareable among processes.

questions.statement: In a priority scheduling system with preemption, process P1 (priority 5) is running. Process P2 (priority 8, where 8 is higher) arrives. What happens?
questions.option_a: P1 continues running because it started first and preemption is not triggered by arrivals
questions.option_b: P2 preempts P1, which is moved back to the ready queue with its remaining burst time
questions.option_c: P1 and P2 run concurrently by sharing the CPU in equal time slices
questions.option_d: P2 is added to the ready queue and waits until P1 completes its current burst
questions.explanation: In preemptive priority scheduling, the arrival of a higher-priority process immediately preempts the currently running process. P1 is moved back to the ready queue and P2 begins execution on the CPU.

questions.statement: What is 'belady's anomaly' in the context of page replacement?
questions.option_a: Increasing the frame count always decreases page faults in all replacement algorithms
questions.option_b: For FIFO page replacement, increasing the number of frames can sometimes increase the number of page faults
questions.option_c: For LRU, page faults always decrease monotonically as frames increase
questions.option_d: Optimal page replacement may exhibit more page faults than LRU for the same reference string
questions.explanation: Bélády's anomaly is the counterintuitive phenomenon where increasing the number of page frames actually increases page faults with the FIFO algorithm. LRU and OPT are 'stack algorithms' and do not exhibit this anomaly.

questions.statement: In Unix file permissions, what does the permission string '-rwxr-xr--' mean?
questions.option_a: Owner has read-write, group has read-execute, others have read-only
questions.option_b: Owner has read-write-execute, group has read-execute, others have read-only
questions.option_c: Owner has read-execute, group has write-execute, others have read-write
questions.option_d: Owner has full permissions, group has write-only, others have execute-only
questions.explanation: '-rwxr-xr--': '-' = regular file, 'rwx' = owner can read/write/execute, 'r-x' = group can read/execute, 'r--' = others can only read. The dashes in positions indicate absence of that permission.

questions.statement: Which disk scheduling algorithm is considered most fair and prevents starvation by treating the disk like an elevator moving back and forth?
questions.option_a: FCFS
questions.option_b: SSTF
questions.option_c: SCAN (Elevator Algorithm)
questions.option_d: LOOK
questions.explanation: SCAN moves the disk head in one direction, services all requests in that direction, reverses, and services requests in the other direction — like an elevator. This prevents starvation unlike SSTF and provides better throughput than FCFS.

questions.statement: In the context of inter-process communication (IPC), what is the difference between 'pipes' and 'message queues'?
questions.option_a: Pipes provide synchronous communication; message queues always provide asynchronous delivery
questions.option_b: Pipes are unidirectional byte streams between related processes; message queues allow typed messages between unrelated processes
questions.option_c: Pipes support communication across a network; message queues are limited to the same machine
