questions.option_d: Pipes preserve message boundaries; message queues merge data into a continuous byte stream
questions.explanation: Pipes are unidirectional byte streams typically used between a parent and child process. Message queues allow typed, prioritized messages between unrelated processes, and messages can be retrieved out of order by type.

questions.statement: What is the primary goal of an operating system's 'memory compaction'?
questions.option_a: To combine fragmented free memory areas into a single large contiguous block
questions.option_b: To compress file data to increase effective disk storage capacity
questions.option_c: To reorganize the page table to speed up virtual address translation
questions.option_d: To move all process data to the lower addresses and stack to high addresses
questions.explanation: Memory compaction relocates all processes to one end of memory, consolidating all free space into one large contiguous block. This eliminates external fragmentation but is expensive as it requires updating all addresses.

questions.statement: A system implements the readers-writers problem. Multiple readers can read simultaneously, but a writer needs exclusive access. What is the key synchronization requirement?
questions.option_a: Writers must wait for all current readers to finish, and new readers must wait if a writer is waiting
questions.option_b: Readers must acquire a mutual exclusion lock to prevent other readers from reading simultaneously
questions.option_c: Writers must acquire a separate high-priority lock that immediately interrupts all current readers
questions.option_d: All readers and writers must execute sequentially in strict arrival order
questions.explanation: In the readers-writers problem, multiple concurrent readers are allowed. A writer needs exclusive access: it must wait for all active readers to finish. Variants differ in whether new readers are blocked when a writer is waiting.

questions.statement: In the context of file systems, what is a 'superblock'?
questions.option_a: The first directory entry in a file system containing the root directory structure
questions.option_b: A special block that stores critical metadata about the file system structure, size, and status
questions.option_c: A block allocated at the end of a file to store its checksum for integrity verification
questions.option_d: A reserved block that caches recently modified inode entries for fast access
questions.explanation: The superblock contains critical file system metadata: total size, block size, number of free blocks/inodes, file system state, and mount information. Its corruption makes the file system unmountable.

questions.statement: What is the key purpose of the 'nice' value in Unix/Linux process scheduling?
questions.option_a: It specifies the memory priority of a process for physical frame allocation
questions.option_b: It allows users to adjust the scheduling priority of a process relative to others
questions.option_c: It defines the signal handling behavior for inter-process communication
questions.option_d: It sets the maximum CPU time a process can use before being terminated
questions.explanation: The 'nice' value (-20 to +19) adjusts a process's scheduling priority. A higher nice value makes a process 'nicer' (lower priority, getting less CPU time). Root can set negative values for higher priority.

questions.statement: In the context of deadlock prevention, which strategy eliminates the 'circular wait' condition?
questions.option_a: Allowing preemption of resources from blocked processes
questions.option_b: Requiring processes to request all needed resources at once before starting
questions.option_c: Assigning a total ordering to all resource types and requiring processes to request resources in increasing order
questions.option_d: Ensuring that each resource type can only be held by one process at a time
questions.explanation: Circular wait prevention assigns a global numerical ordering to all resource types. Processes must request resources in strictly increasing order, preventing the circular dependency that forms a deadlock cycle.

questions.statement: What is 'address space layout randomization' (ASLR) and why does the OS use it?
questions.option_a: It randomizes the order of processes in the scheduling queue to improve fairness
questions.option_b: It randomizes the virtual address placement of key memory regions to make exploits harder
questions.option_c: It randomizes I/O device allocation to prevent resource monopolization
questions.option_d: It randomizes the page replacement order to avoid thrashing in memory-intensive workloads
questions.explanation: ASLR randomizes the base addresses of the stack, heap, and shared libraries each time a program runs. This makes it much harder for attackers to predict target addresses for exploits like buffer overflows.

questions.statement: In a multilevel queue scheduling system, processes are divided into foreground (interactive) and background (batch) queues. What is the typical policy for CPU allocation between queues?
questions.option_a: Each queue gets equal CPU time to ensure complete fairness across all process types
questions.option_b: Foreground queue gets higher priority (e.g., 80% CPU time) and uses Round Robin; background uses FCFS
questions.option_c: Background processes always run first because they are more computationally intensive
questions.option_d: Both queues share a single scheduling algorithm applied uniformly across all processes
questions.explanation: Multilevel Queue gives foreground (interactive) processes higher priority and often more CPU time, using Round Robin for responsiveness. Background batch jobs run with FCFS during remaining CPU time, preventing starvation.

questions.statement: What is the key difference between 'hard real-time' and 'soft real-time' systems?
questions.option_a: Hard real-time systems use preemptive scheduling; soft real-time systems use cooperative scheduling
questions.option_b: In hard real-time, missing a deadline is catastrophic; in soft real-time, missing a deadline is undesirable but tolerable
questions.option_c: Hard real-time systems are embedded systems; soft real-time systems are exclusively desktop OS
questions.option_d: Hard real-time processes are at the highest priority; soft real-time processes share priority with other tasks
questions.explanation: In hard real-time systems (e.g., aircraft control, pacemakers), missing any deadline causes system failure. In soft real-time systems (e.g., multimedia streaming), occasional deadline misses degrade quality but are not catastrophic.

questions.statement: In Unix, what is the purpose of the 'wait()' system call in a parent process?
questions.option_a: To suspend execution until a specified time has elapsed
questions.option_b: To pause until a child process terminates and collect its exit status
questions.option_c: To wait for a specific signal from another process or the kernel
questions.option_d: To block until a requested I/O operation on a file descriptor completes
questions.explanation: The wait() system call blocks the parent process until one of its child processes terminates. It also retrieves the child's exit status, allowing the OS to remove the zombie process table entry.

questions.statement: What is 'memory-mapped I/O'?
questions.option_a: A technique where device registers are mapped into the process's virtual address space for direct access
questions.option_b: A method of DMA where the device controller maps its buffer to a shared physical page
questions.option_c: An I/O method where the OS maps all I/O operations to file system calls
questions.option_d: A technique where device driver memory is isolated from kernel memory for security
questions.explanation: Memory-mapped I/O maps device registers and buffers into the processor's address space. Programs can access I/O devices using ordinary load/store instructions rather than special I/O instructions.

questions.statement: In the context of virtual memory, what is the 'working set model'?
questions.option_a: A model that predicts future page accesses based on access frequency
questions.option_b: A model defining the set of pages a process is actively using in a given time window
questions.option_c: A model that tracks the total number of frames allocated to each process
questions.option_d: A model that identifies pages that should be permanently locked in physical memory
questions.explanation: The working set model (Denning) tracks the set of pages used by a process in the last Δ time units. Allocating enough frames to hold the working set prevents thrashing, as the process won't generate excessive page faults.

questions.statement: Which file organization method provides the fastest access time for records with known positions, as each record can be accessed with a direct calculation?
questions.option_a: Sequential file organization
questions.option_b: Indexed file organization
questions.option_c: Hashed file organization
questions.option_d: Relative (Direct Access) file organization
questions.explanation: Relative (direct access) file organization computes the physical location of a record directly from its logical record number, providing O(1) access time. Sequential access requires scanning, and indexed access requires an index lookup.

questions.statement: In the context of operating system security, what is 'privilege separation'?
questions.option_a: Encrypting sensitive data with different keys based on user access level
questions.option_b: Running different parts of an application with different (minimal) privilege levels
questions.option_c: Using separate user accounts for different applications on the same machine
questions.option_d: Dividing physical memory between kernel and user processes
questions.explanation: Privilege separation divides an application into components with different privilege levels, so that a compromise of a low-privilege component limits the damage. It follows the principle of least privilege.

questions.statement: A system has 5 processes and 3 identical resource instances. The current allocation is: P1=1, P2=2, P3=1, P4=0, P5=1. Maximum needs: P1=2, P2=2, P3=3, P4=1, P5=2. Available=1. Is a safe sequence possible?
questions.option_a: No, because total resources are insufficient for all maximum claims
questions.option_b: Yes: P4→P1→P2→P5→P3 is a safe sequence
questions.option_c: Yes: P1→P2→P3→P4→P5 is a safe sequence
questions.option_d: No, because P3 can never be satisfied
questions.explanation: Available=1. P4 needs max 1, has 0, needs 1 more — P4 runs, frees 0+1=releases 0 wait. Let me recalculate: Total=1+2+1+0+1=5+available=1=6. Max total=2+2+3+1+2=10. Need: P1=1,P2=0,P3=2,P4=1,P5=1. With available=1: P2(need=0)runs,frees 2, avail=3; P1(need=1)runs,frees 1,avail=3; P4(need=1)runs,frees 0,avail=3; P5(need=1)runs,frees 1,avail=3; P3(need=2)runs. Safe sequence: P2→P1→P4→P5→P3. Option_b is correct.

questions.statement: What is the primary difference between 'logical I/O' and 'physical I/O' in operating systems?
questions.option_a: Logical I/O deals with files and records; physical I/O deals with raw blocks on disk
questions.option_b: Logical I/O is faster because it bypasses the kernel; physical I/O goes through system calls
questions.option_c: Logical I/O is handled by device drivers; physical I/O is handled by user applications
questions.option_d: Logical I/O always involves network operations; physical I/O involves only local storage
questions.explanation: Logical I/O is presented to applications as named files and records, abstracted by the file system. Physical I/O is the actual reading/writing of data blocks on the storage hardware, managed by device drivers.

questions.statement: In the context of the producer-consumer problem, what is the purpose of the 'full' semaphore?
questions.option_a: It protects the shared buffer from concurrent access by multiple producers
questions.option_b: It counts available empty slots, blocking the producer when the buffer is full
questions.option_c: It counts the number of filled slots, blocking the consumer when the buffer is empty
questions.option_d: It signals the producer to start producing when the buffer is completely empty
questions.explanation: The 'full' semaphore counts the number of filled slots in the buffer. Consumer threads wait on 'full' when it equals zero (buffer empty). The 'empty' semaphore counts available slots and blocks producers when the buffer is full.

questions.statement: Which memory allocation strategy assigns the smallest free partition that is large enough to satisfy a memory request?
questions.option_a: First Fit
questions.option_b: Worst Fit
questions.option_c: Best Fit
questions.option_d: Next Fit
questions.explanation: Best Fit searches all free partitions and selects the smallest one that satisfies the request, minimizing wasted space within the allocated partition. However, it tends to create many tiny unusable fragments over time.

questions.statement: In Unix/Linux, what does the 'fork-exec' pattern accomplish?
questions.option_a: It creates a child thread and assigns it a new function to execute concurrently
questions.option_b: It creates a child process (fork) and then replaces its memory image with a new program (exec)
questions.option_c: It creates a new process and then waits for it to complete before the parent continues
questions.option_d: It duplicates a file descriptor and then redirects it to a new device
questions.explanation: fork() creates a child copy of the parent, and exec() replaces the child's memory with a new program. This pattern is how shells launch commands: fork a child, exec the desired program, and the parent waits for completion.

questions.statement: What does 'TLB shootdown' refer to in multiprocessor operating systems?
questions.option_a: A hardware mechanism to automatically invalidate stale TLB entries across all CPUs
questions.option_b: The process of sending IPIs (inter-processor interrupts) to all other CPUs to invalidate TLB entries after a page table modification
questions.option_c: A performance optimization that removes unused TLB entries to make room for new mappings
questions.option_d: A security mechanism that clears the TLB on every context switch to prevent information leakage
questions.explanation: In multi-core systems, when a page table entry is modified (e.g., page unmapped), the OS must send TLB shootdown IPIs to all CPUs to invalidate their stale TLB entries, ensuring memory access correctness.

questions.statement: In the context of deadlock recovery, which approach has the least impact on system performance but is only applicable to certain types of systems?
questions.option_a: Terminating all deadlocked processes simultaneously
questions.option_b: Preempting resources from deadlocked processes
questions.option_c: Rolling back and restarting deadlocked processes from a checkpoint
questions.option_d: Using the Banker's Algorithm to detect and resolve deadlocks
questions.explanation: Checkpoint-based rollback restores processes to a safe pre-deadlock state. It has minimal performance impact when checkpoints are frequent and applies to systems where process state can be saved and restored.

questions.statement: What is the main purpose of a 'bootloader' in the OS startup process?
questions.option_a: It manages the hardware power supply during the system boot sequence
questions.option_b: It loads and transfers control to the OS kernel from persistent storage
questions.option_c: It provides the initial user interface before the OS is fully loaded
questions.option_d: It tests all hardware components for faults before the OS begins loading
questions.explanation: A bootloader (e.g., GRUB) is the first program run after firmware/BIOS. It locates the OS kernel on storage, loads it into memory, and transfers CPU control to it. It may also provide a boot menu for multiple OS selection.

questions.statement: In the context of file systems, what is the purpose of 'fsck' (file system check)?
questions.option_a: To defragment the disk by moving file blocks to contiguous locations
questions.option_b: To scan and repair inconsistencies in the file system after an unclean shutdown
questions.option_c: To securely erase deleted file data to prevent recovery by forensic tools
questions.option_d: To check file permissions and fix incorrect ownership assignments
questions.explanation: fsck scans the file system metadata structures (inodes, directories, free block lists) for inconsistencies caused by unclean shutdowns and repairs them, preventing data corruption from spreading.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the 'nice' command output range in Unix, specifically the value of -20?
questions.option_a: It indicates the lowest possible scheduling priority for a process
questions.option_b: It indicates the highest scheduling priority (most CPU time), reserved for privileged processes
questions.option_c: It represents a neutral priority equal to all other default processes
questions.option_d: It indicates the process has no scheduling priority and runs only during idle time
questions.explanation: In Unix, nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to +19 (lowest priority). A nice value of -20 gives the process the most CPU time. Only root can set negative nice values, as they impact other processes.

questions.statement: In the context of memory management, what is 'segmentation'?
questions.option_a: Dividing physical memory into equal-sized frames and process memory into equal-sized pages
questions.option_b: Dividing a process's logical address space into variable-sized segments based on logical units
questions.option_c: Compacting all free memory into a single contiguous block periodically
questions.option_d: Splitting a large process across multiple fixed-size memory partitions
questions.explanation: Memory segmentation divides a process's address space into logical units (code, stack, heap, data) of variable sizes. Each segment has a base and limit, and access to each segment can be controlled independently.

questions.statement: In operating systems, what is the key distinction between 'hard links' and 'symbolic links' when the original file is deleted?
questions.option_a: Both hard links and symbolic links become dangling when the original file is deleted
questions.option_b: A hard link still provides access to the file data; a symbolic link becomes dangling
questions.option_c: A symbolic link still provides access via the directory path; a hard link fails
questions.option_d: Both hard links and symbolic links are automatically removed when the original is deleted
questions.explanation: A hard link points directly to the inode; deleting the original removes one link but the data persists as long as any hard link exists. A symbolic link stores a path; if the target is deleted, the symlink becomes dangling.

questions.statement: In the context of thread synchronization, what is a 'condition variable' used for?
questions.option_a: To count the number of active threads currently executing in a critical section
questions.option_b: To allow threads to wait for a specific condition to become true before proceeding
questions.option_c: To enforce mutual exclusion on a shared data structure in a multi-threaded program
questions.option_d: To set the priority of a thread within the scheduling queue of the OS
questions.explanation: A condition variable allows threads to atomically release a mutex and block while waiting for a condition to become true. When another thread signals the condition variable, waiting threads are woken up to recheck the condition.

questions.statement: In memory management, what is the effect of increasing the page size on a system?
questions.option_a: Smaller page size increases internal fragmentation and reduces the page table size
questions.option_b: Larger page size reduces internal fragmentation but increases the page table size
questions.option_c: Larger page size may increase internal fragmentation but reduces page table size and TLB pressure
questions.option_d: Smaller page size improves disk I/O performance during page fault handling
questions.explanation: Larger pages mean fewer entries in the page table (reducing table size and TLB entries needed), but waste more memory at the end of a last page (increased internal fragmentation). Disk I/O also transfers more useful data per fault.

questions.statement: In the context of I/O scheduling, what does the 'C-SCAN' algorithm do differently from 'SCAN'?
questions.option_a: C-SCAN services requests in both directions like SCAN but skips the middle of the disk
questions.option_b: C-SCAN moves in one direction, services all requests, then jumps back to the start without servicing on the return
questions.option_c: C-SCAN selects the closest request to the current head position rather than moving unidirectionally
questions.option_d: C-SCAN gives priority to newly arrived requests over requests already in the queue
questions.explanation: C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) moves in one direction, services all requests, then jumps back to the start of the disk without servicing on the return trip, providing more uniform wait times than SCAN's uneven treatment of requests near the middle.

questions.statement: What is 'demand paging with prepaging' and how does it improve performance?
questions.option_a: It replaces demand paging by loading all pages at startup to eliminate page faults
questions.option_b: It loads the faulted page and prefetches additional nearby pages to reduce future page faults
questions.option_c: It increases the page size dynamically when many page faults occur in a short period
questions.option_d: It priorities page loading for high-priority processes over lower-priority ones
questions.explanation: Prepaging extends demand paging by also loading pages likely to be needed soon (e.g., sequentially adjacent pages) along with the faulted page, exploiting spatial locality to reduce subsequent page faults.

questions.statement: In the context of OS protection rings, what is the significance of ring 0?
questions.option_a: It is the user application layer with the least privilege for security isolation
questions.option_b: It is the highest privilege level where the OS kernel runs with unrestricted hardware access
questions.option_c: It is a virtualization layer used only in hypervisor-based environments
questions.option_d: It is the interrupt handler layer that runs between kernel and user space
questions.explanation: Ring 0 (kernel mode) is the highest privilege level in x86 architecture. Code running in ring 0 has unrestricted access to all hardware and memory. User applications run in ring 3 with restricted access.

questions.statement: What does the acronym POSIX stand for in the context of operating systems?
questions.option_a: Portable Operating System Interface — a set of standards for Unix-compatible OS APIs
questions.option_b: Process Optimization Standard Interface — guidelines for efficient system call design
questions.option_c: Parallel Operations System Index — a benchmark for multi-core OS performance
questions.option_d: Platform-Oriented Software Interface eXchange — a protocol for OS-to-OS communication
questions.explanation: POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) is an IEEE standard defining the OS interface for Unix-compatible systems, ensuring software portability. The 'X' acknowledges Unix heritage. The other options are fabricated.

questions.statement: In process management, what is 'inter-process communication' (IPC) and which method is fastest for communicating between two processes on the same machine?
questions.option_a: IPC is thread synchronization; mutexes are fastest for same-machine communication
questions.option_b: IPC is the mechanism for processes to exchange data; shared memory is the fastest method
questions.option_c: IPC is the OS scheduling mechanism; pipes are fastest for same-machine communication
questions.option_d: IPC is the method for remote procedure calls; sockets are fastest for same-machine communication
questions.explanation: IPC allows processes to exchange data and synchronize. Shared memory is the fastest IPC method because it avoids copying — both processes map the same physical memory pages. Pipes and sockets involve data copying.

questions.statement: In a system using the clock page replacement algorithm, what does a reference bit value of 1 indicate?
questions.option_a: The page has not been accessed since it was loaded and is a good replacement candidate
questions.option_b: The page has been recently accessed and should be given another chance before replacement
questions.option_c: The page is currently locked in memory and cannot be replaced
questions.option_d: The page has been modified and must be written to disk before replacement
questions.explanation: The clock algorithm's reference bit is set to 1 by hardware when a page is accessed. During replacement, if a page's bit is 1, it is cleared (given a second chance) and the hand moves on. Pages with bit 0 are replaced.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the 'umask' value in Unix/Linux file permission management?
questions.option_a: It encrypts files with a specified key before writing them to disk
questions.option_b: It defines the permissions that are removed (masked out) when new files are created
questions.option_c: It specifies the minimum permissions required to read a file
questions.option_d: It sets the maximum permission level a user can grant to their own files
questions.explanation: The umask (user file creation mask) specifies which permission bits are turned off when new files or directories are created. A umask of 022 removes write permission for group and others from new files (666 & ~022 = 644).

questions.statement: In a preemptive scheduling environment, a process's priority is dynamically adjusted based on how much CPU time it has consumed recently. What type of scheduling does this describe?
questions.option_a: Fixed Priority Scheduling
questions.option_b: Multilevel Queue Scheduling
questions.option_c: Aging-based Priority Scheduling
questions.option_d: Dynamic Multilevel Feedback Queue Scheduling
questions.explanation: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) dynamically adjusts process priority based on CPU behavior — processes that use too much CPU time are moved to lower-priority queues; I/O-bound processes retain or gain priority.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the 'fork bomb' in the context of OS security?
questions.option_a: It is a technique to crash a process by writing to a null pointer
questions.option_b: It is a denial-of-service attack where a process recursively forks until system resources are exhausted
questions.option_c: It is a buffer overflow attack targeting the fork() system call implementation
questions.option_d: It is a method to escalate privileges by exploiting the parent-child process relationship
questions.explanation: A fork bomb (e.g., ':(){ :|:& };:' in bash) creates processes that recursively fork, exponentially consuming PIDs, memory, and CPU until the system becomes unresponsive. Resource limits (ulimit) can mitigate it.

questions.statement: In memory management, what is the 'resident set' of a process?
questions.option_a: The set of all pages ever accessed by a process during its entire lifetime
questions.option_b: The subset of a process's pages currently loaded in physical memory
questions.option_c: The set of pages a process is predicted to access in the near future
questions.option_d: The set of pages that have been modified and must be written back to disk
questions.explanation: The resident set is the collection of a process's pages currently in physical memory (RAM). A small resident set increases page faults; too large a resident set reduces the number of processes that can run concurrently.

questions.statement: What distinguishes a 'kernel thread' from a 'user thread' with regard to blocking system calls?
questions.option_a: Both kernel and user threads block all threads in the process when one makes a blocking call
questions.option_b: A kernel thread blocking on a system call does not block other kernel threads; a user thread blocking may block all user threads in the process
questions.option_c: A user thread can make blocking calls without affecting other user threads due to hardware support
questions.option_d: Kernel threads cannot make blocking system calls as they run in privileged mode
questions.explanation: Kernel threads are managed by the OS — blocking one does not affect others. With user threads on a many-to-one model, one blocking call (which the kernel sees as a process block) stops all threads in that process.

questions.statement: In the context of operating system design, what is a 'system call' and why must it use a controlled entry mechanism?
questions.option_a: A system call is an API function that any application can call to run kernel code directly
questions.option_b: A system call is a controlled interface allowing user programs to request privileged OS services via a trap instruction
questions.option_c: A system call is a direct memory access mechanism for user programs to read kernel data structures
questions.option_d: A system call is a signal sent between processes to coordinate concurrent execution
questions.explanation: A system call uses a trap (software interrupt) to safely transfer execution to the kernel at a predefined entry point. Controlled entry prevents user programs from jumping to arbitrary kernel addresses, which would be a security vulnerability.

questions.statement: In the context of process synchronization, what is the 'test-and-set' instruction, and why is hardware support required?
questions.option_a: It is a high-level synchronization construct that requires OS kernel support
questions.option_b: It is an atomic instruction that reads a memory word and sets it to true in a single indivisible operation
questions.option_c: It is a software-only solution that uses busy-waiting to implement mutual exclusion
questions.option_d: It is a memory fence instruction that ensures write ordering across CPU cores
questions.explanation: test-and-set is a hardware-supported atomic instruction: it reads the current value of a memory location and sets it to 1 in one uninterruptible step. Hardware atomicity is necessary because a non-atomic read-then-write creates a race condition.

questions.statement: In the context of file systems, what is the primary purpose of a 'directory'?
questions.option_a: To store the actual binary content of files in a structured format
questions.option_b: To map human-readable file names to inode numbers or other file identifiers
questions.option_c: To define the access permissions for groups of related files
questions.option_d: To allocate disk blocks for new files created in the file system
questions.explanation: A directory is a special file that stores mappings from file names to inode numbers (or other identifiers). It allows the OS to translate a human-readable path into the internal identifier for a file's metadata.

questions.statement: What is the main purpose of 'virtual memory' in modern operating systems?
questions.option_a: To provide a backup of physical memory contents to disk for fault tolerance
questions.option_b: To give each process the illusion of a large, private address space independent of physical RAM size
questions.option_c: To increase CPU cache size by using RAM as a second-level cache
questions.option_d: To allow multiple operating systems to run simultaneously on the same physical hardware
questions.explanation: Virtual memory provides each process with an isolated virtual address space that can be larger than physical RAM. The OS maps virtual pages to physical frames on demand, enabling process isolation and efficient memory use.

questions.statement: In the context of CPU scheduling metrics, what does 'throughput' measure?
questions.option_a: The total time from process submission to its completion
questions.option_b: The fraction of time the CPU is executing user processes (not idle)
questions.option_c: The number of processes completed per unit of time
questions.option_d: The average time a process spends waiting in the ready queue
questions.explanation: Throughput measures the number of processes completed per unit time. It is a system-level performance metric. Turnaround time measures per-process time; CPU utilization measures idleness; waiting time is queue delay.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of 'page table base register' (PTBR) in memory management?
questions.option_a: It caches the most recently accessed page table entries for TLB misses
questions.option_b: It stores the physical address of the page table for the currently running process
questions.option_c: It defines the maximum allowed page table size for a process
questions.option_d: It contains the base address of the physical memory frame allocation pool
questions.explanation: The PTBR (CR3 in x86) stores the physical base address of the page table for the currently executing process. During a context switch, the PTBR is updated to point to the new process's page table.

questions.statement: In the context of file systems, what is the advantage of 'indexed allocation' over linked allocation?
questions.option_a: Indexed allocation avoids the overhead of maintaining a separate index block
questions.option_b: Indexed allocation supports direct random access to any block without sequential traversal
questions.option_c: Indexed allocation eliminates external fragmentation unlike linked allocation
questions.option_d: Indexed allocation allows files to grow dynamically without preallocating an index
questions.explanation: Indexed allocation stores all block pointers for a file in an index block, enabling O(1) random access to any file block. Linked allocation requires traversing the linked list to reach the nth block, which is O(n).

questions.statement: In the context of real-time operating systems, what does 'rate monotonic scheduling' (RMS) assign as priority?
questions.option_a: Priority is assigned based on deadlines — the task with the earliest deadline runs first
questions.option_b: Priority is fixed and inversely proportional to period — shorter period tasks get higher priority
questions.option_c: Priority is dynamically assigned based on CPU utilization of each real-time task
questions.option_d: Priority is assigned based on worst-case execution time — shortest execution gets highest priority
questions.explanation: RMS assigns fixed priorities inversely proportional to the task period (shorter period = higher priority). It is optimal among fixed-priority algorithms and can guarantee schedulability for task sets with utilization ≤ ln(2) ≈ 69.3%.

questions.statement: What is the key issue with 'busy-waiting' (spinlock) synchronization and when is it acceptable?
questions.option_a: Busy-waiting blocks the process in the OS scheduler and prevents context switches
questions.option_b: Busy-waiting wastes CPU cycles continuously checking a condition; it is acceptable when the wait time is very short relative to context switch cost
questions.option_c: Busy-waiting prevents deadlocks because the process never sleeps while holding a lock
questions.option_d: Busy-waiting always deadlocks when two threads each spin waiting for the other
questions.explanation: Spinlocks waste CPU cycles looping while waiting, but on multiprocessors where the wait is expected to be shorter than a context switch overhead, spinning is more efficient than sleeping and re-scheduling.

questions.statement: In a system with 2 CPUs and 4 threads, what is the maximum level of true parallelism achievable?
questions.option_a: 1 thread at a time because the OS serializes all thread execution
questions.option_b: 2 threads simultaneously, one per CPU core
questions.option_c: 4 threads simultaneously because all can run on separate hardware
questions.option_d: 3 threads simultaneously because one CPU handles OS overhead
questions.explanation: True parallelism requires separate CPU cores. With 2 CPUs, exactly 2 threads can execute simultaneously. The remaining threads wait in the ready queue. More CPUs would be needed for greater parallelism.

questions.statement: In memory management, what is the difference between 'first fit' and 'best fit' allocation strategies?
questions.option_a: First fit always results in less fragmentation than best fit over time
questions.option_b: First fit allocates the first partition large enough; best fit allocates the smallest sufficient partition
questions.option_c: First fit is faster than best fit but uses more total memory for each allocation
questions.option_d: Best fit always results in faster allocation but more total wasted memory
questions.explanation: First fit searches from the beginning and allocates the first hole large enough (O(n) in worst case but faster on average). Best fit searches all holes and picks the smallest sufficient one, minimizing wasted space per allocation.

questions.statement: What is the primary function of the 'interrupt handler' (ISR) in an operating system?
questions.option_a: To check for errors in all I/O operations currently in progress
questions.option_b: To respond to hardware interrupts by saving CPU state and executing the appropriate service routine
questions.option_c: To prevent user processes from executing system calls during critical kernel operations
questions.option_d: To schedule the next process to run when the current process yields the CPU
questions.explanation: When a hardware interrupt occurs, the CPU automatically saves its state and transfers control to the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). The ISR handles the event (e.g., I/O completion), then restores CPU state and resumes.

questions.statement: In the context of threading models, what does 'many-to-many' thread mapping achieve?
questions.option_a: Multiple user threads are multiplexed onto a single kernel thread for efficiency
questions.option_b: Multiple user threads are multiplexed across a pool of kernel threads, allowing true parallelism and non-blocking
questions.option_c: Each user thread maps to exactly one kernel thread for maximum kernel visibility
questions.option_d: Each kernel thread maps to many user threads running sequentially on one CPU
questions.explanation: The many-to-many (M:N) model maps M user threads to N kernel threads (N ≤ M). This allows true parallelism across CPUs while enabling blocking calls to not block all threads, combining benefits of both models.

questions.statement: In disk management, what is the purpose of 'disk formatting' and what are its two levels?
questions.option_a: Low-level: initializes hardware sectors; High-level: creates the file system structure
questions.option_b: Low-level: defragments disk blocks; High-level: encrypts the partition
questions.option_c: Low-level: tests disk sectors; High-level: partitions the disk into volumes
questions.option_d: Low-level: creates the file system; High-level: installs the OS bootloader
questions.explanation: Low-level (physical) formatting initializes sectors with headers, trailers, and error correction codes on the physical disk. High-level (logical) formatting installs the file system structure (superblock, inodes, etc.) on a partition.

questions.statement: What is the distinction between 'protection' and 'security' in operating systems?
questions.option_a: Protection refers to network security; security refers to memory isolation
questions.option_b: Protection is the OS mechanism controlling process access to resources; security deals with defending against malicious threats
questions.option_c: Protection encrypts user data; security provides authentication for login
questions.option_d: Protection prevents hardware failures; security prevents software bugs
questions.explanation: Protection is the internal OS mechanism that controls which processes can access which resources (e.g., access control, memory boundaries). Security is the broader concern of defending the system against external threats and malicious users.

questions.statement: In the context of process states, what does it mean for a process to be in the 'new' state?
questions.option_a: The process has been created and is ready to be scheduled for CPU execution
questions.option_b: The process is being created and its PCB and resources are being initialized
questions.option_c: The process has completed execution and is waiting for its parent to collect its exit status
questions.option_d: The process has been swapped out to disk by the medium-term scheduler
questions.explanation: The 'new' state means the process is being created — the OS is initializing its PCB, allocating its address space, and loading the program. It transitions to 'ready' once initialization is complete.

questions.statement: What mechanism does the OS use to prevent a process from accessing memory belonging to another process?
questions.option_a: Process isolation is enforced by the compiler by generating bounds-checked code
questions.option_b: Hardware memory protection uses base/limit registers or page tables to trap illegal accesses
questions.option_c: All processes run in the same address space but use software flags to indicate ownership
questions.option_d: The OS periodically scans all memory accesses and terminates processes that access wrong memory
questions.explanation: Hardware memory protection via base/limit registers (in simple systems) or page tables (in virtual memory systems) ensures that any attempt by a process to access memory outside its allocated range causes a trap to the OS.

questions.statement: In CPU scheduling, what is 'turnaround time' for a process?
questions.option_a: The time a process spends waiting in the ready queue for CPU
questions.option_b: The time from process submission to process completion
questions.option_c: The time the process is actively executing on the CPU
questions.option_d: The time between a process's creation and its first execution on the CPU
questions.explanation: Turnaround time = completion time - arrival time. It encompasses waiting in the ready queue, executing on the CPU, and waiting for I/O. It is the key metric for batch system performance evaluation.

questions.statement: In the context of file system recovery, what is the difference between 'journaling' and 'checkpointing'?
questions.option_a: Journaling records disk block changes; checkpointing records CPU register states
questions.option_b: Journaling logs operations before they commit for crash recovery; checkpointing saves a consistent snapshot of the file system state periodically
questions.option_c: Journaling defragments the file system during idle periods; checkpointing compresses old log entries
questions.option_d: Journaling is used only for metadata; checkpointing protects both metadata and file data
questions.explanation: Journaling (write-ahead logging) records intended operations before execution, enabling replay after a crash. Checkpointing creates periodic consistent snapshots of the file system, allowing recovery to the last checkpoint.

questions.statement: What does 'demand segmentation' combine with demand paging to address in memory management?
questions.option_a: It combines fixed-size allocation with demand loading to eliminate both fragmentation types
questions.option_b: It uses variable-size logical segments as the unit of memory management, loading segments on demand
questions.option_c: It uses large segments to reduce the number of page table entries needed
questions.option_d: It eliminates the need for the TLB by using hardware segment registers for all translations
questions.explanation: Demand segmentation uses the programmer-visible segment (code, stack, data, heap) as the unit of allocation and loads segments on demand. When combined with paging (segmented paging), it provides logical structure with efficient memory use.

questions.statement: In an OS with round-robin scheduling, what is the effect of setting the time quantum too small?
questions.option_a: CPU utilization improves because processes switch more frequently
questions.option_b: Context switch overhead dominates, reducing CPU efficiency for useful work
questions.option_c: Process response time increases because each process waits longer between turns
questions.option_d: The CPU scheduler selects longer processes more often to reduce switching
questions.explanation: An extremely small quantum means the CPU spends most time doing context switches (saving/loading registers and updating memory maps) rather than executing process instructions, dramatically reducing throughput.

questions.statement: In the context of OS design, what is the 'kernel' responsible for?
questions.option_a: Rendering the user interface and managing window display on screen
questions.option_b: Managing hardware resources, process scheduling, memory management, and providing system call interfaces
questions.option_c: Compiling and linking user application code for hardware-specific execution
questions.option_d: Enforcing software license agreements and access control for installed applications
questions.explanation: The kernel is the core of the OS and manages hardware abstraction, CPU scheduling, memory management, I/O device management, and provides the system call interface through which applications access OS services.

questions.statement: Which of the following is the PRIMARY role of an operating system?
questions.option_a: Execute user applications directly
questions.option_b: Act as an intermediary between hardware and user applications, managing resources
questions.option_c: Provide antivirus protection for the system
questions.option_d: Connect the computer to the internet
questions.explanation: The OS abstracts hardware complexity, manages resources (CPU, memory, storage, I/O), and provides a consistent environment for applications. Without the OS, every application would need its own hardware drivers.

questions.statement: A system call differs from a regular function call because:
questions.option_a: System calls are faster than regular function calls
questions.option_b: System calls cause a switch from user mode to kernel mode, allowing restricted access to OS services
questions.option_c: System calls cannot return values to the calling application
questions.option_d: System calls are only available in compiled languages
questions.explanation: System calls cross the privilege boundary. The SYSCALL/INT instruction triggers a hardware-enforced switch from ring 3 (user mode) to ring 0 (kernel mode). The kernel validates the request and performs the privileged operation. Regular function calls stay within the same privilege level.

questions.statement: What is the difference between a program and a process?
questions.option_a: A program is written in high-level language; a process is machine code
questions.option_b: A program is a static file on disk; a process is a running instance of a program with state, resources, and a PCB
questions.option_c: A process is always more secure than a program
questions.option_d: Programs can only run once; processes can run multiple times
questions.explanation: A program (firefox.exe) is a static file. A process is a dynamic execution — it has a process ID, state (running/waiting), allocated memory, open files, and a PCB. Running Firefox twice creates two processes from the same program.

questions.statement: Which process state indicates the process is waiting for an I/O operation to complete?
questions.option_a: Ready
questions.option_b: Running
questions.option_c: Waiting (Blocked)
questions.option_d: Suspended
questions.explanation: Waiting/Blocked: the process cannot proceed until an event (I/O completion, timer, signal) occurs. It's removed from the ready queue and placed in a waiting queue for the specific event. When I/O completes, it moves back to Ready.

questions.statement: In a system with one CPU, how many processes can be in the "Running" state simultaneously?
questions.option_a: As many as needed
questions.option_b: Limited only by available memory
questions.option_c: Exactly one
questions.option_d: One per user logged in
questions.explanation: One CPU can execute exactly one instruction stream at a time. Only ONE process can be in the Running state on a single-core CPU at any instant. Multiple CPUs/cores would allow multiple simultaneous running processes (one per core).

questions.statement: What does fork() return to the CHILD process?
questions.option_a: The child's PID
questions.option_b: The parent's PID
questions.option_d: -1 (indicating it's the child)
questions.explanation: fork() returns different values to parent and child. To parent: child's PID (positive number). To child: 0. This is how parent and child distinguish themselves — check the return value. -1 means fork() failed (no new process created).

questions.statement: A "zombie process" occurs when:
questions.option_a: A malware process pretends to be a legitimate system process
questions.option_b: A process has terminated but its parent hasn't called wait() to collect the exit status
questions.option_c: A process is waiting indefinitely for a resource
questions.option_d: A process consumes excessive CPU time
questions.explanation: Zombie: terminated process whose PCB hasn't been cleaned up. Exit status is preserved until the parent calls wait(). Zombie consumes minimal resources (just the PCB entry) but occupies a PID. If the parent terminates without calling wait(), the orphaned zombie is reparented to PID 1 (init/systemd) which reaps it.

questions.statement: Round Robin scheduling is particularly suited for:
questions.option_a: Batch processing systems with long jobs
questions.option_b: Real-time systems requiring deterministic response
questions.option_c: Time-sharing/interactive systems requiring good response time for all users
questions.option_d: Single-user desktop systems with one process at a time
questions.explanation: RR gives each process a time quantum (10-100ms), then preempts and runs the next. No process waits too long — excellent response time. Suitable for interactive systems (servers, desktops). Batch systems prefer SJF/priority for throughput. Real-time systems use specialized schedulers.

questions.statement: Belady's Anomaly affects which page replacement algorithm?
questions.option_a: OPT (Optimal)
questions.option_b: LRU (Least Recently Used)
questions.option_c: FIFO (First In First Out)
questions.option_d: Clock (Second Chance)
questions.explanation: Belady's Anomaly: for FIFO, adding MORE physical frames can actually INCREASE page faults. LRU and OPT do not suffer from this anomaly (they are "stack algorithms"). This counterintuitive behavior is one reason FIFO is not commonly used.

questions.statement: A "critical section" in the context of concurrent programming is:
questions.option_a: The most important function in a program
questions.option_b: Code that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by multiple threads simultaneously
questions.option_c: Sections of the OS kernel that are protected from user access
questions.option_d: Code that cannot be optimized by the compiler
questions.explanation: Critical section: the region of code accessing shared mutable state (shared variables, files, data structures). Only ONE thread at a time should execute any process's critical section. Synchronization mechanisms (mutex, semaphore) protect critical sections.

questions.statement: The four necessary conditions for deadlock are:
questions.option_a: Mutual exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
questions.option_b: Starvation, Livelock, Priority Inversion, Resource Exhaustion
questions.option_c: Concurrency, Synchronization, Communication, Coordination
questions.option_d: CPU Bound, I/O Bound, Memory Bound, Network Bound
questions.explanation: Coffman conditions (1971): ALL four must hold simultaneously for deadlock. Eliminating ANY one prevents deadlock. Mutual Exclusion (resources not shareable), Hold and Wait (holding resources while waiting), No Preemption (resources can't be forcibly taken), Circular Wait (cyclic dependency).

questions.statement: Banker's Algorithm is used for:
questions.option_a: Detecting deadlocks after they occur
questions.option_b: Preventing deadlocks by rejecting resource allocation requests that would lead to unsafe states
questions.option_c: Recovering from deadlocks by terminating processes
questions.option_d: Encrypting financial transactions in banking software
questions.explanation: Banker's Algorithm (Dijkstra): deadlock AVOIDANCE. Before granting a resource request, simulate the allocation and check if the resulting state is "safe" (a safe execution sequence exists for all processes). If safe: grant. If unsafe: make the requesting process wait. Named after analogy to a banker who won't lend money if it would prevent meeting all customers' maximum demands.

questions.statement: Virtual memory allows:
questions.option_a: Multiple CPUs to share the same memory space
questions.option_b: Processes to use more memory than physically available by storing inactive pages on disk
questions.option_c: Memory to be accessed more quickly through caching
questions.option_d: Different processes to directly access each other's memory
questions.explanation: Virtual memory creates the illusion of a large address space. Only active pages need to be in RAM. Inactive pages are stored on swap space (disk). The OS pages data in/out as needed. A 32-bit process can have 4GB virtual address space even if the machine has 1GB RAM.

questions.statement: A TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) improves performance by:
questions.option_a: Increasing physical memory capacity
questions.option_b: Caching recent virtual-to-physical address translations to avoid slow page table lookups in memory
questions.option_c: Buffering disk I/O requests for batch processing
questions.option_d: Translating high-level language instructions to machine code
questions.explanation: Without TLB: every memory access = 2 memory accesses (page table lookup + actual access) — 2× overhead. TLB caches recent translations. With ~99% hit rate, effective access time ≈ normal access time. TLB is in CPU hardware, extremely fast (1-2 cycles).

questions.statement: When a page fault occurs:
questions.option_a: The CPU resets and the program crashes
questions.option_b: The OS detects the page is not in RAM, fetches it from disk, updates the page table, and restarts the faulting instruction
questions.option_c: The process is terminated due to invalid memory access
questions.option_d: The TLB flushes all cached entries
questions.explanation: Page fault is handled transparently: (1) MMU detects page not in RAM, triggers trap. (2) OS page fault handler runs. (3) OS finds page on disk (swap). (4) Evicts a page if necessary. (5) Loads requested page from disk to a frame. (6) Updates page table. (7) Restarts the instruction. Process resumes as if nothing happened — just slightly slower.

questions.statement: "Thrashing" in virtual memory systems occurs when:
questions.option_a: Excessive context switches waste CPU time
questions.option_b: A process page faults constantly because it has fewer frames than its working set needs
questions.option_c: The OS uses too much memory for its own data structures
questions.option_d: Disk I/O speed is a bottleneck for system performance
questions.explanation: Thrashing: process spends more time handling page faults than executing. Every few instructions: page fault → wait for disk → bring in page → evict another page → soon need that evicted page → another page fault. CPU utilization drops to near zero. Fix: increase physical RAM or reduce multiprogramming degree.

questions.statement: In Linux file permissions, chmod 644 file.txt sets:
questions.option_a: Owner: rwx, Group: r, Others: r
questions.option_b: Owner: rw, Group: r, Others: r
questions.option_c: Owner: rw, Group: rw, Others: r
questions.option_d: Owner: r, Group: rw, Others: rw
questions.explanation: Octal 644: 6=rw, 4=r, 4=r. Owner: read+write (6=4+2). Group: read only (4). Others: read only (4). Standard for data files — owner can read and write, everyone else can read only.

questions.statement: What does the inode in a Unix file system store?
questions.option_a: The file's name and directory location
questions.option_b: File metadata (permissions, timestamps, size, owner) and pointers to data blocks — but NOT the filename
questions.option_c: The file's actual content
questions.option_d: The file's encryption key
questions.explanation: Inode contains: file type, permissions, owner/group, timestamps (atime/mtime/ctime), link count, size, and direct/indirect pointers to data blocks. Notably, the filename is NOT in the inode — it's in the directory entry that maps name → inode number. Hard links work by having multiple directory entries point to the same inode.

questions.statement: RAID 5 requires a minimum of how many disks?
questions.option_a: 2 disks
questions.option_b: 3 disks
questions.option_c: 4 disks
questions.option_d: 5 disks
questions.explanation: RAID 5 uses distributed parity. With N disks, usable capacity = (N-1) × disk_size. Minimum: 3 disks — 2 for data, 1 equivalent for distributed parity. With 3 × 1TB drives: 2TB usable, survives 1 drive failure. RAID 6 requires minimum 4 disks.

questions.statement: DMA (Direct Memory Access) reduces CPU load by:
questions.option_a: Allowing multiple processes to access memory simultaneously
questions.option_b: Letting a dedicated DMA controller transfer data between devices and memory without CPU involvement for each byte
questions.option_c: Caching frequently accessed data in CPU registers
questions.option_d: Compressing data to reduce the amount that needs to be transferred
questions.explanation: DMA: CPU programs the DMA controller (source, destination, byte count), then does other work. DMA controller performs the entire transfer independently. CPU only involved at start (setup) and end (completion interrupt). Without DMA: CPU must move every byte — completely occupied during large transfers.

questions.statement: The "convoy effect" in FCFS scheduling occurs when:
questions.option_a: Processes are scheduled in the wrong priority order
questions.option_b: Short processes are stuck waiting behind a long CPU-bound process
questions.option_c: Too many processes are in the waiting state simultaneously
questions.option_d: The OS scheduler makes convoy (group) decisions instead of individual ones
questions.explanation: Convoy effect: if P1 (burst=24ms) arrives first, then P2 (3ms) and P3 (3ms), P2 and P3 wait 24ms each. Average wait = 17ms. If scheduled in order P2, P3, P1: average wait = 3ms. The long process "convoys" all subsequent processes — FCFS unfair to short processes.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a "semaphore" in OS synchronization?
questions.option_a: A signal for inter-process communication over networks
questions.option_b: An integer variable with atomic wait() and signal() operations used to control access to shared resources
questions.option_c: A hardware timer used by the scheduler for time-slicing
questions.option_d: A flag indicating that a process is waiting for I/O
questions.explanation: Semaphore (Dijkstra): integer S. wait(S): if S>0, S--; else block. signal(S): S++; if threads blocked, wake one. Binary semaphore (0/1) acts as mutex. Counting semaphore (N) allows N concurrent accesses. Used to solve producer-consumer, reader-writer, and other synchronization problems.

questions.statement: Which scheduling algorithm is provably optimal (minimizes average waiting time) but impractical to implement?
questions.option_a: Round Robin
questions.option_b: First Come First Served
questions.option_c: Shortest Job First (non-preemptive)
questions.option_d: Priority Scheduling
questions.explanation: SJF is provably optimal for minimizing average waiting time. Impractical: requires knowing each process's next CPU burst in advance. We can estimate (exponential averaging) but not know exactly. Preemptive SJF (SRTF) is also optimal but preemptive.

questions.statement: What is "thrashing" and what is the primary solution?
questions.option_a: Excessive context switching; solution is fewer processes
questions.option_b: Too many page faults because processes have insufficient physical memory; solution is adding more RAM or reducing multiprogramming degree
questions.option_c: Disk I/O overload; solution is faster disks
questions.option_d: Network congestion in distributed systems; solution is better bandwidth
questions.explanation: Thrashing: working set (active pages needed) exceeds available frames. Constant page faults. Solution: (1) Add physical RAM (most effective), (2) Reduce number of simultaneous processes (fewer processes sharing RAM), (3) Use working set model to ensure each process has enough frames.

questions.statement: In the context of OS memory management, what is "external fragmentation"?
questions.option_a: Wasted space within allocated memory blocks
questions.option_b: Memory fragmented between CPU caches
questions.option_c: Free memory that exists in small, non-contiguous pieces and cannot satisfy large allocation requests
questions.option_d: Memory pages stored on external (disk) storage
questions.explanation: External fragmentation: total free memory is sufficient for a request, but it's scattered in small non-contiguous pieces. A request for 100MB contiguous memory fails even if 200MB is free in small chunks. Solved by paging (no need for contiguous memory) or compaction (expensive — move processes to consolidate free space).

questions.statement: A mutex differs from a semaphore in that:
questions.option_a: Mutexes are for inter-process communication; semaphores are for intra-process synchronization
questions.option_b: A mutex must be released by the same thread that acquired it (ownership); semaphores can be signaled by any thread
questions.option_c: Mutexes allow multiple concurrent accesses; semaphores allow only one
questions.option_d: They are identical — mutex is just another name for a binary semaphore
questions.explanation: Mutex ownership: the thread that locks the mutex must unlock it. Prevents one thread from releasing a lock held by another thread. Binary semaphore has no ownership — any thread can signal it. This matters for priority inheritance (to solve priority inversion) which requires knowing who holds the mutex.

questions.statement: What is "priority inversion" and how is it addressed?
questions.option_a: Low-priority processes are incorrectly given high priority; addressed by re-examining scheduling policy
questions.option_b: A high-priority process waits for a resource held by a low-priority process, which is in turn preempted by medium-priority processes; addressed by priority inheritance
questions.option_c: Process priorities are inverted from what was requested; addressed by priority verification
questions.option_d: High priority processes always run last; addressed by priority reversal
questions.explanation: Priority inversion: HP (high-priority) needs resource held by LP (low-priority). MP (medium-priority) preempts LP (higher priority than LP, lower than HP). LP can't release the resource while preempted. HP is effectively blocked by MP — inversion! Priority inheritance: LP temporarily inherits HP's priority until it releases the resource. Famous case: Mars Pathfinder (1997) experienced priority inversion.

questions.statement: Journaling in file systems (ext4, NTFS) provides what benefit?
questions.option_a: Faster write performance through write caching
questions.option_b: Faster recovery after a crash — the journal records intended changes, enabling consistent state restoration without full disk scan
questions.option_c: Automatic file defragmentation
questions.option_d: Encryption of sensitive file data
questions.explanation: Journaling: before modifying file system structures, write a journal entry describing the intended changes. If crash occurs: journal is replayed (changes committed or rolled back). No need for lengthy fsck scan. Recovery takes seconds instead of potentially hours (for large disks without journaling).

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the "working set" concept in virtual memory management?
questions.option_a: The set of programs currently running on the system
questions.option_b: The set of pages a process is actively using in a given time interval — used to determine how many frames a process needs
questions.option_c: The maximum amount of work a CPU can perform per second
questions.option_d: The set of system calls a process is allowed to make
questions.explanation: Working set W(t, Δ): pages referenced in the time interval [t-Δ, t]. Allocate at least working_set_size frames to each process. If allocated frames < working set → thrashing. Working set model: dynamically adjust frame allocation based on actual usage patterns.

questions.statement: In virtual memory, what is "copy-on-write" (CoW)?
questions.option_a: All memory writes are copied to backup storage immediately
questions.option_b: After fork(), parent and child share the same physical pages read-only; a copy is made only when a process tries to write
questions.option_c: File writes are copied to a transaction log before being applied
questions.option_d: CPU writes to memory are copied to a cache first
questions.explanation: CoW optimization for fork(): instead of immediately copying all parent's memory to child (expensive), mark all shared pages as read-only. If either process reads: use the shared page (fast). If either process WRITES: THEN make a copy of that specific page and give the writing process its own copy. For exec() after fork(), most pages are never written — CoW makes fork() nearly free.

questions.statement: An LRU page replacement algorithm works by:
questions.option_a: Replacing the page that was loaded first (oldest)
questions.option_b: Replacing the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future
questions.option_c: Replacing the page that was used least recently (hasn't been accessed for the longest time)
questions.option_d: Replacing a random page to minimize implementation complexity
questions.explanation: LRU (Least Recently Used): evict the page whose last access was furthest in the past. Based on temporal locality — recently used pages are likely to be used again. Good approximation of OPT. Expensive to implement exactly (need timestamp per access). Clock algorithm approximates LRU efficiently.

questions.statement: What is the difference between RAID 0 and RAID 1?
questions.option_a: RAID 0 is older; RAID 1 is a newer version
questions.option_b: RAID 0 stripes data for performance with NO redundancy; RAID 1 mirrors data for redundancy with NO performance gain for writes
questions.option_c: RAID 0 uses parity; RAID 1 uses striping
questions.option_d: RAID 1 is faster than RAID 0 for all operations
questions.explanation: RAID 0 (striping): write/read speed × number of disks, but no redundancy — one disk fails → ALL data lost. RAID 1 (mirroring): full copy on each disk — one disk fails → other still has data. Read speed can double (can read from either disk). Write speed same as one disk (must write to both).

questions.statement: The "no preemption" condition required for deadlock means:
questions.option_a: The OS scheduler cannot interrupt a running process
questions.option_b: Resources held by a process cannot be forcibly taken away — the process must voluntarily release them
questions.option_c: Threads cannot preempt each other during critical sections
questions.option_d: I/O operations cannot be interrupted once started
questions.explanation: No preemption: a process holding resource R cannot have R forcibly taken. It must explicitly release it. Violating this condition (allowing preemption) is one way to prevent deadlock — take resources from blocked processes and give to waiting ones (only feasible for some resource types).

questions.statement: What does ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) prevent?
questions.option_a: Stack overflow due to deep recursion
questions.option_b: Exploitation of buffer overflows by randomizing memory layout — attackers can't hardcode exploit addresses
questions.option_c: Unauthorized access to other processes' memory
questions.option_d: Memory leaks in long-running applications
questions.explanation: ASLR: each time a program runs, the stack, heap, and library base addresses are randomized. Exploit code that hardcodes "jump to address 0xbffff890" fails because the stack is at a different address this run. Combined with NX bit (non-executable memory), makes exploitation dramatically harder.

questions.statement: A monolithic kernel differs from a microkernel in that:
questions.option_a: Monolithic kernels are smaller and more efficient
questions.option_b: All OS services run in kernel space in a monolithic kernel; microkernels move most services to user space
questions.option_c: Monolithic kernels support more hardware
questions.option_d: Microkernels are older than monolithic kernels
questions.explanation: Monolithic: everything in one big kernel program — process scheduling, memory management, file systems, device drivers, networking. Fast but: bug anywhere can crash everything. Microkernel: only core services (scheduling, memory, IPC) in kernel. Others (file systems, device drivers) as user-space servers. More fault-isolated but IPC overhead.

questions.statement: In Linux, what does the command kill -9 PID do?
questions.option_a: Pauses the process with the given PID
questions.option_b: Sends SIGKILL to the process — immediately terminates it; cannot be caught or ignored
questions.option_c: Removes the process from the scheduler for 9 seconds
questions.option_d: Reduces the process's priority by 9
questions.explanation: kill sends signals. Signal 9 = SIGKILL. Unlike other signals (which processes can catch and handle gracefully), SIGKILL is handled directly by the kernel — the process is immediately terminated with no chance to clean up. Use when a process doesn't respond to SIGTERM (signal 15 — graceful termination request).

questions.statement: What is "internal fragmentation" in memory management?
questions.option_a: Memory fragmentation inside the OS kernel
questions.option_b: Wasted space WITHIN allocated memory blocks — when allocated block is larger than requested size
questions.option_c: Memory fragmented between multiple processes
questions.option_d: Fragmented data within a single file on disk
questions.explanation: Internal fragmentation: allocated memory is larger than needed. In fixed partitioning: 100MB partition for a 70MB process wastes 30MB internally. In paging: last page of a process may be partially filled — a 1-byte file occupies a full 4KB page, wasting 4,095 bytes. External fragmentation is the opposite: free space fragmented between allocations.

questions.statement: The Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling algorithm suffers from what problem?
questions.option_a: Long processes never get CPU time (starvation)
questions.option_b: Short processes never get CPU time
questions.option_c: Requires knowing the length of next CPU burst in advance, which is not generally known
questions.option_d: Cannot handle processes with different priorities
questions.explanation: SJF requires the next CPU burst duration. We can only ESTIMATE this (using exponential averaging of past bursts). For exact SJF, starvation of long processes is also a concern if short jobs keep arriving. Non-preemptive SJF: once a job starts, it runs to completion of its burst — so long jobs eventually run.

questions.statement: What is "swapping" in operating system memory management?
questions.option_a: Exchanging data between CPU registers and cache
questions.option_b: Moving an entire process from main memory to disk (and back) to free up memory for other processes
questions.option_c: Switching between two active processes
questions.option_d: Exchanging data between two running processes via shared memory
questions.explanation: Swapping: entire processes moved to a "swap area" on disk when memory is needed for other processes. When swapped process needs to run again, it's brought back to memory (may get a different physical location). Distinct from paging (which moves individual pages). Modern systems prefer paging over whole-process swapping.

questions.statement: In the producer-consumer problem, what prevents the producer from adding items when the buffer is FULL?
questions.option_a: A mutex that prevents both threads from accessing the buffer simultaneously
questions.option_b: A semaphore counting empty slots — initialized to buffer capacity; producer wait()s on it, blocking when count reaches 0
questions.option_c: A conditional variable that checks if count < capacity
questions.option_d: Memory protection that prevents writing beyond the buffer
questions.explanation: empty semaphore: initialized to N (buffer capacity). Producer: wait(empty) — decrements empty count (blocks if 0, meaning no empty slots). When consumer removes an item: signal(empty) — increments empty count (may unblock a waiting producer). The mutex provides exclusive access to the buffer itself.

questions.statement: What is "context switching" and what overhead does it introduce?
questions.option_a: Changing application windows in a GUI; introduces display refresh overhead
questions.option_b: Saving the current process's state (registers, PC) and loading another process's state; introduces pure overhead — no useful work done
questions.option_c: Switching between different programming contexts; no significant overhead
questions.option_d: Moving processes between CPU cores; introduces cache invalidation overhead
questions.explanation: Context switch: when OS preempts a running process to schedule another. Must: save all CPU registers + program counter to PCB, load new process's registers from its PCB. ~1-10 microseconds. During this time, no user-mode work is done. High context switch rate wastes CPU. Modern CPUs minimize overhead; hardware context switching (multiple register sets) exists in some CPUs.

questions.statement: The /proc filesystem in Linux contains:
questions.option_a: Processing scripts and batch job files
questions.option_b: Virtual files representing kernel data structures and process information — not real files on disk
questions.option_c: Temporary files created during process execution
questions.option_d: Configuration files for system processes
questions.explanation: /proc is a virtual filesystem (no disk storage). cat /proc/cpuinfo reads CPU info directly from kernel data structures. cat /proc/1234/status reads information about process 1234. cat /proc/meminfo reads memory statistics. All created dynamically by the kernel on access. Also /sys for hardware/device information.

questions.statement: What is "demand paging"?
questions.option_a: Pages are loaded when users request them via a special system call
questions.option_b: Pages are loaded into memory only when they are first accessed, not all at process startup
questions.option_c: Memory pages are dynamically allocated based on application demand
questions.option_d: The OS demands payment of memory from applications
questions.explanation: Demand paging: at process creation, only the minimum pages needed are loaded (or even none). When a page is accessed that isn't in memory → page fault → load from disk. Benefit: faster startup (don't need to load everything), less memory wasted (unused pages never loaded). Cost: initial page faults on first access to each page.

questions.statement: In disk scheduling, the C-SCAN algorithm provides what advantage over SCAN?
questions.option_a: Faster seek time by going in both directions
questions.option_b: More uniform wait time — by sweeping in one direction only and jumping back to the start, all disk locations have similar maximum wait time
questions.option_c: Better sequential read performance
questions.option_d: Lower CPU overhead for scheduling decisions
questions.explanation: SCAN sweeps back and forth — locations at the center of the disk are serviced twice as often as locations at the ends (served on both passes). C-SCAN: only services requests while moving in one direction. At the end, jumps back to start. Uniform service — each location is served approximately once per sweep. More fair.

questions.statement: What is a "race condition" in concurrent programming?
questions.option_a: Competition between two processes for CPU scheduling priority
questions.option_b: A situation where the outcome of concurrent operations depends on the unpredictable order of execution
questions.option_c: A performance issue where one process is faster than another
questions.option_d: Deadlock caused by two processes racing to acquire resources
questions.explanation: Race condition: when two or more threads access shared data and the result depends on the order of execution. Thread 1 reads X (10), Thread 2 reads X (10), Thread 1 writes X+1 (11), Thread 2 writes X+1 (11) — result is 11 instead of 12. The "race" between threads produced incorrect output. Solved by proper synchronization (mutex, semaphore).

questions.statement: Process creation via fork() creates a child process that:
questions.option_a: Shares all memory with the parent (no copying)
questions.option_b: Has a completely independent copy of the parent's address space
questions.option_c: Gets a copy-on-write view of the parent's address space, sharing physical pages until a write occurs
questions.option_d: Starts with an empty address space
questions.explanation: Modern fork() uses Copy-on-Write (CoW). Parent and child initially share the same physical pages (read-only). When either writes to a page, a private copy is made for the writing process. The pages are not copied until they need to diverge. Makes fork() fast — if followed by exec(), most pages are never written to (exec() replaces them anyway).

questions.statement: In the Readers-Writers problem, what is "second readers-writers" problem?
questions.option_a: A second version of the algorithm with improved performance
questions.option_b: Writers are given priority — once a writer is waiting, no new readers can start, preventing writer starvation
questions.option_c: Multiple writers are allowed simultaneously
questions.option_d: Both readers and writers have equal priority
questions.explanation: Second readers-writers: once a writer is waiting, new readers are blocked (even if current readers are active). Writer waits for current readers to finish, then gets exclusive access. Readers might starve if writers constantly arrive. First readers-writers: readers are prioritized — a reader never waits if only readers are active. Writers can starve.

questions.statement: What is the primary advantage of paging over contiguous memory allocation?
questions.option_a: Paging is faster for sequential access
questions.option_b: Paging eliminates external fragmentation — any page can go in any frame, no need for contiguous free memory
questions.option_c: Paging uses less memory overhead
questions.option_d: Paging improves CPU cache utilization
questions.explanation: Paging's key benefit: a 100MB process doesn't need 100MB of CONTIGUOUS physical memory. Its 25,000 pages can be scattered across any available frames. External fragmentation is eliminated. (Internal fragmentation remains — the last page may be partially full.)

questions.statement: The UEFI "Secure Boot" feature prevents:
