questions.option_a: Unauthorized user account creation during boot
questions.option_b: Booting from unauthorized/tampered bootloaders by checking digital signatures
questions.option_c: Network booting to prevent unauthorized remote access
questions.option_d: Hardware changes being made during the boot process
questions.explanation: Secure Boot: UEFI checks the digital signature of the bootloader (and optionally kernel) against a database of trusted signatures before executing. If the bootloader has been tampered with (rootkit/bootkit infection), its signature won't match → boot refused. Prevents persistent boot-level malware.

questions.statement: What is "address space layout" in the context of a process?
questions.option_a: The arrangement of files in the process's home directory
questions.option_b: The organization of a process's virtual memory into segments: text (code), data, heap, stack
questions.option_c: The physical memory map showing which RAM chips are installed
questions.option_d: The network addresses allocated to the process for communication
questions.explanation: A process's address space contains: Text/Code (read-only program instructions, low addresses), Data segment (initialized global variables), BSS (uninitialized globals), Heap (grows upward with malloc/new), Stack (grows downward with function calls and local variables). Understanding this layout is essential for understanding buffer overflows and memory corruption vulnerabilities.

questions.statement: A process's PCB (Process Control Block) stores:
questions.option_a: Data related only to process termination
questions.option_b: All information needed to manage the process: PID, state, program counter, registers, memory info, open files, scheduling info
questions.option_c: The history of the process's execution on disk
questions.option_d: The source code of the process
questions.explanation: All information needed to manage the process: PID, state, program counter, registers, memory info, open files, scheduling info.

questions.statement: Preemptive scheduling means:
questions.option_a: The OS can forcibly remove a running process from the CPU before it voluntarily releases it
questions.option_b: The process voluntarily yields the CPU
questions.option_c: The process pre-empts other tasks by increasing its priority
questions.option_d: The process executes without interruption
questions.explanation: The OS can forcibly remove a running process from the CPU before it voluntarily releases it.

questions.statement: The "ready queue" in process scheduling contains:
questions.option_a: Processes that have finished execution
questions.option_b: All processes that are ready to run and waiting for CPU time
questions.option_c: Processes waiting for I/O operations
questions.option_d: Processes in the suspended state
questions.explanation: All processes that are ready to run and waiting for CPU time.

questions.statement: A thread shares with its sibling threads within the same process:
questions.option_a: Its own stack and registers
questions.option_b: The entire CPU state
questions.option_c: Code, data (global variables), and open files
questions.option_d: Memory limits specific to the thread
questions.explanation: Code, data (global variables), and open files. Stack and registers are private.

questions.statement: "Aging" in scheduling prevents:
questions.option_a: Deadlock — by forcing process execution
questions.option_b: Starvation — gradually increasing the priority of processes that have waited a long time
questions.option_c: Thrashing — by paging out old data
questions.option_d: Priority inversion — by setting a maximum priority
questions.explanation: Starvation — gradually increasing the priority of processes that have waited a long time.

questions.statement: The SCAN disk scheduling algorithm is also known as:
questions.option_a: The elevator algorithm — moves in one direction servicing requests, then reverses
questions.option_b: The shortest seek time first algorithm
questions.option_c: The circular scan algorithm
questions.option_d: The sequential algorithm
questions.explanation: The elevator algorithm — moves in one direction servicing requests, then reverses.

questions.statement: In a page table, the "valid bit" indicates:
questions.option_a: If the page is executable
questions.option_b: Whether the page is currently in physical memory (1 = in memory, 0 = not in memory/paged out)
questions.option_c: If the page has been modified
questions.option_d: If the page is shared between processes
questions.explanation: Whether the page is currently in physical memory (1 = in memory, 0 = not in memory/paged out).

questions.statement: exec() after fork() in Unix:
questions.option_a: Ends the execution of the parent process
questions.option_b: Creates a new thread within the child process
questions.option_c: Replaces the child's address space with a new program, while inheriting file descriptors and PID
questions.option_d: Duplicates the parent's memory entirely
questions.explanation: Replaces the child's address space with a new program, while inheriting file descriptors and PID.

questions.statement: A "pipe" in Unix IPC provides:
questions.option_a: A unidirectional byte stream channel between two processes (e.g., parent to child)
questions.option_b: A bidirectional communication link for network traffic
questions.option_c: A mechanism for shared memory
questions.option_d: A way to signal hardware interrupts
questions.explanation: A unidirectional byte stream channel between two processes (e.g., parent to child).

questions.statement: Mutual exclusion in operating systems means:
questions.option_a: Processes must exclude each other from running simultaneously
questions.option_b: Only one process can be in its critical section at a time
questions.option_c: Resources are mutually shared between all processes
questions.option_d: No two processes can access the same file on disk
questions.explanation: Only one process can be in its critical section at a time.

questions.statement: The difference between kill and pkill in Linux:
questions.option_a: kill kills all processes; pkill kills only user processes
questions.option_b: kill targets by PID; pkill targets by process name
questions.option_c: kill stops a process temporarily; pkill kills it permanently
questions.option_d: kill requires root privileges; pkill does not
questions.explanation: kill targets by PID; pkill targets by process name.

questions.statement: "Garbage collection" in SSD management refers to:
questions.option_a: Deleting temporary files from the OS
questions.option_b: Cleaning up memory leaks in user applications
questions.option_c: Reclaiming flash blocks by copying valid pages to clean blocks, then erasing old blocks
questions.option_d: Removing orphaned process control blocks
questions.explanation: Reclaiming flash blocks by copying valid pages to clean blocks, then erasing old blocks.

questions.statement: What does ulimit control in Linux?
questions.option_a: User login limits
questions.option_b: Resource limits for processes: max open files, max memory, max CPU time, max stack size
questions.option_c: Network bandwidth usage
questions.option_d: The maximum length of command line arguments
questions.explanation: Resource limits for processes: max open files, max memory, max CPU time, max stack size.

questions.statement: The difference between a hard link and a symbolic link:
questions.option_a: Hard links point to directories; symbolic links point to files
questions.option_b: Hard link: another directory entry pointing to the SAME inode. Symbolic link: a file containing the path to another file
questions.option_c: Hard links can cross file systems; symbolic links cannot
questions.option_d: Symbolic links are faster than hard links
questions.explanation: Hard link: another directory entry pointing to the SAME inode. Symbolic link: a file containing the path to another file.

questions.statement: I/O bound vs CPU bound processes:
questions.option_a: I/O bound requires high CPU; CPU bound requires high disk access
questions.option_b: I/O bound: spends most time waiting for I/O. CPU bound: spends most time computing. I/O bound benefits more from higher CPU scheduling priority
questions.option_c: Both terms mean the same thing
questions.option_d: CPU bound processes are always given lower priority by default
questions.explanation: I/O bound: spends most time waiting for I/O. CPU bound: spends most time computing. I/O bound benefits more from higher CPU scheduling priority.

questions.statement: The purpose of the nice value in Linux scheduling:
questions.option_a: Adjusts a process's priority — positive nice = lower priority (being "nice" to others), negative nice = higher priority
questions.option_b: Increases the visual appeal of GUI applications
questions.option_c: Determines how nicely a process handles network errors
questions.option_d: Limits the memory usage of a process
questions.explanation: Adjusts a process's priority — positive nice = lower priority (being "nice" to others), negative nice = higher priority.

questions.statement: What is "memory-mapped I/O"?
questions.option_a: Using main memory to simulate a hard drive
questions.option_b: Device registers mapped into the physical address space — CPU accesses them with regular load/store instructions
questions.option_c: Caching network requests in memory
questions.option_d: Allocating memory to a specific process ID
questions.explanation: Device registers mapped into the physical address space — CPU accesses them with regular load/store instructions.

questions.statement: An interrupt handler (ISR) is executed:
questions.option_a: In a user-space application thread
questions.option_b: As a background batch job
questions.option_c: At kernel privilege level (ring 0), saving/restoring process state
questions.option_d: Only when the system reboots
questions.explanation: At kernel privilege level (ring 0), saving/restoring process state.

questions.statement: "Segmentation fault" (SIGSEGV) occurs when:
questions.option_a: A network packet is segmented improperly
questions.option_b: A process accesses memory outside its allocated address space or violates memory protection
questions.option_c: The hard drive becomes physically fragmented
questions.option_d: An instruction fails to compile
questions.explanation: A process accesses memory outside its allocated address space or violates memory protection.

questions.statement: The page table is stored in:
questions.option_a: The CPU cache only
questions.option_b: Main memory (RAM), with recent entries cached in the TLB
questions.option_c: The hard drive swapping area
questions.option_d: ROM (Read-Only Memory)
questions.explanation: Main memory (RAM), with recent entries cached in the TLB.

questions.statement: "Swapping" an entire process to disk:
questions.option_a: Permanently deletes the process
questions.option_b: Frees physical memory for other processes; the swapped process can be brought back to run again
questions.option_c: Is a technique used only in real-time systems
questions.option_d: Increases CPU cache size
questions.explanation: Frees physical memory for other processes; the swapped process can be brought back to run again.

questions.statement: The clock algorithm for page replacement:
questions.option_a: Measures the exact time a page was loaded
questions.option_b: Replaces pages randomly based on system time
questions.option_c: Approximates LRU using a reference bit and a "clock hand" that sweeps through pages
questions.option_d: Is a hardware clock inside the memory controller
questions.explanation: Approximates LRU using a reference bit and a "clock hand" that sweeps through pages.

questions.statement: In RAID 6, how many simultaneous drive failures can be tolerated?
questions.option_a: One
questions.option_b: Two simultaneous drive failures (uses two parity blocks distributed across all drives)
questions.option_c: Three
questions.option_d: Four
questions.explanation: Two simultaneous drive failures (uses two parity blocks distributed across all drives).

questions.statement: mmap() system call is used to:
questions.option_a: Move files between directories
questions.option_b: Monitor network map activity
questions.option_c: Map files or devices into a process's virtual address space; also used for anonymous memory allocation
questions.option_d: Manage multiprocessor memory affinity
questions.explanation: Map files or devices into a process's virtual address space; also used for anonymous memory allocation.

questions.statement: Kernel threads vs user threads — when one kernel thread blocks on I/O:
questions.option_a: All threads in the process block
questions.option_b: Other kernel threads continue running (OS knows about each thread). For user threads without kernel support, all threads block
questions.option_c: The entire OS halts
questions.option_d: The thread is automatically killed
questions.explanation: Other kernel threads continue running (OS knows about each thread). For user threads without kernel support, all threads block.

questions.statement: The purpose of a "watchdog timer" in embedded/OS systems:
questions.option_a: Measures the time it takes to boot the system
questions.option_b: Reset the system if the software doesn't periodically reset the timer — detects hung/deadlocked systems
questions.option_c: Limits the time users can log in
questions.option_d: Tracks network latency
questions.explanation: Reset the system if the software doesn't periodically reset the timer — detects hung/deadlocked systems.

questions.statement: Hierarchical page tables (multi-level paging) solve:
questions.option_a: The problem of slow CPU cache access
questions.option_b: The issue of external fragmentation
questions.option_c: The large page table size problem — instead of one contiguous page table, use a tree of smaller tables; only allocate page table pages that are actually used
questions.option_d: The problem of disk latency
questions.explanation: The large page table size problem — instead of one contiguous page table, use a tree of smaller tables; only allocate page table pages that are actually used.

questions.statement: In OS scheduling, what is "starvation"?
questions.option_a: A process waiting indefinitely for resources because higher-priority processes always preempt it
questions.option_b: A system running out of disk space
questions.option_c: A CPU with no processes to execute
questions.option_d: A network link dropping packets due to congestion
questions.explanation: A process waiting indefinitely for resources because higher-priority processes always preempt it.

questions.statement: The difference between wait() and waitpid() in Unix:
questions.option_a: wait() is non-blocking; waitpid() is blocking
questions.option_b: wait() waits for any child; waitpid() waits for a specific child by PID
questions.option_c: wait() is used for threads; waitpid() for processes
questions.option_d: wait() returns immediately; waitpid() has a timeout
questions.explanation: wait() waits for any child; waitpid() waits for a specific child by PID.

questions.statement: File system "mounting" means:
questions.option_a: Formatting a disk drive
questions.option_b: Attaching a file system (from a device, network, or virtual source) to a directory in the existing file system tree
questions.option_c: Installing an OS on a new hard drive
questions.option_d: Copying files from one partition to another
questions.explanation: Attaching a file system (from a device, network, or virtual source) to a directory in the existing file system tree.

questions.statement: The purpose of /dev/null in Unix:
questions.option_a: Stores deleted files temporarily
questions.option_b: Provides random numbers for cryptography
questions.option_c: Discards all data written to it; returns EOF when read. Used to suppress output
questions.option_d: Acts as a fallback directory for the OS
questions.explanation: Discards all data written to it; returns EOF when read. Used to suppress output.

questions.statement: Multiprocessor scheduling differs from single-processor because:
questions.option_a: It doesn't require preemptive scheduling
questions.option_b: Must consider affinity (process prefers to run on same CPU for cache warmth) and load balancing across cores
questions.option_c: All processes must run on all processors simultaneously
questions.option_d: Priority scheduling is not used in multiprocessor systems
questions.explanation: Must consider affinity (process prefers to run on same CPU for cache warmth) and load balancing across cores.

questions.statement: NX (No-Execute) bit in page tables prevents:
questions.option_a: Unauthorized users from logging in
questions.option_b: Executing code from data pages (stack, heap) — defeats most buffer overflow exploits
questions.option_c: Data from being written to disk
questions.option_d: Memory pages from being swapped out
questions.explanation: Executing code from data pages (stack, heap) — defeats most buffer overflow exploits.

questions.statement: What does /proc/meminfo show in Linux?
questions.option_a: Memory usage statistics: total RAM, free RAM, buffers, cached, swap usage
questions.option_b: Details of the CPU cache
questions.option_c: The memory layout of the currently running process
questions.option_d: A list of processes consuming the most memory
questions.explanation: Memory usage statistics: total RAM, free RAM, buffers, cached, swap usage.

questions.statement: The "completely fair scheduler" (CFS) in Linux uses:
questions.option_a: A strict First-Come-First-Served policy
questions.option_b: A round-robin quantum of exactly 1ms
questions.option_c: Virtual runtime to allocate CPU time proportionally — processes with less CPU time get priority
questions.option_d: Random selection of the next process to run
questions.explanation: Virtual runtime to allocate CPU time proportionally — processes with less CPU time get priority.

questions.statement: NTFS (Windows file system) advantages over FAT32 include:
questions.option_a: Smaller cluster sizes for less internal fragmentation
questions.option_b: Faster formatting times
questions.option_c: File-level security permissions, journaling, file size >4GB, better reliability
questions.option_d: Better compatibility with older DOS systems
questions.explanation: File-level security permissions, journaling, file size >4GB, better reliability.

questions.statement: In virtual memory, "page sharing" allows:
questions.option_a: Data to be shared across network connections
questions.option_b: Multiple processes to share the same physical page for read-only data (like shared libraries), saving memory
questions.option_c: Processes to write to each other's memory spaces without restriction
questions.option_d: The OS to distribute pages across multiple hard drives
questions.explanation: Multiple processes to share the same physical page for read-only data (like shared libraries), saving memory.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the "sticky bit" on a Unix directory (like /tmp)?
questions.option_a: It prevents files from being moved out of the directory
questions.option_b: Only the file's owner (or root) can delete files in that directory, even if others have write permission
questions.option_c: It makes all files executable by default
questions.option_d: It forces all new files to be owned by root
questions.explanation: Only the file's owner (or root) can delete files in that directory, even if others have write permission.

questions.statement: fork() versus vfork():
questions.option_a: vfork() creates a thread; fork() creates a process
questions.option_b: They are identical; vfork() is just an older alias
questions.option_c: vfork() is an older optimization where child shares parent's address space without copy-on-write (parent blocks until child exec() or exit()); largely superseded by CoW fork()
questions.option_d: fork() is only for background processes
questions.explanation: vfork() is an older optimization where child shares parent's address space without copy-on-write (parent blocks until child exec() or exit()); largely superseded by CoW fork().

questions.statement: An OS "shell" is:
questions.option_a: The physical casing around the computer
questions.option_b: A command interpreter that provides a user interface to the OS — reads commands and arranges for their execution
questions.option_c: The outermost layer of network security
questions.option_d: A graphical desktop environment only
questions.explanation: A command interpreter that provides a user interface to the OS — reads commands and arranges for their execution.

questions.statement: Segmentation provides what security benefit?
questions.option_a: It encrypts each segment with a different key
questions.option_b: Code segments can be marked execute-only/no-write; data segments read-write/no-execute — separate permissions per segment type
questions.option_c: It isolates the network traffic for each application
questions.option_d: It prevents fragmentation of the hard drive
questions.explanation: Code segments can be marked execute-only/no-write; data segments read-write/no-execute — separate permissions per segment type.

questions.statement: "Thrashing" can be detected by:
questions.option_a: Low disk I/O activity
questions.option_b: Frequent process terminations
questions.option_c: Very high page fault rate combined with very low CPU utilization — CPU mostly waiting for pages to be loaded from disk
questions.option_d: High CPU temperature warnings
questions.explanation: Very high page fault rate combined with very low CPU utilization — CPU mostly waiting for pages to be loaded from disk.

questions.statement: What is "preemptive multitasking"?
questions.option_a: Tasks preempt the OS scheduler for priority
questions.option_b: The OS can forcibly interrupt a running process and switch to another — time-sharing systems use this to give all processes fair CPU time
questions.option_c: The user manually switches between tasks
questions.option_d: Processes voluntarily give up the CPU when they finish
questions.explanation: The OS can forcibly interrupt a running process and switch to another — time-sharing systems use this to give all processes fair CPU time.

questions.statement: File system "inodes" are pre-allocated at:
questions.option_a: The moment a file is saved
questions.option_b: File system creation time (mkfs). A file system can run out of inodes before running out of disk space if many small files are created
questions.option_c: System boot time
questions.option_d: During OS updates
questions.explanation: File system creation time (mkfs). A file system can run out of inodes before running out of disk space if many small files are created.

questions.statement: The purpose of fsck (filesystem check):
questions.option_a: To format a new drive
questions.option_b: Scan and repair file system inconsistencies (usually after unclean shutdown without journaling)
questions.option_c: To defragment files
questions.option_d: To compress unused data
questions.explanation: Scan and repair file system inconsistencies (usually after unclean shutdown without journaling).

questions.statement: In memory allocation, the "best fit" strategy:
questions.option_a: Always allocates the largest block available
questions.option_b: Finds the smallest free block that can satisfy the request — minimizes wasted space per allocation but tends to create many small unusable fragments
questions.option_c: Allocates the first block that fits
questions.option_d: Allocates memory sequentially from the start of RAM
questions.explanation: Finds the smallest free block that can satisfy the request — minimizes wasted space per allocation but tends to create many small unusable fragments.

questions.statement: "Kernel panic" (Linux) / "Blue Screen of Death" (Windows) occurs when:
questions.option_a: A user enters the wrong password too many times
questions.option_b: The hard drive is completely full
questions.option_c: The OS encounters an unrecoverable error — typically a kernel bug, hardware failure, or critical driver crash in kernel mode
questions.option_d: A new software update is required
questions.explanation: The OS encounters an unrecoverable error — typically a kernel bug, hardware failure, or critical driver crash in kernel mode.

questions.statement: /etc/fstab in Linux contains:
questions.option_a: User passwords
questions.option_b: File system mount configurations — which devices should be mounted where at boot time, with what options
questions.option_c: Network routing tables
questions.option_d: The history of previously typed commands
questions.explanation: File system mount configurations — which devices should be mounted where at boot time, with what options.

questions.statement: Process "affinity" in multiprocessor scheduling means:
questions.option_a: Processes that frequently communicate run together
questions.option_b: Preference to schedule a process on the same CPU it previously ran on — improves cache utilization (warm cache)
questions.option_c: Processes are evenly distributed across all cores
questions.option_d: High priority processes get more CPU time
questions.explanation: Preference to schedule a process on the same CPU it previously ran on — improves cache utilization (warm cache).

questions.statement: The key difference between hard real-time and soft real-time OS:
questions.option_a: Hard real-time runs on hardware; soft real-time is virtualized
questions.option_b: Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a system failure (aircraft, pacemaker). Soft real-time: missing a deadline degrades quality but isn't catastrophic (video streaming, interactive UI)
questions.option_c: Hard real-time refers to permanent storage; soft real-time refers to RAM
questions.option_d: There is no practical difference between the two
questions.explanation: Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a system failure (aircraft, pacemaker). Soft real-time: missing a deadline degrades quality but isn't catastrophic (video streaming, interactive UI).

questions.statement: The term "Software Crisis" was coined at which conference and in which year?
questions.option_a: ACM Conference, 1975
questions.option_b: IEEE Software Engineering Conference, 1972
questions.option_c: NATO Software Engineering Conference, 1968
questions.option_d: International Software Engineering Congress, 1970
questions.explanation: The NATO Software Engineering Conference in Garmisch, Germany, 1968, specifically coined the term "software crisis" to describe the epidemic of failed software projects.

questions.statement: Which characteristic of software makes it fundamentally different from physical engineering artifacts?
questions.option_a: Software is always cheaper to produce
questions.option_b: Software does not degrade physically but must evolve as the world changes
questions.option_c: Software never needs maintenance
questions.option_d: Software can be manufactured identically once created
questions.explanation: Software doesn't wear out physically but must change as business rules, technology, and user needs evolve. A program that ran correctly in 1990 may still run correctly but be irrelevant because the world changed.

questions.statement: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental activities in all software processes?
questions.option_a: Specification
questions.option_b: Marketing
questions.option_c: Validation
questions.option_d: Evolution
questions.explanation: The four fundamental activities are: Specification (defining requirements), Design and Implementation, Validation (testing), and Evolution (maintenance). Marketing is a business activity, not a software process activity.

questions.statement: In the Waterfall model, what is the PRIMARY disadvantage that makes it unsuitable for most modern projects?
questions.option_a: It produces too much documentation
questions.option_b: Requirements must be completely and correctly specified before development begins, making it unable to accommodate change
questions.option_c: It requires too many developers
questions.option_d: It doesn't include a testing phase
questions.explanation: The waterfall's fundamental problem: requirements are frozen in Phase 1. Discovering wrong requirements in Phase 4 (testing) requires going back to Phase 1 — enormously expensive. Modern projects have evolving requirements that waterfall cannot accommodate.

questions.statement: The V-Model extends the Waterfall model by:
questions.option_a: Adding a requirements review at the end
questions.option_b: Explicitly mapping each development phase to a corresponding testing phase
questions.option_c: Adding an iteration cycle
questions.option_d: Replacing documentation with working software
questions.explanation: The V-Model's key contribution: each left-arm development phase (requirements, design, implementation) explicitly pairs with a right-arm testing phase (acceptance testing, system testing, unit testing). Testing is planned during the corresponding development phase, not as an afterthought.

questions.statement: Which process model treats risk management as its central organizing principle and explicitly requires risk analysis at each iteration?
questions.option_a: Waterfall
questions.option_b: Incremental
questions.option_c: Spiral
questions.option_d: V-Model
questions.explanation: Barry Boehm's Spiral model has risk analysis as one of its four quadrants in every spiral. The project continues to the next spiral ONLY if risks identified in the current spiral are resolved.

questions.statement: The Incremental model's primary advantage over Waterfall is:
questions.option_a: It requires less documentation
questions.option_b: It delivers working software earlier and incorporates user feedback between increments
questions.option_c: It has fewer development phases
questions.option_d: It always costs less to implement
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery means users get value earlier (not waiting 18 months for everything) and feedback from real use of earlier increments improves later increments.

questions.statement: A software project is building a life-support system for a hospital with very stable, well-understood requirements and extremely high reliability demands. Which process model is MOST appropriate?
questions.option_a: Scrum
questions.option_b: Kanban
questions.option_c: V-Model / Waterfall with formal verification
questions.option_d: XP with pair programming
questions.explanation: Life-critical systems with stable requirements and high reliability demands are the ideal use case for V-Model/Waterfall. The formal documentation, verification at each phase, and defined testing phases satisfy regulatory requirements and reduce safety risk.

questions.statement: What is meant by "software process" in the context of software engineering?
questions.option_a: The hardware processes that run software
questions.option_b: A structured set of activities, methods, and practices used to develop and maintain software
questions.option_c: The compilation process that converts source code to machine code
questions.option_d: The business processes that software automates
questions.explanation: A software process defines WHAT activities to perform, WHO performs them, WHEN they're performed, and HOW they're performed. It's the organizational framework for software development.

questions.statement: Which statement about the Waterfall model is CORRECT?
questions.option_a: It was designed for projects with rapidly changing requirements
questions.option_b: It delivers working software in regular short intervals
questions.option_c: It was originally proposed for large government/military contracts with stable requirements
questions.option_d: It encourages customer involvement throughout development
questions.explanation: Waterfall's origins are in large, contractual government and military software projects where requirements were stable, formal documentation was required at each phase, and teams were large and distributed.

questions.statement: In the Incremental model, what determines which features are built in the first increment?
questions.option_a: Features that are alphabetically first
questions.option_b: The most critical/highest-priority features that deliver the most business value
questions.option_c: The features that are easiest to implement
questions.option_d: Features requested most recently by stakeholders
questions.explanation: The highest-priority features go first. This ensures users get the most valuable functionality earliest, and if the project is cancelled, the most important features have already been delivered.

questions.statement: Which of the following is a characteristic of the Spiral model that distinguishes it from all other models?
questions.option_a: Use of agile principles
questions.option_b: Fixed-length iterations
questions.option_c: Each spiral cycle includes explicit risk identification, analysis, and resolution
questions.option_d: Requirements must be frozen before development begins
questions.explanation: The Spiral model's unique characteristic is explicit risk management at each spiral. Every iteration begins with risk identification and analysis, and potentially terminates the project if risks cannot be resolved.

questions.statement: In the V-Model, Acceptance Testing corresponds to which development phase?
questions.option_a: System Design
questions.option_b: Architecture Design
questions.option_c: Requirements Specification
questions.option_d: Module Design
questions.explanation: Acceptance tests verify that the system meets user requirements — defined at the Requirements Specification phase. The V-Model directly maps: Requirements → Acceptance Testing.

questions.statement: Which process model is BEST described as "build a little, test a little, release a little"?
questions.option_a: Waterfall
questions.option_b: Spiral
questions.option_c: Incremental
questions.option_d: V-Model
questions.explanation: The Incremental model's essence is building and releasing in functional pieces, each delivering value and generating feedback for the next piece.

questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of a software process model?
questions.option_a: To determine the programming language to use
questions.option_b: To provide a framework for organizing and managing development activities
questions.option_c: To ensure projects are always delivered on time
questions.option_d: To eliminate the need for testing
questions.explanation: Process models provide frameworks — they organize and sequence development activities, define roles, and specify deliverables. They don't guarantee success but provide structure for managing complex development efforts.

questions.statement: Lehman's Law of Continuing Change states:
questions.option_a: Software complexity always decreases over time
questions.option_b: Software systems must continually adapt to their changing environment or become less useful
questions.option_c: All software eventually becomes bug-free
questions.option_d: Software development always takes longer than planned
questions.explanation: Lehman's observation from studying large systems over decades: systems that don't adapt become progressively less useful and are eventually replaced. Software must evolve or die.

questions.statement: Which type of software maintenance accounts for the LARGEST proportion of total maintenance effort?
questions.option_a: Corrective maintenance (fixing bugs)
questions.option_b: Adaptive maintenance (adapting to environment changes)
questions.option_c: Perfective maintenance (improving/enhancing the system)
questions.option_d: Preventive maintenance (preventing future failures)
questions.explanation: Perfective maintenance (enhancements and improvements) accounts for approximately 50% of maintenance effort. Users always want more features and better performance. Corrective is ~20%, adaptive ~25%, preventive ~5%.

questions.statement: A hospital information system is running on Windows XP (no longer supported by Microsoft). The hospital needs to upgrade it to run on Windows 11. What type of maintenance is this?
questions.option_a: Corrective maintenance
questions.option_b: Adaptive maintenance
questions.option_c: Perfective maintenance
questions.option_d: Preventive maintenance
questions.explanation: Adaptive maintenance adapts the system to external environment changes. The external environment (OS version) changed — the software must adapt. The system isn't broken; it must adapt to remain functional.

questions.statement: What is "technical debt" in software engineering?
questions.option_a: Money owed by a software company for technical equipment
questions.option_b: The cost of rework caused by shortcuts taken during development that must be addressed later with interest
questions.option_c: Technical skills a developer needs to acquire
questions.option_d: The difference between estimated and actual project cost
questions.explanation: Technical debt is the metaphor (from Ward Cunningham) comparing shortcuts in code to financial debt — both accrue "interest" over time. Quick solutions today create harder-to-fix problems tomorrow.

questions.statement: Which statement about legacy systems is MOST accurate?
questions.option_a: Legacy systems are always technically inferior and should be immediately replaced
questions.option_b: Legacy systems cannot be integrated with modern systems
questions.option_c: Legacy systems continue to be used because they perform critical functions, despite being based on outdated technology
questions.option_d: Legacy systems never have any technical debt
questions.explanation: Legacy systems persist because they do something valuable — critical business functions that would be expensive and risky to migrate. The technology is old; the business value may be high.

questions.statement: The Agile Manifesto values "Responding to change over following a plan." This means:
questions.option_a: Agile projects never have plans
questions.option_b: Plans are useless in Agile
questions.option_c: While planning has value, the ability to adapt to change is more valuable
questions.option_d: Agile projects change requirements every day
questions.explanation: The manifesto says "over" not "instead of." Plans have value. But the ability to adapt as you learn more is more valuable than slavishly following a plan made when you knew the least.

questions.statement: In Scrum, which role is responsible for prioritizing the Product Backlog?
questions.option_a: Scrum Master
questions.option_b: Development Team
questions.option_c: Project Manager
questions.option_d: Product Owner
questions.explanation: The Product Owner owns the Product Backlog. Only the Product Owner can add items, reprioritize items, and decide what gets built in what order. The Scrum Master facilitates; the Development Team executes.

questions.statement: What is the Scrum Master's PRIMARY responsibility?
questions.option_a: Writing code and delivering features
questions.option_b: Managing the project budget and timeline
questions.option_c: Serving the team — removing impediments, coaching on Scrum, facilitating ceremonies
questions.option_d: Representing the customer's interests in backlog prioritization
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master is a servant-leader. They don't manage the team — they serve it by removing obstacles, coaching Scrum principles, and protecting the team from external disruption.

questions.statement: What does "time-boxed" mean in the context of a Scrum Sprint?
questions.option_a: The Sprint can be extended if work is incomplete
questions.option_b: The Sprint always ends on its fixed end date — scope is reduced, not the time
questions.option_c: The Sprint has a minimum of 4 weeks
questions.option_d: Sprint length changes based on project complexity
questions.explanation: Time-boxing means the Sprint's duration is fixed and cannot be extended. If not all committed work is complete, it goes back to the backlog — the Sprint end date never moves.

questions.statement: A team's Sprint Review shows working software to stakeholders. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this event?
questions.option_a: Measuring team performance and calculating velocity
questions.option_b: Demonstrating working software to gather feedback and update the backlog
questions.option_c: Planning the next Sprint
questions.option_d: Celebrating the completion of the Sprint
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review is a feedback mechanism. Seeing working software prompts real feedback from stakeholders — "this works, but I actually need it to also do X." This feedback updates the backlog for future Sprints.

questions.statement: In the Daily Scrum, each team member answers three questions. Which of the following is NOT one of the three standard questions?
questions.option_a: What did I do yesterday to help the team reach the Sprint Goal?
questions.option_b: What will I do today to help the team reach the Sprint Goal?
questions.option_c: How many story points have I completed this week?
questions.option_d: Are there any impediments blocking me or the team?
questions.explanation: Story point counting is NOT a Daily Scrum question. The three questions focus on coordination: yesterday's work, today's plan, and blockers. The Daily Scrum is not a status report.

questions.statement: The Sprint Retrospective differs from the Sprint Review in that:
questions.option_a: The Retrospective is shorter than the Review
questions.option_b: The Review is about the process; the Retrospective is about the product
questions.option_c: The Retrospective focuses on improving the PROCESS; the Review demonstrates the PRODUCT
questions.option_d: Only the Scrum Master attends the Retrospective
questions.explanation: Sprint Review: demonstrate working software (product focus). Sprint Retrospective: reflect on HOW the team works (process focus). Both are essential but address different dimensions.

questions.statement: Which Agile framework uses Work In Progress (WIP) limits and a continuous flow model instead of fixed-length sprints?
questions.option_a: Scrum
questions.option_b: XP (Extreme Programming)
questions.option_c: SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework)
questions.option_d: Kanban
questions.explanation: Kanban uses WIP limits and continuous flow — work items flow through stages without fixed-length sprints. Scrum uses sprints. Kanban is better suited for support, operations, and maintenance work.

questions.statement: Test-Driven Development (TDD) follows which sequence?
questions.option_a: Code → Test → Refactor
questions.option_b: Design → Code → Test
questions.option_c: Red (failing test) → Green (minimal code to pass) → Refactor
questions.option_d: Test → Deploy → Monitor
questions.explanation: TDD's Red-Green-Refactor cycle: write a failing test (Red), write minimum code to pass it (Green), improve the code without changing behavior (Refactor). Test is written FIRST.

questions.statement: A user story follows which standard format?
questions.option_a: "The system shall [action] when [condition]"
questions.option_b: "As a [user type], I want [goal], so that [benefit]"
questions.option_c: "Feature: [name], Priority: [level], Effort: [points]"
questions.option_d: "[Actor] [Action] [Object] [Outcome]"
questions.explanation: The standard user story template captures: who wants it (user type), what they want (goal/desire), and why (business benefit). This format keeps stories focused on user value.

questions.statement: Functional requirements describe:
questions.option_a: How fast the system must respond
questions.option_b: How many users the system must support
questions.option_c: What the system must DO — specific behaviors, functions, and services
questions.option_d: What security measures the system must implement
questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe WHAT the system does — specific behaviors. Non-functional requirements describe HOW WELL it does it (performance, security, reliability).

questions.statement: "The system must be available 99.9% of the time" is an example of:
questions.option_a: A functional requirement
questions.option_b: A non-functional requirement (availability)
questions.option_c: A user story
questions.option_d: A technical constraint
questions.explanation: Availability (99.9% uptime) is a non-functional requirement describing a quality attribute — how reliably the system performs, not what it does. Functional: "The system shall allow users to check their balance." Non-functional: "The system shall respond within 2 seconds."

questions.statement: Which requirement quality attribute means that every requirement must be testable — you can objectively determine if the system satisfies it?
questions.option_a: Complete
questions.option_b: Consistent
questions.option_c: Unambiguous
questions.option_d: Verifiable
questions.explanation: Verifiable: you can prove/disprove the requirement is met. "The system shall be fast" is NOT verifiable. "The system shall respond to login requests within 1.5 seconds" IS verifiable.

questions.statement: In requirements elicitation, which technique is MOST valuable for discovering requirements that users don't think to mention because they seem obvious to them?
questions.option_a: Questionnaires
questions.option_b: Observation/Ethnography
questions.option_c: Interviews
questions.option_d: Document analysis
questions.explanation: Observation reveals what users actually do, not what they think they do or think to mention. Watching a nurse navigate 5 screens to find medication history reveals a requirement no nurse would have articulated in an interview.

questions.statement: What is "scope creep" in a software project?
questions.option_a: The gradual deterioration of software quality
questions.option_b: The gradual, uncontrolled expansion of project scope beyond original agreed boundaries
questions.option_c: The increase in team size during development
questions.option_d: The process of adding test coverage gradually
questions.explanation: Scope creep is the enemy of project schedules and budgets. Requirements are added continuously without formal change control or resource/schedule adjustment, causing the project to bloat uncontrollably.

questions.statement: In use case diagrams, the "include" relationship means:
questions.option_a: One use case optionally extends another
questions.option_b: One use case always includes/uses the behavior of another use case
questions.option_c: An actor is included in the system boundary
questions.option_d: A use case includes all possible scenarios
questions.explanation: "Include" means the base use case ALWAYS requires the behavior of the included use case. "Authenticate User" is included by all main use cases — you always authenticate before doing anything.

questions.statement: "The system shall be user-friendly" violates which requirement quality attribute?
questions.option_a: Complete
questions.option_b: Traceable
questions.option_c: Verifiable/Unambiguous
questions.option_d: Consistent
questions.explanation: "User-friendly" is ambiguous (means different things to different people) and not verifiable (no objective test can determine if the system IS user-friendly). A verifiable alternative: "A new user shall be able to register an account in under 5 minutes without assistance."

questions.statement: What is the Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document?
questions.option_a: The source code specification
questions.option_b: A comprehensive document describing all system requirements — functional, non-functional, and constraints
questions.option_c: The software testing plan
questions.option_d: The project management plan
questions.explanation: The SRS is the primary requirements artifact — a complete, consistent, unambiguous specification of all requirements. It is the contract between what the system must do and what will be built.

questions.statement: Pair programming is an XP practice where:
questions.option_a: Two programmers alternate working on different features
questions.option_b: Two programmers work at one computer — one writes code (driver), the other reviews in real-time (navigator)
questions.option_c: A programmer and a tester pair to write and test code simultaneously
questions.option_d: Two programmers independently solve the same problem and compare solutions
questions.explanation: Pair programming: one computer, two programmers. Driver writes code. Navigator watches, thinks ahead, catches mistakes, suggests improvements. They switch roles regularly. Benefits: fewer bugs, knowledge sharing, better design.

questions.statement: The "Definition of Done" (DoD) in Scrum is:
questions.option_a: A list of features that will be completed in the Sprint
questions.option_b: The acceptance criteria for a specific user story
questions.option_c: A shared understanding of what criteria a Product Backlog Item must meet to be considered complete
questions.option_d: The Sprint Goal
questions.explanation: DoD is team-level: applies to ALL stories. It defines "done" for the team — might include: coded, unit tested, integration tested, code reviewed, documentation updated. Acceptance criteria is story-specific.

questions.statement: Which design principle states that a module should have only ONE reason to change?
questions.option_a: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_b: Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.option_c: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.option_d: Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.explanation: SRP: a class/module should have one and only one reason to change — meaning it has one responsibility. Multiple responsibilities mean multiple reasons to change, creating fragile code.

questions.statement: In software design, "low coupling" means:
questions.option_a: Modules share minimal data and have minimal dependencies on each other
questions.option_b: Modules are tightly interconnected
questions.option_c: The system has few modules
questions.option_d: All modules communicate through a central module
questions.explanation: Low coupling: modules are largely independent. Changes in one module minimally affect others. This is GOOD — it makes the system easier to maintain and modify.

questions.statement: Which type of cohesion is considered BEST in software design?
questions.option_a: Logical cohesion
questions.option_b: Temporal cohesion
questions.option_c: Coincidental cohesion
questions.option_d: Functional cohesion
questions.explanation: Functional cohesion: every element of the module contributes to ONE well-defined function. A module that does exactly ONE thing, does it well, and does nothing else is ideally cohesive.

questions.statement: The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be:
questions.option_a: Open for modification and closed for extension
questions.option_b: Open for extension and closed for modification
questions.option_c: Open for testing and closed for deployment
questions.option_d: Open to all users and closed to external systems
questions.explanation: OCP: add NEW behavior by adding NEW code (open for extension), without modifying existing tested code (closed for modification). Achieved through abstractions and polymorphism.

questions.statement: Which software architecture pattern separates an application into Model (data/logic), View (presentation), and Controller (intermediary)?
questions.option_a: Layered architecture
questions.option_b: Microservices architecture
questions.option_c: MVC (Model-View-Controller)
questions.option_d: Event-driven architecture
questions.explanation: MVC separates: Model (business logic and data), View (user interface), Controller (handles user input, coordinates model and view). Used in web frameworks like Django, Rails, Spring MVC.

questions.statement: What is the PRIMARY advantage of microservices architecture over monolithic architecture?
questions.option_a: Microservices are always faster than monoliths
questions.option_b: Microservices require fewer developers
questions.option_c: Individual services can be deployed, scaled, and updated independently
questions.option_d: Microservices eliminate the need for databases
questions.explanation: Independent deployment and scaling is the defining advantage. Update the Payment Service without redeploying the Recommendation Service. Scale the Order Service without scaling the User Service.

questions.statement: In a three-tier architecture, where should business logic reside?
questions.option_a: Presentation tier (user interface)
questions.option_b: Middle tier (application/business logic tier)
questions.option_c: Data tier (database)
questions.option_d: Distributed across all three tiers equally
questions.explanation: Business logic belongs in the middle tier (application/business logic layer). The presentation tier handles display. The data tier handles storage. Business rules — calculations, workflows, validations — belong in the middle.

questions.statement: Which design principle says "High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules — both should depend on abstractions"?
questions.option_a: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.option_b: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_c: Interface Segregation Principle
questions.option_d: Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.explanation: DIP: instead of BusinessLogic depending on MySQLDatabase (concrete), BusinessLogic depends on DatabaseInterface (abstraction). MySQLDatabase implements DatabaseInterface. Decoupling achieved.

questions.statement: What is "information hiding" in software design?
questions.option_a: Encrypting data for security
questions.option_b: Hiding implementation details within a module so they cannot be accessed from outside — only the interface is exposed
questions.option_c: Removing comments from source code
questions.option_d: Preventing users from seeing system errors
questions.explanation: Information hiding (Parnas, 1972): hide the design decisions that are most likely to change. If implementation details are hidden, they can be changed without affecting anything that uses the module.

questions.statement: Which of the following is an example of GOOD coupling (low coupling)?
questions.option_a: Module A directly reads and modifies Module B's internal database tables
questions.option_b: Module A calls Module B's public API function, passing exactly the parameters needed and receiving a return value
questions.option_c: Module A and Module B both read from the same global variable
questions.option_d: Module A passes a control flag to Module B telling it how to behave
questions.explanation: Passing needed parameters and receiving a result is data coupling — the best type. No shared global state, no internal access, no control flags.

questions.statement: Event-driven architecture is characterized by:
questions.option_a: All communication through synchronous function calls
questions.option_b: A central database that all components query
questions.option_c: Components communicating through events — producers emit events, consumers react to them asynchronously
questions.option_d: One main controller component directing all other components
questions.explanation: Event-driven: producers publish events without knowing who's interested. Consumers subscribe to events they care about. Loosely coupled — producer and consumer don't know about each other.

questions.statement: The Liskov Substitution Principle is violated when:
questions.option_a: A child class has more methods than its parent
questions.option_b: A parent class has abstract methods
questions.option_c: A child class cannot be used wherever the parent class is expected without breaking program correctness
questions.option_d: A class implements an interface
questions.explanation: LSP: you should be able to use a subclass instance anywhere its superclass is expected. If Square extends Rectangle but breaks the contract that width and height can be set independently, you can't substitute Square for Rectangle — LSP violation.

questions.statement: What is the PRIMARY benefit of the layered architecture pattern?
questions.option_a: It always produces the fastest applications
questions.option_b: It separates concerns into distinct layers — each layer has a well-defined responsibility and depends only on the layer below
questions.option_c: It eliminates the need for a database
questions.option_d: It requires fewer developers to build
questions.explanation: Layered architecture's strength: separation of concerns. Presentation developers work independently of database developers. A layer can be replaced (Oracle → PostgreSQL) without affecting layers above.

questions.statement: Which principle of UI design states that the system should always keep users informed about what is happening?
questions.option_a: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
questions.option_b: Consistency and Standards
questions.option_c: Visibility of System Status
questions.option_d: User Control and Freedom
questions.explanation: Visibility of System Status: always communicate what's happening. Progress bars, "Saving...", "3 of 10 uploaded", green checkmarks when done. Users shouldn't have to wonder if the system is working.

questions.statement: Wireframes in UI design are used to:
questions.option_a: Define the exact visual design with colors and images
questions.option_b: Write the HTML code for the interface
questions.option_c: Communicate layout, structure, and content without the distraction of visual design details
questions.option_d: Test user interactions with the fully functional system
questions.explanation: Wireframes are low-fidelity representations (boxes, lines, labels) that communicate structure. They're created before visual design to agree on layout and content. Changing a wireframe is fast; changing a designed page is slow.

questions.statement: WCAG accessibility guidelines primarily aim to:
questions.option_a: Improve search engine optimization
questions.option_b: Make web content accessible to people with disabilities
questions.option_c: Standardize programming languages used in web development
questions.option_d: Improve website loading speed
questions.explanation: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) ensures web content is accessible to users with visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive disabilities. Required by law in many countries.

questions.statement: What is "abstraction" in software design?
questions.option_a: Making code hard to understand through complex syntax
questions.option_b: Representing complex systems through simplified models that expose only essential characteristics
questions.option_c: Removing all comments from code
questions.option_d: Converting source code to binary
questions.explanation: Abstraction hides complexity behind a simplified interface. A List abstracts the complexity of memory management and pointer manipulation behind simple add(), get(), remove() operations.

questions.statement: Which statement about the MVC pattern is TRUE?
questions.option_a: The Model should contain UI rendering logic
questions.option_b: The View should contain business logic for efficiency
questions.option_c: The Model is independent of the View — the same model can have multiple different views
questions.option_d: The Controller directly renders HTML output
questions.explanation: Model independence is a key MVC benefit. The same Customer model can have a web view (HTML), a mobile view (mobile UI), and an API view (JSON) — all using the same model without code duplication.

questions.statement: What is the correct order of testing levels from smallest to largest scope?
questions.option_a: System Testing → Integration Testing → Unit Testing → Acceptance Testing
questions.option_b: Unit Testing → Integration Testing → System Testing → Acceptance Testing
questions.option_c: Acceptance Testing → System Testing → Integration Testing → Unit Testing
questions.option_d: Unit Testing → System Testing → Integration Testing → Acceptance Testing
questions.explanation: Testing progresses from smallest unit (individual functions) → combining units (integration) → complete system (system testing) → user validation (acceptance). Each level builds on the previous.

questions.statement: In software testing, what is a "regression test"?
questions.option_a: A test that checks if the system regresses in performance under load
questions.option_b: A test run after changes to verify existing functionality was not broken by the changes
questions.option_c: A statistical analysis of defect trends over time
questions.option_d: Testing performed by going back through requirements
questions.explanation: Regression testing: re-running previously passing tests after changes. "Did fixing bug A break features B, C, and D?" Automation is essential — manually running thousands of regression tests is impractical.

questions.statement: Black-box testing is characterized by:
questions.option_a: Testing based on knowledge of internal implementation
questions.option_b: Testing that only covers error conditions
questions.option_c: Testing based on specifications — tester knows inputs and expected outputs, NOT internal code
questions.option_d: Testing performed only in the dark
questions.explanation: Black-box: tester sees inputs and outputs, not internal code. Tests are derived from specifications, not code. Appropriate for system testing and acceptance testing.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of "equivalence partitioning" in test design?
questions.option_a: Dividing the development team into equal groups
questions.option_b: Distributing test effort equally across all functions
questions.option_c: Dividing input into classes where any value from the class will produce the same result — reducing the number of test cases needed
questions.option_d: Ensuring each developer writes an equal number of tests
questions.explanation: Equivalence partitioning: values in the same "class" will be handled identically. Instead of testing every age from 0 to 150, test one from each class: valid (e.g., 30), too young (e.g., 15), too old (e.g., 70). Same result within each class.

questions.statement: "Boundary value analysis" tests values:
questions.option_a: At the center of each equivalence partition
questions.option_b: At and just beyond the boundaries between equivalence partitions
questions.option_c: Randomly selected from each partition
questions.option_d: Only at extreme minimum and maximum values
questions.explanation: Errors cluster at boundaries. For valid range 18-65: test 17 (just below), 18 (minimum boundary), 65 (maximum boundary), 66 (just above). Boundary values are where bugs hide.

questions.statement: Which testing type verifies that individual units of code work correctly in isolation?
questions.option_a: Integration testing
questions.option_b: System testing
questions.option_c: Unit testing
questions.option_d: Acceptance testing
questions.explanation: Unit testing targets the smallest testable piece — a function, method, or class. External dependencies (databases, APIs) are replaced with mocks. Tests run fast and in isolation.

questions.statement: The MOST effective and economical way to prevent defects from reaching production is:
questions.option_a: Extensive system testing before release
questions.option_b: Beta testing with selected users
questions.option_c: Formal code inspections and reviews combined with automated testing throughout development
questions.option_d: Hiring more QA engineers for final testing
questions.explanation: Defect prevention (reviews, inspections) is cheaper than defect detection (testing) which is cheaper than defect correction in production. Finding a bug in review costs a fraction of finding it after release.

questions.statement: Cyclomatic complexity of a module measures:
questions.option_a: How long the module takes to compile
questions.option_b: The number of classes the module uses
questions.option_c: The number of independent paths through the module's code
questions.option_d: The number of lines of code in the module
questions.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe) counts independent execution paths. Calculated as: CC = number of decision points + 1. Higher CC = more complex, more test cases needed, higher defect risk.

questions.statement: What does CMMI Level 3 (Defined) signify?
questions.option_a: Processes are unpredictable and reactive
questions.option_b: Processes are defined, documented, and consistently applied organization-wide
questions.option_c: Processes use statistical quality control
questions.option_d: Processes are being continuously improved based on quantitative data
questions.explanation: CMMI Level 3: organization has documented, standard processes tailored for each project. Level 1 = chaos, Level 2 = managed per project, Level 3 = organization-wide standard, Level 4 = quantitatively managed, Level 5 = optimizing.

questions.statement: ISO 9001 certification for a software company primarily demonstrates:
questions.option_a: The company's software has zero defects
questions.option_b: The company uses a specific programming language
questions.option_c: The company has a quality management system that consistently produces customer-satisfying products
questions.option_d: The company employs more than 100 developers
questions.explanation: ISO 9001 certifies the PROCESS (quality management system), not the product. It demonstrates that the organization has systematic processes for ensuring quality and continuous improvement.

questions.statement: User Acceptance Testing (UAT) is conducted by:
questions.option_a: The development team
questions.option_b: QA engineers
questions.option_c: Actual end users or their representatives
questions.option_d: External security auditors
questions.explanation: UAT is conducted by end users (or business representatives acting on their behalf). Its purpose is to verify the system meets BUSINESS NEEDS — not just technical specifications. Technical testing can confirm the specs were met; UAT confirms the specs were correct.

questions.statement: What is "defect density"?
questions.option_a: Number of tests per developer
questions.option_b: Number of defects per unit of software size (KLOC or Function Points)
questions.option_c: Density of the development team per square meter
questions.option_d: Number of defects per hour of testing
questions.explanation: Defect density = defects / size. Used to compare quality across modules and over time. Module A at 2 defects/KLOC vs Module B at 20 defects/KLOC — Module B needs attention.

questions.statement: TDD (Test-Driven Development) produces which unintended but valuable side effect?
questions.option_a: Eliminates the need for integration testing
questions.option_b: A comprehensive unit test suite that serves as regression protection and living documentation
questions.option_c: Reduces the number of developers needed
questions.option_d: Automatically generates user documentation
questions.explanation: When you write tests before code for EVERY piece of functionality, you end up with a complete test suite. This suite: catches regressions immediately, documents intended behavior, enables confident refactoring.

questions.statement: Which statement about formal code inspections (Fagan Inspections) is TRUE?
questions.option_a: They are less effective than testing at finding defects
questions.option_b: They are only useful for finding syntax errors
questions.option_c: Studies show they find 60-90% of defects and provide better ROI than testing alone
questions.option_d: They can only be performed after system testing
questions.explanation: Fagan inspections are among the most effective defect detection techniques. IBM studies found that every hour in inspection saves 3-5 hours in testing. They find design flaws that testing might miss entirely.

questions.statement: What is "velocity" in Scrum?
questions.option_a: How fast developers type code
questions.option_b: The number of bugs fixed per Sprint
questions.option_c: The amount of work (in story points) a team completes per Sprint — used for future planning
questions.option_d: The speed of code deployment to production
questions.explanation: Velocity = story points completed per Sprint. Used for prediction: with 200 points remaining and average velocity 40 points/sprint, approximately 5 more sprints (10 weeks at 2-week sprints) remain.

questions.statement: What is the PRIMARY purpose of code refactoring?
questions.option_a: Adding new features while rewriting existing code
questions.option_b: Improving internal code structure without changing external behavior
questions.option_c: Translating code from one programming language to another
questions.option_d: Removing all comments to reduce file size
questions.explanation: Refactoring: improve the code's design and structure WITHOUT changing what it does externally. The system behaves identically before and after. Tests verify this — they must all pass after refactoring.

questions.statement: Which of the following BEST describes "software quality assurance" vs "software testing"?
questions.option_a: QA finds defects; testing prevents them
questions.option_b: Testing finds defects in the product; QA ensures the development PROCESS produces quality products
questions.option_c: QA is done by developers; testing is done by users
questions.option_d: Testing happens before QA in the development lifecycle
questions.explanation: QA is process-focused (are we doing development correctly?). Testing is product-focused (does this product work?). QA prevents defects; testing detects them. Both are necessary.

questions.statement: The "Iron Triangle" of project management consists of:
questions.option_a: Cost, Quality, and Team Size
questions.option_b: Scope, Schedule, and Cost — all three in permanent tension
questions.option_c: Planning, Execution, and Monitoring
questions.option_d: Requirements, Design, and Testing
questions.explanation: The triple constraint (Iron Triangle): Scope, Schedule, Cost. Change one and at least one other must change. Fix all three and something else (often quality) suffers. This is a law of project management.

questions.statement: What is the CRITICAL PATH in a project network diagram?
questions.option_a: The path requiring the most documentation
questions.option_b: The path through the most complex technical components
questions.option_c: The longest sequence of dependent activities — its duration equals the minimum project completion time
questions.option_d: The path with the highest risk
questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest path through the project network. Its total duration = minimum time to complete the project. Any delay on the critical path directly delays the project finish date.

questions.statement: "Float" (or "slack") in project scheduling means:
questions.option_a: The project budget contingency
questions.option_b: How much a non-critical activity can be delayed without delaying the project
questions.option_c: The percentage of work remaining
questions.option_d: The time between two critical path activities
questions.explanation: Float = amount an activity can slip without affecting the project end date. Critical path activities have ZERO float. Non-critical activities have positive float — they have scheduling flexibility.

questions.statement: The COCOMO model is used for:
questions.option_a: Managing software configuration
questions.option_b: Estimating software development effort based on project size
questions.option_c: Designing database schemas
questions.option_d: Measuring software quality
questions.explanation: COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model) estimates effort and schedule from software size (KLOC) and project type. Basic formula: Effort = a × (KLOC)^b where a and b depend on project type.

questions.statement: In risk management, "risk transfer" means:
questions.option_a: Moving a risk from one team member to another
questions.option_b: Documenting the risk and forgetting about it
questions.option_c: Moving the risk to a third party (insurance, fixed-price contract, warranty)
questions.option_d: Increasing the risk probability
questions.explanation: Risk transfer: you still have the potential for loss, but a third party bears the financial consequence. Insurance transfers financial risk to the insurer. Fixed-price contracts transfer schedule/cost risk to the vendor.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a Software Configuration Management (SCM) system?
questions.option_a: Configuring operating systems for software deployment
questions.option_b: Tracking and controlling changes to software artifacts throughout the lifecycle
questions.option_c: Managing the configuration of user preferences
questions.option_d: Setting up development environments for new team members
questions.explanation: SCM tracks all changes to all artifacts (code, docs, tests, configs): who changed what, when, why. It enables reproducibility (what was in the March 15 release?), rollback (revert to previous working version), and parallel development (branches).

questions.statement: A "baseline" in software configuration management is:
questions.option_a: The minimum acceptable performance level
questions.option_b: The starting point for a new project
questions.option_c: A formally approved, fixed version of a configuration item — a reference point for further development
questions.option_d: The development team's code style guidelines
questions.explanation: A baseline marks a significant milestone — requirements baseline, design baseline, release baseline. It freezes a version for reference. The requirements baseline for version 2 is used to track what changed from requirements baseline for version 1.

questions.statement: What is "risk exposure" and how is it calculated?
questions.option_a: The emotional impact of a risk on the team; cannot be calculated
questions.option_b: Risk Probability × Risk Impact — the overall severity of a risk
questions.option_c: The number of team members exposed to project risks
questions.option_d: How often risks are reviewed in risk meetings
questions.explanation: Risk Exposure = Probability × Impact. A low-probability, high-impact risk might have the same exposure as a high-probability, low-impact risk. Risk exposure allows comparing and prioritizing different risks.

questions.statement: Which risk mitigation strategy involves changing plans to eliminate the risk entirely?
questions.option_a: Risk acceptance
questions.option_b: Risk transfer
questions.option_c: Risk mitigation
questions.option_d: Risk avoidance
questions.explanation: Risk avoidance: change your approach to eliminate the risk. "We risk the new ML library not working" → use a proven library instead. The risk no longer exists.

questions.statement: A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) must satisfy which rule?
questions.option_a: All tasks must have equal duration
questions.option_b: The 100% Rule — the WBS must capture 100% of the project's work, no more, no less
questions.option_c: Tasks must be assigned to specific individuals
questions.option_d: The WBS must have exactly 5 levels of hierarchy
questions.explanation: The 100% Rule: WBS captures ALL work, nothing is missed, nothing is counted twice. Missing items lead to unrealistic schedules and budgets. Duplicate items inflate estimates.

questions.statement: SQL Injection attacks exploit:
questions.option_a: Weak encryption of database files
questions.option_b: Untrusted user input being executed as SQL commands due to lack of parameterization
questions.option_c: Weak administrator passwords
questions.option_d: Unpatched operating system vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: SQL injection: user input containing SQL code is interpreted as SQL commands. Prevention: parameterized queries (prepared statements) treat user input as pure data, never code.

questions.statement: The OWASP Top 10 is:
questions.option_a: The top 10 programming languages for web development
questions.option_b: Ten rules for writing clean code
questions.option_c: A list of the most critical security risks in web applications
questions.option_d: The top 10 software frameworks recommended for security
questions.explanation: OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) Top 10 lists the most common and critical web application security vulnerabilities. Knowing these is essential for any web developer or security engineer.

questions.statement: The "Principle of Least Privilege" in security engineering states:
questions.option_a: Users should have the fewest possible features in the UI
questions.option_b: Every user, process, and component should have only the minimum privileges necessary to perform its function
questions.option_c: Security measures should be as simple (least complex) as possible
questions.option_d: System access should require the fewest authentication steps possible
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits damage from compromise. If an attacker takes over a database account that has only SELECT on specific tables, they can't DROP tables or access other schemas. If the account has full admin rights, the attacker owns the entire database.

questions.statement: "Defense in Depth" in security engineering means:
questions.option_a: Making the security measures hard to understand (security through obscurity)
questions.option_b: Using one very strong security control rather than many weaker ones
questions.option_c: Using multiple layers of security controls so failure of one layer doesn't mean complete system compromise
questions.option_d: Encrypting data deeply — multiple times with different algorithms
questions.explanation: Defense in depth: layers of security. Network firewall → Application firewall → Input validation → Access control → Encryption → Monitoring. An attacker who bypasses one layer still faces others.

questions.statement: STRIDE threat model categorizes which of the following as a threat?
questions.option_a: Poor documentation, Slow performance, High cost, Bad design
questions.option_b: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege
questions.option_c: Software bugs, Hardware failures, Network outages, User errors
questions.option_d: Missing requirements, Incomplete testing, Technical debt, Poor architecture
questions.explanation: STRIDE is Microsoft's threat categorization: Spoofing (impersonation), Tampering (data modification), Repudiation (denying actions), Information Disclosure (data exposure), Denial of Service (availability attack), Elevation of Privilege (unauthorized privilege gain).

questions.statement: A system that fails by DENYING ACCESS when an error occurs is said to:
questions.option_a: Fail open
questions.option_b: Fail secure (fail closed)
questions.option_c: Fail gracefully
questions.option_d: Fail loudly
questions.explanation: Fail secure / fail closed: when in doubt or in failure, deny access. A gate that fails OPEN lets anyone through — security failure. A gate that fails CLOSED lets no one through — secure but inconvenient. For security systems, always fail closed.

questions.statement: Which OWASP Top 10 vulnerability involves users accessing data or functionality they're not authorized to access?
questions.option_a: SQL Injection
questions.option_b: Broken Access Control
questions.option_c: Security Misconfiguration
questions.option_d: Cryptographic Failures
questions.explanation: Broken Access Control: user manipulates URL from /account/123 to /account/124 and sees another user's account. The system failed to verify that the requesting user is authorized to access that specific account.
