questions.statement: "Refactoring" and "adding new features" are different because:
questions.option_a: Refactoring is faster than adding features
questions.option_b: Refactoring changes internal code structure without changing external behavior; features change behavior
questions.option_c: Only senior developers can refactor
questions.option_d: Refactoring requires rewriting the entire system
questions.explanation: Refactoring: same behavior, better internal structure. Feature addition: new or changed behavior. The test suite tells the difference — after refactoring, all existing tests pass. After adding a feature, new tests are added that previously didn't exist.

questions.statement: What does "continuous integration" (CI) mean in modern software development?
questions.option_a: Integrating all features at the end of the project
questions.option_b: Developers integrate code into a shared repository multiple times daily, triggering automated builds and tests each time
questions.option_c: Continuously adding new team members to the project
questions.option_d: Running integration tests once per week
questions.explanation: CI: commit frequently + automated build + automated tests. If code breaks anything, the team knows in minutes — not days. The "main" branch is always in a working, deployable state.

questions.statement: Adaptive maintenance is triggered by:
questions.option_a: Finding a bug in the software
questions.option_b: Users requesting new features
questions.option_c: Changes in the external environment — OS, hardware, regulations, integrated systems
questions.option_d: Performance problems discovered during usage
questions.explanation: Adaptive: the software must ADAPT to external changes. Tax law changes, OS updates that break the app, payment gateway API changes, government regulation requiring new data fields — all trigger adaptive maintenance.

questions.statement: Which software quality attribute measures how easily the software can be modified without introducing defects?
questions.option_a: Reliability
questions.option_b: Portability
questions.option_c: Maintainability
questions.option_d: Efficiency
questions.explanation: Maintainability: how easy is it to change? Low maintainability = high cost to change + high risk of introducing bugs. High maintainability = changes are easy, safe, and predictable.

questions.statement: The Agile principle "Working software is the primary measure of progress" means:
questions.option_a: Documentation is irrelevant in Agile
questions.option_b: The only thing that matters is how much code is written
questions.option_c: A completed specification document is as valuable as working software
questions.option_d: Actual functioning software is more meaningful evidence of progress than any other artifact
questions.explanation: In waterfall, projects can be "on schedule" while producing documents. No value delivered until month 18. Agile measures progress by working software in users' hands. "We have delivered 3 of 10 planned features" is more meaningful than "we've written 200 pages of specs."

questions.statement: Which of the following describes the Fagan Inspection process correctly?
questions.option_a: Informal walkthrough where the author presents their work
questions.option_b: Automated static analysis of code for bugs
questions.option_c: A structured, formal review with defined phases: planning, overview, preparation, inspection, rework, follow-up
questions.option_d: Testing performed by end users in their own environment
questions.explanation: Fagan inspection is a formal, structured, multi-phase process. It's more rigorous and more effective than informal walkthrough. Studies show it finds 60-90% of defects before testing.

questions.statement: When should security be addressed in the Software Development Lifecycle?
questions.option_a: Only during the testing phase
questions.option_b: Only after deployment when vulnerabilities are discovered
questions.option_c: Throughout all phases — requirements through deployment and operations
questions.option_d: Only during the design phase
questions.explanation: Security must be built in, not bolted on. Security requirements in requirements phase. Threat modeling in design. Secure coding in implementation. Security testing in test phase. Secure deployment. Monitoring in operations. Security in one phase only is catastrophically insufficient.

questions.statement: A software project was delivered on time and within budget but users rarely use it because it doesn't solve their actual problems. This failure represents:
questions.option_a: A testing failure — insufficient testing caused defects
questions.option_b: A requirements failure — the right thing was built incorrectly
questions.option_c: A requirements failure — the wrong thing was built correctly (even though it met specifications)
questions.option_d: A maintenance failure — the system was not maintained after delivery
questions.explanation: Building the wrong thing correctly is the most expensive failure — you spend full project cost delivering something useless. This is requirements engineering's greatest challenge: ensuring the specifications reflect actual user needs, not just what users said they needed.

questions.statement: What does SDLC stand for in the context of software engineering?
questions.option_a: System Design Life Cycle
questions.option_b: Software Deployment Life Cycle
questions.option_c: Software Development Life Cycle
questions.option_d: System Development Life Cycle
questions.explanation: SDLC stands for Software Development Life Cycle, which is the structured process of planning, creating, testing, and deploying software. Options A, B, and D use the same initials but incorrect expansions.

questions.statement: A development team notices that their project requirements keep changing every week, causing missed deadlines. Which process model is best suited to handle this situation?
questions.option_a: Waterfall Model
questions.option_b: V-Model
questions.option_c: Spiral Model
questions.option_d: Agile Model
questions.explanation: Agile is designed to accommodate frequently changing requirements through iterative sprints and continuous stakeholder collaboration. Waterfall and V-Model are rigid and ill-suited for volatile requirements.

questions.statement: Which software quality attribute refers to how easily a system can be modified to correct faults or adapt to new environments?
questions.option_a: Reliability
questions.option_b: Maintainability
questions.option_c: Portability
questions.option_d: Efficiency
questions.explanation: Maintainability is the ease with which a software system can be modified to fix defects, improve performance, or adapt to a changed environment. Reliability refers to consistent performance, not ease of modification.

questions.statement: A software architect is designing a system where each service runs independently and communicates over APIs. Which architectural style is being used?
questions.option_a: Layered Architecture
questions.option_b: Monolithic Architecture
questions.option_c: Microservices Architecture
questions.option_d: Event-Driven Architecture
questions.explanation: Microservices Architecture decomposes a system into small, independently deployable services that communicate via APIs. Monolithic Architecture packages all functionality into a single deployable unit.

questions.statement: During a sprint retrospective, a Scrum team identifies that their Definition of Done was never properly established. What is the most likely consequence of this oversight?
questions.option_a: Sprint velocity increases unpredictably
questions.option_b: Incomplete features are repeatedly marked as done
questions.option_c: The product owner loses voting rights in planning
questions.option_d: Daily standups become redundant
questions.explanation: Without a clear Definition of Done, team members apply inconsistent standards, leading to features being marked complete before they truly meet acceptance criteria. This causes quality debt to accumulate.

questions.statement: What does COCOMO stand for in software project estimation?
questions.option_a: Constructive Cost Model
questions.option_b: Computational Complexity Overhead Model
questions.option_c: Constructive Component Optimization Model
questions.option_d: Calculated Cost Operations Model
questions.explanation: COCOMO stands for Constructive Cost Model, an algorithmic software cost estimation model developed by Barry Boehm. The other options use the same initials but are fabricated expansions.

questions.statement: A tester executes test cases without knowledge of the internal code structure. Which testing technique is being applied?
questions.option_a: White-box Testing
questions.option_b: Gray-box Testing
questions.option_c: Black-box Testing
questions.option_d: Unit Testing
questions.explanation: Black-box testing evaluates software functionality without any knowledge of its internal implementation. White-box testing, by contrast, requires knowledge of the code structure.

questions.statement: Which SDLC phase is primarily responsible for identifying what the software system must do without specifying how it will do it?
questions.option_a: System Design
questions.option_b: Requirements Engineering
questions.option_c: Software Maintenance
questions.option_d: Implementation
questions.explanation: Requirements Engineering captures what the system must accomplish (functional and non-functional requirements) without defining implementation details. System Design addresses the 'how' of the solution.

questions.statement: A project manager observes that a team of 5 developers constantly misunderstands each other's code modules. Which metric would best quantify the degree of interdependency between those modules?
questions.option_a: Cyclomatic Complexity
questions.option_b: Lines of Code
questions.option_c: Coupling
questions.option_d: Cohesion
questions.explanation: Coupling measures the degree of interdependence between software modules. High coupling indicates that modules are tightly bound, making changes and understanding harder. Cohesion measures how well elements within a module belong together.

questions.statement: In the Spiral Model of software development, what is the PRIMARY activity during the risk analysis quadrant?
questions.option_a: Writing system specifications
questions.option_b: Evaluating alternatives and resolving uncertainties
questions.option_c: Developing and verifying the next-level product
questions.option_d: Planning the next iteration objectives
questions.explanation: The risk analysis quadrant of the Spiral Model focuses on identifying, evaluating, and mitigating risks before committing to the next cycle. Planning objectives occurs in a separate quadrant.

questions.statement: What does the acronym UML stand for?
questions.option_a: Unified Modeling Language
questions.option_b: Universal Markup Language
questions.option_c: Unified Module Linkage
questions.option_d: Universal Modeling Logic
questions.explanation: UML stands for Unified Modeling Language, a standardized visual language for specifying, constructing, and documenting software systems. The other options are fabricated expansions of the same letters.

questions.statement: A team using Extreme Programming (XP) writes automated tests before writing any production code. What practice are they following?
questions.option_a: Continuous Integration
questions.option_b: Pair Programming
questions.option_c: Test-Driven Development
questions.option_d: Refactoring
questions.explanation: Test-Driven Development (TDD) requires writing a failing test case before writing production code to make it pass. This practice is a core XP practice distinct from pair programming or continuous integration.

questions.statement: Which type of software maintenance involves modifying a system to correct discovered faults after deployment?
questions.option_a: Adaptive Maintenance
questions.option_b: Perfective Maintenance
questions.option_c: Corrective Maintenance
questions.option_d: Preventive Maintenance
questions.explanation: Corrective maintenance addresses bugs and failures discovered after the software has been deployed. Adaptive maintenance handles changes to the environment, while perfective maintenance improves performance or adds features.

questions.statement: A software engineer notices that a class in the codebase handles user authentication, generates PDF reports, and manages database connections simultaneously. Which design principle is being violated?
questions.option_a: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_b: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.option_c: Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.option_d: Interface Segregation Principle
questions.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class should have only one reason to change. Assigning multiple unrelated responsibilities to one class violates this principle and reduces maintainability.

questions.statement: During a code review, a reviewer finds that a new subclass overrides a parent class method in a way that breaks the parent class's expected behavior. Which SOLID principle is violated?
questions.option_a: Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.option_b: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_c: Interface Segregation Principle
questions.option_d: Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle states that objects of a subclass must be substitutable for objects of the parent class without altering program correctness. Overriding a method to break expected behavior directly violates this.

questions.statement: What does SRS stand for in software requirements documentation?
questions.option_a: System Requirements Summary
questions.option_b: Software Requirements Specification
questions.option_c: Structured Requirements Schema
questions.option_d: Software Resource Schedule
questions.explanation: SRS stands for Software Requirements Specification, a document that comprehensively describes the intended behavior, constraints, and interfaces of a software system. The other options are fabricated expansions.

questions.statement: A development team switches from monthly releases to deploying code multiple times per day using automated pipelines. Which practice best describes this change?
questions.option_a: Waterfall Delivery
questions.option_b: Continuous Deployment
questions.option_c: Feature Branching
questions.option_d: Regression Testing
questions.explanation: Continuous Deployment automates the release of every validated code change to production, enabling multiple deployments per day. Feature branching is a version control strategy, not a deployment frequency practice.

questions.statement: Which software design pattern defines a one-to-many dependency where all dependents are notified automatically when a subject's state changes?
questions.option_a: Singleton Pattern
questions.option_b: Factory Pattern
questions.option_c: Observer Pattern
questions.option_d: Strategy Pattern
questions.explanation: The Observer Pattern establishes a subscription mechanism where multiple objects (observers) are notified and updated automatically when another object (subject) changes state. The Singleton Pattern ensures only one instance of a class exists.

questions.statement: A project team is conducting a walkthrough of their requirements document with stakeholders to find ambiguities early. Which review technique are they using?
questions.option_a: Formal Inspection
questions.option_b: Technical Review
questions.option_c: Peer Review
questions.option_d: Requirements Walkthrough
questions.explanation: A Requirements Walkthrough is an informal review where the author guides stakeholders through the document to identify ambiguities and inconsistencies. A Formal Inspection follows a stricter, structured process with defined roles.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a Configuration Management System in software engineering?
questions.option_a: To automate user interface design workflows
questions.option_b: To track and control changes to software artifacts over time
questions.option_c: To calculate the total cost of a software project
questions.option_d: To schedule and assign developer tasks in sprints
questions.explanation: Software Configuration Management (SCM) systems track and control changes to source code, documentation, and other artifacts, ensuring consistency and traceability. Task scheduling is handled by project management tools.

questions.statement: A company wants to ensure their web application handles 10,000 simultaneous users without degrading response time. Which type of testing addresses this requirement?
questions.option_a: Smoke Testing
questions.option_b: Acceptance Testing
questions.option_c: Load Testing
questions.option_d: Regression Testing
questions.explanation: Load Testing evaluates system behavior under expected and peak load conditions to ensure performance requirements are met. Regression testing verifies that existing functionality has not been broken by new changes.

questions.statement: Which Agile artifact serves as a prioritized list of all desired features and requirements for a product?
questions.option_a: Sprint Backlog
questions.option_b: Release Plan
questions.option_c: Product Backlog
questions.option_d: Burndown Chart
questions.explanation: The Product Backlog is a prioritized list of all features, enhancements, and fixes desired for a product, maintained by the Product Owner. The Sprint Backlog contains only the items selected for the current sprint.

questions.statement: In software testing, what does the term 'regression testing' primarily aim to verify?
questions.option_a: That new features work correctly before release
questions.option_b: That previously working functionality has not been broken by new changes
questions.option_c: That the system meets security vulnerability standards
questions.option_d: That code coverage exceeds the defined threshold
questions.explanation: Regression testing ensures that modifications to the codebase have not introduced defects in previously working functionality. Verifying new features is the goal of functional or acceptance testing.

questions.statement: A senior developer proposes extracting a group of related functions spread across multiple classes into a single, cohesive class. Which refactoring goal does this serve?
questions.option_a: Reducing cyclomatic complexity
questions.option_b: Increasing coupling between modules
questions.option_c: Improving cohesion within the module
questions.option_d: Eliminating dead code paths
questions.explanation: Grouping related functions into a single class increases cohesion, meaning the class has a single, well-defined purpose. Cohesion and coupling are inversely desirable—high cohesion and low coupling is the ideal.

questions.statement: What does the acronym CASE stand for in software engineering tools?
questions.option_a: Computer-Aided Software Engineering
questions.option_b: Collaborative Application Source Environment
questions.option_c: Code Analysis and Syntax Engine
questions.option_d: Component-Aided System Execution
questions.explanation: CASE stands for Computer-Aided Software Engineering, referring to tools that support the software development process through automation of tasks like modeling, coding, and testing. The other options are fabricated expansions.

questions.statement: A software project has a low fault detection rate during testing but a high number of faults reported post-release. What does this most likely indicate?
questions.option_a: The testing team lacked sufficient hardware resources
questions.option_b: The test cases were not adequately covering the requirements
questions.option_c: The development team used an inappropriate programming language
questions.option_d: The project manager did not schedule enough sprint meetings
questions.explanation: A low fault detection rate coupled with high post-release faults indicates poor test coverage—the test cases failed to exercise sufficient functionality and edge cases to expose existing defects.

questions.statement: Which software architecture pattern separates an application into three interconnected components: data, presentation, and logic?
questions.option_a: Client-Server Architecture
questions.option_b: Service-Oriented Architecture
questions.option_c: Peer-to-Peer Architecture
questions.option_d: Model-View-Controller Architecture
questions.explanation: The Model-View-Controller (MVC) Architecture separates an application into the Model (data), View (presentation), and Controller (logic) components. Client-Server architecture describes the distribution of roles between machines.

questions.statement: During requirements elicitation, a business analyst uses structured questions to gather information from domain experts one at a time. Which technique is being used?
questions.option_a: Focus Groups
questions.option_b: Interviews
questions.option_c: Observation
questions.option_d: Questionnaires
questions.explanation: Interviews involve structured or semi-structured one-on-one conversations with stakeholders to elicit requirements. Focus groups involve multiple stakeholders simultaneously, while questionnaires are written instruments.

questions.statement: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a Gantt chart in software project management?
questions.option_a: Tracking defect density over time
questions.option_b: Visualizing the schedule of project tasks and their durations
questions.option_c: Mapping dependencies between software modules
questions.option_d: Measuring team velocity across sprints
questions.explanation: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart used to visualize project tasks, their scheduled start and end dates, and their durations. Defect tracking and module dependency mapping are done using other specialized tools.

questions.statement: Which type of software requirement specifies constraints on how the system must perform rather than what it must do?
questions.option_a: Functional Requirement
questions.option_b: Domain Requirement
questions.option_c: Non-Functional Requirement
questions.option_d: Business Requirement
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements specify system qualities such as performance, security, and usability—constraints on how the system behaves rather than specific behaviors. Functional requirements describe what the system must do.

questions.statement: A team is implementing a feature where a class cannot be directly instantiated and instead provides a shared instance through a static method. Which design pattern is this?
questions.option_a: Factory Method Pattern
questions.option_b: Prototype Pattern
questions.option_c: Singleton Pattern
questions.option_d: Builder Pattern
questions.explanation: The Singleton Pattern ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it, typically through a static method. The Factory Method Pattern deals with object creation through subclass delegation.

questions.statement: What does the term 'technical debt' refer to in software engineering?
questions.option_a: The financial cost of purchasing development licenses
questions.option_b: The implied cost of rework caused by choosing quick solutions over better long-term approaches
questions.option_c: The budget overrun caused by adding unplanned features
questions.option_d: The overhead costs of training new developers on a codebase
questions.explanation: Technical debt represents the future cost of rework accumulated by taking shortcuts or making suboptimal design decisions to meet immediate deadlines. It is a metaphor for deferred code quality work.

questions.statement: In risk management, which strategy involves transferring the impact of a risk to a third party?
questions.option_a: Risk Avoidance
questions.option_b: Risk Mitigation
questions.option_c: Risk Acceptance
questions.option_d: Risk Transfer
questions.explanation: Risk Transfer shifts the financial or operational impact of a risk to a third party, such as through insurance or contracts. Risk Mitigation reduces the probability or impact of a risk occurring.

questions.statement: A Scrum team has a velocity of 40 story points per sprint. Their product backlog contains 200 story points. Approximately how many sprints will it take to complete the backlog?
questions.option_a: 4 sprints
questions.option_b: 5 sprints
questions.option_c: 8 sprints
questions.option_d: 10 sprints
questions.explanation: Dividing the total backlog (200 story points) by the team's velocity (40 story points per sprint) gives 5 sprints. This is a basic sprint planning calculation used in Agile estimation.

questions.statement: Which type of UML diagram is best suited to show the sequence of messages exchanged between objects during a specific use case?
questions.option_a: Class Diagram
questions.option_b: Component Diagram
questions.option_c: Sequence Diagram
questions.option_d: Activity Diagram
questions.explanation: A Sequence Diagram shows the chronological order of messages exchanged between objects to accomplish a specific function or use case. A Class Diagram shows static structure and relationships between classes.

questions.statement: What does the acronym IEEE stand for in the context of software engineering standards?
questions.option_a: International Engineering and Electronics Enterprise
questions.option_b: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
questions.option_c: Integrated Environment for Engineering Execution
questions.option_d: International Evaluation for Electronics and Engineering
questions.explanation: IEEE stands for Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, the professional organization that publishes widely-used software engineering standards. The other options are fabricated expansions of the same initials.

questions.statement: A developer discovers that a module in the system can only be reused if three other unrelated modules are also included. What software quality problem does this illustrate?
questions.option_a: Low cohesion within the module
questions.option_b: High coupling between modules
questions.option_c: Insufficient cyclomatic complexity
questions.option_d: Poor code readability
questions.explanation: High coupling means a module is tightly dependent on multiple other modules, making independent reuse difficult. Low cohesion means a module has unrelated internal responsibilities, which is a different problem.

questions.statement: Which testing level focuses on verifying that individual units of source code work correctly in isolation?
questions.option_a: Integration Testing
questions.option_b: System Testing
questions.option_c: Unit Testing
questions.option_d: Acceptance Testing
questions.explanation: Unit Testing verifies the smallest testable parts of a software system in isolation from external dependencies. Integration Testing verifies that multiple units work correctly together.

questions.statement: A software project manager identifies that the critical path of a project passes through the database design task. What does this imply?
questions.option_a: The database design task has the highest budget allocation
questions.option_b: Any delay in database design will directly delay the project completion
questions.option_c: The database design task has the most assigned developers
questions.option_d: The database design task can be safely postponed without impact
questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks that determines the minimum project duration. Any delay in a task on the critical path directly extends the overall project end date.

questions.statement: What is the main purpose of a software inspection, as distinct from a walkthrough?
questions.option_a: To demonstrate working software to the product owner
questions.option_b: To detect defects through a formal, structured review with defined roles
questions.option_c: To plan the tasks for the next development iteration
questions.option_d: To train junior developers on the codebase
questions.explanation: A software inspection is a formal, rigorous defect detection technique with defined roles (moderator, author, inspectors) and a documented process. A walkthrough is less formal and typically author-led.

questions.statement: Which software metric measures the number of linearly independent paths through a program's source code?
questions.option_a: Function Point
questions.option_b: Lines of Code
questions.option_c: Halstead Volume
questions.option_d: Cyclomatic Complexity
questions.explanation: Cyclomatic Complexity, defined by Thomas McCabe, counts the number of linearly independent paths through a program, serving as a measure of its testability and maintainability. Function Points measure functional size.

questions.statement: A system is described as being able to recover from a hardware failure and resume normal operation within two minutes. Which quality attribute is being specified?
questions.option_a: Scalability
questions.option_b: Availability
questions.option_c: Portability
questions.option_d: Recoverability
questions.explanation: Recoverability refers to a system's ability to re-establish its performance level and recover data affected by a failure within a specified time. Availability measures the proportion of time the system is operational.

questions.statement: In a software project following the V-Model, which development phase directly corresponds to system testing?
questions.option_a: Unit Design
questions.option_b: Detailed Design
questions.option_c: System Requirements
questions.option_d: High-Level Design
questions.explanation: In the V-Model, System Testing validates the entire system against the System Requirements specification. Each testing phase on the right side of the V corresponds to a development phase on the left side.

questions.statement: Which Agile ceremony is specifically intended to allow the team to improve its own processes and collaboration at the end of each iteration?
questions.option_a: Sprint Review
questions.option_b: Sprint Planning
questions.option_c: Daily Scrum
questions.option_d: Sprint Retrospective
questions.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is held at the end of each sprint to allow the team to reflect on and improve their process, collaboration, and tooling. The Sprint Review focuses on inspecting the product increment.

questions.statement: A software company maintains a separate environment that is identical to production, used only for final validation before each release. What is this environment called?
questions.option_a: Development Environment
questions.option_b: Test Environment
questions.option_c: Staging Environment
questions.option_d: Integration Environment
questions.explanation: A Staging Environment is an environment that mirrors production as closely as possible and is used for final validation testing before a release is deployed to production. It catches environment-specific defects.

questions.statement: What does the acronym FURPS stand for in software quality models?
questions.option_a: Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability
questions.option_b: Flexibility, Usability, Robustness, Performance, Scalability
questions.option_c: Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Portability, Security
questions.option_d: Flexibility, Uniformity, Reliability, Performance, Supportability
questions.explanation: FURPS stands for Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, and Supportability, a quality model used to classify software requirements. The other options alter one or more of the correct terms.

questions.statement: A developer uses a version control system to create an isolated copy of the main codebase to develop a new feature without affecting the stable release. What is this isolated copy called?
questions.option_a: A Commit
questions.option_b: A Tag
questions.option_c: A Branch
questions.option_d: A Fork
questions.explanation: A Branch is an isolated copy of the codebase within the same repository used to develop features or fixes without affecting the main codebase. A Fork is a separate copy of an entire repository, typically on a different account.

questions.statement: Which software design concept ensures that a module's implementation details are hidden from other modules, exposing only a well-defined interface?
questions.option_a: Abstraction
questions.option_b: Encapsulation
questions.option_c: Polymorphism
questions.option_d: Inheritance
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides a module's internal implementation details and exposes only a well-defined interface for interaction, reducing dependencies. Abstraction is a broader concept of modeling only essential aspects of an entity.

questions.statement: A team's burndown chart shows that the remaining work line is consistently above the ideal progress line throughout the sprint. What does this indicate?
questions.option_a: The team is ahead of schedule
questions.option_b: The team is not completing work fast enough to meet the sprint goal
questions.option_c: The team has too few user stories in the backlog
questions.option_d: The product owner added stories after sprint planning
questions.explanation: A burndown chart line consistently above the ideal line indicates the team is completing work more slowly than planned, signaling a risk of not meeting the sprint goal. Being ahead of schedule would show the line below ideal.

questions.statement: Which security principle in software engineering states that components should only have access to the information and resources necessary for their legitimate purpose?
questions.option_a: Defense in Depth
questions.option_b: Fail-Safe Defaults
questions.option_c: Least Privilege
questions.option_d: Separation of Duties
questions.explanation: The Principle of Least Privilege dictates that each component or user should be granted only the minimum access rights needed for its function. Defense in Depth is a layered security strategy.

questions.statement: What is the key distinguishing characteristic of a use case diagram in UML?
questions.option_a: It shows the timing of messages between objects
questions.option_b: It depicts the physical deployment of software components
questions.option_c: It captures functional requirements from the user's perspective
questions.option_d: It describes the internal state transitions of an object
questions.explanation: Use Case Diagrams capture the functional requirements of a system by showing interactions between external actors and the system's use cases. State diagrams capture object state transitions.

questions.statement: A software team applies the principle that once a module is released, its interface should never be changed, only extended. Which SOLID principle does this represent?
questions.option_a: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.option_b: Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.option_c: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_d: Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification, allowing new functionality without changing existing, tested code. This prevents breaking dependent modules.

questions.statement: Which process model is best described as a sequential set of phases where each phase must be completely finished before the next begins?
questions.option_a: Incremental Model
questions.option_b: Prototyping Model
questions.option_c: Waterfall Model
questions.option_d: RAD Model
questions.explanation: The Waterfall Model is a strictly sequential process where each phase (Requirements, Design, Implementation, Testing, Maintenance) must be completed before the next begins. Incremental models deliver working software in multiple iterations.

questions.statement: In software project management, what does the term 'scope creep' refer to?
questions.option_a: The gradual increase in project budget due to inflation
questions.option_b: The uncontrolled expansion of project requirements beyond what was originally agreed
questions.option_c: The slow decline in team productivity during long sprints
questions.option_d: The progressive accumulation of unresolved technical debt
questions.explanation: Scope creep is the uncontrolled growth of project scope, where new features or requirements are added without proper change control processes, often leading to cost and schedule overruns.

questions.statement: A software architect chooses to place business logic, data access, and presentation in completely separate layers that communicate through defined interfaces. What architectural pattern is this?
questions.option_a: Microservices Architecture
questions.option_b: Event-Driven Architecture
questions.option_c: Layered (N-Tier) Architecture
questions.option_d: Repository Pattern
questions.explanation: Layered (N-Tier) Architecture organizes a system into layers—such as Presentation, Business Logic, and Data Access—where each layer has a specific responsibility and communicates only with adjacent layers.

questions.statement: Which type of software prototype is built quickly to explore requirements but is discarded after the concepts are validated?
questions.option_a: Evolutionary Prototype
questions.option_b: Horizontal Prototype
questions.option_c: Throwaway Prototype
questions.option_d: Vertical Prototype
questions.explanation: A Throwaway (or Exploratory) Prototype is built quickly to clarify ambiguous requirements and is then discarded, not evolved into the final product. An Evolutionary Prototype is refined incrementally into the final system.

questions.statement: What is the role of a Product Owner in the Scrum framework?
questions.option_a: Facilitating all Scrum ceremonies and removing team impediments
questions.option_b: Writing and executing all test cases for each sprint
questions.option_c: Maximizing product value by managing and prioritizing the Product Backlog
questions.option_d: Assigning tasks to individual developers each day
questions.explanation: The Product Owner is responsible for maximizing the value of the product by managing the Product Backlog, setting priorities, and representing stakeholder interests. The Scrum Master facilitates ceremonies and removes impediments.

questions.statement: An application crashes when a user enters a negative number in a field that expects only positive integers. Which testing technique would most effectively catch this bug?
questions.option_a: Statement Coverage Testing
questions.option_b: Boundary Value Analysis
questions.option_c: Equivalence Partitioning
questions.option_d: Mutation Testing
questions.explanation: Boundary Value Analysis tests input values at the boundaries of valid and invalid partitions, such as -1, 0, and 1 for a positive-integer field, directly targeting this class of defect. Equivalence Partitioning divides inputs into valid and invalid groups but may not test exact boundaries.

questions.statement: Which software quality attribute measures the proportion of time that a system is operational and accessible to users?
questions.option_a: Reliability
questions.option_b: Maintainability
questions.option_c: Availability
questions.option_d: Scalability
questions.explanation: Availability is the proportion of time a system is in a functioning, accessible state, often expressed as a percentage (e.g., 99.9%). Reliability refers to the system's ability to perform its required function without failure.

questions.statement: What does the acronym DFD stand for in structured analysis?
questions.option_a: Dynamic Functional Design
questions.option_b: Data Flow Diagram
questions.option_c: Distributed File Descriptor
questions.option_d: Design Framework Diagram
questions.explanation: DFD stands for Data Flow Diagram, a graphical representation of how data moves through a system, showing processes, data stores, and external entities. The other options are fabricated expansions.

questions.statement: A developer is asked to improve the internal structure of existing code without changing its external behavior. What is this process called?
questions.option_a: Debugging
questions.option_b: Refactoring
questions.option_c: Reverse Engineering
questions.option_d: Re-engineering
questions.explanation: Refactoring is the disciplined technique of restructuring existing code to improve its internal design, readability, or maintainability without altering its external, observable behavior. Debugging involves finding and fixing defects.

questions.statement: Which Agile estimation technique uses a series of cards with values representing story point estimates, and team members reveal their estimates simultaneously to avoid anchoring bias?
questions.option_a: Affinity Estimation
questions.option_b: Three-Point Estimation
questions.option_c: Planning Poker
questions.option_d: T-Shirt Sizing
questions.explanation: Planning Poker is a consensus-based Agile estimation technique where team members simultaneously reveal their estimates using Fibonacci-valued cards, reducing anchoring bias and promoting discussion.

questions.statement: In software architecture, what is a key disadvantage of a monolithic architecture compared to microservices?
questions.option_a: It requires more network bandwidth for component communication
questions.option_b: Scaling the entire application is necessary even when only one component has high load
questions.option_c: It cannot support relational databases as a data store
questions.option_d: It prevents the use of continuous integration pipelines
questions.explanation: A major drawback of monolithic architecture is that the entire application must be scaled even if only one part requires additional resources. Microservices allow independent scaling of individual services.

questions.statement: A software team uses automated tools to automatically build, test, and merge code changes multiple times per day. Which practice is this?
questions.option_a: Continuous Delivery
questions.option_b: Continuous Deployment
questions.option_c: Continuous Integration
questions.option_d: Agile Retrospective
questions.explanation: Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of automatically building and testing code every time a developer pushes changes to a shared repository. Continuous Delivery extends CI by automating the release process to a staging environment.

questions.statement: Which type of coupling is considered the most undesirable in software design?
questions.option_a: Data Coupling
questions.option_b: Stamp Coupling
questions.option_c: Control Coupling
questions.option_d: Content Coupling
questions.explanation: Content Coupling is the most undesirable form, occurring when one module directly accesses or modifies the internal data or code of another module, breaking encapsulation. Data Coupling, where modules share only the necessary data through parameters, is the most desirable.

questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of a feasibility study conducted at the beginning of a software project?
questions.option_a: To assign team roles and responsibilities
questions.option_b: To determine whether the proposed system is technically and economically viable
questions.option_c: To define the coding standards for the project
questions.option_d: To write the initial version of the SRS document
questions.explanation: A feasibility study assesses whether a proposed software project is viable from technical, economic, operational, and scheduling perspectives before committing resources. It informs the decision to proceed or abandon the project.

questions.statement: A user interface designer ensures that the most frequently used actions are accessible within three clicks from any screen. Which UI design principle is being applied?
questions.option_a: Consistency
questions.option_b: Feedback
questions.option_c: Affordance
questions.option_d: Efficiency
questions.explanation: Efficiency is a UI design principle aimed at minimizing the number of steps required to accomplish common tasks, directly reflected in the 'three-click rule' heuristic. Consistency means the interface behaves predictably across screens.

questions.statement: Which software testing technique involves modifying source code in small ways to check whether the test suite can detect the changes?
questions.option_a: Fuzzing
questions.option_b: Boundary Testing
questions.option_c: Mutation Testing
questions.option_d: Regression Testing
questions.explanation: Mutation Testing introduces small, deliberate faults (mutations) into the source code to evaluate whether the existing test suite can detect them, measuring test suite effectiveness. Fuzzing involves providing random or malformed inputs.

questions.statement: What does the term 'baseline' mean in software configuration management?
questions.option_a: The minimum performance threshold a system must achieve
questions.option_b: A formally reviewed and approved version of a software artifact that serves as the basis for future changes
questions.option_c: The initial set of functional requirements before any changes are made
questions.option_d: The codebase state before any developer branches are merged
questions.explanation: A baseline in SCM is a formally reviewed, agreed-upon version of a software artifact that can only be changed through a formal change control process. It serves as a stable reference point for future development.

questions.statement: A project has a Planned Value (PV) of $80,000, Actual Cost (AC) of $90,000, and Earned Value (EV) of $70,000. What is the Cost Variance (CV)?
questions.option_a: $10,000 (over budget)
questions.option_b: $20,000 (over budget)
questions.option_c: –$20,000 (over budget)
questions.option_d: –$10,000 (over budget)
questions.explanation: Cost Variance (CV) = EV – AC = $70,000 – $90,000 = –$20,000. A negative CV indicates the project is over budget. A positive CV would indicate under-budget performance.

questions.statement: Which model of software maintenance classifies maintenance into corrective, adaptive, perfective, and preventive categories?
questions.option_a: Carnegie Mellon Model
questions.option_b: Lehman's Laws
questions.option_c: Lientz and Swanson Model
questions.option_d: ISO/IEC 14764 Model
questions.explanation: The Lientz and Swanson Model classifies software maintenance into four categories: corrective, adaptive, perfective, and preventive. This is one of the most cited early empirical studies of software maintenance activity.

questions.statement: In object-oriented design, which principle states that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules, but both should depend on abstractions?
questions.option_a: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.option_b: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_c: Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.option_d: Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.explanation: The Dependency Inversion Principle requires that both high-level and low-level modules depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on each other directly. This decouples modules and makes the system more flexible and testable.

questions.statement: A company's application requires 99.999% uptime, meaning it cannot be unavailable for more than approximately 5 minutes per year. What does this metric define?
questions.option_a: Recovery Time Objective
questions.option_b: Mean Time Between Failures
questions.option_c: Service Level Agreement
questions.option_d: Availability Requirement
questions.explanation: The 99.999% uptime figure is a specific availability requirement often expressed in SLAs, but as a system property it defines the availability non-functional requirement. SLA is a contract between provider and customer that may contain this metric.

questions.statement: Which diagram in UML is used to show the physical deployment of software components on hardware nodes?
questions.option_a: Component Diagram
questions.option_b: Deployment Diagram
questions.option_c: Package Diagram
questions.option_d: Composite Structure Diagram
questions.explanation: A UML Deployment Diagram shows how software components are distributed across physical hardware nodes (servers, devices). A Component Diagram shows the logical organization of software components and their dependencies.

questions.statement: What is the term for a software defect that only appears under specific conditions, such as a particular sequence of user actions, and is difficult to reproduce consistently?
questions.option_a: A latent bug
questions.option_b: A Heisenbug
questions.option_c: An intermittent bug
questions.option_d: A regression bug
questions.explanation: An intermittent bug is a defect that appears inconsistently and is difficult to reproduce reliably, making it challenging to diagnose and fix. A Heisenbug is a specific type of bug that changes behavior when being observed or debugged.

questions.statement: A team practicing Kanban uses a board to limit the number of tasks in the 'In Progress' column to three at a time. What concept does this limit implement?
questions.option_a: Sprint Commitment
questions.option_b: Work in Progress (WIP) Limit
questions.option_c: Definition of Done
questions.option_d: Throughput Constraint
questions.explanation: Work in Progress (WIP) Limits are a core Kanban practice that restricts the number of tasks in each stage of the workflow to reduce context switching, identify bottlenecks, and improve flow.

questions.statement: Which software architecture style processes data as a series of transformations where the output of one component is the input to the next?
questions.option_a: Blackboard Architecture
questions.option_b: Broker Architecture
questions.option_c: Pipe-and-Filter Architecture
questions.option_d: Repository Architecture
questions.explanation: The Pipe-and-Filter architecture processes data streams through a sequence of independent filter components connected by pipes, where each filter transforms the data and passes it to the next. Compiler design is a classic example.

questions.statement: What does the acronym MVC stand for in software design patterns?
questions.option_a: Module-View-Controller
questions.option_b: Model-Validation-Component
questions.option_c: Model-View-Controller
questions.option_d: Module-Validation-Component
questions.explanation: MVC stands for Model-View-Controller, a design pattern that separates an application into three components. The other options use the same initials but substitute incorrect words for 'View' or 'Model'.

questions.statement: A software team has identified that a specific third-party library they depend on is no longer receiving security patches. Which risk response strategy involves replacing the library with a maintained alternative?
questions.option_a: Risk Acceptance
questions.option_b: Risk Avoidance
questions.option_c: Risk Mitigation
questions.option_d: Risk Transfer
questions.explanation: Replacing a vulnerable library with a maintained alternative actively reduces the probability of a security incident, which is the goal of Risk Mitigation. Risk Avoidance would mean eliminating the feature entirely.

questions.statement: In the context of software testing, what is a 'test oracle'?
questions.option_a: A specialized database used to store test results
questions.option_b: A mechanism or document that determines whether a test has passed or failed
questions.option_c: A tool that automatically generates test cases from requirements
questions.option_d: A senior tester responsible for approving the test plan
questions.explanation: A test oracle is the means by which a tester determines the expected outcome of a test and judges whether the system produced the correct result. It can be a specification, a reference implementation, or domain expert knowledge.

questions.statement: Which Agile framework, commonly used for large-scale implementations, divides the organization into Agile Release Trains (ARTs)?
questions.option_a: Crystal
questions.option_b: SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework)
questions.option_c: DSDM
questions.option_d: LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum)
questions.explanation: SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) organizes large enterprises into Agile Release Trains (ARTs), which are long-lived teams of Agile teams aligned to a common mission. LeSS and DSDM are different scaling frameworks that do not use this concept.

questions.statement: A system's response time increases from 200ms to 2000ms when the number of users doubles. This behavior most directly indicates a problem with which quality attribute?
questions.option_a: Reliability
questions.option_b: Security
questions.option_c: Scalability
questions.option_d: Maintainability
questions.explanation: Scalability is a system's ability to handle increased load without unacceptable performance degradation. A tenfold increase in response time from doubling users indicates poor scalability. Reliability refers to consistent fault-free operation.

questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of a software quality audit?
questions.option_a: To measure developer productivity using lines of code
questions.option_b: To independently verify that software processes and products comply with defined standards and plans
questions.option_c: To demonstrate the system's features to end users before release
questions.option_d: To identify and assign defects found during code review
questions.explanation: A software quality audit is an independent review of software processes and products to verify conformance with standards, plans, and regulations. It is different from a product inspection, which focuses on finding defects.

questions.statement: Which requirement elicitation technique is most useful when the domain knowledge is tacit and experts find it difficult to articulate their knowledge verbally?
questions.option_a: Surveys
questions.option_b: Prototyping
questions.option_c: Interviews
questions.option_d: Document Analysis
questions.explanation: Prototyping is effective when tacit knowledge is involved, as users can react to and validate a concrete artifact more easily than describing abstract requirements verbally. Interviews are useful but less effective for tacit, non-verbalized knowledge.

questions.statement: In software engineering, what is 'software entropy'?
questions.option_a: The gradual increase in a software system's disorder, complexity, and degradation over time
questions.option_b: The total energy consumed by a software system during execution
questions.option_c: The randomness introduced into algorithms to improve security
questions.option_d: The measure of data unpredictability within a database
questions.explanation: Software entropy, inspired by the physics concept, refers to the tendency of software systems to become increasingly disorganized, complex, and difficult to maintain over time as changes accumulate without proper design discipline.

questions.statement: A developer writes a function that accepts a base class parameter but tests confirm it works correctly with all subclass instances. Which SOLID principle is being demonstrated?
questions.option_a: Open/Closed Principle
questions.option_b: Interface Segregation Principle
questions.option_c: Single Responsibility Principle
questions.option_d: Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle is demonstrated when code using a base class type works correctly with any subclass instance, confirming that subclasses genuinely extend, rather than break, the behavior of the base class.

questions.statement: What does the acronym CMMI stand for in software process improvement?
questions.option_a: Capability Maturity Model Integration
questions.option_b: Continuous Management and Metrics Initiative
questions.option_c: Capability Management and Measurement Index
questions.option_d: Continuous Maturity Model Integration
questions.explanation: CMMI stands for Capability Maturity Model Integration, a process improvement framework that helps organizations improve their software development processes across five maturity levels. The other options are fabricated expansions.

questions.statement: A testers' team finds that 80% of defects are concentrated in 20% of the modules. Which software quality principle does this observation reflect?
questions.option_a: The Pareto Principle
questions.option_b: The Pesticide Paradox
questions.option_c: Defect Clustering
questions.option_d: Error Seeding
questions.explanation: Defect Clustering is the testing principle that a small number of modules tend to contain the majority of defects, which aligns with the Pareto (80/20) observation. Recognizing clustering helps target testing efforts effectively.

questions.statement: Which software process activity is responsible for ensuring that the software product correctly implements all specified requirements?
questions.option_a: Validation
questions.option_b: Verification
questions.option_c: Configuration Management
questions.option_d: Quality Assurance
questions.explanation: Verification ensures the software correctly implements the specified requirements (building the product right), while Validation ensures the right product was built (it meets user needs). These are distinct activities in quality management.

questions.statement: A software company stores all source code, build scripts, and configuration files in a central system that tracks every version of every file. What type of system is this?
questions.option_a: Issue Tracking System
questions.option_b: Continuous Integration Server
questions.option_c: Version Control System
questions.option_d: Build Automation System
questions.explanation: A Version Control System (VCS) tracks and manages changes to files over time, maintaining a history of every version. Issue tracking systems manage bugs and tasks; CI servers automate builds triggered by code changes.

questions.statement: In the context of user interface design, which principle states that the system should always keep users informed about what is happening through appropriate feedback?
questions.option_a: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
questions.option_b: User Control and Freedom
questions.option_c: Visibility of System Status
questions.option_d: Error Prevention
questions.explanation: Visibility of System Status, one of Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics, requires that the system always communicate its current state to users through timely feedback. Error Prevention is a separate heuristic about designing to prevent mistakes.

questions.statement: What is the key difference between software validation and software verification?
questions.option_a: Validation checks code syntax while verification checks functionality
questions.option_b: Verification confirms the product is built right; validation confirms the right product was built
questions.option_c: Validation is performed by developers while verification is performed by testers
questions.option_d: Verification occurs after deployment while validation occurs during development
questions.explanation: This is the classic V&V distinction: Verification asks 'Are we building the product right?' (conformance to specification), while Validation asks 'Are we building the right product?' (fitness for user needs). Both are independent quality activities.

questions.statement: Which design pattern provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem by creating a single entry point?
questions.option_a: Adapter Pattern
questions.option_b: Proxy Pattern
questions.option_c: Facade Pattern
questions.option_d: Decorator Pattern
questions.explanation: The Facade Pattern provides a unified, simplified interface to a complex subsystem, hiding its complexity from client code. The Adapter Pattern translates one interface into another; the Proxy Pattern controls access to an object.

questions.statement: During a post-mortem analysis, a team discovers that the majority of their schedule delays were caused by underestimating integration tasks. Which estimation technique could have best addressed this by explicitly modeling task dependencies and uncertainties?
questions.option_a: Function Point Analysis
questions.option_b: PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique)
questions.option_c: Lines of Code Estimation
questions.option_d: Story Point Estimation
questions.explanation: PERT uses three-point estimates (optimistic, pessimistic, most likely) and models task dependencies, making it effective for capturing scheduling uncertainties in complex projects. Function Point Analysis measures functional size, not schedule duration.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of static analysis tools in software quality assurance?
questions.option_a: To measure the system's response time under concurrent user loads
questions.option_b: To examine source code for defects and style violations without executing the program
questions.option_c: To generate test data and inject it into a running system
questions.option_d: To monitor memory allocation during program execution
questions.explanation: Static analysis tools inspect source code without executing it to identify potential defects, security vulnerabilities, and coding standard violations. Dynamic analysis, by contrast, examines behavior during program execution.

questions.statement: A project stakeholder requests a feature midway through the project that significantly changes the system architecture. What process should the team follow?
questions.option_a: Immediately implement the feature to satisfy the stakeholder
questions.option_b: Reject the request outright as it is outside the original scope
questions.option_c: Submit the request through the formal change control process for evaluation
questions.option_d: Defer all architecture changes until after the final release
questions.explanation: A formal change control process evaluates the impact of proposed changes on cost, schedule, and scope before approval. Immediately implementing or outright rejecting changes are both poor practices that bypass governance.

questions.statement: In software testing terminology, what is the difference between an error, a fault, and a failure?
questions.option_a: They are synonyms used interchangeably in modern testing practice
questions.option_b: An error is a human mistake causing a fault in code; a fault may cause a failure during execution
questions.option_c: A failure is a developer mistake; a fault is a tester's oversight; an error is a user mistake
questions.option_d: An error occurs at runtime; a fault is a design problem; a failure is a requirements gap
questions.explanation: In IEEE terminology: an Error is a human action that produces incorrect code (a Fault/Defect); a Fault in the code, when triggered, causes a Failure (incorrect system behavior). These are distinct concepts in the defect taxonomy.

questions.statement: Which software architecture pattern uses a central event bus where components publish and subscribe to events without knowing each other's identity?
questions.option_a: Layered Architecture
questions.option_b: Pipe-and-Filter Architecture
questions.option_c: Event-Driven Architecture
questions.option_d: Repository Architecture
questions.explanation: Event-Driven Architecture decouples components by having them communicate through events on a shared bus. Publishers and subscribers have no direct knowledge of each other, promoting loose coupling and scalability.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of 'code coverage' as a metric in software testing?
questions.option_a: To measure the number of bugs found per lines of code written
questions.option_b: To quantify the proportion of source code executed by a test suite
questions.option_c: To assess how closely the code follows documented coding standards
questions.option_d: To count the number of distinct code paths tested per sprint
questions.explanation: Code coverage measures the percentage of source code statements, branches, or paths that are exercised by a test suite, serving as a proxy for test thoroughness. High coverage does not guarantee defect-free code but indicates untested areas.

questions.statement: A software team is using a process where requirements are gathered, a small working version is built, demonstrated to users, and refined in repeated cycles. Which model does this describe?
questions.option_a: Waterfall Model
questions.option_b: V-Model
questions.option_c: Iterative Prototyping Model
questions.option_d: Big Bang Model
questions.explanation: The Iterative Prototyping Model repeatedly builds, demonstrates, and refines working prototypes based on user feedback until the requirements are fully understood and the product is acceptable. This is distinct from Waterfall's single-pass approach.

questions.statement: Which attribute of a good software requirement states that it must be testable—that is, there must be a way to verify whether the system has met it?
questions.option_a: Completeness
questions.option_b: Consistency
questions.option_c: Verifiability
questions.option_d: Traceability
questions.explanation: Verifiability requires that a requirement can be objectively confirmed as met or not met through testing, review, or analysis. Ambiguous or unmeasurable requirements cannot be verified, making them unacceptable in a formal SRS.

questions.statement: A large e-commerce company needs to ensure that a failure in the payment service does not cascade and bring down the entire platform. Which software design pattern is most applicable?
questions.option_a: Retry Pattern
questions.option_b: Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.option_c: Bulkhead Pattern
questions.option_d: Throttle Pattern
questions.explanation: The Circuit Breaker Pattern prevents cascading failures by detecting repeated failures in a service and temporarily stopping requests to it, allowing the rest of the system to remain functional. The Bulkhead Pattern isolates failures by partitioning resources.

questions.statement: What does the term 'software process maturity' refer to in the context of the CMMI model?
questions.option_a: The age of the software application currently in production
questions.option_b: The degree to which an organization's software processes are defined, measured, and continuously improved
questions.option_c: The number of successful projects completed by a software team
questions.option_d: The proportion of senior developers to junior developers in an organization
questions.explanation: Software process maturity in CMMI refers to how well-defined, consistently followed, measured, and continuously improved an organization's processes are. Higher maturity levels correspond to more disciplined and optimized processes.

questions.statement: A developer applies the DRY principle while reviewing a codebase. What does DRY stand for, and what specific problem is the developer trying to eliminate?
questions.option_a: Don't Repeat Yourself; the developer is eliminating duplicated code or knowledge
questions.option_b: Design Right Yourself; the developer is eliminating poor design patterns
questions.option_c: Develop Reliable Yields; the developer is improving test coverage
questions.option_d: Document Resources Yearly; the developer is improving code comments
questions.explanation: DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself, a principle that states every piece of knowledge should have a single, authoritative representation in the system. The developer is eliminating code duplication that creates maintenance burdens.

questions.statement: Which type of software testing is performed by the end-users in their own environment to validate the software before formal acceptance?
questions.option_a: Alpha Testing
questions.option_b: Usability Testing
questions.option_c: System Testing
questions.option_d: Beta Testing
questions.explanation: Beta Testing is performed by real end-users in their actual operating environment, providing feedback on usability and defects before final release. Alpha Testing is conducted internally by the development organization, not end-users in the field.

questions.statement: What is the primary role of a Software Configuration Management (SCM) audit?
questions.option_a: To review the team's adherence to the Agile sprint schedule
questions.option_b: To verify that configuration items are accurately recorded and that the process is being followed correctly
questions.option_c: To evaluate the performance and compensation of software developers
questions.option_d: To approve changes requested by product stakeholders
questions.explanation: An SCM audit verifies that configuration items are correctly identified, recorded, and controlled, and that the defined SCM processes are being followed. It ensures the integrity of the configuration baseline.

questions.statement: A software architect recommends that a new high-traffic API be implemented as a stateless service. What is the PRIMARY advantage of this design decision?
questions.option_a: Stateless services can process requests faster than stateful services in all cases
questions.option_b: Any server instance can handle any request, enabling straightforward horizontal scaling
questions.option_c: Stateless services consume significantly less storage than stateful services
questions.option_d: Stateless services eliminate the need for authentication mechanisms
questions.explanation: Stateless services do not store client session information between requests, meaning any server instance can handle any client request. This allows horizontal scaling by simply adding more server instances without session affinity concerns.

questions.statement: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'software reuse' in engineering practice?
questions.option_a: Recycling old, deprecated code libraries that are no longer maintained
questions.option_b: Using existing software components, patterns, or frameworks to build new systems more efficiently
questions.option_c: Running the same test suite on multiple versions of a product
questions.option_d: Adopting the same project management methodology across different teams
questions.explanation: Software reuse involves deliberately using existing, tested software assets—components, libraries, frameworks, or design patterns—to build new systems, reducing development cost and time while improving reliability.

questions.statement: In Agile development, which ceremony is a brief daily synchronization meeting where team members share progress, plans, and impediments?
questions.option_a: Sprint Planning
questions.option_b: Sprint Review
questions.option_c: Sprint Retrospective
questions.option_d: Daily Scrum
questions.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a short, time-boxed (typically 15-minute) meeting held each day where team members synchronize on what they did yesterday, what they plan today, and any impediments. Sprint Planning and Review are longer ceremonies at sprint boundaries.

questions.statement: A project team is building a safety-critical medical device software. Which standard is most directly applicable to ensuring the safety of the software?
questions.option_a: ISO 9001
questions.option_b: IEEE 830
questions.option_d: CMMI Level 3
questions.explanation: IEC 62304 is the international standard specifically for the lifecycle requirements of medical device software, covering development, maintenance, and risk management. ISO 9001 is a general quality management standard not specific to medical software.

questions.statement: Which type of software architecture would be most appropriate for a system where the correctness of individual components must be independently verifiable, such as a flight control system?
questions.option_a: Microservices Architecture
questions.option_b: Component-Based Architecture
questions.option_c: Monolithic Architecture
questions.option_d: Service-Oriented Architecture
questions.explanation: Component-Based Architecture structures a system as a collection of independently verifiable, encapsulated components with well-defined interfaces. This supports formal verification of individual components, which is critical in safety-critical systems.

questions.statement: What is a key benefit of using design patterns in software engineering?
questions.option_a: They guarantee zero defects in the final software product
questions.option_b: They provide tested, reusable solutions to commonly occurring design problems
questions.option_c: They eliminate the need for software documentation
questions.option_d: They automatically generate source code from UML diagrams
questions.explanation: Design patterns are reusable, well-documented solutions to recurring design problems that have been validated through community experience. They do not guarantee zero defects or eliminate the need for documentation.

questions.statement: A senior developer reviews code and notices that a function is 400 lines long and handles file I/O, data parsing, and report generation simultaneously. This is a classic example of which anti-pattern?
questions.option_a: God Object
questions.option_b: Spaghetti Code
questions.option_c: Long Method
questions.option_d: Shotgun Surgery
questions.explanation: The Long Method anti-pattern describes functions or methods that are excessively long and handle too many responsibilities, making them hard to understand, test, and maintain. God Object refers to a class that knows too much or does too much.

questions.statement: Which level of the CMMI model is characterized by processes being documented, standardized, and consistently followed across the organization?
questions.option_a: Level 1: Initial
questions.option_b: Level 2: Managed
questions.option_c: Level 3: Defined
questions.option_d: Level 4: Quantitatively Managed
questions.explanation: CMMI Level 3 (Defined) is characterized by processes being documented, standardized, and tailored from the organization's standard process set. Level 2 (Managed) has project-level processes established but not yet standardized organization-wide.

questions.statement: In requirements engineering, what is the difference between a functional requirement and a non-functional requirement?
questions.option_a: Functional requirements describe user interface layouts; non-functional requirements describe data models
questions.option_b: Functional requirements specify what the system does; non-functional requirements specify how well it does it
questions.option_c: Functional requirements are mandatory; non-functional requirements are optional suggestions
questions.option_d: Functional requirements apply to the backend; non-functional requirements apply to the frontend
questions.explanation: Functional requirements define specific behaviors and functions the system must perform, while non-functional requirements (quality attributes) define constraints on how the system performs them, such as speed, reliability, and security.

questions.statement: A software team discovers that their automated test suite takes four hours to run, causing significant delays in their CI pipeline. Which strategy would most effectively reduce this problem without reducing test coverage?
questions.option_a: Deleting the slowest-running test cases to speed up execution
questions.option_b: Running all tests sequentially but on faster hardware
questions.option_c: Parallelizing test execution across multiple machines
questions.option_d: Removing automated tests and relying solely on manual testing
questions.explanation: Parallelizing test execution distributes tests across multiple machines or processes, reducing total execution time without removing any test coverage. Deleting tests or removing automation reduces coverage and quality confidence.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a 'software project charter' as a formal document?
questions.option_a: To define the coding standards and style guidelines for the project
questions.option_b: To formally authorize the project and grant the project manager authority to allocate resources
questions.option_c: To list all the functional requirements identified during elicitation
questions.option_d: To provide a detailed schedule of all tasks and milestones
questions.explanation: A project charter formally authorizes a project, defines its objectives and scope at a high level, and grants the project manager the authority to apply organizational resources. It is different from a project plan, which provides detailed scheduling.

questions.statement: Which software testing principle states that testing can show the presence of defects but cannot prove their absence?
questions.option_a: Exhaustive Testing is Impossible
questions.option_b: Defect Clustering
questions.option_c: Pesticide Paradox
questions.option_d: Testing Shows Presence of Defects
questions.explanation: This is one of the fundamental principles of software testing: testing can confirm that defects exist but cannot conclusively prove a system is defect-free. This principle, associated with Dijkstra, underlies the need for risk-based testing.

questions.statement: A team notices that running the same test suite repeatedly no longer finds new bugs. Which testing principle explains this phenomenon?
questions.option_a: Defect Clustering
questions.option_b: The Pesticide Paradox
questions.option_c: Absence-of-Errors Fallacy
questions.option_d: Early Testing Principle
questions.explanation: The Pesticide Paradox states that if the same tests are repeated, they will eventually stop finding new defects. To counter this, tests must be regularly reviewed and new tests written to cover new or changed functionality.

questions.statement: In software security engineering, which attack type involves injecting malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users?
questions.option_a: SQL Injection
questions.option_b: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
questions.option_c: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
questions.option_d: Buffer Overflow
questions.explanation: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) involves injecting malicious client-side scripts into web pages that other users view, potentially stealing session cookies or credentials. SQL Injection targets database queries, not client-side script execution.

questions.statement: Which software metric measures the size of software based on user-visible functionality rather than lines of code?
questions.option_a: Cyclomatic Complexity
questions.option_b: Halstead Metric
questions.option_c: Function Point
questions.option_d: Code Churn
questions.explanation: Function Points measure software size from the user's perspective based on inputs, outputs, files, and interfaces, making it language-independent. Cyclomatic Complexity measures code structural complexity, not functional size.

questions.statement: A team using Scrum realizes their sprint velocity is highly inconsistent, ranging from 20 to 60 story points per sprint. What is the most likely root cause?
questions.option_a: The product backlog is insufficiently detailed
questions.option_b: Story point estimates are inconsistent and not calibrated properly
questions.option_c: The Scrum Master is not attending daily standups
questions.option_d: The sprint duration changes from sprint to sprint
questions.explanation: Inconsistent velocity is most commonly caused by poor estimation calibration—the team is not applying a consistent definition of story point value across different items or sprints, leading to wide variance in measured output.

questions.statement: What is the main goal of software architecture evaluation methods such as ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method)?
questions.option_a: To measure the code quality of individual software components
