questions.option_b: To analyze how well an architecture satisfies quality attribute requirements and identify tradeoffs
questions.option_c: To verify that the software meets all functional requirements
questions.option_d: To estimate the total cost of the software development effort
questions.explanation: ATAM is a structured method for evaluating software architectures by analyzing how architectural decisions affect quality attributes and revealing tradeoffs between competing quality goals, such as performance versus security.

questions.statement: A software company implements a policy requiring that every code change be reviewed and approved by at least two other developers before merging. Which software quality practice does this implement?
questions.option_a: Pair Programming
questions.option_b: Peer Code Review
questions.option_c: Static Analysis
questions.option_d: Automated Testing
questions.explanation: Peer Code Review requires that code changes be examined by other developers before integration to identify defects, enforce standards, and share knowledge. Pair Programming involves two developers working simultaneously on the same code.

questions.statement: In project planning, what does the critical path method (CPM) identify?
questions.option_a: The most expensive sequence of tasks in a project
questions.option_b: The longest path of dependent tasks that determines the earliest project completion date
questions.option_c: The set of tasks with the highest risk of failure
questions.option_d: The sequence of tasks assigned to the most skilled developers
questions.explanation: CPM identifies the longest sequence of dependent tasks through a project network, which determines the minimum possible project duration. Any delay to tasks on the critical path directly delays the project end date.

questions.statement: A software requirement states: 'The system shall respond to user queries within two seconds under normal load.' This is an example of which type of requirement?
questions.option_a: Functional Requirement
questions.option_b: Domain Requirement
questions.option_c: Interface Requirement
questions.option_d: Performance Requirement
questions.explanation: A performance requirement is a type of non-functional requirement specifying measurable performance constraints. Stating a maximum response time of two seconds under normal load is a classic performance requirement specification.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of regression testing in Agile development?
questions.option_a: To evaluate whether the team achieved the sprint goal
questions.option_b: To verify that new code changes have not broken existing functionality
questions.option_c: To measure the team's story point velocity for the past sprint
questions.option_d: To check that newly written test cases have adequate code coverage
questions.explanation: Regression testing confirms that changes made in the current sprint have not introduced defects in previously working functionality. In Agile, automated regression suites are run continuously to detect breakages early.

questions.statement: Which software maintenance category involves modifying a system to use a new database platform after the original vendor discontinues support?
questions.option_a: Corrective Maintenance
questions.option_b: Perfective Maintenance
questions.option_c: Adaptive Maintenance
questions.option_d: Preventive Maintenance
questions.explanation: Adaptive Maintenance modifies a system to accommodate changes in its operating environment, such as new hardware, operating systems, or third-party software platforms. Corrective Maintenance fixes defects in the existing system.

questions.statement: A security engineer recommends encrypting sensitive data both at rest and in transit. Which security principle does this implement?
questions.option_a: Least Privilege
questions.option_b: Defense in Depth
questions.option_c: Non-Repudiation
questions.option_d: Separation of Duties
questions.explanation: Defense in Depth is a layered security strategy that applies multiple independent security controls so that if one layer fails, others still protect the system. Encrypting data at rest and in transit is a classic multi-layer application.

questions.statement: What is the primary objective of software risk management throughout a project lifecycle?
questions.option_a: To eliminate all risks before the project begins
questions.option_b: To identify, assess, and mitigate risks proactively to minimize their impact on the project
questions.option_c: To document all risks that occurred for post-project lessons learned
questions.option_d: To transfer all project risks to the customer through contract clauses
questions.explanation: Software risk management is the ongoing process of identifying potential problems early, assessing their likelihood and impact, and developing response strategies to minimize their effect on project success.

questions.statement: Which software quality attribute defines the degree to which a system can be transferred from one environment or platform to another?
questions.option_a: Scalability
questions.option_b: Maintainability
questions.option_c: Interoperability
questions.option_d: Portability
questions.explanation: Portability is the ease with which software can be transferred from one hardware, operating system, or software environment to another. Interoperability is the ability to exchange and use information with other systems.

questions.statement: A development team is asked to add a new payment gateway to an existing e-commerce application. The current architecture requires changes to the core transaction processing module, the UI, and the database schema simultaneously. What architectural problem does this reveal?
questions.option_a: High cohesion within the modules
questions.option_b: Insufficient logging and monitoring
questions.option_c: High coupling between the modules
questions.option_d: Inadequate test coverage
questions.explanation: The need to modify multiple unrelated modules for a single feature change indicates high coupling, where modules are excessively interdependent. A well-designed, loosely coupled system would require changes in only the relevant module.

questions.statement: What is the main purpose of a feasibility study in the context of software risk management?
questions.option_a: To produce the initial functional requirements specification
questions.option_b: To assess technical, financial, and operational viability before committing to development
questions.option_c: To create a detailed project schedule with milestones
questions.option_d: To select the programming languages and frameworks for the project
questions.explanation: A feasibility study evaluates whether a proposed project is achievable from technical, economic, legal, and operational perspectives before major resources are committed, directly supporting informed risk decision-making.

questions.statement: In a Scrum project, who is responsible for removing impediments that block the development team's progress?
questions.option_a: The Product Owner
questions.option_b: The Development Team collectively
questions.option_c: The Project Sponsor
questions.option_d: The Scrum Master
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master is responsible for removing impediments that prevent the Development Team from making progress. The Product Owner manages the backlog; the Team self-organizes work; the Scrum Master facilitates and protects the team.

questions.statement: What does the acronym API stand for in software engineering?
questions.option_a: Application Process Integration
questions.option_b: Automated Programming Interface
questions.option_c: Application Programming Interface
questions.option_d: Advanced Protocol Integration
questions.explanation: API stands for Application Programming Interface, a set of rules and definitions that allows different software applications to communicate with each other. The other options use the same initials but are fabricated expansions.

questions.statement: A software team uses a tool that automatically checks each committed code change against a predefined set of coding rules and flags violations before the code is merged. Which type of tool is this?
questions.option_a: Dynamic Analysis Tool
questions.option_b: Profiling Tool
questions.option_c: Static Code Analysis (Linting) Tool
questions.option_d: Mutation Testing Tool
questions.explanation: A static code analysis or linting tool examines source code without executing it to enforce coding standards, identify potential bugs, and flag style violations. Dynamic analysis tools analyze code behavior during execution.

questions.statement: Which Agile principle most directly supports the practice of continuous technical excellence and good design?
questions.option_a: Welcome changing requirements
questions.option_b: Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility
questions.option_c: Working software over comprehensive documentation
questions.option_d: The best architectures emerge from self-organizing teams
questions.explanation: The Agile Manifesto principle 'Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility' directly supports practices like refactoring, code review, and clean architecture as enablers of sustainable Agile delivery.

questions.statement: A project manager uses a risk matrix to plot identified risks by their likelihood and impact. A risk with high likelihood and high impact should receive which priority response?
questions.option_a: Risk Acceptance
questions.option_b: Risk Monitoring
questions.option_c: Immediate Risk Mitigation or Avoidance
questions.option_d: Low-priority documentation
questions.explanation: A risk with both high likelihood and high impact falls in the critical zone of a risk matrix and demands immediate attention through aggressive mitigation or avoidance strategies. Acceptance is appropriate only for low-impact or low-likelihood risks.

questions.statement: What is the key difference between 'alpha testing' and 'beta testing'?
questions.option_a: Alpha testing uses automated scripts; beta testing uses manual testers
questions.option_b: Alpha testing is done by internal developers or testers; beta testing is done by external end-users
questions.option_c: Alpha testing occurs before system testing; beta testing occurs before integration testing
questions.option_d: Alpha testing evaluates performance; beta testing evaluates security
questions.explanation: Alpha testing is conducted in a controlled environment by internal developers or a dedicated testing team. Beta testing is performed by external, real-world end-users in their actual environment before general availability.

questions.statement: Which software engineering concept refers to the idea that a system should continue to function correctly even when one of its components fails?
questions.option_a: Scalability
questions.option_b: Fault Tolerance
questions.option_c: High Availability
questions.option_d: Graceful Degradation
questions.explanation: Fault Tolerance is the property of a system that allows it to continue operating correctly even when one or more of its components fail. Graceful Degradation allows continued partial operation, while High Availability focuses on minimizing downtime.

questions.statement: A software team performs a series of tests that specifically verify the system behaves correctly at the boundaries of input ranges, such as testing with the exact minimum and maximum allowed values. What testing technique is this?
questions.option_a: Equivalence Class Partitioning
questions.option_b: Decision Table Testing
questions.option_c: Boundary Value Analysis
questions.option_d: State Transition Testing
questions.explanation: Boundary Value Analysis focuses test cases on values at and just beyond the edges of valid input ranges, as defects are most commonly found at these boundaries. Equivalence Class Partitioning divides inputs into groups assumed to behave the same way.

questions.statement: What does the acronym OWASP stand for in the context of web and software security?
questions.option_a: Open Web Application Security Project
questions.option_b: Official Web Application Standards Program
questions.option_c: Open Web Access Security Protocol
questions.option_d: Organized Web Application Software Platform
questions.explanation: OWASP stands for Open Web Application Security Project, a nonprofit foundation that produces freely available resources on web application security, including the well-known OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities list.

questions.statement: In software configuration management, what is the purpose of a Change Control Board (CCB)?
questions.option_a: To review and approve or reject proposed changes to baselined software artifacts
questions.option_b: To manage the daily task assignments of the development team
questions.option_c: To oversee the hiring and onboarding of new software engineers
questions.option_d: To select and approve vendor tools used in the development process
questions.explanation: A Change Control Board (CCB) is a group responsible for reviewing, approving, or rejecting proposed changes to baselined software artifacts, ensuring that changes are evaluated for their impact on cost, schedule, and quality.

questions.statement: A system architect designs a service that can be deployed as multiple identical instances behind a load balancer, with no shared state between instances. Which architectural quality is this design optimizing for?
questions.option_a: Maintainability
questions.option_b: Portability
questions.option_c: Horizontal Scalability
questions.option_d: Security
questions.explanation: Designing stateless, identical service instances that can run behind a load balancer optimizes horizontal scalability, allowing the system to handle increased load by simply adding more instances without architectural changes.

questions.statement: Which of the following is an example of a non-functional requirement?
questions.option_a: The system shall allow users to reset their password via email.
questions.option_b: The system shall display search results within 1.5 seconds for 95% of queries.
questions.option_c: The system shall support user account creation with username and password.
questions.option_d: The system shall send email notifications upon order confirmation.
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements specify quality constraints on how the system performs. A 1.5-second response time for 95% of queries is a performance (non-functional) requirement. The other options describe specific system behaviors, which are functional requirements.

questions.statement: In software testing, what is 'test data management'?
questions.option_a: The process of writing, organizing, and executing test scripts
questions.option_b: Planning, generating, and maintaining the data used as input for test execution
questions.option_c: Tracking and reporting the results of test runs in a test management tool
questions.option_d: Automating the deployment of test environments using infrastructure scripts
questions.explanation: Test data management involves planning, creating, securing, and maintaining input data for tests, ensuring tests have appropriate, realistic, and compliant data. This is distinct from managing test scripts or test infrastructure.

questions.statement: A software engineer proposes that the team adopt a practice where the complete source code of the application is always in a releasable state, with every build producing a potentially shippable product increment. This most closely describes which DevOps principle?
questions.option_a: Infrastructure as Code
questions.option_b: Blue-Green Deployment
questions.option_c: Continuous Delivery
questions.option_d: Shift-Left Testing
questions.explanation: Continuous Delivery ensures the codebase is always in a releasable state by automating build, test, and deployment processes through a pipeline, producing a potentially shippable increment after every validated build.

questions.statement: Which UML diagram type is most appropriate for modeling all possible states of an object and the events that cause transitions between those states?
questions.option_a: Activity Diagram
questions.option_b: Sequence Diagram
questions.option_c: State Machine Diagram
questions.option_d: Collaboration Diagram
questions.explanation: A State Machine (Statechart) Diagram models the distinct states an object can be in and the events or conditions that trigger transitions between states. Activity Diagrams model the flow of control in a process or workflow.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of 'pair programming' as practiced in Extreme Programming (XP)?
questions.option_a: To double the output of a development team by having two developers work on separate features simultaneously
questions.option_b: To have one developer write code while another continuously reviews it, catching defects in real time
questions.option_c: To train junior developers by shadowing senior developers during debugging sessions
questions.option_d: To allow developers to alternate between coding and documentation tasks more efficiently
questions.explanation: In pair programming, one developer (driver) writes code while the other (navigator) continuously reviews it. This catches defects immediately, improves design quality, and spreads knowledge, but does not double throughput.

questions.statement: A software project manager identifies that the project schedule has a Schedule Performance Index (SPI) of 0.75. What does this indicate?
questions.option_a: The project is ahead of schedule by 25%
questions.option_b: The project is over budget by 25%
questions.option_c: The project is behind schedule, completing only 75% of planned work
questions.option_d: The project has completed 75% of total deliverables
questions.explanation: SPI = EV / PV. An SPI of 0.75 means the project is achieving only 75 cents of planned value for every dollar of work scheduled, indicating the project is 25% behind its planned schedule. An SPI above 1.0 indicates ahead of schedule.

questions.statement: What does the term 'agile manifesto' refer to?
questions.option_a: A detailed framework specifying all Scrum ceremonies and their time boxes
questions.option_b: A legal document governing open-source software licenses
questions.option_c: A statement of four core values and twelve principles guiding Agile software development
questions.option_d: A set of coding best practices for test-driven development
questions.explanation: The Agile Manifesto, published in 2001, is a concise document articulating four core values and twelve guiding principles for Agile software development. It is not a detailed framework (like Scrum) or a legal or coding document.

questions.statement: In software design, what is meant by 'separation of concerns'?
questions.option_a: Ensuring that each developer on the team is responsible for a separate module
questions.option_b: Dividing a software system into distinct sections, each addressing a separate aspect of the system's functionality
questions.option_c: Separating the development environment from the production environment
questions.option_d: Dividing requirements into functional and non-functional categories
questions.explanation: Separation of Concerns is a design principle for dividing a system into distinct sections that each address a separate concern or aspect of functionality, reducing complexity and improving maintainability. It is a design principle, not a team management or environment practice.

questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of a burndown chart in Agile project management?
questions.option_a: To display the distribution of story points across each team member
questions.option_b: To visualize the amount of work remaining versus time elapsed in a sprint
questions.option_c: To compare the current sprint's velocity against past sprint averages
questions.option_d: To track the number of defects found per day during a sprint
questions.explanation: A burndown chart plots the amount of work remaining (y-axis) against time (x-axis) within a sprint, providing a visual indication of whether the team is on track to complete all committed work by the sprint end.

questions.statement: Which type of testing verifies that two or more software components work correctly together after being individually tested?
questions.option_a: Unit Testing
questions.option_b: System Testing
questions.option_c: Integration Testing
questions.option_d: Acceptance Testing
questions.explanation: Integration Testing verifies that individual modules or components work correctly when combined, testing the interfaces and interactions between them. Unit Testing validates components in isolation; System Testing validates the complete system.

questions.statement: A software system needs to allow third-party vendors to add new features without modifying the core application code. Which architectural mechanism best supports this requirement?
questions.option_a: Inheritance hierarchies
questions.option_b: Plugin/Extension Architecture
questions.option_c: Layered Architecture
questions.option_d: Monolithic Design
questions.explanation: A Plugin/Extension Architecture exposes well-defined extension points that allow third parties to add functionality without touching core application code, directly supporting the Open/Closed Principle at the architectural level.

questions.statement: Which software engineering term describes the practice of writing the minimum code necessary to pass a test, then refactoring it to improve quality?
questions.option_a: Defensive Programming
questions.option_b: Red-Green-Refactor Cycle
questions.option_c: Behavior-Driven Development
questions.option_d: Code-First Development
questions.explanation: The Red-Green-Refactor cycle is the core rhythm of TDD: write a failing test (Red), write minimum code to pass it (Green), then improve the code structure without changing behavior (Refactor). This drives incremental, clean development.

questions.statement: A team conducting a sprint review invites stakeholders to inspect the product increment and provide feedback. What is the PRIMARY goal of this ceremony?
questions.option_a: To assign blame for incomplete user stories
questions.option_b: To inspect the increment and adapt the product backlog based on feedback
questions.option_c: To evaluate individual developer performance metrics
questions.option_d: To plan the technical tasks for the upcoming sprint
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review's primary goal is to inspect the completed increment with stakeholders and adapt the Product Backlog based on their feedback, ensuring the product evolves in the right direction. Performance evaluation and task planning are separate activities.

questions.statement: In software architecture, what is a 'quality attribute scenario' used for?
questions.option_a: To describe a specific user story in the product backlog
questions.option_b: To concretely specify a desired quality attribute as a testable, measurable condition
questions.option_c: To document the API contracts between microservices
questions.option_d: To outline the steps in a software release procedure
questions.explanation: A quality attribute scenario precisely defines a quality attribute requirement in a testable form, specifying the stimulus, source, environment, artifact, response, and response measure. This makes abstract quality goals concrete and verifiable.

questions.statement: A software project has accumulated so much technical debt that adding new features takes five times longer than it should. The team proposes dedicating an entire sprint to addressing only technical debt. This is commonly called a what?
questions.option_a: A Hotfix Sprint
questions.option_b: A Hardening Sprint
questions.option_c: A Tech Debt Sprint
questions.option_d: A Refactoring Sprint
questions.explanation: A Tech Debt Sprint (sometimes called a Refactoring or Hardening Sprint) is a sprint dedicated exclusively to addressing accumulated technical debt—improving code quality, paying down shortcuts—without delivering new user-visible features.

questions.statement: What does the acronym CI/CD stand for in modern software development practices?
questions.option_a: Code Integration/Code Deployment
questions.option_b: Continuous Inspection/Continuous Delivery
questions.option_c: Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (or Deployment)
questions.option_d: Component Integration/Component Deployment
questions.explanation: CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (or Deployment), a set of practices that automate the building, testing, and release of software. The other options are fabricated or incorrect expansions of the same initials.

questions.statement: The HTTP method that should be used to RETRIEVE a list of products from an API is:
questions.option_a: POST
questions.option_b: PUT
questions.option_c: GET
questions.option_d: FETCH
questions.explanation: GET retrieves resources. It is safe (doesn't modify state) and idempotent. POST creates resources, PUT updates them. There is no HTTP method called FETCH.

questions.statement: An API returns status code 401. What does this mean?
questions.option_a: Resource not found
questions.option_b: Server error
questions.option_c: Authentication required — user must log in
questions.option_d: Access forbidden — user lacks permission
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized: authentication is required. The user is not logged in (or token is invalid). 403 Forbidden: user IS authenticated but lacks permission. 404: not found. 500: server error.

questions.statement: What is the correct HTTP status code for a successfully CREATED resource?
questions.option_a: 200 OK
questions.option_b: 201 Created
questions.option_c: 204 No Content
questions.option_d: 202 Accepted
questions.explanation: 201 Created: the POST request succeeded and a new resource was created. 200 OK is for successful GET/PUT/PATCH. 204 No Content is typically used for successful DELETE.

questions.statement: DNS (Domain Name System) is responsible for:
questions.option_a: Encrypting data between client and server
questions.option_b: Translating domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses
questions.option_c: Managing HTTP request routing
questions.option_d: Storing web page content
questions.explanation: DNS is the internet's "phone book" — translates human-readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses that computers use to connect to each other.

questions.statement: What does "stateless" mean in the context of HTTP?
questions.option_a: HTTP cannot handle state changes
questions.option_b: Each HTTP request is completely independent — the server has no memory of previous requests
questions.option_c: The server maintains state for all users permanently
questions.option_d: Stateless means HTTP is unreliable
questions.explanation: HTTP statelessness: each request must contain all information needed. The server doesn't remember previous interactions. This is why we need cookies, sessions, and tokens to maintain state across requests.

questions.statement: HTTPS differs from HTTP by:
questions.option_a: Using a different port (443 vs 80) and encrypting all communication with TLS
questions.option_b: Being faster than HTTP in all cases
questions.option_c: Only encrypting passwords
questions.option_d: Requiring a login to access any page
questions.explanation: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS encryption. Uses port 443 (HTTP uses 80). Encrypts ALL communication — headers, body, URLs — not just passwords.

questions.statement: Which HTTP method is IDEMPOTENT (calling it multiple times produces the same result as calling it once)?
questions.option_a: POST
questions.option_b: GET and DELETE
questions.option_c: Only PUT
questions.option_d: None are idempotent
questions.explanation: GET (retrieves same data multiple times — no side effects), PUT (replacing with same data multiple times — same result), DELETE (deleting same resource multiple times — after first success, subsequent calls say "not found" but state is same — deleted). POST is NOT idempotent — posting the same data twice creates two records.

questions.statement: In HTTP/2 compared to HTTP/1.1, what significant improvement was introduced?
questions.option_a: Support for HTTPS
questions.option_b: Multiplexing — multiple requests/responses simultaneously on one connection
questions.option_c: Support for cookies
questions.option_d: Larger file size support
questions.explanation: HTTP/2's key improvement: multiplexing allows multiple request/response pairs over a single TCP connection simultaneously. HTTP/1.1 could only handle one at a time per connection.

questions.statement: What does a Content Security Policy (CSP) header do?
questions.option_a: Compresses page content for faster delivery
questions.option_b: Restricts which sources scripts, styles, and other resources can be loaded from
questions.option_c: Controls which users can access the site
questions.option_d: Caches content on the client
questions.explanation: CSP is a security header that tells browsers which sources are trusted for scripts, styles, images, etc. It prevents XSS attacks by blocking scripts from untrusted sources.

questions.statement: The HTTP OPTIONS method is used to:
questions.option_a: Configure server settings
questions.option_b: Retrieve server logs
questions.option_c: Discover which HTTP methods a server supports for a resource
questions.option_d: Update resource options/settings
questions.explanation: OPTIONS is used for "preflight" requests in CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) — the browser asks the server what methods it supports before sending the actual request.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the Cache-Control: max-age=86400 HTTP header?
questions.option_a: The server will delete the resource after 86400 seconds
questions.option_b: The client should cache the resource for 86400 seconds (1 day)
questions.option_c: The resource was created 86400 seconds ago
questions.option_d: The maximum file size is 86400 bytes
questions.explanation: max-age=86400 tells the browser to cache this resource and serve it from cache for 86400 seconds (24 hours) without re-requesting from the server.

questions.statement: What is the CORRECT order of steps when a user visits a website for the first time?
questions.option_a: HTTPS → DNS → TCP → HTTP request → Response
questions.option_b: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → Server processes → HTTP response
questions.option_c: HTTP → DNS → Server → Response
questions.option_d: TCP → DNS → HTTP → Response
questions.explanation: The correct order: DNS (resolve domain to IP) → TCP connection (three-way handshake) → TLS handshake (for HTTPS) → HTTP request → Server processes → HTTP response.

questions.statement: Which status code should a server return when a user tries to access a resource they're authenticated but not authorized to access?
questions.option_a: 401 Unauthorized
questions.option_b: 404 Not Found
questions.option_c: 403 Forbidden
questions.option_d: 405 Method Not Allowed
questions.explanation: 403 Forbidden: user IS authenticated (server knows who they are) but does NOT have permission. 401 Unauthorized means not authenticated (must log in).

questions.statement: What does REST stand for in web API design?
questions.option_a: Remote Execution of Server Technology
questions.option_b: Representational State Transfer
questions.option_c: Reliable Endpoint Serving Technology
questions.option_d: Resource Exchange Standard Technology
questions.explanation: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems, defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation.

questions.statement: In a RESTful API, which URL design is CORRECT?
questions.option_a: /getAllUsers (GET), /createUser (POST)
questions.option_b: /users (GET for list, POST for create)
questions.option_c: /user/fetch, /user/save
questions.option_d: /api?action=getUsers, /api?action=createUser
questions.explanation: REST uses nouns (resources), not verbs in URLs. The HTTP method (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) expresses the action. /users with different HTTP methods is the correct RESTful design.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the SameSite=Strict cookie attribute?
questions.option_a: Makes the cookie available only on HTTPS connections
questions.option_b: Prevents the cookie from being sent on cross-site requests, protecting against CSRF
questions.option_c: Makes the cookie accessible only to server-side code
questions.option_d: Restricts the cookie to a specific subdomain
questions.explanation: SameSite=Strict prevents the cookie from being sent when the request originates from a different domain (cross-site). This eliminates CSRF attacks that rely on the browser automatically sending cookies.

questions.statement: WebSockets differ from regular HTTP requests because:
questions.option_a: WebSockets are faster for all types of requests
questions.option_b: WebSockets provide a persistent, bidirectional connection — server can push data to client without polling
questions.option_c: WebSockets automatically encrypt data
questions.option_d: WebSockets can only be used for binary data
questions.explanation: WebSockets maintain an open connection where EITHER party can send data at any time. HTTP is request-response — server can only respond to client requests. WebSockets enable real-time features like chat and live updates.

questions.statement: What is the HTTP 304 status code used for?
questions.option_a: Partial content delivered (range request)
questions.option_b: Resource has moved permanently
questions.option_c: Cached content is still valid — use the local cache
questions.option_d: Request processing is not yet complete
questions.explanation: 304 Not Modified: the browser asked "has this changed since last time?" (using If-Modified-Since or ETag headers). The server responds "no, use what you have cached." Saves bandwidth — no content is transferred.

questions.statement: Which HTML element is SEMANTICALLY correct for the main navigation of a website?
questions.option_a: <div class="navigation">
questions.option_b: <menu>
questions.option_c: <nav>
questions.option_d: <ul class="nav">
questions.explanation: <nav> is the semantic element specifically for navigation links. Screen readers use it to announce navigation sections to users, allowing them to skip navigation with screen reader shortcuts.

questions.statement: What does the alt attribute on an tag provide?
questions.option_a: Alternative source if the image doesn't load
questions.option_b: A text description of the image for screen readers and when the image doesn't load
questions.option_c: An alternative link for the image
questions.option_d: The image file format alternative
questions.explanation: alt text serves: screen readers (read to visually impaired users), search engines (index image content), cases where image fails to load (displayed in its place), and text browsers.

questions.statement: The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration at the start of an HTML document:
questions.option_a: Declares the document as an HTML template
questions.option_b: Specifies the author of the document
questions.option_c: Tells the browser to render in standards mode using HTML5
questions.option_d: Imports the HTML library
questions.explanation: <!DOCTYPE html> signals HTML5 and triggers "standards mode" in browsers. Without it, browsers may use "quirks mode" — an old backward-compatibility rendering mode with inconsistent behavior.

questions.statement: Which CSS selector selects ALL direct children <li> elements of a <ul>?
questions.option_a: ul li
questions.option_b: ul > li
questions.option_c: ul + li
questions.option_d: ul ~ li
questions.explanation: ul > li is the child combinator — selects <li> elements that are DIRECT children of <ul>. ul li (descendant) selects any <li> inside <ul> at any depth.

questions.statement: With box-sizing: border-box, if an element has width: 300px, padding: 20px, and border: 5px, its total rendered width is:
questions.option_a: 350px
questions.option_b: 300px
questions.option_c: 280px
questions.option_d: 320px
questions.explanation: With border-box, the width includes padding and border. Total width stays 300px regardless of padding and border values. Without border-box (content-box default), it would be 350px.

questions.statement: What is CSS specificity used to determine?
questions.option_a: How fast CSS rules are applied
questions.option_b: Which CSS rule wins when multiple rules target the same element and property
questions.option_c: The order in which CSS files are loaded
questions.option_d: Whether CSS is valid
questions.explanation: When multiple CSS rules conflict, specificity determines which rule wins. Higher specificity beats lower, regardless of source order. ID selectors beat class selectors beat element selectors.

questions.statement: In Flexbox, justify-content: space-between distributes items:
questions.option_a: With equal space around each item (including edges)
questions.option_b: With equal space BETWEEN items, no space at the edges
questions.option_c: Centered with equal space on both sides
questions.option_d: At the start of the flex container
questions.explanation: space-between: items spread to edges, equal space only BETWEEN items. space-around: equal space on all sides. space-evenly: mathematically equal space including edges.

questions.statement: The CSS display: grid property with grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) creates:
questions.option_a: Exactly 3 columns
questions.option_b: As many 200px minimum columns as fit — responsive without media queries
questions.option_c: One column that grows to fill space
questions.option_d: Fixed 200px columns
questions.explanation: auto-fill creates as many columns as fit. minmax(200px, 1fr) makes each column at least 200px wide and maximum 1fr. On a 800px container: 4 columns. On 400px: 2 columns. No media queries needed.

questions.statement: Which CSS unit is RELATIVE to the root element's (html) font size?
questions.option_a: em
questions.option_c: rem
questions.option_d: vw
questions.explanation: rem = Root EM. If the root font size is 16px, 1rem = 16px, 2rem = 32px. em is relative to the PARENT element's font size (compounds with nesting). rem doesn't compound.

questions.statement: A media query @media (max-width: 768px) applies styles when:
questions.option_a: The screen is WIDER than 768px
questions.option_b: The screen is NARROWER than or equal to 768px
questions.option_c: The screen is exactly 768px
questions.option_d: The device has a 768px physical resolution
questions.explanation: max-width: 768px means "apply these styles when the viewport width is 768px or less." This is the desktop-first approach — start with desktop, add media queries for smaller screens.

questions.statement: What does position: sticky do in CSS?
questions.option_a: Fixes an element at a position relative to the viewport always
questions.option_b: The element scrolls with the page until it reaches a threshold, then sticks
questions.option_c: Positions the element relative to its parent
questions.option_d: Removes the element from the normal document flow
questions.explanation: sticky is a hybrid of relative and fixed. The element scrolls normally until it hits the threshold (top: 0), then it "sticks" to that position as the page scrolls. Navigation bars that stick at the top after scrolling past them use this.

questions.statement: In the CSS cascade, which has the highest specificity?
questions.option_a: A class selector (.active)
questions.option_b: An element selector (p)
questions.option_c: An inline style (style="color: red")
questions.option_d: An ID selector (#header)
questions.explanation: Specificity order (lowest to highest): element (0,0,0,1), class/attribute/pseudo-class (0,0,1,0), ID (0,1,0,0), inline style (1,0,0,0). !important overrides all (not a specificity level — it's a different mechanism).

questions.statement: The HTML <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> tag is used to:
questions.option_a: Set the actual screen resolution
questions.option_b: Enable responsive design by making the viewport match the device width
questions.option_c: Declare the website's language
questions.option_d: Set the page zoom level permanently
questions.explanation: Without this tag, mobile browsers zoom out to show the full desktop-width page. This tag makes the viewport match the device's actual width, enabling responsive design to work correctly.

questions.statement: What is the correct HTML for a radio button group where only one option can be selected at a time?
questions.option_a: Different name attributes and same id
questions.option_b: Same name attribute on all radio inputs in the group
questions.option_c: Using type="select" instead of type="radio"
questions.option_d: Adding unique attribute to each radio button
questions.explanation: Radio buttons in a group share the same name attribute. The browser enforces that only one radio button per name group can be selected at a time. Different names = independent groups.

questions.statement: What CSS property creates the visual space BETWEEN an element's content and its border?
questions.option_a: margin
questions.option_b: border-spacing
questions.option_c: padding
questions.option_d: gap
questions.explanation: Padding: space between content and border (inside the element). Margin: space outside the border (between elements). Gap: space between flex/grid items.

questions.statement: Which CSS pseudo-class targets an element when the user's mouse hovers over it?
questions.option_a: :active
questions.option_b: :hover
questions.option_c: :focus
questions.option_d: :visited
questions.explanation: :hover activates when mouse pointer is over the element. :active when the element is being clicked (pressed). :focus when the element has keyboard/programmatic focus. :visited for visited links.

questions.statement: The <figure> and <figcaption> HTML elements are BEST used for:
questions.option_a: Creating decorative borders around content
questions.option_b: Self-contained content with an optional caption — like images, code blocks, or diagrams
questions.option_c: Creating figure/shape drawings with CSS
questions.option_d: Displaying numerical figures and statistics
questions.explanation: <figure> wraps self-contained content that could be removed from the flow without affecting the document's meaning. <figcaption> provides a caption. Commonly used for images with captions, code examples, quotes.

questions.statement: In CSS Grid, grid-column: 1 / -1 means:
questions.option_a: Column 1 to column -1 (invalid)
questions.option_b: The item spans from the first column line to the LAST column line (full width)
questions.option_c: The item is hidden (negative value)
questions.option_d: The item is placed in the last column
questions.explanation: In CSS Grid, negative line numbers count from the end. -1 is the last line of the grid. So 1 / -1 means from the first line to the last line — spanning the full width of the grid.

questions.statement: The @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) media query:
questions.option_a: Applies styles when the website has a dark background
questions.option_b: Applies styles when the user's operating system is set to dark mode
questions.option_c: Applies styles only in Chrome
questions.option_d: Is used for accessibility for visually impaired users
questions.explanation: This media query detects the OS-level dark mode preference. When the user has dark mode enabled in their OS/browser settings, these styles apply — enabling automatic dark mode support.

questions.statement: Which HTML element should be used for the most important heading on a page, and how many should a page typically have?
questions.option_a: <h1>, and multiple throughout the page
questions.option_b: <h1>, and typically only one per page
questions.option_c: <h2>, always
questions.option_d: <title>, exactly one
questions.explanation: <h1> is the page's primary heading — its main topic. Most accessibility guidelines and SEO best practices recommend one <h1> per page. Multiple <h1> elements are technically valid HTML5 but discouraged.

questions.statement: CSS transition: all 0.3s ease will:
questions.option_a: Animate only color changes
questions.option_b: Create a 0.3-second smooth transition for ALL CSS property changes
questions.option_c: Apply only to hover effects
questions.option_d: Delay all CSS changes by 0.3 seconds without animation
questions.explanation: This transition applies to ALL CSS property changes (color, transform, opacity, size, etc.) with a 0.3-second duration using the ease timing function (starts fast, slows at end).

questions.statement: Which statement about CSS Flexbox vs CSS Grid is TRUE?
questions.option_a: Flexbox is for two-dimensional layouts; Grid is for one-dimensional
questions.option_b: Flexbox is for one-dimensional layouts (row OR column); Grid is for two-dimensional (rows AND columns)
questions.option_c: They are identical and interchangeable
questions.option_d: Grid is always better and should replace Flexbox
questions.explanation: Flexbox: one dimension at a time (either a row of items or a column). Grid: two dimensions simultaneously (rows AND columns). They complement each other — often used together.

questions.statement:
What is the output of this JavaScript code?
console.log(typeof null);
questions.option_a: "null"
questions.option_b: "undefined"
questions.option_c: "object"
questions.option_d: "string"
questions.explanation: typeof null === "object" is a famous JavaScript bug from 1995 that was never fixed to maintain backward compatibility. null is not actually an object.

questions.statement: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: == is for numbers, === is for strings
questions.option_b: === is strict equality (no type coercion); == is loose equality (coerces types)
questions.option_c: == checks type only; === checks value only
questions.option_d: They are identical in modern JavaScript
questions.explanation: === (strict): must be same TYPE and same VALUE. 5 === "5" is false. == (loose): coerces types. 5 == "5" is true (string "5" coerced to number). Always use ===.

questions.statement: What does the const keyword guarantee in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: The variable's value can never change
questions.option_b: The variable's binding cannot be reassigned, but object properties can still be modified
questions.option_c: The variable is immutable and deeply frozen
questions.option_d: The variable can only hold primitive values
questions.explanation: const prevents reassignment of the variable binding. const obj = {}; obj = {} throws an error. But const obj = {}; obj.name = "Ali" works — you're modifying the object, not reassigning the variable.

questions.statement: What does the Fetch API return?
questions.option_a: The response body directly
questions.option_b: A Promise that resolves to a Response object
questions.option_c: An XMLHttpRequest object
questions.option_d: JSON data automatically
questions.explanation: fetch() returns a Promise. When resolved, it gives a Response object. You must then call .json(), .text(), or .blob() on the Response to get the body (which also returns a Promise).

questions.statement: What is "event bubbling" in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: Events are queued and processed in order
questions.option_b: When an event fires on an element, it also fires on all ancestor elements in order
questions.option_c: Events bubble up from the event queue to the call stack
questions.option_d: Multiple events triggered simultaneously
questions.explanation: When you click a button inside a div, the click event fires on the button, then bubbles up to the div, then the section, then the body, then document. You can stop bubbling with event.stopPropagation().

questions.statement: What is the purpose of event.preventDefault()?
questions.option_a: Stop the event from bubbling to parent elements
questions.option_b: Prevent the browser's default behavior for this event (e.g., form submission, link navigation)
questions.option_c: Delete the event handler
questions.option_d: Delay the event processing
questions.explanation: preventDefault() stops the browser's built-in response to the event. For form submit: prevents page reload. For link click: prevents navigation. For key events: prevents character insertion.

questions.statement: In JavaScript, a Promise can be in which states?
questions.option_a: Loading, Done, Failed
questions.option_b: Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected
questions.option_c: Open, Closed, Error
questions.option_d: Running, Complete, Cancelled
questions.explanation: A Promise is: Pending (operation in progress), Fulfilled (operation succeeded — .then() runs), or Rejected (operation failed — .catch() runs). A Promise can only transition from Pending to either Fulfilled or Rejected — never back.

questions.option_a: "number"
questions.option_b: "function"
questions.option_c: "object"
questions.option_d: "undefined"
questions.explanation: An async function ALWAYS returns a Promise, even if you return a non-Promise value. test() returns Promise<number>, not 42. typeof Promise === "object". To get 42, you'd need await test().

questions.statement: What does Array.prototype.reduce() do?
questions.option_a: Reduces the array to only unique elements
questions.option_b: Removes elements from the array
questions.option_c: Accumulates array elements into a single value using a callback function
questions.option_d: Sorts the array in ascending order
questions.explanation: reduce(callback, initialValue) applies the callback to an accumulator and each element, resulting in a single value. [1,2,3,4].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0) → 10.

questions.statement: What is a "closure" in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: A way to close/terminate a function
questions.option_b: A function that has access to variables from its outer scope even after the outer function returns
questions.option_c: An encapsulated class in JavaScript
questions.option_d: A method to close browser tabs from JavaScript
questions.explanation: Closure: a function "closes over" variables from its enclosing scope. Those variables persist in memory as long as the closure exists. Enables private state, factory functions, memoization.

questions.statement: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
questions.option_a: localStorage is for larger files; sessionStorage is for smaller data
questions.option_b: localStorage persists indefinitely; sessionStorage is cleared when the tab/browser is closed
questions.option_c: sessionStorage is server-side; localStorage is client-side
questions.option_d: They are identical in all ways
questions.explanation: Both store key-value pairs in the browser. localStorage: persists until explicitly cleared. sessionStorage: cleared when the tab closes. Both are accessible only on the same origin.

questions.statement: Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]) behaves how when one promise rejects?
questions.option_a: It continues with the remaining promises and returns results for successful ones
questions.option_b: It immediately rejects with the first rejection reason
questions.option_c: It returns undefined for rejected promises
questions.option_d: It retries the rejected promise
questions.explanation: Promise.all fails fast: if ANY promise rejects, the whole Promise.all immediately rejects. Use Promise.allSettled if you want results from all promises regardless of success/failure.

questions.statement: What does the ?. (optional chaining) operator do?
questions.option_a: Makes a property optional in TypeScript
questions.option_b: Safely accesses a nested property — returns undefined instead of throwing if an intermediate value is null/undefined
questions.option_c: Creates optional parameters in function definitions
questions.option_d: Conditionally assigns a value
questions.explanation: user?.address?.city returns undefined if user or user.address is null/undefined, instead of throwing TypeError: Cannot read properties of null.

questions.statement: Event delegation is the practice of:
questions.option_a: Delegating event handling to a web server
questions.option_b: Attaching ONE event handler to a parent element to handle events from all its children
questions.option_c: Using multiple event listeners on the same element
questions.option_d: Delegating events to setTimeout for delayed handling
questions.explanation: Instead of attaching handlers to 1000 list items (memory-expensive), attach ONE handler to the parent list. Use event.target to determine which item was clicked. Works for dynamically added items too.

questions.statement: In the JavaScript event loop, what is the "call stack"?
questions.option_a: A list of all event listeners currently registered
questions.option_b: The LIFO structure where JavaScript tracks function execution
questions.option_c: The queue of pending async operations
questions.option_d: The browser's rendering queue
questions.explanation: The call stack is where JavaScript executes code. Functions are pushed when called, popped when they return. Only one function executes at a time. Stack overflow occurs when recursion runs without a base case.

questions.statement: What is the spread operator (...) used for in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: Only for function rest parameters
questions.option_b: Expanding an iterable (array, object) into individual elements
questions.option_c: Creating infinite sequences
questions.option_d: Spreading code across multiple files
questions.explanation: Spread expands: Math.max(...[3,1,4,1,5]) expands array to Math.max(3,1,4,1,5). {...obj1, ...obj2} merges objects. [...arr1, ...arr2] concatenates arrays.

questions.statement: Array.prototype.map() is different from Array.prototype.forEach() because:
questions.option_a: map is faster than forEach
questions.option_b: map returns a new array with transformed elements; forEach returns undefined
questions.option_c: forEach can only work with numbers; map works with any type
questions.option_d: map modifies the original array; forEach doesn't
questions.explanation: map creates and returns a NEW array. forEach is for side effects — it returns undefined. Use map when you need a transformed array. Use forEach when you need to iterate for side effects (logging, DOM updates).

questions.statement: What is "hoisting" in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: Moving large files to a CDN for faster delivery
questions.option_b: JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope during compilation
questions.option_c: Elevating functions to higher performance mode
questions.option_d: Loading scripts before the DOM is ready
questions.explanation: Hoisting: var declarations and function declarations are moved to the top of their scope during compilation. So you can call a function before its declaration appears in code. let and const are hoisted but not initialized — accessing them before declaration causes a ReferenceError (Temporal Dead Zone).

questions.statement: What is the purpose of async/await syntax?
questions.option_a: Makes JavaScript code run in parallel threads
questions.option_b: Enables writing asynchronous code that looks like synchronous code, using Promises underneath
questions.option_c: Replaces the need for Promises entirely
questions.option_d: Only works for HTTP requests
questions.explanation: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises. It makes Promise-based code look synchronous and sequential, improving readability. Under the hood, it's still Promises.

questions.statement: What does document.querySelector("#main") return if no element with id="main" exists?
questions.option_a: An empty NodeList
questions.option_b: undefined
questions.option_c: null
questions.option_d: An error is thrown
questions.explanation: querySelector returns null if no matching element is found. querySelectorAll returns an empty NodeList. Attempting to access properties on null throws a TypeError.

questions.option_a: A then B
questions.option_b: B then A
questions.option_c: Both simultaneously
questions.option_d: Only B (setTimeout with 0 is ignored)
questions.explanation: setTimeout is a Web API — it runs asynchronously. Even with 0ms delay, the callback goes to the callback queue and only executes when the call stack is empty. console.log("B") runs on the call stack first. Output: B then A.

questions.statement: What is destructuring in JavaScript?
questions.option_a: Breaking down objects/arrays into smaller pieces for garbage collection
questions.option_b: Extracting values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables
questions.option_c: A way to destruct/delete variables
questions.option_d: Converting objects to JSON strings
questions.explanation: Destructuring: const { name, age } = user; creates variables name and age from user object. const [first, second] = array; creates variables from array positions. Cleaner than const name = user.name; const age = user.age;.

questions.statement: In React, what is a "component"?
questions.option_a: A separate JavaScript file
questions.option_b: A reusable, self-contained piece of UI — a function that returns JSX
questions.option_c: A CSS class applied to HTML elements
questions.option_d: A database record
questions.explanation: A React component is a function (or class) that returns JSX — a description of what to render. Components are the building blocks of React UIs, composable and reusable.

questions.statement: What does the key prop serve in React lists?
questions.option_a: Acts as a CSS selector for the element
questions.option_b: Helps React identify which items changed, were added, or removed — enabling efficient DOM updates
questions.option_c: Encrypts the data in the list item
questions.option_d: Creates a unique CSS class for styling
questions.explanation: key is React's mechanism for tracking list items. When items change, React uses keys to determine what changed vs what moved. Without keys, React must re-render the entire list. With keys, only changed items re-render.

questions.statement: The React useState hook returns:
questions.option_a: The current state and a function to re-render
questions.option_b: An array with the current state value and a function to update it
questions.option_c: The previous state and the new state
questions.option_d: A boolean indicating if state has changed
questions.explanation: const [count, setCount] = useState(0) — array destructuring. count is the current value. setCount is the updater function. Calling setCount(newValue) triggers a re-render with the new value.

questions.statement: The React useEffect hook runs:
questions.option_a: Before the component renders (similar to constructor)
questions.option_b: After every render by default, or when specified dependencies change
questions.option_c: Only once during the entire application lifecycle
questions.option_d: Only when the user interacts with the component
questions.explanation: By default, useEffect runs after every render. With a dependency array [dep], it runs only when dep changes. With an empty array [], it runs only once after the first render (like componentDidMount).

questions.statement: What is the Virtual DOM in React?
questions.option_a: A physical copy of the DOM stored on the server
questions.option_b: A lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM that React uses to minimize actual DOM updates
questions.option_c: A virtual machine that runs React applications
questions.option_d: A CSS framework that mimics DOM behavior
questions.explanation: React's Virtual DOM: a JavaScript object that mirrors the real DOM. When state changes, React creates a new Virtual DOM, diffs it with the previous one (reconciliation), and applies ONLY the minimum necessary changes to the real DOM.

questions.statement: In a REST API, what is the correct response for a request to DELETE /api/products/123 when the product doesn't exist?
questions.option_a: 200 OK with empty body
questions.option_b: 204 No Content
questions.option_c: 404 Not Found
questions.option_d: 400 Bad Request
questions.explanation: If the product doesn't exist, it cannot be deleted. Return 404 Not Found. 204 No Content would be the response for a successful deletion. Some APIs return 404 for "delete of non-existent resource"; others argue 204 (idempotent — the end state is the same).

questions.statement: What is middleware in Express.js?
questions.option_a: Software between the database and the server
questions.option_b: Functions that have access to req and res and can execute code, modify them, or call the next middleware
questions.option_c: A separate server that handles authentication
questions.option_d: The process of compressing server responses
questions.explanation: Express middleware: functions in the request-response pipeline. They run sequentially, can modify request/response, end the cycle, or call next() to pass to the next middleware.

questions.statement: JWT (JSON Web Token) solves which problem with session-based authentication?
questions.option_a: JWTs encrypt user passwords
questions.option_b: JWTs eliminate the need for server-side session storage, making authentication stateless
questions.option_c: JWTs are more secure because they cannot be decoded
questions.option_d: JWTs allow users to log in without a password
questions.explanation: Session-based auth requires server to store sessions (database/memory overhead, scaling issues). JWTs are self-contained — all user info is in the token, cryptographically signed. Server verifies signature without storage lookup.

questions.statement: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is prevented primarily by:
questions.option_a: Using HTTPS
questions.option_b: Sanitizing/escaping user input before rendering it as HTML, and using Content Security Policy
questions.option_c: Rate limiting login attempts
questions.option_d: Storing sessions server-side
questions.explanation: XSS occurs when user-supplied content is rendered as executable HTML. Prevention: treat user input as data (use textContent not innerHTML), sanitize with DOMPurify if HTML is needed, and use CSP headers to restrict script execution.

questions.statement: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is prevented by:
questions.option_a: Encrypting all form data
questions.option_b: Using CSRF tokens on state-changing requests and/or SameSite cookie attribute
questions.option_c: Validating the user's IP address
questions.option_d: Using POST instead of GET for all requests
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits that browsers auto-send cookies with cross-site requests. Prevention: CSRF tokens (attacker can't get the token due to same-origin policy) and SameSite=Strict cookies (not sent cross-site at all).

questions.statement: The "Principle of Least Privilege" applied to a web application's database account means:
questions.option_a: Using the simplest database possible
questions.option_b: The database account should have only the minimum permissions required (e.g., only SELECT on certain tables, not DROP)
questions.option_c: Limiting database queries to small result sets
questions.option_d: Allowing the database account to be used by only one developer
questions.explanation: If an attacker compromises the web application, the damage is limited by the database account's permissions. An account with SELECT only can't DROP tables or export all user data.

questions.statement: What is SQL injection and how is it prevented?
questions.option_a: A technique for optimizing SQL queries; prevented by using indexes
questions.option_b: An attack where malicious SQL is injected into user input; prevented by parameterized queries
questions.option_c: A method for injecting data into databases; prevented by input length limits
questions.option_d: An attack on the database server directly; prevented by firewalls
questions.explanation: SQL injection: user input containing SQL code is concatenated into a query and executed. Prevention: parameterized queries (prepared statements) treat user input as data, never as code.

questions.statement: What does PWA (Progressive Web App) enable that a regular website cannot?
questions.option_a: Better SEO rankings
questions.option_b: Support for all programming languages
questions.option_c: Offline functionality, push notifications, and installation to the home screen
questions.option_d: Access to all device hardware
questions.explanation: PWAs use Service Workers (offline/background) and Web App Manifest (installability). They can work without internet, receive push notifications, and be "installed" like native apps. Regular websites cannot do these.

questions.statement: In GraphQL, what is the key advantage over REST APIs?
questions.option_a: GraphQL is always faster than REST
questions.option_b: The client specifies exactly what data it needs — no over-fetching or under-fetching
questions.option_c: GraphQL automatically generates documentation
questions.option_d: GraphQL supports only JSON format while REST doesn't
questions.explanation: GraphQL lets the client request exactly the fields it needs (no more, no less) in a single request. REST endpoints return fixed data structures — you either get too much (over-fetching) or need multiple requests (under-fetching).

questions.statement: What is the purpose of an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) in web development?
questions.option_a: Maps images to HTML elements
questions.option_b: Translates between database tables and programming language objects, allowing database operations without raw SQL
questions.option_c: Manages browser object models
questions.option_d: Maps URL routes to controllers
questions.explanation: ORMs like Sequelize, Mongoose, SQLAlchemy let developers interact with databases using their programming language's patterns (objects, methods) instead of writing SQL. Trade-off: abstraction for some performance overhead.

questions.statement: What does Content-Type: application/json in an HTTP request header tell the server?
questions.option_a: The server should respond with JSON
questions.option_b: The request body contains JSON-formatted data
questions.option_c: The request is from a JSON-compatible browser
questions.option_d: JSONP is being used
questions.explanation: The Content-Type request header declares the format of the REQUEST BODY. application/json tells the server "the body I'm sending is JSON, please parse it as JSON."

questions.statement: In React, what happens when you call setState() or a state setter from useState()?
questions.option_a: The component is immediately destroyed and recreated
questions.option_b: The state updates synchronously, then React updates the DOM
questions.option_c: React schedules a re-render — the component function re-runs with the new state value
questions.option_d: Only child components re-render
questions.explanation: State updates trigger re-renders. React doesn't update state immediately (batching optimization). Instead, it schedules a re-render where the component function runs again with the new state value.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of the HttpOnly cookie flag?
questions.option_a: Restricts the cookie to HTTPS connections only
questions.option_b: Makes the cookie inaccessible to JavaScript — only sent in HTTP headers
questions.option_c: Makes the cookie available only from the HTTP server, not CDN
questions.option_d: Limits the cookie's size
questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies cannot be accessed via document.cookie in JavaScript. This prevents XSS attacks from stealing session cookies. Even if an attacker injects JavaScript, they cannot read HttpOnly cookies.

questions.statement: Lazy loading images with loading="lazy" means:
questions.option_a: Images load slowly to save bandwidth
questions.option_b: Images only load when they're about to enter the viewport
questions.option_c: Images load in low quality first, then high quality
questions.option_d: Images load after all JavaScript has executed
questions.explanation: Lazy loading defers image loading until the image is close to the viewport. Significantly reduces initial page load time and data usage for pages with many images below the fold.

questions.statement: What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network) and why is it used?
questions.option_a: A tool for compressing CSS and JavaScript files
questions.option_b: A network of geographically distributed servers that serve static assets from locations close to users
questions.option_c: A database replication system
questions.option_d: A monitoring tool for web applications
questions.explanation: CDN: distributed servers worldwide. A user in Karachi gets images from a CDN server in Pakistan (30ms) instead of a US origin server (300ms). Reduces latency, reduces load on origin server, improves reliability.

questions.statement: What is code splitting in modern web development?
questions.option_a: Dividing code between frontend and backend developers
questions.option_b: Breaking JavaScript bundles into smaller chunks loaded on-demand
questions.option_c: Splitting CSS into separate files per component
questions.option_d: Distributing code across multiple servers
questions.explanation: Code splitting (supported by Webpack, Vite): instead of one massive JavaScript bundle, split into chunks. Load only what's needed for the current page. Other chunks load on-demand when needed. Dramatically improves initial load time.

questions.statement: Browser caching with Cache-Control: immutable, max-age=31536000 is most appropriately used for:
questions.option_a: HTML pages that change frequently
questions.option_b: API responses from dynamic endpoints
questions.option_c: Versioned static assets (JS, CSS files with content hash in filename)
questions.option_d: Images that users upload
questions.explanation: When filenames include content hashes (e.g., app.a1b2c3d4.js), the file never changes — a different content generates a different hash, hence different filename. These files can be aggressively cached forever. HTML should not be cached this way (it references the hashed files).

questions.statement: What is the purpose of minification in web development?
questions.option_a: Reducing image resolution to save storage
questions.option_b: Removing whitespace, comments, and shortening variable names in JS/CSS to reduce file size
questions.option_c: Compressing images with lossy algorithms
questions.option_d: Reducing the number of features in a web application
questions.explanation: Minification removes all unnecessary characters (whitespace, comments) and shortens variable names in JavaScript and CSS. A 100KB file becomes 60KB without changing functionality, reducing download time.

questions.statement: End-to-End (E2E) tests with Playwright/Cypress test:
questions.option_a: Individual JavaScript functions in isolation
questions.option_b: Database queries and ORM operations
questions.option_c: Complete user journeys in a real browser — from user action to expected outcome
questions.option_d: API endpoints without a browser
questions.explanation: E2E tests automate a real browser to test complete flows: "user fills login form, submits, is redirected to dashboard, sees their name." Tests the entire stack — frontend, API, database — working together.

questions.statement: What does Lighthouse measure and provide?
questions.option_a: Backend server performance metrics
questions.option_b: Automated auditing of Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO with scores and recommendations
questions.option_c: Database query performance
questions.option_d: JavaScript bundle size analysis
questions.explanation: Lighthouse (built into Chrome DevTools) scores your page 0-100 on Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO, and PWA criteria. Provides specific recommendations for improvements.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of environment variables in web applications?
questions.option_a: Variables that automatically change based on the user's environment (device, browser)
questions.option_b: Configuration values (database passwords, API keys) stored separately from code — different values for dev/staging/production
questions.option_c: CSS variables that change based on screen size
questions.option_d: JavaScript variables declared with var (function-scoped)
questions.explanation: Environment variables separate configuration from code. Different values for different environments. NEVER commit secrets (passwords, API keys) to version control — use environment variables and .gitignore.

questions.statement: What is Docker and why is it used in web development?
questions.option_a: A CSS framework for creating container elements
questions.option_b: A containerization tool that packages applications and their dependencies for consistent running across environments
questions.option_c: A database management tool
questions.option_d: A JavaScript testing framework
questions.explanation: Docker packages an application and ALL its dependencies (runtime, libraries, config) into a container image. The container runs identically on any machine with Docker. Solves "works on my machine" problems.

questions.statement: Continuous Integration (CI) in web development means:
questions.option_a: Continuously updating the UI without page reloads
questions.option_b: Automatically running tests and builds when code is committed to the repository
questions.option_c: Continuously monitoring server uptime
questions.option_d: Regular backups of the database
questions.explanation: CI: every code commit triggers automated: linting, testing, building. If anything fails, the team is immediately notified. The main branch always has passing tests. Catches problems early when they're cheap to fix.

questions.statement: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) in the context of modern web frameworks?
questions.option_a: Rendering images on a dedicated server
questions.option_b: The server runs JavaScript to generate fully rendered HTML, which is sent to the browser
questions.option_c: Distributing server load across multiple machines
questions.option_d: Using CSS on the server to style HTML
questions.explanation: SSR: the server (running Node.js) executes the frontend JavaScript, fetches data, renders the component tree to HTML, and sends complete HTML. Benefits: fast initial paint, SEO-friendly (HTML is indexed, not JavaScript).

questions.statement: TypeScript adds what to JavaScript?
questions.option_a: New runtime features not available in JavaScript
questions.option_b: Static type checking — type annotations that are checked at compile time
questions.option_c: Built-in performance optimization
questions.option_d: Server-side execution capability
questions.explanation: TypeScript is JavaScript + types. The type annotations are removed during compilation (transpilation to JS). TypeScript catches type errors during development — before the code runs.

questions.statement: aria-label is used to:
questions.option_a: Label JavaScript variables for accessibility
questions.option_b: Provide an accessible name for UI elements that have no visible text label
questions.option_c: Add labels to database fields
questions.option_d: Label sections of CSS code
questions.explanation: aria-label provides a text label for screen readers when there's no visible text (like icon-only buttons). <button aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button> — screen readers announce "Close dialog button", not just "✕".

questions.statement: What does the defer attribute on a <script> tag do?
questions.option_a: Delays the script execution by 1 second
questions.option_b: Downloads the script in parallel with HTML parsing, but executes AFTER the HTML parsing is complete
questions.option_c: Makes the script optional — only loads if needed
questions.option_d: Defers the script to the cache for future use
questions.explanation: defer: script downloads in parallel (doesn't block HTML parsing), but executes after the full HTML document is parsed. Maintains script execution order. Contrast with async (executes as soon as downloaded, may interrupt parsing).

questions.statement: Rate limiting in web APIs is implemented to:
questions.option_a: Limit the size of data returned by each request
questions.option_b: Prevent abuse by limiting how many requests a client can make in a given time window
questions.option_c: Limit the rate at which the database grows
questions.option_d: Control download speeds for file transfers
questions.explanation: Rate limiting: "max 100 requests per 15 minutes per IP." Prevents: brute force attacks on login, API abuse, DDoS amplification via expensive endpoints, scrapers.

questions.statement: In web security, what does the Secure cookie flag do?
questions.option_a: Encrypts the cookie's value
questions.option_b: Ensures the cookie is only transmitted over HTTPS connections, never HTTP
questions.option_c: Prevents the cookie from being modified
questions.option_d: Makes the cookie available only to authenticated users
questions.explanation: Secure flag: the browser will only send this cookie over encrypted HTTPS connections. On HTTP connections, the cookie is not sent. This prevents cookie theft on non-encrypted connections.

questions.statement: What is the difference between sessionStorage and a server-side session?
questions.option_a: They are identical — both store data on the server
questions.option_b: sessionStorage stores data in the browser (client-side), server sessions store data on the server
questions.option_c: Server sessions are more secure because they're in the database
questions.option_d: sessionStorage is permanent; server sessions expire after 30 minutes
questions.explanation: sessionStorage: data in the browser, only for that tab's lifetime. Server sessions: session ID in cookie, actual data on server (in memory or database). Server sessions are generally more secure (sensitive data not sent to client).

questions.statement: What problem does the SameSite=Lax cookie attribute solve?
questions.option_a: Makes cookies work with HTTPS only
questions.option_b: A compromise between security and usability — blocks cross-site request cookies except for top-level GET navigation
questions.option_c: Allows cookies to be shared across subdomains
questions.option_d: Enables cookies on mobile browsers
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax blocks cookies on cross-site subrequests (form POSTs, iframes, XHR) but allows them when navigating to the site via a link. This prevents CSRF while allowing "login with another site" flows.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of package.json in a Node.js project?
questions.option_a: Packages and compresses JavaScript files for deployment
questions.option_b: Defines project metadata, dependencies, scripts, and configuration for Node.js projects
questions.option_c: Contains the packaged (compiled) JavaScript
questions.option_d: Stores environment variables for the project
questions.explanation: package.json is the project's manifest: name, version, description, scripts (npm run build, npm test), dependencies (production), devDependencies (development tools), and configuration.

questions.statement: Which statement about React's virtual DOM reconciliation is TRUE?
questions.option_a: React completely re-renders the entire DOM on every state change
questions.option_b: React rebuilds the entire real DOM and replaces it
questions.option_c: React compares new and old Virtual DOM trees, calculates minimal changes, and applies only those to the real DOM
