questions.option_c: Items that frequently co-occur are always causally related
questions.option_d: The most frequent items have the highest association rules
questions.explanation: Apriori property: if an itemset {A,B} is frequent (support ≥ min_support), then all its subsets {A}, {B} must also be frequent. Contrapositive: if {A} is infrequent, then {A,B,C,...} is also infrequent. This prunes the search space exponentially.

questions.statement: What does model.eval() do in PyTorch?
questions.option_a: Evaluates the model's accuracy on test data
questions.option_b: Switches the model to inference mode, disabling dropout and batch normalization training behavior
questions.option_c: Starts model training
questions.option_d: Prints model architecture summary
questions.explanation: model.eval() sets the model to evaluation mode: Dropout layers use all neurons (no dropping). BatchNorm layers use running statistics (not batch statistics). Always call before inference/evaluation. Complement is model.train() for training mode.

questions.statement: Amazon's abandoned AI hiring tool that penalized female candidates exemplifies which AI bias type?
questions.option_a: Measurement bias — wrong measurement tools
questions.option_b: Historical bias — training on historical hiring data that reflected gender discrimination in tech hiring
questions.option_c: Aggregation bias — not separating male and female models
questions.option_d: Deployment bias — bias introduced during deployment
questions.explanation: Amazon's tool was trained on 10 years of resume submissions, mostly from men (reflecting the tech industry's gender imbalance). The model learned historical patterns, penalizing anything associated with female applicants — perpetuating the historical bias it was trained on.

questions.statement: In the context of ML pipelines, what is the risk of "target leakage"?
questions.option_a: Model predicting the same output for all inputs
questions.option_b: Using features that contain information about the target that would not be available at prediction time
questions.option_c: Training data leaking into the test set
questions.option_d: Sensitive target information being exposed
questions.explanation: Target leakage: a feature is correlated with the target because it is caused by or measured at the same time as the target. Example: including "hospitalized" as a feature to predict "will be hospitalized." The feature already contains the answer. Model shows unrealistically high performance.

questions.statement: What is the "attention mechanism" in seq2seq models?
questions.option_a: A technique to make models focus on processing important training examples
questions.option_b: A mechanism allowing the decoder to look at all encoder hidden states when generating each output token, weighted by relevance
questions.option_c: A method for detecting when the model is not paying attention
questions.option_d: Prioritizing certain training samples during gradient updates
questions.explanation: Attention: when generating output token t, the decoder can "attend" to different parts of the input sequence with varying weights. For machine translation: generating "bank" in French focuses on the source token "bank." This solves the bottleneck of compressing the entire input into one vector.

questions.statement: Which statement about Deep Learning vs Traditional ML is MOST accurate?
questions.option_a: Deep learning always outperforms traditional ML
questions.option_b: Deep learning is better for unstructured data (images, text, audio) and large datasets; traditional ML is often better for structured/tabular data with limited samples
questions.option_c: Traditional ML is obsolete since deep learning's emergence
questions.option_d: Deep learning requires less data than traditional ML
questions.explanation: Deep learning excels for unstructured data where automatic feature discovery matters (images, text, audio) and when massive data is available. For tabular data with thousands of records, XGBoost/Random Forest often match or outperform deep learning while being faster to train and easier to interpret.

questions.statement: The CIA Triad in cyber security stands for:
questions.option_a: Control, Investigation, Assessment
questions.option_b: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
questions.option_c: Cryptography, Identity, Authentication
questions.option_d: Compliance, Integrity, Auditing
questions.explanation: CIA Triad: Confidentiality (only authorized access), Integrity (data not modified), Availability (accessible when needed). All security controls ultimately protect one or more of these three properties.

questions.statement: Which cryptographic property ensures that a sender cannot deny having sent a message?
questions.option_a: Confidentiality
questions.option_b: Integrity
questions.option_c: Non-repudiation
questions.option_d: Availability
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation: the sender cannot later deny having sent the message, because only they had the private key used to create the digital signature. This is critical in legal/financial contexts.

questions.statement: AES-256 uses which key size?
questions.option_a: 128 bits
questions.option_b: 192 bits
questions.option_c: 256 bits
questions.option_d: 512 bits
questions.explanation: AES-256 uses a 256-bit key with 14 rounds. AES also comes in 128-bit (10 rounds) and 192-bit (12 rounds) variants. AES-256 provides the highest security level and is used in military/government applications.

questions.statement: The "key distribution problem" solved by asymmetric cryptography refers to:
questions.option_a: How to distribute cryptography software to end users
questions.option_b: How to securely share a symmetric encryption key over an insecure channel
questions.option_c: How to manage large numbers of cryptographic keys
questions.option_d: How to distribute certificate authority trust
questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption requires both parties to share the same secret key. But how do you securely exchange that key over an insecure internet connection? Asymmetric cryptography solves this — public keys can be freely distributed; only the private key (never transmitted) can decrypt.

questions.statement: What makes bcrypt more suitable for password hashing than SHA-256?
questions.option_a: bcrypt produces longer hashes
questions.option_b: bcrypt is intentionally slow (computationally expensive), making brute-force attacks impractical
questions.option_c: bcrypt cannot be reversed like SHA-256 can
questions.option_d: bcrypt automatically encrypts the result
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is designed to be FAST (useful for checksums). bcrypt is designed to be SLOW — deliberately introduces computational cost. At cost factor 12, computing one hash takes ~100ms. An attacker can try only ~10 passwords/second vs. billions/second with SHA-256. Dramatically increases brute-force cost.

questions.statement: What does "salting" a password hash accomplish?
questions.option_a: Makes the password longer and more complex
questions.option_b: Adds a random unique value to each password before hashing, defeating rainbow table attacks
questions.option_c: Encrypts the hash for additional security
questions.option_d: Sends the hash to a salt server for validation
questions.explanation: Salting: add a unique random value (salt) to each password before hashing. Two identical passwords get different salts → different hashes. Rainbow tables (precomputed hash→password tables) become useless because they'd need to be rebuilt for every unique salt. Without salting, an attacker finding a hash collision cracks ALL users with that password simultaneously.

questions.statement: In public key cryptography, what does Alice use to encrypt a message she wants to send ONLY to Bob?
questions.option_a: Alice's private key
questions.option_b: Alice's public key
questions.option_c: Bob's public key
questions.option_d: Bob's private key
questions.explanation: To send an encrypted message to Bob that ONLY Bob can read, Alice encrypts with BOB's PUBLIC key. Only Bob's PRIVATE key can decrypt. Alice's keys are used for signing (proving the message came from Alice) — not for encrypting messages TO Bob.

questions.statement: A digital certificate primarily binds:
questions.option_a: A domain name to an IP address
questions.option_b: A public key to an identity, verified by a Certificate Authority
questions.option_c: A user's identity to their private key
questions.option_d: An organization's name to its email address
questions.explanation: A digital certificate (X.509) contains: subject identity, subject's PUBLIC key, issuer (CA), validity period, and CA's digital signature. The CA's signature proves "this public key belongs to this identity." Anyone with the CA's public key can verify the certificate's authenticity.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of "forward secrecy" in TLS connections using ECDHE?
questions.option_a: Forward secrecy ensures data sent in the future remains encrypted
questions.option_b: If the server's long-term private key is later compromised, past session traffic cannot be decrypted
questions.option_c: It ensures TLS 1.3 is used instead of older versions
questions.option_d: Forward secrecy prevents replay attacks
questions.explanation: With forward secrecy (using ephemeral key exchange like ECDHE), a new temporary key pair is generated for EACH session. The session key is never stored. Even if an attacker records all your HTTPS traffic today and later steals the server's private key, they cannot decrypt the recorded traffic — those session keys are gone.

questions.statement: SQL injection is MOST effectively prevented by:
questions.option_a: Input length validation
questions.option_b: Parameterized queries (prepared statements)
questions.option_c: Encoding special characters in the URL
questions.option_d: Using a Web Application Firewall
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries completely separate the SQL code from the data. User input is always treated as pure data — never interpreted as SQL syntax. No matter what a user types, it cannot change the query structure. WAFs help but can be bypassed. Input validation helps but isn't sufficient alone.

questions.statement: Which XSS type stores the malicious script in the server's database and delivers it to all users who view the affected content?
questions.option_a: Reflected XSS
questions.option_b: DOM-based XSS
questions.option_c: Stored (Persistent) XSS
questions.option_d: Universal XSS
questions.explanation: Stored XSS: attacker submits malicious script as content (comment, username, product review). It's saved to the database. Every user who views that content receives and executes the malicious script. Most dangerous type — automatically affects all users without requiring them to click a special link.

questions.statement: The HTTPOnly flag on a cookie prevents:
questions.option_a: The cookie from being sent over HTTP (non-HTTPS) connections
questions.option_b: JavaScript from accessing the cookie value, protecting it from XSS theft
questions.option_c: The cookie from being stored for more than one HTTP session
questions.option_d: Cross-origin requests from including the cookie
questions.explanation: HTTPOnly: the browser refuses to expose this cookie to JavaScript (document.cookie). Even if an XSS attack executes malicious script on your page, it cannot steal HTTPOnly session cookies. The cookie is still sent automatically by the browser on HTTP requests — it's just hidden from JavaScript.

questions.statement: A CSRF attack succeeds because:
questions.option_a: The victim's browser is infected with malware
questions.option_b: The browser automatically includes session cookies with requests to authenticated sites, even when the request originates from a different site
questions.option_c: The server doesn't use HTTPS, allowing traffic interception
questions.option_d: The victim uses a weak password
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic cookie inclusion. When you visit a malicious site, your browser is already logged into your bank. The malicious page makes a cross-site request to your bank. The browser automatically attaches your bank session cookie. The bank thinks the request is from you. CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies break this attack.

questions.statement: What distinguishes a virus from a worm?
questions.option_a: Viruses encrypt data; worms delete data
questions.option_b: Viruses attach to files and require user action to spread; worms self-replicate autonomously across networks
questions.option_c: Worms only affect Windows; viruses affect all OS
questions.option_d: Viruses are more dangerous than worms
questions.explanation: Virus: needs host file + user action (open the infected file). Worm: self-contained, exploits network vulnerabilities to spread automatically without any user interaction. WannaCry was a worm — it spread to 200,000 systems in 150 countries in hours without anyone clicking anything.

questions.statement: What is a "zero-day" vulnerability?
questions.option_a: A vulnerability patched within the same day it's discovered
questions.option_b: A vulnerability unknown to the vendor with no patch available, discovered before the vendor has any time to fix it
questions.option_c: A vulnerability that takes zero time to exploit
questions.option_d: A vulnerability in day-zero software (beta releases)
questions.explanation: Zero-day: vendor has had "zero days" to fix it. The vulnerability is unknown to the vendor. No patch exists. No signatures exist in security tools. Attacks exploiting it are extremely difficult to detect and defend against. Nation-state actors pay millions of dollars for reliable zero-days.

questions.statement: Ransomware's "double extortion" technique refers to:
questions.option_a: Demanding payment twice from the same victim
questions.option_b: Encrypting data AND exfiltrating it — threatening to publish stolen data if ransom isn't paid
questions.option_c: Using two separate encryption keys requiring two separate payments
questions.option_d: Attacking both the company and its customers simultaneously
questions.explanation: Double extortion: (1) Encrypt data (ransom for decryption key) + (2) Steal data before encrypting (ransom threat: "pay or we publish your customer data/trade secrets"). Defeats the "we have backups, we won't pay" strategy. Modern ransomware groups almost universally use double extortion.

questions.statement: The Principle of Least Privilege means:
questions.option_a: Users should have simple, easy-to-remember passwords
questions.option_b: Security should be as simple as possible
questions.option_c: Each user, system, and process should have only the minimum access necessary to perform its function
questions.option_d: The least important users have the fewest privileges
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits blast radius. If a compromised account has only read access to one table, the attacker has only read access to that table. If the account has admin access, the attacker owns everything. Least privilege is one of the most important and most frequently violated security principles.

questions.statement: Which access control model assigns permissions to roles rather than individual users?
questions.option_a: DAC (Discretionary Access Control)
questions.option_b: MAC (Mandatory Access Control)
questions.option_c: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)
questions.option_d: ACL (Access Control List)
questions.explanation: RBAC: permissions are assigned to roles (Database Admin, Developer, Auditor). Users are assigned to roles. User inherits the role's permissions. When a user leaves, remove them from their roles — permissions are gone. Far easier to manage than individual permission assignment at scale.

questions.statement: MFA "push notification fatigue" attacks work by:
questions.option_a: Overwhelming the authentication server with requests
questions.option_b: Sending the victim constant MFA approval requests until, out of frustration or confusion, they click approve
questions.option_c: Using fake push notifications that look identical to real ones
questions.option_d: Intercepting push notifications through a MITM attack
questions.explanation: MFA fatigue (also called "MFA bombing"): attacker has the victim's username and password (obtained from a breach/phishing). They continuously trigger MFA push notifications to the victim's phone. Eventually — at 2 AM, while commuting — the victim clicks "approve" to stop the notifications. Uber was breached in 2022 through MFA fatigue attack.

questions.statement: A penetration test differs from a vulnerability assessment because:
questions.option_a: Penetration tests are automated; vulnerability assessments are manual
questions.option_b: Penetration tests attempt to actually exploit vulnerabilities to demonstrate impact; vulnerability assessments only identify them
questions.option_c: Vulnerability assessments are more thorough than penetration tests
questions.option_d: Penetration tests only cover web applications; vulnerability assessments cover entire networks
questions.explanation: Vulnerability assessment: identify potential vulnerabilities (automated scanning + some manual verification). No exploitation. Penetration test: go further — actually attempt to exploit identified vulnerabilities to prove they're exploitable and demonstrate the potential impact. Both require written authorization from the system owner.

questions.statement: What is "shoulder surfing" in the context of physical security?
questions.option_a: A technique for climbing security fences
questions.option_b: Observing someone's screen or keyboard from nearby to steal sensitive information
questions.option_c: A social engineering technique using LinkedIn
questions.option_d: Planting listening devices in conference rooms
questions.explanation: Shoulder surfing: observing from nearby as someone types a password, PIN, or views sensitive information. Simple, low-tech but effective. Prevention: screen privacy filters, physical awareness, being mindful of surroundings when entering credentials.

questions.statement: SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) primarily provides:
questions.option_a: Automatic response to all security incidents
questions.option_b: Centralized collection, correlation, and analysis of security events to detect and investigate incidents
questions.option_c: Encryption of all network communications
questions.option_d: Vulnerability scanning of IT assets
questions.explanation: SIEM collects logs from all sources (firewalls, servers, applications, endpoints), normalizes them to a common format, applies correlation rules to identify attack patterns across multiple events, and generates prioritized alerts for security analysts. It's the central nervous system of a Security Operations Center.

questions.statement: Which of these is the CORRECT order for digital forensics evidence collection according to order of volatility?
questions.option_a: Hard disk → RAM → CPU registers → Network connections
questions.option_b: CPU registers → RAM → Network connections → Hard disk
questions.option_c: Hard disk → Network connections → RAM → CPU registers
questions.option_d: Network connections → Hard disk → RAM → CPU registers
questions.explanation: Order of volatility (most to least volatile): CPU registers/cache → RAM → Network state → Running processes → Temporary filesystem → Disk storage. Collect most volatile first — once power is removed, CPU registers and RAM contents are lost forever. Disk data persists.

questions.statement: A "chain of custody" document in digital forensics tracks:
questions.option_a: The sequence of events that led to a security incident
questions.option_b: Every person who had possession of or access to digital evidence, when, and why
questions.option_c: The blockchain records related to cryptocurrency transactions in cybercrime
questions.option_d: The network path taken by malicious traffic
questions.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented record proving evidence integrity. Any gap — unaccounted time, unauthorized access — can result in evidence being inadmissible in court. Defense attorneys specifically look for chain of custody gaps to challenge evidence.

questions.statement: GDPR's breach notification requirement mandates reporting to supervisory authorities within:
questions.option_a: 24 hours
questions.option_b: 48 hours
questions.option_c: 72 hours
questions.option_d: 7 business days
questions.explanation: GDPR Article 33: data controllers must notify the supervisory authority (e.g., ICO in UK, CNIL in France) within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in risk to individuals.

questions.statement: What is "defense in depth"?
questions.option_a: A deep vulnerability that requires significant effort to exploit
questions.option_b: Using multiple layers of security controls so that if one fails, others continue to provide protection
questions.option_c: Having a dedicated security team providing 24/7 protection
questions.option_d: Encrypting data at multiple levels for maximum security
questions.explanation: Defense in depth: no single security control is perfect or unbreakable. By layering multiple controls (perimeter firewall + network segmentation + host firewall + endpoint protection + encryption + monitoring + incident response), an attacker must breach multiple layers — dramatically increasing difficulty and detection probability.

questions.statement: What is the SolarWinds attack best characterized as?
questions.option_a: SQL injection attack against SolarWinds' website
questions.option_b: A supply chain attack where malicious code was introduced into a legitimate software update
questions.option_c: A ransomware attack against SolarWinds' infrastructure
questions.option_d: A phishing attack targeting SolarWinds employees
questions.explanation: SolarWinds: attackers (APT29/Cozy Bear, Russian SVR) compromised SolarWinds' build system. A backdoor (SUNBURST) was added to the legitimate Orion software update, signed with SolarWinds' certificate, and distributed to 18,000 customers. This is the definition of a supply chain attack — poisoning the upstream software before it reaches victims.

questions.statement: Kerckhoffs's Principle states that a cryptographic system:
questions.option_a: Should be secret from all except authorized cryptographers
questions.option_b: Should be secure even if everything about the system is publicly known, except the key
questions.option_c: Should use multiple encryption algorithms for maximum security
questions.option_d: Should be updated at least annually to maintain security
questions.explanation: Kerckhoffs (1883): security should rely entirely on the secrecy of the key, NOT on the secrecy of the algorithm. The algorithm can be (and should be) public — allowing independent review and analysis. Secret algorithms cannot be independently validated and typically hide weaknesses.

questions.statement: What is "credential stuffing"?
questions.option_a: Filling in fake credentials to waste an attacker's time
questions.option_b: Using previously leaked (username, password) pairs from one breach to attempt login at other services
questions.option_c: Brute-forcing credentials by trying all combinations
questions.option_d: Stuffing credentials into malware to extract them from systems
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing: password reuse is epidemic. When Netflix is breached and email/password combinations leak, attackers try those SAME credentials on banking, email, and shopping sites. People who use the same password everywhere are especially vulnerable. MFA and password managers are the defenses.

questions.statement: In incident response, "eradication" refers to:
questions.option_a: Deleting all data related to the incident to prevent further exposure
questions.option_b: Removing the root cause of the incident — malware, backdoors, exploited vulnerabilities
questions.option_c: Eliminating affected systems by reinstallation only
questions.option_d: The legal process of prosecuting attackers
questions.explanation: Eradication phase: after containing the incident, remove all traces of the attacker — malware, backdoors, persistence mechanisms, attacker-created accounts. Also includes patching the exploited vulnerability and hardening the environment. Followed by recovery (restoring normal operations).

questions.statement: A rootkit is most accurately described as:
questions.option_a: Software that accesses files stored in the root directory
questions.option_b: Malware that hides its presence and the presence of other malware from the OS and security tools
questions.option_c: Software that requires root/admin privileges to run
questions.option_d: A tool for legally auditing root-level system access
questions.explanation: Rootkits: designed to hide. They intercept OS API calls to conceal files, processes, and network connections associated with malware. Detection is extremely difficult by definition (the OS lies to security tools). Some kernel-mode rootkits require booting from external trusted media to detect.

questions.statement: What is the "CVSS score" used for?
questions.option_a: Measuring the attacker's skill level required for exploitation
questions.option_b: A standardized numerical rating (0-10) of a vulnerability's severity
questions.option_c: Scoring security teams' incident response performance
questions.option_d: Certifying security professionals' competency
questions.explanation: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) 0-10: low (0.1-3.9), medium (4.0-6.9), high (7.0-8.9), critical (9.0-10.0). Factors include: attack vector, complexity, privileges required, user interaction, scope, impact on confidentiality/integrity/availability. Log4Shell: CVSS 10.0.

questions.statement: "Living off the land" attacks use:
questions.option_a: Physical access to servers housed in data centers
questions.option_b: Legitimate built-in OS tools (PowerShell, WMI) for malicious purposes, making detection harder
questions.option_c: Agricultural metaphors to describe prolonged cyber espionage campaigns
questions.option_d: Sustainable, low-power attack infrastructure to avoid detection
questions.explanation: Living off the land (LotL): attackers use tools already present on the system (PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation, certutil, mshta). No malicious files to detect. Security tools looking for "malware files" miss LotL attacks. Behavioral analysis is required for detection.

questions.statement: The WannaCry ransomware spread so rapidly because:
questions.option_a: It was sent via email attachments to millions of users
questions.option_b: It exploited EternalBlue — an NSA-developed exploit targeting Windows SMBv1, spreading automatically without user interaction
questions.option_c: It was distributed through a compromised software update
questions.option_d: It exploited a vulnerability in WordPress affecting millions of websites
questions.explanation: WannaCry used EternalBlue (leaked from NSA by Shadow Brokers) to exploit a critical SMBv1 buffer overflow. It spread automatically across networks without any user clicking anything — scanning for vulnerable systems and infecting them. Organizations with unpatched Windows and accessible SMBv1 were vulnerable.

questions.statement: What does a "bug bounty program" provide?
questions.option_a: Rewards for software developers who write bug-free code
questions.option_b: A legal, structured way for external security researchers to report vulnerabilities in exchange for recognition or payment
questions.option_c: Insurance coverage for software bugs that cause data breaches
questions.option_d: A testing environment where developers can report their own bugs
questions.explanation: Bug bounties: companies invite security researchers to find and responsibly disclose vulnerabilities. Researchers are rewarded (money, swag, recognition) instead of prosecuted. Companies get vetted security testing from thousands of researchers globally. Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and many others run bug bounties.

questions.statement: Steganography differs from encryption because:
questions.option_a: Steganography is more secure than encryption
questions.option_b: Steganography hides the existence of a message within other data; encryption hides the content but not the existence
questions.option_c: Steganography uses mathematical algorithms; encryption uses codes
questions.option_d: They are the same concept with different names
questions.explanation: Encryption: everyone knows a secret message exists, but only authorized parties can read it (the message is scrambled). Steganography: the secret message is hidden within apparently innocent data (a photo, audio file) — no one knows a message exists. Combining both provides maximum security: hide an encrypted message steganographically.

questions.statement: What is the Pegasus spyware primarily known for?
questions.option_a: Ransomware targeting corporate networks
questions.option_b: Advanced nation-state spyware that exploits zero-click vulnerabilities to infect iOS/Android devices of journalists and activists
questions.option_c: Banking trojan targeting mobile payment applications
questions.option_d: Botnet software that recruits smartphones for DDoS attacks
questions.explanation: Pegasus (NSO Group, Israel): commercial spyware sold to governments. Uses zero-click exploits (infects devices without any user interaction through iMessage/WhatsApp vulnerabilities). Exfiltrates everything. Discovered on devices of journalists (Jamal Khashoggi's associates), human rights activists, politicians. Major controversy over surveillance abuse.

questions.statement: A "mantrap" (airlock) in physical security prevents:
questions.option_a: Rodents and pests from entering server rooms
questions.option_b: Tailgating — someone following an authorized person through a secured door
questions.option_c: Piracy of software installed on computers
questions.option_d: Unauthorized removal of physical equipment
questions.explanation: Mantrap: two-door vestibule. First door opens (badge/pin/biometric). Person enters. First door closes. Second door won't open until identity fully verified. If unauthorized: person is trapped between doors (security can respond). Prevents tailgating (piggybacking on someone else's legitimate access).

questions.statement: What is OSINT (Open Source Intelligence)?
questions.option_a: Intelligence gathered from open-source software vulnerabilities
questions.option_b: Gathering information about targets from publicly available sources (websites, social media, DNS records, job postings)
questions.option_c: An open-source platform for sharing threat intelligence
questions.option_d: Intelligence used in open-source software development
questions.explanation: OSINT: passive reconnaissance using publicly available information. A security researcher/attacker can learn: company's tech stack (job postings), employee names/roles (LinkedIn), IP ranges (WHOIS), email format (hunter.io), exposed services (Shodan), sensitive files (Google dork: site:company.com filetype:pdf confidential). All without touching the target's systems.

questions.statement: Which law governs cybercrime in Pakistan?
questions.option_a: Computer Emergency Response Act 2012
questions.option_b: Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016
questions.option_c: Digital Rights Protection Ordinance 2018
questions.option_d: Information Technology Act 2015
questions.explanation: PECA 2016: Pakistan's primary cybercrime legislation. Criminalizes unauthorized access, data interception, cyberstalking, hate speech, child pornography, electronic fraud, identity theft. FIA (Federal Investigation Agency) Cybercrime Wing investigates PECA violations.

questions.statement: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is needed because:
questions.option_a: Current encryption is too slow for modern computers
questions.option_b: Sufficiently powerful quantum computers could use Shor's algorithm to break current RSA/ECC cryptography
questions.option_c: Quantum computers have already broken current encryption
questions.option_d: Post-quantum refers to removing quantum randomness from cryptographic keys
questions.explanation: Shor's algorithm on a quantum computer could factor large numbers exponentially faster, breaking RSA/ECC/DH. Current practical quantum computers are too small, but "harvest now, decrypt later" is already happening. NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) resistant to quantum attacks.

questions.statement: What is "security through obscurity" and why is it insufficient?
questions.option_a: Hiding servers in geographic obscurity; insufficient because attackers use internet scanning
questions.option_b: Relying on secrecy of design/implementation as the primary security mechanism; insufficient because once the design is discovered, all security evaporates
questions.option_c: Using obscure programming languages for security software; insufficient because all languages have vulnerabilities
questions.option_d: Encrypting data in an obscure format; insufficient because encryption alone isn't enough
questions.explanation: Security through obscurity: "no one will figure out how we did this." Problem: designs are reverse-engineered, insiders leak information, researchers discover the mechanism. When obscurity fails, ALL security fails. Proper security must remain secure even when the design is public (Kerckhoffs's Principle).

questions.statement: In the context of PKI, what does a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) contain?
questions.option_a: A list of expired certificates
questions.option_b: A list of certificates that have been revoked before their expiration date, due to compromise or other reasons
questions.option_c: A list of trusted Certificate Authorities
questions.option_d: A list of certificates pending renewal
questions.explanation: CRL: list of serial numbers of certificates that have been revoked (private key compromised, certificate incorrectly issued, owner identity changed). Browsers check CRL or use OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) before trusting a certificate. Revocation checking is critical — otherwise a stolen private key could still be used after the certificate should no longer be trusted.

questions.statement: Fileless malware is particularly dangerous because:
questions.option_a: It is invisible to human eyes in file directories
questions.option_b: It runs entirely in memory using legitimate OS tools, leaving no files on disk for traditional antivirus to detect
questions.option_c: It is immune to deletion by security software
questions.option_d: It corrupts file systems making files inaccessible
questions.explanation: Fileless malware: runs in memory only, uses legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI). Traditional antivirus that scans files finds nothing. Detection requires behavioral analysis, memory scanning, and monitoring of legitimate tool usage patterns. Increasingly common in sophisticated attacks.

questions.statement: What is the MAIN difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.option_a: Authentication is for systems; authorization is for people
questions.option_b: Authentication verifies identity (WHO are you?); authorization verifies permissions (WHAT can you do?)
questions.option_c: Authentication uses passwords; authorization uses certificates
questions.option_d: They are the same process with different names
questions.explanation: Authentication: prove your identity (username + password + MFA). Authorization: once you're authenticated, what are you allowed to do? Authenticated users might not be authorized for every action. These are separate, sequential steps — you can't authorize someone whose identity you haven't verified.

questions.statement: An SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) attack causes:
questions.option_a: The client's browser to make requests to unauthorized servers
questions.option_b: The server to make HTTP requests to unintended destinations controlled by the attacker
questions.option_c: Cross-server session sharing allowing horizontal privilege escalation
questions.option_d: Server log forgery to hide evidence of intrusion
questions.explanation: SSRF: attacker tricks the server into making HTTP requests to internal services not accessible from the internet. Classic attack: SSRF to reach AWS metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), retrieve IAM role credentials, use them to access S3 buckets. Capital One breach used this technique.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) as distinct from an IDS?
questions.option_a: IPS detects; IDS prevents
questions.option_b: IPS sits inline in network traffic and can BLOCK threats in real-time; IDS is out-of-band and only detects/alerts
questions.option_c: IPS protects against application layer attacks; IDS protects network layer
questions.option_d: They are identical — just different product names
questions.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System): out-of-band, monitors traffic passively, cannot block. Only detects and alerts. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): sits inline in the traffic path, can DROP malicious packets in real-time. IPS risk: false positives block legitimate traffic. IDS risk: real attacks get through while you're alerted.

questions.statement: Security "hardening" of a system involves:
questions.option_a: Installing the strongest available firewall
questions.option_b: Reducing the attack surface by removing unnecessary features, services, and permissions; applying security configurations
questions.option_c: Encrypting all data stored on the system
questions.option_d: Installing the latest OS and all updates
questions.explanation: Hardening: eliminate everything unnecessary. Each installed service, open port, and software package is a potential attack vector. Remove unused services. Close unused ports. Apply principle of least privilege. Change defaults. Apply CIS Benchmarks. The goal: minimize what can be attacked.

questions.statement: Which of the following best describes a "supply chain attack"?
questions.option_a: Physical theft of hardware from a company's supply chain
questions.option_b: Compromising software or hardware upstream (vendor, developer, update mechanism) to affect all downstream customers
questions.option_c: Attacking a company's inventory management system
questions.option_d: Disrupting physical supply chains through cyber means
questions.explanation: Supply chain attacks compromise the source — a trusted vendor's software, build system, or update mechanism. The attacker then reaches all customers of that vendor. Extremely powerful because victims trust the vendor. SolarWinds, Kaseya, NPM package compromises, Log4Shell (dependency) — all supply chain related.

questions.statement: What is the "kill chain" model in cyber security?
questions.option_a: A model for eliminating malware processes in the correct order
questions.option_b: Lockheed Martin's model describing the stages of a cyber attack: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, C2, Actions
questions.option_c: A supply chain attack methodology
questions.option_d: The sequence of events leading to a system shutdown
questions.explanation: Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin, 2011): Reconnaissance (gather info) → Weaponization (create malware) → Delivery (phishing, USB) → Exploitation (vulnerability triggered) → Installation (malware installed) → Command & Control (attacker connects) → Actions on Objectives (steal data, encrypt). Defenders can disrupt the kill chain at any stage — stopping the attack.

questions.statement: The Mitre ATT&CK framework provides:
questions.option_a: A certification framework for cyber security professionals
questions.option_b: A comprehensive knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used in real attacks
questions.option_c: A legal framework for attributing cyber attacks to nation states
questions.option_d: A technical standard for implementing access control systems
questions.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK: a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary TTPs based on real-world observations. Organized by tactics (Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, etc.) and techniques (specific methods). Used by defenders to assess detection coverage, threat hunting, and incident response.

questions.statement: What is "threat intelligence" in cyber security?
questions.option_a: The combined IQ of an organization's security team
questions.option_b: Evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats, including context, mechanisms, indicators, and implications
questions.option_c: Automated intelligence gathering from hacking tools
questions.option_d: Government intelligence reports about nation-state cyber capabilities
questions.explanation: Threat intelligence: actionable information about threats that helps organizations make better security decisions. Types: tactical (IOCs — IP addresses, hashes, domains), operational (campaign TTPs), strategic (trends, threat actors). Sources: commercial feeds, ISAC sharing, government advisories (CISA, CERT), open source (MISP, OTX).

questions.statement: An attacker gains access to an intern's account, then escalates to a senior administrator's account, then to domain admin. This is called:
questions.option_a: Vertical privilege escalation only
questions.option_b: Lateral movement followed by vertical privilege escalation
questions.option_c: Horizontal privilege escalation
questions.option_d: Role-based access violation
questions.explanation: Lateral movement: moving from one system/account to another at the same privilege level (intern account → another employee account). Vertical privilege escalation: gaining higher privileges (user → admin → domain admin). Most attacks involve both: compromise low-privilege account, laterally move to find a privileged path, escalate vertically.

questions.statement: What does "data exfiltration" mean in the context of a cyber attack?
questions.option_a: Encrypting data to prevent access
questions.option_b: Unauthorized transfer of data out of an organization's environment to an attacker-controlled location
questions.option_c: Deleting data to deny its use
questions.option_d: Corrupting data to make it unusable
questions.explanation: Exfiltration: the attacker TAKES data out. After gaining access, attackers collect valuable data (credentials, PII, trade secrets, financial data) and transfer it to their infrastructure. In double extortion ransomware: exfiltrate THEN encrypt. DLP (Data Loss Prevention) systems monitor for unusual data outflows.

questions.statement: What is "threat hunting"?
questions.option_a: Searching the dark web for stolen company data
questions.option_b: Proactively searching for signs of threats that have evaded automated detection
questions.option_c: Bug bounty programs that hunt for vulnerabilities
questions.option_d: Hiring penetration testers to hunt for weaknesses
questions.explanation: Threat hunting: security analysts proactively and iteratively search through networks and endpoints looking for malicious activity that has evaded existing automated detections. Starts with a hypothesis ("APT groups targeting our industry use this technique") and looks for evidence of that technique in log data. Complements reactive (alert-based) detection.

questions.statement: Which authentication factor is MOST resistant to phishing?
questions.option_a: SMS OTP
questions.option_b: TOTP (Google Authenticator)
questions.option_c: FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware security key
questions.option_d: Email OTP
questions.explanation: FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys (YubiKey): the cryptographic challenge response includes the domain of the website. If a phishing page at "hb1.com.pk" tries to get the user to authenticate, the security key refuses — the domain doesn't match the registered domain "hbl.com.pk". No credential to phish. SMS OTP and TOTP can be phished in real-time proxy attacks.

questions.statement: The NotPetya malware (2017) is distinguished from typical ransomware because:
questions.option_a: It demanded cryptocurrency payment through Tor
questions.option_b: It was actually a wiper — designed to destroy data with no functional decryption capability
questions.option_c: It specifically targeted government systems
questions.option_d: It was the first ransomware to use RSA encryption
questions.explanation: NotPetya: appeared to be ransomware but the decryption mechanism was broken by design. Victims could never recover their data regardless of payment. It was a destructive cyberweapon deployed by Russian intelligence (Sandworm). $10+ billion in global damage. Maersk had to rebuild its entire IT infrastructure. The "ransomware" disguise was cover for a nation-state destructive attack.

questions.statement: What does "separation of duties" prevent?
questions.option_a: Employees from multitasking on security-sensitive work
questions.option_b: A single person from having complete control over a critical process, requiring collusion for fraud
questions.option_c: Separation of security responsibilities between IT and security teams
questions.option_d: Developers from accessing production systems without separate credentials
questions.explanation: Separation of duties: divide critical tasks so no single person can complete fraud alone. A bank teller can initiate transactions but cannot approve AND modify audit logs. A developer can write code but cannot deploy AND approve the deployment. Fraud requires collusion between multiple people — much harder to execute and easier to detect.

questions.statement: In asymmetric cryptography, which operation uses the PRIVATE key?
questions.option_a: Encrypting a message to send to someone
questions.option_b: Verifying a digital signature
questions.option_c: Creating a digital signature (signing)
questions.option_d: Encrypting the session key
questions.explanation: Private key operations: signing (create signature others can verify) + decrypting (decrypt messages encrypted for you). Public key operations: verifying (verify signature) + encrypting (encrypt messages to send to private key holder). Remember: PRIVATE for signing and decryption. PUBLIC for verifying and encryption.

questions.statement: What is a "honeynet" in cyber security?
questions.option_a: A network sweetened with incentives to attract paying customers
questions.option_b: A decoy network of systems designed to lure and trap attackers, providing intelligence about attack methods
questions.option_c: A legitimate shared network between multiple security companies
questions.option_d: A network of security researchers sharing threat intelligence
questions.explanation: Honeynet: a network of honeypots (decoy systems). Appears to be a real network with valuable assets. Has no legitimate traffic. Any interaction is malicious. Captures attacker TTPs, tools, and objectives. Intelligence gathered is used to improve defenses. Advanced organizations run honeypots to detect insider threats and external reconnaissance.

questions.statement: Why is full-disk encryption important for laptops?
questions.option_a: It prevents unauthorized software installation
questions.option_b: If the laptop is stolen, the attacker cannot read the data even by removing and reading the hard drive on another system
questions.option_c: It prevents the laptop from connecting to untrusted WiFi networks
questions.option_d: It protects the laptop from malware attacks
questions.explanation: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS): encrypts all data on the drive. If a laptop is stolen, the thief cannot bypass the OS login by removing the drive — the data is encrypted with a key derived from the user's password (and typically tied to the TPM chip). Without the key, the data is unreadable even with physical access.

questions.statement: Which of the following is an example of a "logic bomb"?
questions.option_a: A bomb-making tutorial found in a dark web forum
questions.option_b: Malicious code that executes when a specific condition is met (e.g., a certain date, or the perpetrator's employee ID no longer appearing in the payroll database)
questions.option_c: A vulnerability in logical operators in programming languages
questions.option_d: An exploit that triggers when system load reaches capacity
questions.explanation: Logic bomb: malicious code dormant until a specific condition triggers it. An angry sysadmin plants code that deletes all databases if their username is removed from the employee database (they're fired → databases destroyed). Often planted by insiders. Typically not persistent like malware — it's already in the code.

questions.statement: What is "vishing"?
questions.option_a: Vulnerability scanning of critical infrastructure
questions.option_b: Voice phishing — phone calls impersonating legitimate entities to trick victims into revealing sensitive information
questions.option_c: Video-based phishing using deepfake technology
questions.option_d: Virtual server phishing targeting cloud environments
questions.explanation: Vishing (voice phishing): attackers call victims posing as bank fraud department, IRS, tech support, Microsoft, etc. Urgency and authority are used to pressure victims. Common: "Your account has been compromised, verify by providing your PIN/OTP." The Twitter hack began with a vishing call to a Twitter employee.

questions.statement: What is the primary benefit of a "bug bounty" program over traditional security testing?
questions.option_a: Bug bounties are free for the company
questions.option_b: Thousands of diverse external researchers with different skills and perspectives continuously test the application in real-world conditions
questions.option_c: Bug bounty findings are legally protected from disclosure
questions.option_d: Bug bounties eliminate the need for internal security teams
questions.explanation: Bug bounties: engage a global crowd of security researchers with varied specialties. Continuous testing (not one-time engagement). Aligned incentives (paid per valid bug found). Diverse perspectives find vulnerabilities internal teams miss. Cost-efficient: pay only for valid findings. Supplementary to (not replacement for) internal security.

questions.statement: When a certificate authority (CA) is compromised, what is the most serious consequence?
questions.option_a: All websites using that CA's certificates must pay for new certificates
questions.option_b: The attacker can issue fraudulent certificates for ANY domain, enabling undetectable MITM attacks
questions.option_c: All websites go offline until new certificates are issued
questions.option_d: Only websites hosted in the compromised CA's data center are affected
questions.explanation: Compromised CA: can issue fraudulent certificates. A certificate for "hbl.com.pk" signed by a compromised CA will be trusted by all browsers. Attacker could intercept ALL HTTPS traffic to that bank. This is why certificate transparency logs, CAA DNS records, and multi-CA validation exist. Notable: DigiNotar (Dutch CA) was compromised in 2011 — Google and other companies dropped DigiNotar trust immediately.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of DNSSEC?
questions.option_a: Encrypting DNS queries so ISPs can't see what domains you're resolving
questions.option_b: Adding cryptographic signatures to DNS records so resolvers can verify responses are authentic and unmodified
questions.option_c: Blocking malicious domains at the DNS level
questions.option_d: Providing private DNS resolution within corporate networks
questions.explanation: DNSSEC: digital signatures on DNS records. The domain owner signs their DNS records with a private key. Resolvers verify signatures with the public key. A DNS poisoning attack that injects false records would fail signature verification — the records would be rejected. DNSSEC prevents cache poisoning but doesn't encrypt DNS queries (DoH/DoT does that).

questions.statement: What is "pharming"?
questions.option_a: Large-scale phishing campaigns sent to agricultural businesses
questions.option_b: Corrupting DNS (cache poisoning or hosts file modification) to redirect users to malicious sites even when they type the correct URL
questions.option_c: Harvesting credentials from phishing attacks for later use
questions.option_d: Creating fake social media profiles to socially engineer targets
questions.explanation: Pharming: redirect legitimate domain requests to attacker's server. Methods: DNS cache poisoning (inject false DNS records), hosts file modification (malware modifies local hosts file), BGP hijacking (route traffic through attacker). User types the correct URL; gets the attacker's fake site. The URL bar shows the correct domain — very convincing.

questions.statement: A company discovers an unpatched critical vulnerability (CVSS 9.8) in their public-facing web application. They cannot patch it for 2 weeks due to testing requirements. The BEST interim mitigation is:
questions.option_a: Take the application offline for 2 weeks
questions.option_b: Deploy a WAF rule to block exploitation attempts for the specific vulnerability
questions.option_c: Notify all users to not use the application for 2 weeks
questions.option_d: Accept the risk and continue operating until patched
questions.explanation: Virtual patching via WAF: deploy a rule that blocks the specific attack pattern for this vulnerability. Not as good as a real patch (WAF rules can sometimes be bypassed) but dramatically reduces risk while the proper patch is being prepared. Also: increase monitoring for exploitation attempts, apply network-level controls to limit exposure.

questions.statement: What is the difference between "white hat," "black hat," and "grey hat" hackers?
questions.option_a: They use different programming languages
questions.option_b: White hat: authorized security testing; black hat: malicious, unauthorized; grey hat: finds vulnerabilities without authorization but discloses responsibly
questions.option_c: White hat: government; black hat: criminal; grey hat: corporate
questions.option_d: They refer to different levels of technical skill
questions.explanation: White hat: authorized penetration testers, security researchers — legal and ethical. Black hat: malicious attackers — illegal and unethical. Grey hat: may access systems without authorization but don't intend harm, often disclose vulnerabilities. Grey hat activities are still illegal (unauthorized access) even if well-intentioned. The lines between grey and black can be blurry legally.

questions.statement: Why is multi-factor authentication important even if strong passwords are used?
questions.option_a: Strong passwords can still be brute-forced with sufficient computing power
questions.option_b: Passwords can be phished, leaked in breaches, or compromised through credential stuffing without the attacker ever breaking the password
questions.option_c: MFA eliminates the need for strong passwords
questions.option_d: Regulatory compliance requires MFA regardless of password strength
questions.explanation: Even a perfect 30-character password is useless if: it's phished (user types it on a fake site), leaked in a database breach, harvested by malware. MFA's value isn't about password strength — it's that a second factor is required that the attacker typically doesn't have even if they have the password.

questions.statement: What is "credential harvesting" malware designed to do?
questions.option_a: Help users securely store and manage their passwords
questions.option_b: Steal login credentials from browsers, applications, and OS credential stores
questions.option_c: Generate strong credentials for system accounts
questions.option_d: Harvest biometric data for identity verification
questions.explanation: Credential harvesting: malware (infostealers like Redline Stealer, Raccoon) extracts saved passwords from browsers (Chrome, Firefox save encrypted passwords), email clients, VPN clients, and OS credential stores. The harvested credentials are exfiltrated to attacker infrastructure and sold on dark web markets or used for further attacks.

questions.statement: What does "data at rest" versus "data in transit" mean in encryption context?
questions.option_a: Data stored in RAM vs. data on hard drives
questions.option_b: Data stored in databases/files/drives (at rest) vs. data being transmitted over a network (in transit)
questions.option_c: Old archived data vs. recently modified data
questions.option_d: Encrypted data vs. plaintext data
questions.explanation: At rest: data stored on disk, in databases, in file shares, in cloud storage — must be encrypted (AES-256). In transit: data being transmitted over networks — must be encrypted (TLS/HTTPS). Both must be protected. Many organizations encrypt data in transit (HTTPS) but forget at rest — leaving database contents exposed if a server is compromised.

questions.statement: An organization's incident response team discovers a compromised server that is actively exfiltrating data. The FIRST action should be:
questions.option_a: Immediately shut down the server to stop the exfiltration
questions.option_b: Preserve evidence by imaging the server, then isolate it from the network while maintaining forensic integrity
questions.option_c: Continue monitoring without intervention to gather intelligence
questions.option_d: Reset the server's passwords and monitor for continued access
questions.explanation: Balance containment with evidence preservation. Isolate from network (stop exfiltration) but don't power off immediately (volatile evidence in RAM: running processes, network connections, encryption keys). Forensic image first if time permits. Isolation is preferable to complete shutdown — maintains ability to continue forensic analysis. IR plan should specify this procedure in advance.

questions.statement: The "assume breach" mentality in security means:
questions.option_a: Assume all employees are malicious insiders
questions.option_b: Design security controls as if attackers have already gained access, focusing on detection, containment, and minimizing blast radius
questions.option_c: Assume every security control will eventually fail
questions.option_d: Assume the worst-case scenario in risk assessments
questions.explanation: Assume breach: build defenses as if the perimeter has already been penetrated. Focus on: detecting attackers already inside, limiting what they can access (microsegmentation, least privilege), detecting lateral movement, responding quickly. This shifts from "keep attackers out" (increasingly impossible) to "limit damage when they get in."

questions.statement: What is the primary goal of a "cyber security awareness training" program?
questions.option_a: Teach employees to perform penetration testing
questions.option_b: Reduce human error as a security risk by educating employees about threats, safe practices, and their responsibilities
questions.option_c: Train employees to respond to security incidents independently
questions.option_d: Ensure regulatory compliance by documenting training hours
questions.explanation: Security awareness training: 95% of breaches involve human error. Training reduces susceptibility to phishing, social engineering, and unintentional security violations. Key topics: phishing recognition, safe browsing, password hygiene, physical security, incident reporting. Simulated phishing campaigns measure and improve effectiveness.

questions.statement: What makes "spear phishing" more effective than regular phishing?
questions.option_a: Uses better graphics and formatting
questions.option_b: Highly personalized content based on research about the specific target — references real colleagues, projects, and events to appear legitimate
questions.option_c: Sent from more convincing spoofed domains
questions.option_d: Targets higher-value individuals
questions.explanation: Spear phishing: targeted at a specific individual. Attacker researches the target via LinkedIn, company website, social media. Email references: real colleagues' names, recent company news, ongoing projects. Appears to come from a known contact. Success rate dramatically higher than generic phishing. CEO fraud (BEC) is a form of spear phishing.

questions.statement: What is "session hijacking" and how is it prevented?
questions.option_a: Hijacking browser tabs to redirect to malicious content; prevented by popup blockers
questions.option_b: Stealing a user's session token to impersonate them without knowing their password; prevented by HTTPOnly cookies, HTTPS, and session regeneration
questions.option_c: Capturing network sessions for forensic analysis; prevented by encryption
questions.option_d: Taking over dormant user sessions in shared computer labs; prevented by session timeout
questions.explanation: Session hijacking: steal the session cookie/token that proves you're authenticated. Attacker presents the stolen token to the server, which sees a valid token and authenticates the attacker as the legitimate user. Prevention: HTTPOnly cookies (JavaScript can't steal via XSS), HTTPS (encrypted in transit), short session timeouts, session binding to IP/user agent.

questions.statement: What is a "zero trust" network as opposed to a perimeter-based network?
questions.option_a: A network with no firewall or security controls, trusting all traffic
questions.option_b: A network where no device or user is inherently trusted based on network location — all access requires explicit authentication and authorization
questions.option_c: A network designed for testing that trusts no external connections
questions.option_d: An air-gapped network with zero internet connectivity
questions.explanation: Zero Trust: "never trust, always verify." Traditional perimeter: everything inside the firewall is trusted. Zero Trust: being inside the network grants no implicit trust. Every access request authenticated, authorized, encrypted, and logged regardless of origin. Necessary because: cloud, remote work, and mobile destroyed the traditional perimeter.

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a "purple team" in security exercises?
questions.option_a: A neutral team that mediates between red and blue teams
questions.option_b: A collaborative team combining red team (offensive) and blue team (defensive) to improve detection and response capabilities
questions.option_c: A specialized team focused exclusively on physical security
questions.option_d: The executive team that oversees security operations
questions.explanation: Purple team: red team (attackers) and blue team (defenders) work together rather than adversarially. Red team executes a technique → blue team attempts to detect it → both teams analyze gaps → improve detection → repeat. More efficient than traditional red team (which doesn't tell defenders what they did, leaving gaps unfixed).

questions.statement: A CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) provides:
questions.option_a: A secure gateway for employees to access public cloud services with visibility, control, and data security
questions.option_b: A certificate authority specifically for cloud certificate issuance
questions.option_c: Automatic security assessment of cloud configurations
questions.option_d: Cloud-based backup for security policies
questions.explanation: CASB: sits between users and cloud services (SaaS, IaaS). Provides: visibility (what cloud apps are in use, including "shadow IT"), data security (DLP in cloud), compliance (enforce policies), threat protection (detect anomalous access). Critical for enterprises with employees using many cloud services.

questions.statement: MD5 should NOT be used for:
questions.option_a: Checking file integrity against accidental corruption
questions.option_b: Non-security checksums
questions.option_c: Identifying known files in a database
questions.option_d: Security-sensitive hashing (passwords, digital signatures)
questions.explanation: Security-sensitive hashing (passwords, digital signatures). MD5 collisions are easily computable. Still acceptable for non-security checksums (file integrity where collision attacks aren't a threat model).

questions.statement: A "honeypot" is:
questions.option_a: A centralized logging server
questions.option_b: A decoy system designed to lure attackers and study their methods
questions.option_c: A password manager
questions.option_d: A type of malware
questions.explanation: A decoy system designed to lure attackers and study their methods.

questions.statement: AES operates in GCM mode to provide:
questions.option_a: Confidentiality only
questions.option_b: Integrity only
questions.option_c: Both confidentiality (encryption) AND integrity/authentication (authentication tag) — AEAD
questions.option_d: Key distribution
questions.explanation: Both confidentiality (encryption) AND integrity/authentication (authentication tag) — AEAD.

questions.statement: "Tailgating" in physical security means:
questions.option_a: Following an authorized person through a secured door without independently authenticating
questions.option_b: Using weak passwords
questions.option_c: Intercepting network traffic
questions.option_d: Leaving a workstation unlocked
questions.explanation: Following an authorized person through a secured door without independently authenticating.

questions.statement: OWASP stands for:
questions.option_a: Online Web Association of Security Professionals
questions.option_b: Open Web Application Security Project
questions.option_c: Open Wireless Authentication Security Protocol
questions.option_d: Organization for Web and Server Protection
questions.explanation: Open Web Application Security Project.

questions.statement: The main risk of using the same password across multiple sites is:
questions.option_a: Password expiration policies
questions.option_b: Forgetting the password
questions.option_c: Credential stuffing — if one site is breached, all accounts with that password are vulnerable
questions.option_d: Slower login times
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing — if one site is breached, all accounts with that password are vulnerable.

questions.statement: Wireshark is primarily used for:
questions.option_a: Antivirus scanning
questions.option_b: Network packet capture and analysis
questions.option_c: Password cracking
questions.option_d: Web application vulnerability scanning
questions.explanation: Network packet capture and analysis.

questions.statement: A "brute force" attack is:
questions.option_a: Systematically trying all possible values until the correct one is found
questions.option_b: Physically destroying a server
questions.option_c: Tricking a user via email
questions.option_d: Exploiting a software bug
questions.explanation: Systematically trying all possible values until the correct one is found.

questions.statement: HTTPS protects against which attack?
questions.option_a: SQL Injection
questions.option_b: Cross-Site Scripting
questions.option_c: Eavesdropping on network traffic (passive interception)
questions.option_d: Denial of Service
questions.explanation: Eavesdropping on network traffic (passive interception).

questions.statement: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault) primarily protects against:
questions.option_a: Network attacks
questions.option_b: Data theft when a physical device is stolen
questions.option_c: Malware infections
questions.option_d: Phishing emails
questions.explanation: Data theft when a physical device is stolen.

questions.statement: "Pretexting" is a social engineering technique that involves:
questions.option_a: Creating a fabricated scenario (pretext) to manipulate someone into providing information
questions.option_b: Sending malicious attachments
questions.option_c: Guessing passwords
questions.option_d: Bypassing physical security
questions.explanation: Creating a fabricated scenario (pretext) to manipulate someone into providing information.

questions.statement: A DLP (Data Loss Prevention) system monitors for:
questions.option_a: Hard drive failures
questions.option_b: Incoming malware
questions.option_c: Unauthorized transfer of sensitive data outside the organization
questions.option_d: Network outages
questions.explanation: Unauthorized transfer of sensitive data outside the organization.

questions.statement: "Privilege escalation" means:
questions.option_a: Updating user passwords
questions.option_b: Gaining higher system privileges than initially granted
questions.option_c: Granting access to new employees
questions.option_d: Encrypting sensitive files
questions.explanation: Gaining higher system privileges than initially granted.

questions.statement: ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) compared to RSA:
questions.option_a: Provides equivalent security with smaller key sizes, making it more efficient
questions.option_b: Requires much larger key sizes for the same security
questions.option_c: Is a symmetric encryption algorithm
questions.option_d: Is entirely obsolete
questions.explanation: Provides equivalent security with smaller key sizes, making it more efficient.

questions.statement: Log files should be protected from modification because:
questions.option_a: They take up too much disk space
questions.option_b: Attackers routinely delete or modify logs to hide evidence of intrusion
questions.option_c: They slow down the system
questions.option_d: They contain plaintext passwords
questions.explanation: Attackers routinely delete or modify logs to hide evidence of intrusion.

questions.statement: A "pass-the-hash" attack involves:
questions.option_a: Cracking the hash offline
questions.option_b: Intercepting the plaintext password
questions.option_c: Using a captured password hash directly for authentication without cracking it to plaintext
questions.option_d: Changing the hashing algorithm
questions.explanation: Using a captured password hash directly for authentication without cracking it to plaintext.

questions.statement: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is needed to:
questions.option_a: Encrypt hard drives
questions.option_b: Establish trust in public keys by having a trusted third party (CA) bind identities to public keys
questions.option_c: Manage symmetric keys
questions.option_d: Block network intrusions
questions.explanation: Establish trust in public keys by having a trusted third party (CA) bind identities to public keys.

questions.statement: NIST SP 800-61 is the standard for:
questions.option_a: Computer Security Incident Handling
questions.option_b: Cryptographic Algorithms
questions.option_c: Cloud Security
questions.option_d: Physical Access Control
questions.explanation: Computer Security Incident Handling.

questions.statement: Polymorphic malware is designed to:
questions.option_a: Corrupt databases
questions.option_b: Perform DDoS attacks
questions.option_c: Change its signature with each infection to evade signature-based detection
questions.option_d: Steal user passwords
questions.explanation: Change its signature with each infection to evade signature-based detection.

questions.statement: The "principle of complete mediation" requires:
questions.option_a: All data must be encrypted at rest
questions.option_b: Every access to every resource must be checked for authorization — no caching or bypassing of access control checks
questions.option_c: Networks must be segmented
questions.option_d: Users must change passwords every 30 days
questions.explanation: Every access to every resource must be checked for authorization — no caching or bypassing of access control checks.

questions.statement: What does the CIA triad stand for in information security?
questions.option_a: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
questions.option_b: Confidentiality, Identity, Authentication
questions.option_c: Control, Integrity, Authorization
questions.option_d: Compliance, Integrity, Availability
questions.explanation: The CIA triad represents the three core security objectives: Confidentiality (preventing unauthorized access), Integrity (ensuring data accuracy), and Availability (ensuring authorized access when needed).

questions.statement: A company encrypts data with a key that is the same for encryption and decryption. Which type of cryptography is being used?
questions.option_a: Asymmetric Key Cryptography
questions.option_b: Public Key Infrastructure
questions.option_c: Symmetric Key Cryptography
questions.option_d: Hash-based Cryptography
questions.explanation: Symmetric key cryptography uses the same secret key for both encryption and decryption. AES and DES are common examples. Asymmetric cryptography uses a mathematically related key pair (public and private).

questions.statement: What does RSA stand for in public-key cryptography?
questions.option_a: Rivest, Shamir, Adleman
questions.option_b: Random Substitution Algorithm
questions.option_c: Reliable Secure Authentication
questions.option_d: Recursive Secure Algorithm
questions.explanation: RSA stands for Rivest, Shamir, Adleman — the three inventors of the algorithm. The other options use the same initials but are fabricated names.

questions.statement: An attacker sends phishing emails pretending to be the company's IT department, asking employees to reset their passwords via a malicious link. Which attack category is this?
questions.option_a: SQL Injection
questions.option_b: Cross-Site Scripting
questions.option_c: Social Engineering
questions.option_d: Man-in-the-Middle Attack
questions.explanation: Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. Phishing is a form of social engineering where attackers impersonate trusted entities to trick users into divulging credentials.

questions.statement: In the context of public key cryptography, if Alice wants to send Bob a confidential message, which key does she use to encrypt it?
questions.option_a: Alice's private key
questions.option_b: Alice's public key
questions.option_c: Bob's private key
questions.option_d: Bob's public key
questions.explanation: To send a confidential message to Bob, Alice encrypts with Bob's public key. Only Bob's paired private key can decrypt it. Encrypting with Alice's private key would create a digital signature, not confidentiality.

questions.statement: What does 'AES' stand for, and what is its key feature?
questions.option_a: Advanced Encryption Standard — a symmetric block cipher with key sizes of 128, 192, or 256 bits
questions.option_b: Advanced Encryption Standard — an asymmetric cipher using public-private key pairs
questions.option_c: Authenticated Encryption System — a protocol combining encryption with authentication
questions.option_d: Automatic Encryption Service — a cloud-based encryption key management system
questions.explanation: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher operating on 128-bit blocks with key sizes of 128, 192, or 256 bits. It replaced DES and is the current NIST-approved standard for symmetric encryption.

questions.statement: A penetration tester has no prior knowledge of the target system's architecture or defenses. Which type of penetration test is this?
questions.option_a: White-box testing
questions.option_b: Gray-box testing
questions.option_c: Black-box testing
questions.option_d: Red team assessment
questions.explanation: Black-box testing gives the tester no prior information about the target, simulating an external attacker's perspective. White-box provides full knowledge; gray-box provides partial knowledge.

questions.statement: In network security, what does a 'stateful firewall' do that a packet filter firewall cannot?
questions.option_a: It inspects and decrypts HTTPS traffic for malware detection
questions.option_b: It tracks the state of network connections and allows only legitimate traffic in established sessions
questions.option_c: It blocks traffic based on application-layer content like URLs and keywords
questions.option_d: It physically isolates network segments using dedicated hardware switches
questions.explanation: A stateful firewall maintains a connection state table. It tracks TCP handshakes and ensures only packets belonging to established connections are allowed, blocking unsolicited inbound packets. Packet filters only check individual packet headers.

questions.statement: What does 'SQL injection' allow an attacker to do?
questions.option_a: Inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users
questions.option_b: Manipulate database queries by inserting malicious SQL code through input fields
questions.option_c: Intercept network traffic between a user and web server
questions.option_d: Exploit a buffer overflow in the web server's SQL driver
questions.explanation: SQL injection inserts malicious SQL syntax into application input fields. If the application concatenates input into SQL queries, attackers can modify query logic to bypass authentication, extract data, or destroy the database.

questions.statement: In cryptography, what is the purpose of a 'hash function' like SHA-256?
questions.option_a: To encrypt data so that it can be later decrypted with the correct key
questions.option_b: To produce a fixed-size digest of arbitrary input that cannot be reversed
questions.option_c: To generate a symmetric key from a user-provided password
questions.option_d: To sign digital documents with a sender's private key
questions.explanation: A cryptographic hash function produces a fixed-size output (digest) from any input, and is computationally infeasible to reverse (one-way). It is used for integrity verification, password storage, and digital signatures.

questions.statement: A developer discovers that a web application directly includes user input in a system command without sanitization. Which vulnerability class does this represent?
questions.option_a: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
questions.option_b: XML External Entity Injection (XXE)
questions.option_c: Command Injection (OS Command Injection)
questions.option_d: Insecure Deserialization
questions.explanation: Command injection occurs when user input is embedded in OS commands without sanitization. An attacker can inject additional commands (e.g., '; rm -rf /') that execute on the server with the application's OS privileges.

questions.statement: What does 'XSS' stand for, and what is the primary risk it poses?
questions.option_a: Cross-Site Scripting — allows attackers to inject malicious scripts executed in victims' browsers
questions.option_b: XML Server Scripting — allows attackers to access server-side XML data
questions.option_c: Cross-Server Synchronization — allows attackers to sync data between multiple servers
questions.option_d: Exclusive Security Scanning — a vulnerability scanning technique for web applications
questions.explanation: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) injects malicious scripts into web pages that are executed by victims' browsers. Attackers can steal cookies/session tokens, redirect users, or perform actions on their behalf.

questions.statement: In the context of digital forensics, which principle states that the forensic investigator's actions should not alter the original evidence?
questions.option_a: Chain of Custody
questions.option_b: Locard's Exchange Principle
questions.option_c: Integrity Principle
questions.option_d: Evidence Preservation Principle
