questions.explanation: Lost Update: both transactions read the same value, both write back, one update overwrites the other and is lost.

questions.statement: In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), during the shrinking phase, a transaction:
questions.option_a: Can acquire new locks and release old ones freely
questions.option_b: Can only acquire new locks
questions.option_c: Can only release locks — cannot acquire new ones
questions.option_d: Must acquire all locks before any operation
questions.explanation: In 2PL's shrinking phase, ONLY lock releases are allowed. No new locks can be acquired.

questions.statement: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but allows unrepeatable reads?
questions.option_a: Read Uncommitted
questions.option_b: Read Committed
questions.option_c: Repeatable Read
questions.option_d: Serializable
questions.explanation: Read Committed prevents dirty reads (only sees committed data) but allows unrepeatable reads (data can change between reads within a transaction).

questions.statement: Which ACID property ensures that committed transactions survive system crashes?
questions.option_a: Atomicity
questions.option_b: Consistency
questions.option_c: Isolation
questions.option_d: Durability
questions.explanation: Durability ensures committed changes are permanent, surviving even power failures.

questions.statement: A shared lock (S-lock) allows:
questions.option_a: Only one transaction to read at a time
questions.option_b: Multiple transactions to read simultaneously, but no writes
questions.option_c: One transaction to read and write exclusively
questions.option_d: No access — it's a blocking lock
questions.explanation: Shared locks allow concurrent reads. Exclusive locks block all other access.

questions.statement: Which isolation level completely prevents dirty reads, unrepeatable reads, AND phantom reads?
questions.option_a: Read Uncommitted
questions.option_b: Read Committed
questions.option_c: Repeatable Read
questions.option_d: Serializable
questions.explanation: Serializable is the highest isolation level — prevents all three concurrency problems. Slowest but safest.

questions.statement: In a transaction log, <T1, A, 5000, 3000> means:
questions.option_a: Transaction T1 read value 5000 from attribute A and expected 3000
questions.option_b: Transaction T1 changed attribute A from 5000 to 3000
questions.option_c: Transaction T1 will change A to 5000 after 3000 milliseconds
questions.option_d: Transaction T1 is the 5000th transaction, on attribute A with value 3000
questions.explanation: Log format: <TransactionID, DataItem, OldValue, NewValue>. So T1 changed A from 5000 to 3000.

questions.statement: Which operation does the recovery manager perform for transactions that were COMMITTED but whose changes may not have been written to disk before a crash?
questions.option_a: UNDO
questions.option_b: REDO
questions.option_c: ROLLBACK
questions.option_d: ABORT
questions.explanation: REDO re-applies committed transactions that may not have been flushed to disk. UNDO reverses uncommitted transactions.

questions.statement: The purpose of a checkpoint in database recovery is to:
questions.option_a: Create a full database backup
questions.option_b: Limit how far back the recovery process needs to scan the log
questions.option_c: Lock the database for exclusive access
questions.option_d: Commit all pending transactions
questions.explanation: Checkpoints flush in-memory changes to disk and mark a point in the log. Recovery only needs to scan from the last checkpoint forward.

questions.statement: The transaction state "Partially Committed" means:
questions.option_a: Half of the transaction's SQL statements have executed
questions.option_b: The final SQL statement has executed but changes aren't yet on disk
questions.option_c: The transaction was committed but then rolled back
questions.option_d: Only some ACID properties are satisfied
questions.explanation: Partially committed: all SQL statements done, changes in memory buffer — waiting to be flushed to disk. Still vulnerable to failure before full commit.

questions.statement: Which index type stores ALL data pointers at the leaf level with leaves linked together?
questions.option_a: B-Tree index
questions.option_b: B+ Tree index
questions.option_c: Dense index
questions.option_d: Hash index
questions.explanation: B+ Tree stores data only at leaves (linked), making range queries very efficient. B-Tree stores data at all levels.

questions.statement: A clustered index means:
questions.option_a: Multiple indexes are grouped together
questions.option_b: Physical row order on disk matches the index order
questions.option_c: The index is stored in a separate cluster from the data
questions.option_d: Related tables share the same index
questions.explanation: Clustered index: the actual table data is physically ordered according to the index key.

questions.statement: How many clustered indexes can a table have?
questions.option_a: Unlimited
questions.option_b: One per column
questions.option_c: Exactly one
questions.option_d: Maximum of three
questions.explanation: Only ONE clustered index per table — because physical row order can only be in one sequence.

questions.statement: The EXPLAIN command in SQL is used to:
questions.option_a: Add explanatory comments to a query
questions.option_b: View the query execution plan chosen by the optimizer
questions.option_c: Explain the meaning of a column name
questions.option_d: Document stored procedures
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN shows how the database plans to execute a query — whether it uses index or full scan, join order, estimated rows.

questions.statement: Which file organization is best for exact-match searches (finding a specific record by key)?
questions.option_a: Heap file organization
questions.option_b: Sequential file organization
questions.option_c: Hashed file organization
questions.option_d: Indexed file organization
questions.explanation: Hashed organization computes the record location directly from the key value — O(1) exact match. But terrible for range queries.

questions.statement: In query optimization, applying the selection (WHERE) operation as early as possible is beneficial because:
questions.option_a: It increases the number of rows for subsequent operations
questions.option_b: It reduces the size of intermediate results, making subsequent operations faster
questions.option_c: It always uses an index
questions.option_d: It reduces the number of attributes in the result
questions.explanation: Applying selection early reduces data volume that subsequent operations (joins, projections) need to process.

questions.statement: A dense index has an entry for:
questions.option_a: Every block/page of data
questions.option_b: Every record in the data file
questions.option_c: Only the first record of each block
questions.option_d: Only unique key values
questions.explanation: Dense index: one index entry per record. Sparse index: one entry per block/page.

questions.statement: Which index type does MySQL InnoDB use for its primary key by default?
questions.option_a: Hash index
questions.option_b: Bitmap index
questions.option_c: B+ Tree index
questions.option_d: Full-text index
questions.explanation: InnoDB uses B+ Tree for its clustered primary key index (and all secondary indexes). The table data IS the B+ Tree.

questions.statement: According to the CAP theorem, a distributed system can simultaneously guarantee only:
questions.option_a: All three: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
questions.option_b: Any two of the three properties
questions.option_c: Only Consistency and Availability
questions.option_d: Only Partition Tolerance
questions.explanation: CAP theorem: you can only guarantee 2 of 3. Since partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, the real choice is CP or AP.

questions.statement: A banking system that becomes temporarily unavailable during a network partition rather than returning potentially incorrect balance data is choosing:
questions.option_a: AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance)
questions.option_b: CA (Consistency + Availability)
questions.option_c: CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance)
questions.option_d: CAP (all three)
questions.explanation: CP: consistency is prioritized. Better to be unavailable ("service down") than show wrong balance.

questions.statement: MongoDB is a:
questions.option_a: Key-Value database
questions.option_b: Document database
questions.option_c: Column-family database
questions.option_d: Graph database
questions.explanation: MongoDB stores data as JSON-like documents (BSON format). Primary document database.

questions.statement: Redis is primarily used for:
questions.option_a: Storing complex relational data
questions.option_b: Graph traversal queries
questions.option_c: Caching and session management (key-value store)
questions.option_d: Time-series data analytics
questions.explanation: Redis is an in-memory key-value store, excellent for caching (sessions, hot data, counters, leaderboards).

questions.statement: Which NoSQL database type is BEST suited for a social network's friendship/connection data?
questions.option_a: Document database (MongoDB)
questions.option_b: Key-Value database (Redis)
questions.option_c: Column-family database (Cassandra)
questions.option_d: Graph database (Neo4j)
questions.explanation: Graph databases store nodes (users) and edges (friendships), making relationship traversal (friends-of-friends) extremely efficient.

questions.statement: The "E" in BASE (Eventually Consistent) means:
questions.option_a: All nodes have consistent data at all times
questions.option_b: The system will reach a consistent state eventually, though not immediately
questions.option_c: Each transaction is immediately consistent
questions.option_d: External consistency is guaranteed
questions.explanation: Eventually consistent: after updates stop, the system will converge to a consistent state, but intermediate states may differ across nodes.

questions.statement: Horizontal fragmentation in a distributed database means:
questions.option_a: Splitting a table by columns across different sites
questions.option_b: Splitting a table by rows across different sites
questions.option_c: Replicating all data at every site
questions.option_d: Compressing data horizontally
questions.explanation: Horizontal fragmentation splits by rows (e.g., customers in Karachi to one server, Lahore to another). Vertical splits by columns.

questions.statement: In the Two-Phase Commit Protocol (2PC), if ANY participant responds "NO" in Phase 1:
questions.option_a: Only that participant rolls back, others commit
questions.option_b: All participants rollback
questions.option_c: The coordinator retries the transaction
questions.option_d: The transaction waits indefinitely
questions.explanation: 2PC: unanimous YES needed to commit. Any NO → ALL participants must rollback.

questions.statement: Cassandra (column-family database) is classified as which CAP combination?
questions.option_a: CP
questions.option_b: CA
questions.option_c: AP
questions.option_d: CAP
questions.explanation: Cassandra prioritizes Availability and Partition Tolerance (AP). It allows eventual consistency, making it suitable for Netflix, social media, IoT data.

questions.statement: Which SQL statement best represents "Eventual Consistency" in a NoSQL context?
questions.option_a: BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT
questions.option_b: Synchronized replication across all nodes before acknowledging write
questions.option_c: Write acknowledged immediately, changes propagate to replicas asynchronously
questions.option_d: SERIALIZABLE isolation level
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency: write is acknowledged fast, but replicas are updated asynchronously. Different nodes may temporarily have different data.

questions.statement: OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) differs from OLTP primarily in that OLAP:
questions.option_a: Handles real-time transactions like sales and orders
questions.option_b: Is optimized for complex analysis on large historical datasets
questions.option_c: Uses highly normalized schemas for data integrity
questions.option_d: Serves thousands of concurrent end-users making small changes
questions.explanation: OLAP is for analytics (complex queries on historical data). OLTP is for day-to-day transactions (fast, simple operations).

questions.statement: In a Star Schema, the Fact Table contains:
questions.option_a: Descriptive information like product names and customer addresses
questions.option_b: Numeric, measurable data (revenue, quantity, counts)
questions.option_c: The primary keys of all dimension tables only
questions.option_d: Historical snapshots of dimension data
questions.explanation: Fact Table stores measurable business metrics (sales, revenue, quantity). Dimension Tables store descriptive attributes.

questions.statement: The "T" in ETL stands for:
questions.option_a: Transfer
questions.option_b: Truncate
questions.option_c: Transform
questions.option_d: Test
questions.explanation: ETL: Extract (from source), Transform (clean/standardize), Load (into data warehouse).

questions.statement: Which data mining technique groups similar customers together WITHOUT predefined categories?
questions.option_a: Classification
questions.option_b: Clustering
questions.option_c: Association Rule Mining
questions.option_d: Regression
questions.explanation: Clustering is unsupervised — finds natural groupings without predefined labels. Classification uses predefined categories.

questions.statement: The famous "beer and diapers" discovery is an example of:
questions.option_a: Classification
questions.option_b: Clustering
questions.option_c: Association Rule Mining
questions.option_d: Regression
questions.explanation: Association rules discover "if X then Y" patterns in purchase data.

questions.statement: SQL Injection can BEST be prevented by:
questions.option_a: Encrypting all database columns
questions.option_b: Using prepared statements (parameterized queries)
questions.option_c: Implementing a firewall
questions.option_d: Hashing user passwords
questions.explanation: Prepared statements separate SQL code from user data, making injection impossible. The user input is treated as pure data, never executed as SQL.

questions.statement: A Snowflake Schema differs from a Star Schema in that:
questions.option_a: It has no Fact Table
questions.option_b: Dimension tables are normalized into sub-dimension tables
questions.option_c: All data is stored in a single large table
questions.option_d: It only supports OLTP workloads
questions.explanation: Snowflake Schema normalizes dimensions (e.g., Product → Category → Department), reducing redundancy but requiring more joins.

questions.statement: Which property of a Data Warehouse means it stores data accumulated over many years and never deletes historical records?
questions.option_a: Subject-Oriented
questions.option_b: Integrated
questions.option_c: Non-Volatile
questions.option_d: Time-Variant
questions.explanation: Non-volatile: data is loaded and read, but rarely modified or deleted. Historical records are preserved permanently.

questions.statement: Which of the following is an example of a WELL-STRUCTURED problem?
questions.option_a: How can Pakistan improve its education system?
questions.option_b: Find all prime numbers less than 100
questions.option_c: What is the best career path?
questions.option_d: How should a company respond to a PR crisis?
questions.explanation: Finding primes < 100 has a clear starting state (all integers from 2-99), clear goal (identify primes), and clear verification method. A, C, and D have vague goals, contested criteria, and no single correct answer — ill-structured.

questions.statement: Polya's problem-solving framework lists "Looking Back" as the final step. The PRIMARY purpose of this step is:
questions.option_a: Checking that your arithmetic is correct
questions.option_b: Learning from the solution process to improve future problem-solving abilities
questions.option_c: Reviewing the problem statement one more time
questions.option_d: Getting feedback from a supervisor
questions.explanation: "Looking Back" is about reflection and learning: Can you verify the result? Can you derive it differently? Can you use the result for other problems? It's the meta-learning step that converts problem-solving into expertise over time.

questions.statement: A developer receives a bug report saying "the app crashes." The MOST important first step is:
questions.option_a: Immediately look at the database logs
questions.option_b: Restart the server
questions.option_c: Ask clarifying questions: when, for whom, on what device, with what action
questions.option_d: Check if the same issue exists in production
questions.explanation: "The app crashes" is insufficient to diagnose anything. Clarifying questions establish the current state precisely. Without specifics (what action triggers it, which user, which device, which error message), any debugging effort is guesswork.

questions.statement: The "5 Whys" technique is primarily used for:
questions.option_a: Generating five alternative solutions to a problem
questions.option_b: Finding the root cause of a problem by repeatedly asking why the problem occurred
questions.option_c: Scoring solutions on five criteria
questions.option_d: Interviewing five stakeholders to understand requirements
questions.explanation: 5 Whys: ask "Why did this problem occur?" five times, each answer becoming the subject of the next "why." This iterative questioning uncovers root causes rather than symptoms.

questions.statement: Which of the following BEST demonstrates "problem reframing"?
questions.option_a: Solving a problem using a different programming language
questions.option_b: An elevator company adding mirrors to the lobby instead of installing faster elevators to address tenant complaints
questions.option_c: Asking more detailed questions about requirements
questions.option_d: Decomposing a large problem into smaller subproblems
questions.explanation: Reframing changes the fundamental question. Instead of "how do we make the elevator faster?" (the stated problem), the question becomes "why do tenants complain?" (the real problem). The mirror solution addresses the real problem (boredom while waiting) without solving the stated problem (elevator speed).

questions.statement: In root cause analysis, the difference between a SYMPTOM and a ROOT CAUSE is:
questions.option_a: Symptoms are technical; root causes are organizational
questions.option_b: Fixing a symptom provides temporary relief; fixing the root cause prevents recurrence
questions.option_c: Root causes are always hardware-related; symptoms are always software-related
questions.option_d: There is no meaningful difference — they are the same thing
questions.explanation: A symptom is the observable problem. The root cause is the underlying reason. Fixing the symptom (restarting a crashing server) provides temporary relief. Fixing the root cause (memory leak in code) prevents the crash from recurring.

questions.statement: When analyzing constraints for a problem, "soft constraints" are:
questions.option_a: Security constraints that can be bypassed
questions.option_b: Constraints on memory usage only
questions.option_c: Preferences that can be traded off — violated if necessary to satisfy hard constraints
questions.option_d: Constraints that are easy to implement
questions.explanation: Hard constraints: non-negotiable (must be satisfied). Soft constraints: preferences (should be satisfied if possible). "System must handle 10,000 users" — hard. "Response time should be under 1 second" — soft (1.5 seconds might be acceptable).

questions.statement: A problem statement says: "We need a better website." This is poor because it is:
questions.option_a: Too technical
questions.option_b: Not written in English
questions.option_c: Vague, unmeasurable, and doesn't specify current state, desired state, or success criteria
questions.option_d: Too long
questions.explanation: A good problem statement is specific, measurable, and defines current state, desired state, and success criteria. "Better" is not measurable. There's no indication of what's wrong with the current site, what "better" means quantitatively, or how we'd know when we've succeeded.

questions.statement: Decomposing a large problem into smaller sub-problems is most directly an example of which problem-solving approach?
questions.option_a: Pattern recognition
questions.option_b: Abstraction
questions.option_c: Divide and conquer / decomposition
questions.option_d: Inductive reasoning
questions.explanation: Decomposition directly corresponds to the divide and conquer approach: break the large problem into manageable sub-problems, solve each, combine solutions. This is fundamental to both algorithm design and software engineering.

questions.statement: The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because one team used metric units and another used imperial units. This failure is BEST categorized as:
questions.option_a: A hardware failure
questions.option_b: A requirements/specification mismatch — a problem understanding failure
questions.option_c: A software bug
questions.option_d: An operator error
questions.explanation: The root cause was a failure to clearly specify units in the interface definition. Both teams were correct given their own assumptions. The problem was in the specification/communication of requirements — a problem understanding failure, not a technical one.

questions.statement: Which approach is MOST useful when the problem is ill-structured and the goal is unclear?
questions.option_a: Jumping directly to implementation
questions.option_b: Stakeholder interviews, requirements workshops, and prototyping to clarify the goal
questions.option_c: Using the fastest available algorithm
questions.option_d: Finding a similar solved problem and copying the solution
questions.explanation: For ill-structured problems, the first task is to structure them — clarify the goal through stakeholder engagement. Interviews uncover different perspectives. Workshops resolve conflicts. Prototypes make abstract goals concrete and reveal misunderstandings early.

questions.statement: Sensitivity analysis in decision-making asks:
questions.option_a: Whether a decision is ethically sensitive
questions.option_b: How much the optimal decision changes if the assumptions underlying it change
questions.option_c: How sensitive the stakeholders are to the proposed changes
questions.option_d: Whether the system is sensitive to security attacks
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis: "What if our assumptions are wrong by 10%? 20%? Does the decision change?" If a decision only works under a narrow range of assumptions, it's fragile. If it holds across a wide range, it's robust.

questions.statement: The IDEAL problem-solving framework stands for:
questions.option_a: Identify, Design, Execute, Assess, Launch
questions.option_b: Investigate, Develop, Evaluate, Apply, Learn
questions.option_c: Identify, Define, Explore, Act, Look and evaluate
questions.option_d: Initiate, Determine, Experiment, Analyze, Log
questions.explanation: IDEAL (Bransford & Stein): Identify the problem, Define and represent it, Explore possible strategies, Act on strategies, Look back and evaluate. A systematic framework complementing Polya's approach.

questions.statement: "The XY Problem" in technical support refers to:
questions.option_a: Confusion between X-axis and Y-axis in data visualization
questions.option_b: Users asking for help with their attempted solution (Y) instead of their actual underlying problem (X)
questions.option_c: A problem involving two variables X and Y
questions.option_d: An unknown problem where neither X nor Y is identified
questions.explanation: The XY problem: user has problem X, tries solution Y, asks "how do I do Y?" The real answer might be "Y isn't the right approach to X; here's a better solution." Always ask "what are you ultimately trying to accomplish?" before answering the literal question.

questions.statement: When performing functional decomposition of a system, you should:
questions.option_a: Decompose based on who will implement each part
questions.option_b: Break the system into modules based on distinct functions/responsibilities
questions.option_c: Decompose based on the time required for each part
questions.option_d: Always create exactly five sub-problems
questions.explanation: Functional decomposition divides by function/responsibility: authentication module, payment module, notification module, etc. Each module has a clear, distinct function. This aligns with the Single Responsibility Principle and makes systems understandable and maintainable.

questions.statement: A problem has a known starting state, known goal state, but the path is unclear. This is:
questions.option_a: An ill-structured problem because the path is unknown
questions.option_b: A well-structured problem — the path is found through problem-solving
questions.option_c: An unsolvable problem
questions.option_d: An algorithmic problem requiring only computation
questions.explanation: Well-structured problems have defined start and goal states. The challenge is finding the path — that's what problem-solving is! The path doesn't need to be obvious at the start; it needs to be findable through systematic analysis.

questions.statement: Which of the following demonstrates the BEST application of "first principles thinking"?
questions.option_a: "We should use React because all modern companies use React"
questions.option_b: "What do we actually need? Real-time updates for 100 users. Does that require React, or would server-sent events suffice?"
questions.option_c: "Let's copy how Company X solved this problem"
questions.option_d: "The industry standard says to use microservices"
questions.explanation: First principles: break down to fundamental truths and reason from there. Instead of relying on convention ("React is what modern companies use"), we ask "what do we fundamentally need?" and reason from that. This often reveals simpler, better-fitting solutions.

questions.statement: In a requirements meeting, a stakeholder says "the system should be fast." The BEST follow-up action is:
questions.option_a: Accept "fast" as a requirement and prioritize performance
questions.option_b: Ask "how fast? What's the acceptable response time for which operations under what load?"
questions.option_c: Explain that "fast" is a non-functional requirement and will be addressed later
questions.option_d: Benchmark the current system and set a 20% improvement target
questions.explanation: "Fast" is unmeasurable. Convert to specific, measurable, testable requirements: "Search queries must return within 2 seconds for 95% of requests with up to 10,000 concurrent users." This can be tested, designed for, and verified.

questions.statement: The key difference between "hard constraints" and "soft constraints" in problem-solving is:
questions.option_a: Hard constraints come from hardware limitations; soft constraints from software
questions.option_b: Hard constraints must be satisfied; soft constraints are preferences that can be violated if necessary
questions.option_c: Hard constraints are well-understood; soft constraints are ambiguous
questions.option_d: Hard constraints apply to all users; soft constraints apply to specific users
questions.explanation: Hard: non-negotiable, solution invalid if violated. Soft: preferences, can be traded off. "Data must not be lost during a crash" = hard. "Dark mode should be available" = soft. Misidentifying hard as soft (or vice versa) leads to wrong design decisions.

questions.statement: Which problem-solving step does "draw a diagram, introduce suitable notation" belong to?
questions.option_a: Devise a plan
questions.option_b: Carry out the plan
questions.option_c: Look back
questions.option_d: Understand the problem
questions.explanation: In Polya's framework, drawing a diagram and introducing notation are part of UNDERSTANDING the problem. These activities force precise thinking about the problem's elements, constraints, and relationships before attempting to solve it.

questions.statement: An e-commerce company notices their checkout page has a 70% abandonment rate. The MOST appropriate first step in addressing this is:
questions.option_a: Redesign the checkout page immediately
questions.option_b: Add more payment options
questions.option_c: Analyze data to understand WHERE in checkout users leave and WHY
questions.option_d: Reduce the price of products
questions.explanation: Before implementing solutions, understand the problem precisely. Data analysis might reveal abandonment happens at the "shipping cost revealed" step (suggesting fee transparency or free shipping threshold), or at "create account required" (suggesting guest checkout), or at "too many form fields" (suggesting form simplification). The solution depends entirely on the root cause.

questions.statement: Scenario: A software team consistently misses deadlines. Using the "5 Whys," a probable root cause would be discovered after asking:
questions.option_a: Why is the team slow?
questions.option_b: A series of five iterative "why" questions that might reveal: no accurate estimation process, unclear requirements causing rework, missing skills needing training, or unclear priorities
questions.option_c: Why didn't the team work overtime?
questions.option_d: Why was the deadline set too early?
questions.explanation: The 5 Whys is an iterative process. Each answer becomes the subject of the next "why." For deadline misses: Why miss deadlines? → Underestimated effort. Why underestimate? → No historical data on similar tasks. Why no historical data? → No time-tracking system. Why no time tracking? → Never prioritized it. Root cause: Missing time-tracking system.

questions.statement: A project has a tight deadline (1 week) and limited budget (2 developers). The scope includes 50 features. The BEST problem-solving approach is:
questions.option_a: Work 80-hour weeks to complete all 50 features
questions.option_b: Prioritize: deliver the most critical features first (MVP), defer others
questions.option_c: Request a budget increase to hire 10 more developers
questions.option_d: Cancel the project as it's impossible
questions.explanation: The triple constraint (scope, schedule, budget) means something must give. With fixed schedule and budget, scope must be reduced. The answer is prioritization: identify the minimal viable product (MVP) — the features that deliver core value — and deliver those. Additional features can follow.

questions.statement: The Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram categorizes potential causes of a problem into:
questions.option_a: Fast causes and slow causes
questions.option_b: Hardware and software causes
questions.option_c: Major categories (e.g., People, Process, Technology, Environment) with sub-causes branching off each
questions.option_d: Root causes and proximate causes
questions.explanation: The Fishbone diagram: the "head" is the problem (effect). "Bones" are categories of causes (for manufacturing: 6Ms; for software/service: People, Process, Technology, Environment). Causes and sub-causes branch off each bone. Visualizes the entire landscape of potential causes systematically.

questions.statement: Problem reframing is MOST valuable when:
questions.option_a: The problem is simple and well-defined
questions.option_b: The obvious solutions to the stated problem haven't worked or seem too expensive
questions.option_c: Stakeholders are in agreement about the problem
questions.option_d: The technical implementation is straightforward
questions.explanation: Reframing is most needed when conventional thinking is stuck. If all obvious solutions to "how do we make the elevator faster?" are too expensive, questioning the problem itself ("what is the real complaint?") can reveal entirely different solution spaces.

questions.statement: Which argument form is VALID?
questions.option_a: If P then Q; Q is true; therefore P is true
questions.option_b: If P then Q; P is false; therefore Q is false
questions.option_c: If P then Q; P is true; therefore Q is true
questions.option_d: If P then Q; Q is false; therefore P might be true
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens: If P→Q and P is true, then Q MUST be true. This is the fundamental valid deductive argument form. Options A (affirming the consequent) and B (denying the antecedent) are both INVALID fallacies.

questions.statement: The statement "NOT (A AND B)" is logically equivalent to:
questions.option_a: NOT A AND NOT B
questions.option_b: NOT A OR NOT B
questions.option_c: A OR B
questions.option_d: NOT A AND B
questions.explanation: De Morgan's First Law: ¬(A ∧ B) ≡ ¬A ∨ ¬B. When negation distributes inside parentheses, AND becomes OR (and OR becomes AND). Essential for simplifying logical expressions and understanding equivalent conditions in code.

questions.statement: In boolean algebra, which expression evaluates to TRUE when X = FALSE and Y = TRUE?
questions.option_a: X AND Y
questions.option_b: X AND NOT Y
questions.option_c: NOT X AND Y
questions.option_d: NOT X AND NOT Y
questions.explanation: NOT X = NOT FALSE = TRUE. Y = TRUE. TRUE AND TRUE = TRUE. Let's check others: A: FALSE AND TRUE = FALSE. B: FALSE AND FALSE = FALSE. D: TRUE AND FALSE = FALSE.

questions.statement: The truth table for the IMPLICATION (P → Q) shows that P → Q is FALSE only when:
questions.option_a: P is TRUE and Q is TRUE
questions.option_b: P is FALSE and Q is FALSE
questions.option_c: P is TRUE and Q is FALSE
questions.option_d: P is FALSE and Q is TRUE
questions.explanation: P → Q ("If P then Q") is only violated when P is true but Q is false. If I say "If it rains, I'll carry an umbrella" — I only lied if it rained (P=T) and I didn't carry an umbrella (Q=F). All other cases (no rain, or rain + umbrella) are consistent.

questions.statement: The number 42 in hexadecimal is:
questions.option_b: 0x2A
questions.option_d: 0x4A
questions.explanation: 42 in hex: 42 ÷ 16 = 2 remainder 10. 10 in hex = A. So 42 decimal = 2A hex = 0x2A. Verify: 2×16 + 10 = 32 + 10 = 42. ✓

questions.statement: What is 0xFF in decimal?
questions.explanation: 0xFF = F×16 + F = 15×16 + 15 = 240 + 15 = 255. This is the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (2⁸ - 1). Used extensively in masks, RGB colors (each channel 0-255), and byte operations.

questions.statement: The binary number 11010110 in decimal is:
In inductive reasoning, the conclusion is:
questions.option_a: Guaranteed to be true if the premises are true
questions.option_b: Probable but not certain — could be wrong even with true premises
questions.option_c: Always false
questions.option_d: Only valid for mathematical statements
questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning generalizes from specific observations. Even if ALL observed ravens are black, the conclusion "all ravens are black" is not guaranteed (a non-black raven might exist unobserved). This is the fundamental limitation of induction — we cannot achieve certainty from examples alone.

questions.statement: Abductive reasoning is BEST described as:
questions.option_a: Reasoning backward from effects to causes
questions.option_b: Inference to the best explanation — choosing the hypothesis that BEST explains the observations
questions.option_c: Starting from general principles to reach specific conclusions
questions.option_d: Using analogies to solve problems
questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning: given observations, find the hypothesis that, if true, would best explain them. It gives the most plausible explanation, not a guaranteed one. Medical diagnosis, debugging, and detective work primarily use abductive reasoning.

questions.statement: "Correlation does not imply causation." Which example BEST illustrates this?
questions.option_a: Smoking causes lung cancer (proven by multiple studies)
questions.option_b: Countries with higher per capita chocolate consumption win more Nobel Prizes (spurious correlation via wealth)
questions.option_c: Exercise improves cardiovascular health (established through multiple RCTs)
questions.option_d: Code with more comments is easier to maintain (logical relationship)
questions.explanation: Chocolate consumption and Nobel Prizes are both caused by high national wealth (confounding variable). There's no causal mechanism by which eating chocolate makes you more likely to win a Nobel Prize — it's a spurious correlation caused by a shared underlying factor.

questions.statement: Which argument commits the "straw man" fallacy?
questions.option_a: You should trust this analysis because the analyst has 20 years of experience
questions.option_b: "We should test software more." Response: "So you're saying we should never ship any product!"
questions.option_c: After feature X was added, user ratings improved; therefore feature X caused the improvement
questions.option_d: We've only seen five examples, so we can't generalize
questions.explanation: Straw man: misrepresent the opponent's argument in an exaggerated or distorted form, then attack the distorted version. "Test more" became "never ship" — a straw man that's easy to attack but doesn't represent the actual argument. A is appeal to authority. C is confusing correlation with causation. D is awareness of hasty generalization.

questions.statement: In propositional logic, which of the following is a TAUTOLOGY (always true regardless of variable values)?
questions.option_a: P AND Q
questions.option_b: P OR NOT P
questions.option_c: P → Q
questions.option_d: P XOR P
questions.explanation: P OR NOT P: either P is true, or NOT P is true. One of these must always be true. This is the Law of Excluded Middle. P AND Q can be false (when either is false). P → Q is false when P=T and Q=F. P XOR P is always false (exclusive or of identical values).

questions.statement: The logical expression NOT (x < 5) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: NOT (x < 5) means "it is not the case that x is less than 5." This is true when x is 5 or greater: x >= 5. Note: NOT (x < 5) is NOT x > 5 (that would exclude 5). Common off-by-one error in boundary conditions.

questions.statement: Modus Tollens (MT) has the form:
questions.option_a: P; if P then Q; therefore Q
questions.option_b: If P then Q; Q; therefore P
questions.option_c: If P then Q; NOT Q; therefore NOT P
questions.option_d: If P then Q; if Q then R; therefore if P then R
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens: "If P then Q; NOT Q; therefore NOT P." Valid! If the consequence doesn't hold, the antecedent must not hold either. Example: "If it's raining, the ground is wet. The ground is NOT wet. Therefore it is NOT raining." This is logically guaranteed.

questions.statement: Which of the following demonstrates a "hasty generalization" fallacy?
questions.option_a: Based on 1,000 randomized trials, this medication is effective for 85% of patients
questions.option_b: I talked to two developers who prefer Python; therefore all developers prefer Python
questions.option_c: After analyzing logs from 10 million users, we conclude peak usage is 9 PM
questions.option_d: Given that A causes B in laboratory conditions, we conclude A causes B in the real world
questions.explanation: Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from insufficient evidence. Two developers is far too small and likely not representative. The other options use appropriate evidence for their claims.

questions.statement: In a truth table for three variables (P, Q, R), how many rows are needed?
questions.explanation: For n variables, a truth table has 2ⁿ rows. For 3 variables: 2³ = 8 rows. Each row represents a unique combination of T/F for all three variables: TTT, TTF, TFT, TFF, FTT, FTF, FFT, FFF.

questions.statement: The biconditional P ↔ Q is equivalent to:
questions.option_a: P → Q only
questions.option_b: Q → P only
questions.option_c: (P → Q) AND (Q → P) — "P if and only if Q"
questions.option_d: NOT (P → Q)
questions.explanation: Biconditional: P ↔ Q means "P is true if and only if Q is true." It's equivalent to both implications holding: P→Q AND Q→P. It's true when P and Q have the same truth value (both true or both false).

questions.statement: Which number system does the prefix "0b" typically indicate in programming?
questions.option_a: Octal (base 8)
questions.option_b: Binary (base 2)
questions.option_c: Hexadecimal (base 16)
questions.option_d: Decimal (base 10)
questions.explanation: Conventions: 0b prefix = binary, 0x or 0X prefix = hexadecimal, 0 prefix = octal (C/C++/Java), no prefix = decimal. Examples: 0b1010 = 10 (decimal), 0xA = 10 (decimal), 0o12 = 10 (Python octal).

questions.statement: What is -1 represented as in 8-bit two's complement?
The condition if (a != 0 && b/a > 5) avoids a division by zero because of:
questions.option_a: Operator precedence
questions.option_b: Short-circuit evaluation — if a = 0, b/a is never evaluated
questions.option_c: The compiler optimizing out the division
questions.option_d: Implicit casting of a to float
questions.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation: in A && B, if A is false, B is never evaluated (result is already false regardless of B). So if (a != 0 && b/a > 5) — if a=0, a != 0 is false, so b/a is never executed. Essential pattern for safe conditional evaluation.

questions.statement: Which of the following is the CONTRAPOSITIVE of "If it is a cat, then it is an animal"?
questions.option_a: If it is not an animal, then it is not a cat
questions.option_b: If it is an animal, then it is a cat
questions.option_c: If it is not a cat, then it is not an animal
questions.option_d: It is not a cat or it is an animal
questions.explanation: Contrapositive of P → Q is ¬Q → ¬P. "If it is a cat → it is an animal" becomes "If it is not an animal → it is not a cat." The contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original. Option B is the converse (not equivalent). Option C is the inverse (not equivalent).

questions.statement: Floating-point arithmetic produces 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. The CORRECT way to handle this in code is:
questions.option_a: Use integer arithmetic for the comparison
questions.option_b: Accept it as correct — floating-point is always precise
questions.option_c: Compare with a small epsilon: abs(result - 0.3) < 0.0001
questions.option_d: Always use doubles instead of floats
questions.explanation: The root cause is that 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be exactly represented in binary floating-point. Epsilon comparison checks if two values are "close enough." For financial applications, use integers (store amounts in smallest denomination) or Decimal types with exact arithmetic.

questions.statement: A logical expression that is FALSE for all possible input values is called:
questions.option_a: A tautology
questions.option_b: A contradiction (unsatisfiable)
questions.option_c: A contingency
questions.option_d: An invalid expression
questions.explanation: Contradiction (or unsatisfiable formula): false for ALL combinations of variable values. Example: P AND NOT P is always false (nothing can be both P and NOT P). The opposite of a tautology (always true).

questions.statement: Two's complement is used for representing signed integers because:
questions.option_a: It uses less memory than sign-magnitude representation
questions.option_b: It allows arithmetic operations (addition and subtraction) to work correctly for both positive and negative numbers using the same circuit
questions.option_c: It was invented before other representations
questions.option_d: It only works for negative numbers
questions.explanation: Two's complement's brilliant property: the CPU uses the SAME addition circuit for all integers, signed or unsigned. 5 + (-3) = 5 + two's_complement(3) = 00000101 + 11111101 = (1)00000010 = 2. The carry is discarded. No separate subtraction circuit needed.

questions.statement: The De Morgan's law ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q has a direct application in which programming scenario?
questions.option_a: Choosing between FOR and WHILE loops
questions.option_b: Simplifying if not (user_logged_in or has_guest_access) to if not user_logged_in and not has_guest_access
questions.option_c: Optimizing database queries
questions.option_d: Error handling in exception hierarchies
questions.explanation: De Morgan's Law directly translates to code. not (A or B) ≡ not A and not B. Both forms are logically identical. The choice is readability — sometimes one form is clearer in context than the other.

questions.statement: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n log n)
questions.option_c: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. After k comparisons, remaining size is n/2^k. The search ends when n/2^k = 1, i.e., k = log₂n. Therefore O(log n).

questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n²)
questions.option_c: O(n log n)
questions.option_d: O(n³)
questions.explanation: Total operations: when i=1: n ops; i=2: n-1 ops; ... i=n: 1 op. Total = n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²). This is the classic triangular sum pattern.

questions.statement: Which sorting algorithm has the BEST guaranteed worst-case time complexity?
questions.option_a: Quick Sort
questions.option_b: Bubble Sort
questions.option_c: Merge Sort
questions.option_d: Selection Sort
questions.explanation: Merge Sort is always O(n log n) — best, average, AND worst case. Quick Sort: average O(n log n) but worst case O(n²) (sorted input with bad pivot). Bubble and Selection Sort: always O(n²).

questions.statement: The merge step of Merge Sort for two arrays of sizes m and n takes:
questions.option_a: O(m × n) time
questions.option_b: O(m + n) time
questions.option_c: O(log(m + n)) time
questions.option_d: O(m log m + n log n) time
questions.explanation: Merging two sorted arrays requires scanning each element of both arrays once. The process is linear in the total size. O(m + n) time, O(m + n) space for the merged result.

questions.statement: A "divide and conquer" algorithm divides a problem of size n into 2 sub-problems of size n/2, then combines in O(n) time. The overall complexity is:
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n log n)
questions.option_c: O(n²)
questions.option_d: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). By Master Theorem (or drawing the recursion tree): log₂n levels, O(n) work at each level → O(n log n) total. This is Merge Sort's recurrence.

questions.statement: For very large input sizes, which is the MOST dangerous complexity class to have?
questions.option_a: O(n log n)
questions.option_b: O(n²)
questions.option_c: O(2ⁿ)
questions.option_d: O(n³)
questions.explanation: Exponential complexity O(2ⁿ) grows so fast that even n=100 gives 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 10³⁰ operations — effectively infinite. For n=1000, 2^1000 operations — more than atoms in the universe. O(n³) is impractical for large n but at least polynomial.

questions.statement: A hash table has O(1) average case lookup but O(n) worst case. When does the worst case occur?
questions.option_a: When the hash table is completely empty
questions.option_b: When all keys hash to the same bucket (all in one chain)
questions.option_c: When the table has an odd number of buckets
questions.option_d: When searching for a key that doesn't exist
questions.explanation: If all n keys happen to hash to the same bucket, the hash table degenerates to a linked list — O(n) for any lookup. Good hash functions distribute keys uniformly to prevent this. Load factor (n/m) also matters — high load factor increases collision probability.

questions.statement: Which algorithm design technique is BEST suited for the problem: "Find ALL possible subsets of a set of n elements"?
questions.option_a: Greedy (always pick the largest element)
questions.option_b: Dynamic Programming (solve once, reuse)
questions.option_c: Divide and Conquer (split into two halves)
questions.option_d: Backtracking (include or exclude each element)
questions.explanation: Generating all subsets is naturally expressed as backtracking: for each element, branch into two choices (include / exclude). With n elements: 2ⁿ subsets. The recursive tree explores all branches, backtracking to explore alternatives. Total O(2ⁿ) which is unavoidable since there are 2ⁿ subsets.

questions.statement: The greedy algorithm for coin change (always pick the largest coin that fits) is OPTIMAL for which set of denominations?
questions.option_a: {1, 3, 4} — does NOT work, needs dynamic programming
questions.option_b: Standard denominations like {1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100} — works because each denomination is a multiple relationship
questions.option_c: Any arbitrary set of denominations
questions.option_d: Only when all denominations are prime numbers
questions.explanation: Greedy coin change works for standard denominations because each larger coin is a multiple of (or exactly accounts for) smaller ones. For {1, 3, 4}: greedy gives change of 6 as {4, 1, 1} (3 coins); optimal is {3, 3} (2 coins). The greedy property depends on the specific denomination structure.

questions.statement: Dynamic programming is applicable when a problem has which TWO properties?
questions.option_a: Large input size AND multiple processors available
questions.option_b: Optimal substructure AND overlapping subproblems
questions.option_c: Sorted input AND binary search feasibility
questions.option_d: Graph structure AND negative edge weights
questions.explanation: DP conditions: (1) Optimal substructure — optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems. (2) Overlapping subproblems — same subproblems are solved multiple times in naive recursion. Without both, DP may not apply (if no overlap, divide & conquer without memoization is fine).

questions.statement: In the context of complexity, log n (without a base) in Big-O notation means:
questions.option_a: Only log base 10
questions.option_b: Only log base 2
questions.option_c: Any base — they differ only by a constant factor, which Big-O ignores
questions.option_d: Natural log (base e) only
questions.explanation: log_a(n) = log_b(n) / log_b(a). The change-of-base formula shows that different bases differ by a constant multiplicative factor. Since Big-O ignores constant factors, O(log₂n) = O(log₁₀n) = O(ln n). They're all O(log n).

questions.statement: A recursive algorithm for computing Fibonacci naively has time complexity:
questions.option_a: O(n)
questions.option_b: O(n log n)
questions.option_c: O(2ⁿ) — exponential due to recomputation
questions.option_d: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Naive Fibonacci fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). Each call spawns two more calls. fib(n) requires approximately 2ⁿ total calls (exponential) because the same values are recomputed many times. With memoization/DP, it reduces to O(n).

questions.statement: Amortized O(1) for dynamic array insertion means:
questions.option_a: Every single insertion takes exactly 1 operation
questions.option_b: The average cost per insertion, over a long sequence of insertions, is O(1)
questions.option_c: Inserting 1 element always takes constant time regardless of current size
questions.option_d: Memory is always immediately available without allocation
questions.explanation: Amortized analysis: most insertions are O(1). Occasional resizing (doubling) costs O(n) but happens rarely. Total cost for n insertions: O(n). Average per insertion: O(n)/n = O(1) amortized. The key word is AVERAGE over a sequence, not guaranteed for each individual operation.

questions.statement: What is the recurrence relation for binary search?
questions.explanation: Binary search: divide the problem in half (T(n/2)), do constant work to compare and decide direction (O(1)). Solving: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 → T(n) = log₂n = O(log n). Option A is linear recursion (O(n)). Option C is merge sort (O(n log n)). Option D is worse linear (O(n²)).

questions.statement: The space complexity of an iterative Fibonacci algorithm using only two variables is:
questions.option_a: O(n) — stores all previous values
questions.option_b: O(log n) — recursion depth
questions.option_c: O(1) — uses only two variables regardless of n
questions.option_d: O(n²) — builds a table
questions.explanation: Iterative Fibonacci: a, b = 0, 1; for _ in range(n): a, b = b, a+b; return a. Uses only two variables (a and b) regardless of how large n is. The loop counter adds O(1). Total: O(1) space. This is much better than memoized recursion which uses O(n) space for the memo table.

questions.statement: Which of the following BEST describes the time complexity of linear search?
questions.option_a: O(1) because it accesses elements directly
questions.option_b: O(log n) because it eliminates half the elements each step
questions.option_c: O(n) because it may need to check every element
questions.option_d: O(n²) because it compares every element to every other
questions.explanation: Linear search checks elements one by one until found or end reached. Best case: O(1) (first element). Worst case: O(n) (last element or not present). Average case: O(n/2) = O(n). The dominant case (worst/average) is O(n).

questions.statement: Which algorithm BEST fits the pattern: "repeatedly find the minimum element in the unsorted portion and place it at the end of the sorted portion"?
questions.option_a: Bubble Sort
questions.option_b: Insertion Sort
questions.option_c: Selection Sort
questions.option_d: Merge Sort
questions.explanation: Selection Sort: find minimum in unsorted portion, swap to front of unsorted portion (extending the sorted portion). Exactly one swap per pass. Always O(n²) regardless of input order. Minimum number of swaps: n-1.

questions.statement: In Big-O notation, which of the following simplifications is CORRECT?
questions.option_a: O(n² + n) simplifies to O(n)
questions.option_b: O(5n + 3) simplifies to O(n)
questions.option_c: O(n log n) simplifies to O(n²)
questions.option_d: O(1000n) simplifies to O(1)
questions.explanation: Big-O ignores constant multipliers and lower-order terms. O(5n + 3): the dominant term is n; constant 5 is dropped; lower-order constant 3 is dropped → O(n). Option A is wrong: O(n² + n) = O(n²) (n² dominates). Option C is wrong (can't change the fundamental growth rate). Option D is wrong (1000n is still linear O(n)).

questions.statement: A problem that CAN be solved in polynomial time belongs to complexity class:
questions.option_a: NP only
questions.option_b: NP-Complete
questions.option_c: P (and therefore also NP)
questions.option_d: Undecidable
questions.explanation: P ⊆ NP: Every problem in P (solvable in polynomial time) is also in NP (verifiable in polynomial time — if you can solve it, you can certainly verify it). P represents "easily solvable" problems. NP-Complete are the hardest problems in NP.

questions.statement: The sliding window technique is MOST applicable to which type of problem?
questions.option_a: Finding a specific element in an unsorted array
questions.option_b: Finding the maximum sum subarray of fixed length k
questions.option_c: Sorting a partially sorted array
questions.option_d: Finding the shortest path in a graph
questions.explanation: Sliding window: maintain a "window" of k consecutive elements. Slide it by removing the leftmost element and adding the next rightmost element. For fixed-length subarrays (maximum sum, average, etc.), this gives O(n) instead of O(n×k) brute force.

questions.statement: Which of these describes the two-pointer technique?
questions.option_a: Using two debuggers simultaneously to find bugs faster
questions.option_b: Using two indices (often one at each end) and moving them toward each other based on conditions — often for sorted arrays
questions.option_c: Storing two copies of a pointer to prevent memory leaks
questions.option_d: Using two hash tables for O(1) lookups
questions.explanation: Two pointers: one pointer at each end (or both starting at the left). Move them toward each other based on conditions. Classic use: checking palindromes (expand from center), finding two elements summing to a target (sorted array), partitioning arrays. Reduces O(n²) brute force to O(n).

questions.statement: For an algorithm with time complexity O(n log n), if the input doubles from n to 2n, the running time approximately:
questions.option_a: Doubles (2× slower)
questions.option_b: Quadruples (4× slower)
questions.option_c: Slightly more than doubles (2× + small factor)
questions.option_d: Increases logarithmically (barely changes)
questions.explanation: At n: T = c × n log n. At 2n: T = c × 2n × log(2n) = c × 2n × (log 2 + log n) = 2c × n × log n + 2c × n = 2T + 2cn. Slightly more than doubling. For large n, the log term grows slowly so it's approximately 2× with a small additional factor.

questions.statement: Backtracking improves on brute force by:
questions.option_a: Using a faster processor
questions.option_b: Pruning — abandoning partial solutions that cannot lead to valid complete solutions
questions.option_c: Finding approximate solutions faster
questions.option_d: Parallelizing the search across multiple cores
questions.explanation: Backtracking's key insight: if a partial solution violates a constraint, all completions of that partial solution are also invalid — no need to explore them. This "pruning" can dramatically reduce the search space compared to brute force, even though the worst case remains exponential.

questions.statement: In pseudo-random number generation and hash functions, which mathematical operation is most commonly used to ensure the result stays within bounds?
questions.option_a: Integer division
questions.option_b: Modular arithmetic (mod / remainder operation)
questions.option_c: Exponentiation
questions.option_d: Square root
questions.explanation: value mod n produces a result in [0, n-1], ensuring the result stays within the desired range regardless of the input value. Hash functions use hashCode(key) mod tableSize to map arbitrary hash codes to valid array indices.

questions.statement: Which is the MOST efficient way to check if a number n is prime?
questions.option_a: Check divisibility by all numbers from 2 to n-1: O(n)
questions.option_b: Check divisibility by all numbers from 2 to n/2: O(n/2) = O(n)
questions.option_c: Check divisibility by all numbers from 2 to √n: O(√n)
questions.option_d: Check if n is odd: O(1) but wrong (4, 9, 25 are even/odd non-primes)
questions.explanation: If n has a factor d > √n, then n/d < √n is also a factor (we'd have already found it). So we only need to check up to √n. For n = 10,000: only need to check up to 100 (100 vs 9,999 checks). O(√n) is the optimized trial division method.

questions.statement: What does the statement "P ≠ NP" mean intuitively?
questions.option_a: P and NP are unrelated complexity classes
questions.option_b: There exist problems that can be quickly verified but NOT quickly solved
questions.option_c: Every polynomial algorithm can be converted to a non-polynomial one
questions.option_d: Non-deterministic Turing machines are strictly slower than deterministic ones
questions.explanation: P ≠ NP (believed to be true): there exist problems where checking a given solution is fast (polynomial) but finding one is hard (seemingly superpolynomial). Example: Sudoku — verifying a solution is quick, but finding one for complex puzzles seems inherently hard. P ≠ NP would mean this hardness is fundamental.

questions.statement: The "Master Theorem" is used to:
questions.option_a: Determine who wrote an algorithm
questions.option_b: Solve recurrence relations of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) to find time complexity
questions.option_c: Prove that a sorting algorithm is optimal
questions.option_d: Determine the maximum depth of recursion
questions.explanation: Master Theorem provides formulas for solving divide-and-conquer recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d). Three cases based on whether f(n) dominates, matches, or is dominated by the recursive work. Result directly gives Big-O complexity. Essential for analyzing divide-and-conquer algorithms.

questions.statement: Selection Sort always makes exactly how many swaps for n elements?
questions.option_a: n² swaps (one per comparison)
questions.option_b: n log n swaps
questions.option_c: At most n-1 swaps (one per pass)
questions.option_d: Zero swaps (moves without swapping)
questions.explanation: Selection Sort: each pass finds the minimum in the unsorted portion and swaps it to the correct position. One swap per pass (or zero if already in position). n-1 passes → at most n-1 swaps. This makes Selection Sort ideal when write operations are expensive (e.g., flash memory with limited write cycles).

questions.statement: The MAIN disadvantage of Insertion Sort over Merge Sort for large datasets is:
questions.option_a: Insertion Sort is not stable
questions.option_b: Insertion Sort requires O(n) extra memory
questions.option_c: Insertion Sort's O(n²) average/worst case time vs Merge Sort's guaranteed O(n log n)
questions.option_d: Insertion Sort cannot handle duplicate elements
questions.explanation: Insertion Sort: O(n²) average/worst (but O(n) for nearly-sorted data). Merge Sort: always O(n log n). For large n, the quadratic vs linearithmic difference is enormous. However, Insertion Sort is excellent for small arrays (low overhead) — which is why Timsort uses it for small subarrays.

questions.statement: In Big-O notation, if algorithm A has complexity O(n²) and algorithm B has complexity O(n log n), for VERY large n (e.g., n = 10⁶):
questions.option_a: A is faster because n² grows linearly
questions.option_b: B is dramatically faster — n log n ≈ 20×10⁶ vs n² = 10¹² operations
questions.option_c: They perform approximately the same
questions.option_d: A is faster due to simpler constant factors
questions.explanation: For n = 10⁶: n log n ≈ 10⁶ × 20 = 2×10⁷. n² = 10¹². Difference: 50,000× more operations for A. At 10⁹ ops/second: B finishes in ~0.02 seconds; A would take ~1000 seconds. Asymptotic complexity completely dominates constant factors at large n.

questions.statement: The sum of the first n odd numbers (1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n-1)) equals:
questions.option_b: n²
questions.explanation: The sum of the first n odd numbers is always n². Check: n=1: 1=1². n=3: 1+3+5=9=3². n=5: 1+3+5+7+9=25=5². This is a beautiful pattern provable by induction or by visualizing square numbers as L-shapes of odd-numbered dots.

questions.statement: In a geometric sequence where a₁ = 2 and r = 3, what is the 5th term?
If the GCD of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 180, and one number is 36, what is the other?
A Fibonacci sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13... What is the 10th term?
In combinatorics, C(7, 3) (7 choose 3) equals:
questions.explanation: C(7,3) = 7! / (3! × 4!) = (7×6×5) / (3×2×1) = 210 / 6 = 35. This counts the number of ways to choose 3 items from 7 without caring about order. Example: choosing 3 committee members from 7 candidates.

questions.statement: If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3, and A and B are INDEPENDENT events, what is P(A AND B)?
questions.explanation: For independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12. Independence means knowledge of B doesn't change probability of A (and vice versa). If events were mutually exclusive instead: P(A ∩ B) = 0, but that's a different condition.

questions.statement: A data set has mean = 50 and standard deviation = 10. Assuming normal distribution, approximately what percentage of values fall between 30 and 70?
questions.explanation: 30 to 70 is 50 ± 20 = mean ± 2σ (since σ = 10, 2σ = 20). The 68-95-99.7 rule: ±1σ covers 68%, ±2σ covers 95%, ±3σ covers 99.7%.

questions.statement: Which data visualization is MOST appropriate for showing the distribution of exam scores?
questions.option_a: Pie chart
questions.option_b: Line chart
questions.option_c: Histogram
questions.option_d: Scatter plot
questions.explanation: Histogram: shows the distribution (frequency) of a continuous variable by grouping values into bins. Perfect for exam scores distribution. Pie chart: part-to-whole. Line chart: trend over time. Scatter plot: relationship between two variables.

questions.statement: If you flip a fair coin 3 times, what is the probability of getting EXACTLY 2 heads?
questions.explanation: P(exactly 2 heads) = C(3,2) × (1/2)² × (1/2)¹ = 3 × 1/4 × 1/2 = 3/8. The combinations are: HHT, HTH, THH — exactly 3 out of 8 total equally likely outcomes.

questions.statement: In a direct proportion, y = kx. If y = 24 when x = 6, what is y when x = 10?
questions.explanation: First find k: 24 = k × 6 → k = 4. Then: y = 4 × 10 = 40. Direct proportion: y/x is always constant (= k = 4 here).

questions.statement: Bayes' Theorem is MOST relevant to which practical application?
questions.option_a: Sorting large arrays efficiently
questions.option_b: Updating probabilities based on new evidence (spam filtering, medical diagnosis)
questions.option_c: Finding shortest paths in graphs
questions.option_d: Optimizing database queries
questions.explanation: Bayes' Theorem: P(hypothesis | evidence) = P(evidence | hypothesis) × P(hypothesis) / P(evidence). Allows updating prior belief given new evidence. Foundation of Bayesian spam filters, diagnostic AI, fraud detection. Critical wherever beliefs must be updated based on observed data.

questions.statement: Fermi estimation skills are MOST valuable when:
questions.option_a: Solving complex differential equations
questions.option_b: Needing quick, rough-order-of-magnitude estimates when exact data isn't available
questions.option_c: Proving mathematical theorems
questions.option_d: Writing precise technical specifications
questions.explanation: Fermi estimation: make reasonable assumptions, decompose into estimatable sub-quantities, combine for a rough answer. Useful for quickly assessing feasibility, sizing systems, detecting absurd assumptions, and making decisions under uncertainty.

questions.statement: A password uses only lowercase letters (26 options) and is 6 characters long. How many possible passwords exist?
questions.explanation: Each position independently has 26 choices. Since positions are independent: total = 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 × 26 = 26⁶ ≈ 309 million. This is multiplication rule (permutations with repetition). C(26,6) would be choosing 6 DIFFERENT letters from 26 (no repetition, no order).

questions.statement: The birthday paradox says that in a group of 23 people, the probability that two share a birthday is:
questions.option_b: Exactly 50%
questions.option_c: Greater than 50%
questions.option_d: Close to 100%
questions.explanation: The birthday paradox: with 23 people, P(at least two share a birthday) ≈ 50.7%. With 50 people: ~97%. This is counterintuitive because we compare ALL pairs (there are 23×22/2 = 253 pairs with 23 people), not just each person against one specific birthday.

questions.statement: If set A = {1,2,3,4,5} and set B = {4,5,6,7,8}, what is A ∩ B (intersection)?
questions.explanation: Intersection: elements in BOTH A AND B. Both A and B contain 4 and 5. A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} (union). A - B = {1,2,3} (A minus B). B - A = {6,7,8} (B minus A).

questions.statement: An arithmetic sequence has a₁ = 5, d = 4. The sum of the first 10 terms is:
The Sieve of Eratosthenes is used to:
questions.option_a: Test if a single large number is prime
questions.option_b: Efficiently find all prime numbers up to n
questions.option_c: Compute GCD of two numbers
questions.option_d: Generate Fibonacci numbers
questions.explanation: Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark all multiples of each prime as composite. Start at 2 (prime), mark all multiples of 2. Move to next unmarked (3), mark all its multiples. Continue until p² > n. Remaining unmarked numbers are prime. Highly efficient: O(n log log n) — nearly linear.

questions.statement: In a direct inverse proportion scenario: 6 workers complete a job in 8 days. How many days would 4 workers take?
questions.option_a: 5.33 days
questions.option_b: 10 days
questions.option_c: 12 days
questions.option_d: 16 days
questions.explanation: Inverse proportion: workers × days = constant. 6 × 8 = 48 = 4 × d → d = 12 days. As workers decrease, days increase proportionally (inverse relationship).

questions.statement: Which pattern recognition strategy would you use for: "I need to find the longest increasing subarray in an array"?
questions.option_a: Binary search (sorted array property)
questions.option_b: Sliding window (contiguous subarray, expanding/contracting)
questions.option_c: Two pointers (start and end moving toward each other)
questions.option_d: Dynamic programming (subarray length depends on previous subarray)
questions.explanation: Longest increasing CONTIGUOUS subarray: use sliding window. Start a window, expand as long as next element > current. When the pattern breaks, record length and start a new window. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.statement: If a population grows by 10% each year, after how many years does it approximately DOUBLE?
questions.option_a: 7 years
questions.option_b: 10 years
questions.option_c: 14 years
questions.option_d: 20 years
questions.explanation: 7 years — 1.1^7 ≈ 1.95 ≈ 2. The Rule of 72 gives 72/10 = 7.2 years.

questions.statement: Which error would cause a program to crash at runtime but would NOT be detected during compilation?
questions.option_a: Missing semicolon
questions.option_b: Misspelled keyword
questions.option_c: Dividing by a variable that happens to be 0 at runtime
questions.option_d: Wrong number of arguments in a function declaration
questions.explanation: Syntax errors (A, B, D) are detected at compile time. Runtime errors occur during execution when a specific invalid operation is attempted. Division by zero: the code is syntactically correct, but when executed with x=0, the division fails.

questions.statement: A function correctly sorts small arrays but produces wrong results for arrays of 10,000+ elements. The MOST likely cause is:
questions.option_a: The algorithm has a syntax error
questions.option_b: Integer overflow in index calculations or accumulations for large n
questions.option_c: The function uses too much memory
questions.option_d: The programming language doesn't support large arrays
questions.explanation: If the algorithm works for small inputs but fails for large ones, the issue likely involves a value that becomes invalid at large scale. Integer overflow is a classic culprit: index = (left + right) / 2 overflows when left + right > MAX_INT. Fix: mid = left + (right - left) / 2.

questions.statement: A developer uses if (x = 5) intending if (x == 5). This is a:
questions.option_a: Syntax error — most modern compilers/interpreters catch this
questions.option_b: Runtime error — crashes when executed
questions.option_c: Logic error — no error is thrown but behavior is wrong
questions.option_d: Semantic error — same as logic error, but specifically a wrong operation
questions.explanation: In C/Java, x = 5 is an assignment (returns 5, truthy) so if (x = 5) is always true. In Python, this IS a syntax error. Language-dependent. The key insight: this is a logic error (wrong behavior without exception). Many modern languages and linters warn about this pattern.

questions.statement: The off-by-one error in for i in range(len(arr) - 1) when iterating ALL elements of arr is:
questions.option_a: Iterates one extra element
questions.option_b: Skips the last element (index len(arr)-1)
questions.option_c: Starts from index 1 instead of 0
questions.option_d: No error — this is correct
questions.explanation: range(len(arr) - 1) generates indices 0 to len(arr)-2. The last index len(arr)-1 is NEVER visited. Fix: range(len(arr)). Off-by-one errors are among the most common bugs — always check boundary conditions carefully.

questions.statement: Binary search debugging involves:
questions.option_a: Debugging problems with binary search algorithm implementation
questions.option_b: Finding a bug by checking the midpoint of the codebase, determining which half contains the bug, and recursively narrowing down
questions.option_c: Using two separate debuggers simultaneously
questions.option_d: Searching for binary values in memory dumps
questions.explanation: Binary search debugging (e.g., git bisect): find a "known good" and "known bad" commit. Check the middle commit — good or bad? Narrow down to the half containing the bug. Repeat until the exact commit introducing the bug is found. O(log n) for n commits.

questions.statement: "Rubber duck debugging" works primarily because:
questions.option_a: The rubber duck can access documentation
questions.option_b: Explaining the code out loud forces you to confront assumptions and step through logic explicitly, often revealing the bug
questions.option_c: The rubber duck provides emotional support reducing stress
questions.option_d: The physical motion of speaking stimulates problem-solving brain regions
questions.explanation: The act of articulating the problem explicitly forces precise thinking. You discover "I assumed X but actually Y..." while explaining. The duck doesn't need to respond — the value is in the explanation process itself, which often triggers insights.

questions.statement: Which debugging strategy is MOST appropriate for a bug that "sometimes occurs randomly"?
questions.option_a: Add print statements everywhere
questions.option_b: Find the exact input/state that triggers it, then examine the code path for that case
questions.option_c: Restart the system and hope it goes away
questions.option_d: Comment out random sections of code to find which section contains the bug
questions.explanation: Non-deterministic bugs are the hardest to debug. Key: find a reliable reproduction case. Is the randomness related to: timing (race condition), random number generation (set seed), external data (network), or memory state? Once reliably reproduced, the standard debug process applies.

questions.statement: A function calculates (a + b) / 2 intending to find the average of two integers. In C/Java with integer arithmetic, this incorrectly returns 3 for a=3, b=4. Why?
questions.option_a: The addition operation overflows
questions.option_b: Integer division truncates: (3+4)/2 = 7/2 = 3 (not 3.5)
questions.option_c: The precedence is wrong
questions.option_d: a and b are not initialized
questions.explanation: Integer division in C/Java truncates (rounds toward zero): 7/2 = 3, not 3.5. To get the correct average: (double)(a + b) / 2 or (a + b) / 2.0 forces floating-point division.

questions.statement: The MOST effective way to prevent the null pointer exception class of bugs is:
questions.option_a: Always check for null before every method call
questions.option_b: Use null-safe types and Optional/Maybe types, or validate at system boundaries and guarantee non-null internally
questions.option_c: Never use null anywhere
questions.option_d: Handle NullPointerException with try-catch everywhere
questions.explanation: Modern approach: Optional (Java), Maybe (Haskell), nullable types (Kotlin, TypeScript). Null-safe design: validate and handle null at the boundary of your system, then maintain non-null invariants inside. Catching NPE everywhere is reactive; preventing them is proactive and better.

questions.statement: Which statement is TRUE about confirmation bias in debugging?
questions.option_a: Confirmation bias helps debugging by focusing on the most likely causes
questions.option_b: Confirmation bias occurs when you only look for evidence that confirms your hypothesis, ignoring disconfirming evidence
questions.option_c: Confirmation bias is helpful when time is limited
questions.option_d: Confirmation bias only affects non-technical problem solvers
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias in debugging: once you form a hypothesis ("I think the bug is in module X"), you unconsciously focus evidence-gathering on X and dismiss evidence pointing elsewhere. Result: wasted time investigating wrong causes. Scientific debugging requires actively seeking to DISPROVE hypotheses.

questions.statement: Using the SCAMPER technique to innovate on a product, "Eliminate" asks:
questions.option_a: What can we add to make it better?
questions.option_b: What components, features, or steps can be removed while maintaining or improving the core value?
questions.option_c: What rules can we break?
questions.option_d: What other products can this compete with?
questions.explanation: SCAMPER Eliminate: systematically question what can be removed. This leads to simplification — often improving the product. Examples: Apple eliminated the CD drive from MacBooks (controversial but correct). Google eliminated the "submit" button on search (auto-suggests). Eliminating friction is often more impactful than adding features.

questions.statement: In decision-making, "analysis paralysis" is caused by:
questions.option_a: Having too little information to make a decision
questions.option_b: Over-analyzing options to the point where no decision is made, often because of fear of making the wrong choice
questions.option_c: Using the wrong decision framework
questions.option_d: Having too many stakeholders involved
questions.explanation: Analysis paralysis: excessive analysis prevents action. Common causes: fear of imperfect decisions, perfectionism, unclear decision criteria. Bezos's "two-way door" insight: most decisions are reversible — make them quickly and adjust. Save deep analysis for truly irreversible decisions.

questions.statement: Which of the following is a practical application of the "Sliding Window" algorithm pattern?
questions.option_a: Finding if a given string is a palindrome
questions.option_b: Detecting the maximum sum of any subarray of length k
questions.option_c: Finding the shortest path in a weighted graph
questions.option_d: Sorting a nearly-sorted array efficiently
questions.explanation: Classic sliding window: maintain a window of k elements, slide it across the array by removing the leftmost element and adding the next. No need to recompute the entire sum — just update incrementally. O(n) vs O(n×k) brute force.

questions.statement: The "separation of concerns" principle states that:
questions.option_a: Different teams should work on different features
questions.option_b: A system should be divided into parts that each address a separate concern, minimizing overlap
questions.option_c: Business logic and technical implementation should be developed separately
questions.option_d: Development and operations should be separate teams
questions.explanation: Separation of concerns (SoC): each module addresses one concern (presentation, business logic, data access). This leads to low coupling, high cohesion, and maintainable systems. HTML/CSS/JavaScript separation (structure/style/behavior) is a concrete example. MVC architecture another.

questions.statement: Which reasoning type is being used when a doctor concludes "This patient probably has pneumonia based on fever, cough, and X-ray findings"?
questions.option_a: Deductive reasoning — certainty from premises
questions.option_b: Inductive reasoning — generalizing from many patients
questions.option_c: Abductive reasoning — inferring the best explanation for observed symptoms
questions.option_d: Analogical reasoning — comparing to a similar past patient
questions.explanation: Abduction: given observations (fever, cough, X-ray), find the hypothesis (pneumonia) that best explains them. The conclusion is probable, not certain — other conditions might explain the same symptoms. Testing (cultures, further imaging) moves toward deductive confirmation.
